front_matter.use: Keep yourself safe first. Check DRABC (Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation). If not breathing normally and CPR-trained: send for help and start CPR (~100-120/min, full chest recoil, use an AED). Find the condition; read Recognize + Get help fast first.
front_matter.recovery_position: Unconscious but breathing and no suspected spine injury: roll onto side, head tilted back/chin up so the airway stays open and fluids drain, top knee forward for stability; keep checking breathing.

entries.title: Bone fracture (broken bone)
entries.what_it_is: A crack or break in a bone from a fall, blow, or twist. Closed = skin intact; open/compound = wound over the break or bone showing (high infection risk).
entries.recognize: Pain worsening with movement/pressure/weight; swelling and bruising; visible deformity (bent, rotated, shorter than the matching limb); snap/grating felt; loss of use; guarding. Compare to the good side. Children: 'greenstick' may show only pain, swelling, reluctance to use. Elderly hip fracture: shortened, outward-turned leg after a minor fall. Suspect spine fracture after falls from height, hard back/neck blows, or diving — with neck/back pain, tingling, weakness, or numbness.
entries.get_help_fast: Open fracture (bone through skin); limb/digit cold, pale, blue, or numb or no pulse beyond injury; suspected neck/back/skull/hip/pelvis/thigh fracture; heavy bleeding; severe pain or shock. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Keep still and reassure. Support the part in the position found — do not straighten. Expose gently (cut clothing). Control bleeding with pressure around (not on) protruding bone. Immobilize with a padded splint crossing the joint above and below the break; pad bony points; tie firm but not circulation-cutting. Recheck fingers/toes beyond splint for warmth/color/feeling. Elevate if it doesn't worsen pain. Cloth-wrapped cold pack 15-20 min. Suspected spine: don't move unless in danger; keep head/neck/body aligned and still.
entries.do_not: Don't push a protruding bone back in. Don't set/straighten it. Don't move a suspected neck/back injury unless life is at risk. Don't tie over the break or so tight it numbs. Don't give food/drink if surgery possible. Don't let them walk on a possibly broken leg/hip.
entries.after_care: Keep elevated, splinted, still. Recheck circulation/sensation every 15 min; loosen if cold/blue/numb. Watch for rising pain, spreading numbness, or a tense extremely painful limb (compartment syndrome — emergency). Keep open-fracture wounds covered/clean (infection is the field danger). Get professional setting + imaging ASAP.
entries.prevention: Fall-proofing (lighting, clear floors, handrails), especially elderly. Protect the spine on any significant trauma.

entries.title: Severe bleeding (hemorrhage)
entries.what_it_is: Rapid blood loss from a wound. Losing a lot fast causes shock and death, so stopping the flow is the first priority after scene safety.
entries.recognize: Blood pouring, pulsing/spurting (artery), or soaking through fast; large/deep wound; severed/crushed limb. Shock signs: pale, cold, clammy skin; fast weak pulse; rapid shallow breathing; thirst; restlessness then drowsiness; dizziness/fainting; confusion. Internal bleeding after trauma: shock signs plus rigid/swelling belly, coughing/vomiting blood, blood in urine/stool.
entries.get_help_fast: Bleeding won't stop after ~10 min firm pressure; blood spurts; limb severed; shock signs; deep/gaping wound or to neck/chest/abdomen/groin; suspected internal bleeding. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Protect yourself. Press hard and directly on the wound and KEEP pressing (don't lift to look). Soaked through: add cloth on top, keep pressing; never remove the first layer. Raise the part above the heart if no fracture. Lay them down, keep warm, raise legs slightly if no leg/spine/pelvis injury. Uncontrolled limb bleed with pressure failing: proper tourniquet (or improvised wide band + windlass) 5-7 cm above the wound, not over a joint; tighten until bleeding stops; write the time. Neck wound: press directly, don't wrap around. Embedded object: press either side, leave it in.
entries.do_not: Don't remove an embedded object. Don't keep peeking under the dressing. Don't use thin cord/wire as a tourniquet. Don't loosen/release a tourniquet once on. Don't give food/drink. Don't elevate a fractured limb.
entries.after_care: Keep lying down, warm, still; recheck dressing for re-soak and monitor breathing/pulse. Treat for shock. Keep wound covered/clean. Note tourniquet time on the person. Even stopped serious wounds need professional cleaning/closure — get to care.
entries.prevention: Press first, press hard, press long. Most field bleeding deaths come from under-pressing or giving up early.

entries.title: Burns
entries.what_it_is: Tissue damage from heat, scald, flame, chemical, electricity, or sun. Severity depends on depth, size, and location.
entries.recognize: Superficial (1st): red, dry, painful, no blisters. Partial (2nd): blisters, wet, very painful. Full thickness (3rd): white/brown/charred, leathery/waxy, may be numb. Size: person's palm+fingers ~=1% body; bigger than a palm is significant. High-risk sites: face, airway, hands, feet, genitals, burns encircling a limb/joint.
entries.get_help_fast: Large (~palm or more) or any full-thickness; face/airway/hands/feet/genitals or encircling a limb; chemical, electrical, or fire in an enclosed space; inhalation signs (soot around nose/mouth, singed nose hairs, hoarse voice, cough, wheeze, trouble breathing — airway can swell shut); infants/elderly/unwell. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Stop the burning (remove from heat; smother flames; chemicals: brush off dry powder then flush 20+ min, remove contaminated clothing; electrical: power off first). Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water ~20 min, ideally within 3 h. Remove rings/watches/tight clothing near the burn before swelling, but leave anything stuck. Cover loosely with clean non-fluffy cloth or cling film. Keep the whole person warm. If alert and not vomiting, small sips of water.
entries.do_not: No ice, butter, oil, toothpaste, egg, or creams on a fresh burn. Don't break blisters. Don't peel stuck clothing. Don't wrap tight or use fluffy cotton on the burn. Don't delay cooling.
entries.after_care: Keep clean; change the loose dressing gently; watch for infection (rising pain, spreading redness, pus, smell, fever). Keep hydrated; manage pain per clinician/label. Encircling/deep/large burns need urgent professional care. Protect healing skin from sun.
entries.prevention: Cool-water-first reduces burn depth. Suspect airway burns early — they worsen over the first hour.

entries.title: Dehydration
entries.what_it_is: Too little body water and salts from heat, exertion, fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. Dangerous fast in infants, children, elderly, and the ill.
entries.recognize: Mild: thirst, dry mouth/lips, reduced darker urine, tiredness, headache, dizziness on standing. Moderate: very dry mouth, little/no urine, sunken eyes, fast pulse, irritability, skin that stays tented when pinched. Severe (emergency): no urine, very drowsy/unconscious, rapid weak pulse, cold hands/feet, rapid breathing, floppy infant, no tears. Infants: sunken soft spot, few/no wet nappies.
entries.get_help_fast: Can't keep fluids down; very drowsy/confused/unconscious; rapid weak pulse; stops urinating; infant or elderly going downhill; bloody diarrhea with high fever. Severe may need IV fluids. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Give fluids early and steadily. Best: ORS — packets per instructions, or improvise ~1 L clean water + 6 tsp sugar + 1/2 tsp salt (no saltier than tears). Small sips often (a spoonful every 1-2 min for nausea/children), building up. Keep breastfeeding. Rest in shade/cool. Replace losses after each stool/vomit. Continue after they feel better.
entries.do_not: Don't rely on soda/energy drinks/alcohol/caffeine. Don't force big volumes with nausea. Don't exceed the salt recipe. Don't give oral fluids to someone who can't swallow safely.
entries.after_care: Continue ORS until urine is pale/regular and thirst/alertness normal. Treat the cause. Watch for return. Seek care for ongoing losses or inability to drink.
entries.prevention: In heat/illness, drink before thirsty; keep ORS ingredients ready; watch infants and elderly closely.

entries.title: Choking (airway obstruction)
entries.what_it_is: Food or an object blocking the airway. Partial = some air moves; complete = no air, minutes to act.
entries.recognize: Sudden inability to speak/cough/breathe while eating or with an object; hands at throat; silent/weak cough; squeaky or no breathing; panic then blue lips and collapse. Forceful coughing or speaking = partial block, air still moving.
entries.get_help_fast: Blockage doesn't clear with first efforts, or the person weakens/goes unconscious — send for help immediately while you act. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Conscious adult/child >1: encourage hard coughing; if they can't breathe/cough/speak, 5 sharp back blows between shoulder blades (lean them forward), then 5 abdominal thrusts (fist above navel, sharp inward-and-up), alternate until clear or collapse. Infant <1: 5 back blows face-down head-low, then 5 chest thrusts face-up (two fingers, lower breastbone), alternate — no abdominal thrusts. Pregnant/very large: chest thrusts. If unconscious: lower safely, send for help, start CPR if trained; remove an object only if clearly seen.
entries.do_not: No blind finger sweeps. No abdominal thrusts on infants <1 or (carefully) the very pregnant. Don't give water to wash it down. Don't back-slap someone upright coughing well with a partial block.
entries.after_care: After clearing, watch breathing; lingering cough, drooling, pain, or trouble swallowing = something may remain, seek care. Anyone who got thrusts or lost consciousness should be checked for internal injury.
entries.prevention: Cut food small for young children/elderly; don't talk/laugh with a full mouth; keep small objects from infants.

entries.title: Asthma attack
entries.what_it_is: Airways narrow and inflame, making breathing out hard. Triggers: infection, allergens, smoke, cold air, exercise, stress.
entries.recognize: Wheezing (especially out), chest tightness, shortness of breath, persistent cough. Severe (emergency): can't speak full sentences, hunched/straining, fast breathing, rapid pulse, pale/blue lips, exhaustion, agitation or drowsiness, or a quiet 'silent' chest.
entries.get_help_fast: Reliever gives no relief in minutes or is needed again very soon; can't speak in sentences; blue lips; tiring, drowsy, or silent chest; or no inhaler available. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Sit upright, leaning slightly forward, elbows supported — never flat. Keep calm, coach slow steady breaths. Help them use their own reliever (usually blue) as prescribed, ideally via spacer, one puff at a time, repeat per their plan while awaiting help. Loosen tight clothing. Remove from triggers (smoke, dust, cold wind, animals).
entries.do_not: Don't lay them flat. Don't crowd/rush them. Don't assume a severe attack will pass. Don't give someone else's preventer as a rescue. Don't let them over-exert.
entries.after_care: Once settled, rest, warm, calm. If relievers were needed repeatedly or the attack was severe, get a medical review even if they feel fine (can rebound). Identify/avoid the trigger; ensure a working reliever and a known plan.
entries.prevention: Daily preventer as prescribed, triggers avoided, reliever always on hand (an empty reliever is a common cause of a bad attack).

entries.title: Heart attack (and cardiac arrest)
entries.what_it_is: Blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked; muscle starts to die. Can trigger cardiac arrest (heart stops) — then CPR is needed.
entries.recognize: Central chest pain/pressure/heaviness (weight or band), >a few minutes or coming and going; spreading to arm(s), neck, jaw, back, or upper belly; shortness of breath; cold sweat; nausea; lightheadedness; sense of doom; grey/pale. Atypical (women, elderly, diabetics): subtle fatigue, breathlessness, indigestion-like discomfort, 'not right.' Cardiac arrest: sudden collapse, unresponsive, not breathing or only gasping — start CPR now.
entries.get_help_fast: Any suspected heart attack — always an emergency; get help immediately, time is heart muscle. Don't wait to be sure.
entries.do_now: Stop exertion; sit and rest, often half-sitting knees bent. Reassure, keep still. Loosen tight clothing. If conscious, not aspirin-allergic, not bleeding, able to swallow: a single adult aspirin chewed slowly is standard suspected-heart-attack first aid (NOT for suspected stroke). Help with their own prescribed heart medicine (e.g., nitroglycerin). Be ready for CPR + AED if they collapse and stop breathing normally.
entries.do_not: Don't let them walk/exert/'wait it out.' No food or large drinks. No aspirin if allergic, bleeding, or if it might be a stroke. Don't leave them alone. Don't delay calling for help.
entries.after_care: Keep resting, calm, watched until help arrives; be ready to start CPR instantly. Note symptom start time and medicines given. Never 'resolved' at home — hospital clot treatment is essential.
entries.prevention: Learn hands-only CPR and nearest AED location. Early CPR + defibrillation greatly improves survival.

entries.title: Stroke (brain attack)
entries.what_it_is: Blood supply to part of the brain is cut off (clot) or a vessel bleeds. Brain cells die fast — speed to treatment is critical.
entries.recognize: BE-FAST: Balance loss; Eyes (sudden vision loss/double vision); Face droop one side (ask to smile); Arm/leg weakness or numbness one side (ask to raise both); Speech slurred/garbled/word-finding trouble; Time — note the exact start time. Also sudden 'worst ever' headache, sudden confusion, sudden one-sided numbness.
entries.get_help_fast: Any BE-FAST sign — always an emergency; treatments work only within a few hours, so start time is critical. Go now.
entries.do_now: Get emergency help immediately; say 'suspected stroke' + start time. Keep calm and still. Conscious: rest with head/shoulders slightly raised. Drowsy/vomiting/unconscious but breathing: recovery position (often paralyzed side down) to protect the airway. Loosen tight clothing. Stay, monitor breathing, record what you saw and when it began.
entries.do_not: No food, drink, or oral medicines (swallowing often impaired — choking/pneumonia risk). DON'T give aspirin (a stroke may be a bleed). Don't let them 'sleep it off.' Don't self-drive if emergency transport is faster/safer.
entries.after_care: Protect the airway and watch breathing until help arrives; ready for CPR if they deteriorate. Keep the start-time note. Every stroke needs urgent hospital imaging/care.
entries.prevention: Control blood pressure, don't smoke, manage diabetes and irregular heartbeat with a clinician. Teach BE-FAST at home.

entries.title: Diabetic emergency (low or high blood sugar)
entries.what_it_is: Blood sugar too low (fast, harms the brain in minutes) or dangerously high (slower, DKA, deadly over hours-days).
entries.recognize: Low (minutes): shaky, sweaty, pale, pounding heart, hungry, anxious/irritable, confused, slurred, may seem drunk/aggressive, then drowsy/seizure/unconscious. High/DKA (hours-days): intense thirst, frequent urination, dry skin/mouth, blurred vision, nausea/vomiting, belly pain, drowsiness, deep rapid 'sighing' breathing, sweet/fruity breath; progresses to coma.
entries.get_help_fast: Unconscious; seizing; can't swallow safely; deep rapid breathing with fruity breath and vomiting (suspected DKA); or no improvement soon after sugar. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: If awake and able to swallow and unsure which: GIVE SUGAR FIRST (a low must be fixed in minutes; short-term sugar does little harm to a high) — sugary drink, glucose tablets/gel, sweets. Recheck 10-15 min; improvement = it was a low, then give a longer-acting snack. Known low with a glucagon kit + trained helper: use as directed. Unconscious/can't swallow: nothing by mouth — recovery position, get help; trained person may give glucagon. Suspected DKA: needs medical care/fluids/insulin — get help; assist their own insulin only if trained and clearly indicated.
entries.do_not: Nothing by mouth if they can't swallow. Don't give insulin to someone low (can kill). Don't assume — if sugar doesn't help fast, escalate. Don't leave them alone recovering.
entries.after_care: After a low: proper meal + rest; stay and recheck. Find the cause (missed meal, activity, dose, illness). Recurrent/severe episodes and any suspected DKA need a diabetes-plan review.
entries.prevention: Carry fast sugar; eat regularly; check sugar as advised; sick days raise DKA risk.

entries.title: Seizure (convulsion)
entries.what_it_is: A burst of abnormal brain electrical activity. Causes: epilepsy, fever (children), low sugar, head injury, infection, poisoning, withdrawal.
entries.recognize: Generalized: sudden collapse, body stiffens then jerks, eyes may roll, breathing may pause/lips dusky, possible tongue-biting and loss of bladder/bowel control, then a confused exhausted period (minutes to ~1 h). Others: staring/unresponsiveness, lip-smacking/fumbling, sudden confusion. Young children: brief 'febrile' seizure with high fever.
entries.get_help_fast: Lasts >5 min, or one follows another without recovery (status — emergency); first-ever seizure; injured, pregnant, diabetic, high fever with stiff neck, or in water; doesn't breathe normally afterward; very slow/abnormal recovery.
entries.do_now: Protect from injury — clear hard/sharp objects, cushion the head, loosen anything tight at the neck. LET the seizure happen — don't restrain. Time it. When jerking stops, recovery position to keep the airway clear and drain saliva/vomit. Stay, keep warm, speak calmly as they come round. Febrile child: cool gently, treat fever once alert, still seek advice.
entries.do_not: Nothing in the mouth, don't hold the tongue (risk broken teeth, bitten fingers, blocked airway). Don't restrain. No food/drink/medicines until fully alert and swallowing. Don't crowd.
entries.after_care: Let them rest; stay until fully oriented. Note duration and what you saw. First seizure, long one, injury, pregnancy, or abnormal recovery needs assessment. Known epilepsy with a typical brief seizure and full recovery may follow their usual plan — escalate if anything is different.
entries.prevention: Known epilepsy: take medicines as prescribed, sleep well, avoid triggers. Children: manage fevers early.

entries.title: Heat stroke / heat illness
entries.what_it_is: The body overheats faster than it can cool. Heat exhaustion is the warning stage; heat stroke (core overheat with brain effects) is life-threatening.
entries.recognize: Heat cramps: painful cramps with heavy sweating. Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, pale cool clammy skin, weakness, fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, fast weak pulse — mentally clear. Heat stroke (emergency): very high temperature; skin hot and dry OR still sweaty; ALTERED MENTAL STATE (confusion, agitation, slurred speech, staggering, seizures, collapse); rapid pulse/breathing.
entries.get_help_fast: Confusion, agitation, collapse, seizures, or very hot skin (heat stroke) — call for help while cooling. Also if heat exhaustion doesn't improve within ~30 min of cooling + fluids. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Move to shade/cool immediately. Lay down; raise legs if faint. Cool fast by any means: remove excess clothing; wet the skin and fan hard; cool wet cloths/ice packs at neck, armpits, groin; cool-water immersion if safe and monitored (best for heat stroke). Keep cooling until skin feels cool and mental state improves. If fully alert, cool water or ORS in sips.
entries.do_not: No drinks to the confused/not fully conscious. No alcohol. No fever medicines for heat stroke. Don't return to heat/exertion. Don't stop cooling too early in heat stroke.
entries.after_care: Rest in the cool, keep rehydrating; monitor mental state/temperature. Heat stroke can damage brain, kidneys, liver, clotting even after cooling — get review. Avoid heat/hard activity 24-48 h.
entries.prevention: Drink regularly, pace activity, rest in shade, buddy system, never leave anyone/child/pet in a hot vehicle.
