entries.title: Hypothermia and frostbite (dangerous cold)
entries.what_it_is: The body loses heat faster than it makes it, dropping core temperature. Frostbite is local freezing of tissue (fingers, toes, ears, nose, cheeks).
entries.recognize: Hypothermia mild: shivering, cold pale skin, numb hands, clumsiness, slurred speech, tiredness, poor judgment. Moderate-severe: shivering slows/STOPS, worsening confusion/apathy, stumbling, drowsiness, slow weak pulse and slow shallow breathing, collapse; may paradoxically feel hot and undress. Frostbite: skin cold, hard, white/grey-yellow or waxy, numb; may blister on rewarming.
entries.get_help_fast: Very drowsy, confused, stopped shivering, slow/weak pulse, or unconscious (severe hypothermia — emergency, handle extremely gently; rough movement can trigger a fatal rhythm). Also deep/large frostbite.
entries.do_now: Out of cold/wind/wet. Remove wet clothing, insulate with dry layers/sleeping bag, cover head/neck, insulate from the ground. Rewarm the CORE gradually — shared body warmth, warm (not hot) packs to chest/armpits/groin/neck. If fully alert, warm sweet non-alcoholic drinks. Handle gently, keep horizontal. Frostbite: protect from refreezing; rewarm slowly in warm (~body-temperature) water only if no chance of refreezing; pad between digits; keep still.
entries.do_not: Don't rub skin or frostbitten parts. No intense direct heat (fire, hot water, heating pad on bare skin). No alcohol/caffeine. No drinks to the drowsy/confused. Don't let thawed frostbite refreeze. Don't assume a cold, pulseless person is dead until warmed and reassessed ('not dead until warm and dead').
entries.after_care: Keep warm, dry, still; monitor breathing/alertness. Severe hypothermia and significant frostbite need medical care (heart-rhythm and tissue-damage risks). Protect rewarmed tissue; don't pop blisters.
entries.prevention: Layer clothing, stay dry, cover extremities and head, eat/hydrate, avoid alcohol in cold.

entries.title: Anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction)
entries.what_it_is: A rapid whole-body allergic reaction (foods, stings, drugs, latex) that can close the airway and drop blood pressure in minutes. Adrenaline reverses it.
entries.recognize: Rapid onset (minutes to ~1 h) after a trigger, usually 2+ of: swelling of lips/tongue/throat/face; trouble breathing, wheeze, tight/hoarse throat; widespread hives/flushing/itch; vomiting/cramping/diarrhea; dizziness, doom, pale/clammy, fainting/collapse. Any breathing trouble or collapse after a trigger = anaphylaxis until proven otherwise.
entries.get_help_fast: ANY breathing difficulty, throat/tongue swelling or voice change, or faintness/collapse — immediate emergency. Call for help now even as you treat.
entries.do_now: GIVE ADRENALINE auto-injector IMMEDIATELY into the outer mid-thigh (through clothing is fine) if available — the priority, life-saving; don't delay for antihistamines or to 'see.' Remove the trigger (scrape out a sting; stop a drug). Position: flat with legs raised if faint; sit up if breathing is the main problem; on the side if vomiting/drowsy — don't stand them up suddenly. No improvement in 5-15 min and a second injector available: give another dose. Be ready for CPR.
entries.do_not: Don't delay adrenaline (late adrenaline is the main cause of death). Don't rely on antihistamine/inhaler alone for a severe reaction. Don't stand them up or let them walk. Don't assume it's over when symptoms ease (can rebound).
entries.after_care: Everyone who has had anaphylaxis needs urgent medical care even if they recover (biphasic rebound). Keep monitoring breathing/circulation and positioning. Arrange allergist follow-up, a written action plan, and carrying two auto-injectors.
entries.prevention: Strict trigger avoidance; carry in-date auto-injectors; family/companions know how and when to use them.

entries.title: Pneumonia (serious chest infection)
entries.what_it_is: Infection of lung tissue (often bacterial) filling air sacs with fluid so breathing and oxygen suffer. A leading cause of death in children and the elderly.
entries.recognize: Cough (often yellow/green/rusty phlegm), fever/chills, chest pain worse on breathing in or coughing, fast/labored breathing, breathlessness, fatigue, poor appetite. Danger signs: fast breathing (count it), blue lips/fingertips, confusion (elderly), can't drink, chest indrawing/nostril flaring/grunting (children), very high or very low temperature, drowsiness. Count breaths for a full minute at rest — persistently fast breathing is a key warning.
entries.get_help_fast: Fast/labored breathing; blue lips; confusion or severe weakness; can't drink; severe chest pain; chest indrawing/grunting in a child; infant/elderly/pregnant/chronically ill worsening. Usually needs prescribed antibiotics, sometimes oxygen. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Rest; sit upright/propped to ease breathing. Fluids in frequent small sips to loosen secretions and prevent dehydration. Keep warm not overheated. Manage fever with rest/fluids/simple measures per label and age/weight. Encourage gentle coughing; fresh air helps. Count and note breathing rate; watch danger signs. Arrange medical assessment — a clinician must choose any antibiotic.
entries.do_not: Don't ignore fast/labored breathing. No leftover/other-person antibiotics or guessed doses. Don't suppress a productive cough just to silence it. Don't let a struggling child or frail elder 'wait it out.'
entries.after_care: Continue rest/fluids; finish any prescribed antibiotic course fully. Recheck breathing rate and alertness. Re-assess if not improving in 2-3 days or worsening. Energy can take weeks to return.
entries.prevention: Hand hygiene, not smoking, vaccination where available, prompt care of the vulnerable. Counting breaths is the simplest field severity check.

entries.title: Concussion / head injury
entries.what_it_is: A brain injury from a blow/jolt that shakes the brain. Concussion is the milder end; the danger is missing a bleed or swelling inside the skull, which can worsen over hours.
entries.recognize: After a head impact: brief or no loss of consciousness; dazed/stunned/confused; headache; dizziness; nausea/vomiting; blurred/double vision; ringing ears; light/noise sensitivity; memory gaps; slow responses; 'not right,' emotional/irritable. Symptoms can appear/worsen over minutes to hours.
entries.get_help_fast: RED FLAGS (possible brain bleed/skull or neck injury): steadily worsening or severe headache; repeated vomiting; increasing drowsiness/confusion or hard to wake; unequal/unreactive pupils; weakness/numbness/clumsiness or trouble walking/talking; a seizure; clear fluid or blood from nose/ears; bruising around both eyes or behind ears; slurred speech or strange behavior; any neck pain (possible spine injury); any loss of consciousness. Infants: bulging soft spot, constant crying, won't feed, lethargy. If any of these danger signs are present, call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK) or get to the nearest emergency department.
entries.do_now: Stop activity; rest quietly (physical and mental); watch closely for red flags over the next 24 h. Possible neck/spine injury: keep head/neck still and in line, don't move unless in danger, support the head. Cloth-wrapped cold pack to a bump. Keep company; someone should be able to check on them, including waking periodically the first night to confirm they rouse and act normally.
entries.do_not: No return to sport/work/driving/heavy activity while any symptom remains (a second impact while recovering can be catastrophic). Don't leave them alone the first 24 h. No alcohol/sedatives. Don't move a suspected neck injury carelessly. Don't give strong painkillers that mask worsening without advice.
entries.after_care: Rest with a gradual, symptom-guided return and limited screens. Keep watching red flags 24-48 h; seek care immediately if any appear. Get assessment for very young/old, anyone on blood-thinners, any loss of consciousness, or symptoms beyond a few days.
entries.prevention: Helmets and seatbelts; fall-proofing for elderly and very young. On blood-thinners, even a minor head knock deserves review.

entries.title: Food poisoning / gastroenteritis
entries.what_it_is: Illness from contaminated food or water. Usually self-limiting over 1-3 days; the real danger is dehydration, especially in the young, old, pregnant, and ill.
entries.recognize: Nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, diarrhea, usually hours to a day or two after suspect food/water; sometimes fever, headache, aches. Watch the dehydration signs (see dehydration entry): little/dark urine, dry mouth, sunken eyes, dizziness, lethargy.
entries.get_help_fast: Blood or black tarry color in vomit/stool; high or persistent fever; serious dehydration (very little/no urine, sunken eyes, confusion, rapid pulse, floppy child); severe constant belly pain or rigid/swollen belly; unstoppable vomiting; symptoms beyond a few days; recent high-risk travel; infant/elderly/pregnant/chronically ill. Botulism signs (blurred/double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing/breathing, descending weakness after canned/preserved food) — emergency.
entries.do_now: Prioritize fluids — frequent small sips of ORS (see dehydration) or clean water, more after each stool/vomit. Rest. Reintroduce food gently when able — small bland starch (rice, bananas, toast, crackers, soup). Keep breastfeeding infants; ORS between feeds. Strict hand-washing to avoid spreading it.
entries.do_not: No anti-diarrhea drugs (e.g., loperamide) if bloody diarrhea or high fever (can trap infection). Don't force solids during active vomiting. Don't ignore dehydration. No unprescribed antibiotics. Don't prepare food for others while ill.
entries.after_care: Keep rehydrating until urine is pale/normal and symptoms settle; rebuild diet gradually. Seek care if it won't settle, blood appears, or dehydration develops. Clean/disinfect to prevent household spread.
entries.prevention: Safe water (boil/treat), thorough cooking, separate raw/cooked, refrigeration, hand-washing. Discard bulging/damaged cans and off-smelling food.

entries.title: Family medical history and inherited risk
entries.what_it_is: A family health history records important illnesses among relatives. It helps healthcare professionals consider shared risk factors; it cannot diagnose a person or establish that a disease is inevitable.
entries.recognize: This is background information rather than a symptom diagnosis. Useful details are the condition, which relative was affected, and age at diagnosis if known.
entries.get_help_fast: Discuss unusual family patterns, multiple close relatives with the same serious condition, or illness at unusually young ages with a healthcare professional who can advise on screening or genetic counselling. New urgent symptoms need their own prompt assessment, regardless of family history.
entries.do_now: Ask willing relatives about significant conditions on both sides of the family. Record relationship, condition, age when identified if known, and whether details are uncertain. Date each update; share a concise summary with your healthcare professional only with appropriate privacy and consent.
entries.do_not: Do not interpret family stories as genetic test results, predict an individual's risk percentage, or store a relative's private health information without permission.
entries.after_care: Review the list before healthcare visits and correct inaccurate or outdated information. Ask which screening or prevention steps actually apply to you.
entries.prevention: Healthy habits and appropriate, individualized screening can reduce some risks even when family history cannot be changed.
sources: CDC ΓÇö About Family Health History
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Hand and everyday body hygiene
entries.what_it_is: Everyday hygiene can help reduce transmission of infectious illnesses. Cleaning hands is particularly important before food handling and after using the toilet, coughing, or caring for someone ill.
entries.recognize: The need for routine handwashing depends on exposures, not on a diagnosis. Visible dirt, food contamination and contact with body fluids are good reasons to wash with soap and water.
entries.get_help_fast: Hygiene is not a treatment for an infection. Ask a healthcare professional about a wound that appears infected or symptoms that worsen. Difficulty breathing, severe weakness or rapidly spreading symptoms should be assessed urgently rather than managed through cleaning alone.
entries.do_now: When available, wash hands with soap and clean water, rubbing all surfaces for at least 20 seconds and drying with a clean material. If hands are not visibly dirty and water is unavailable, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, following its label. Keep personal supplies reasonably clean.
entries.do_not: Do not substitute hand sanitizer for soap and water when hands are visibly soiled if washing is available. Do not put cleaning chemicals or disinfectants on broken skin or inside body openings.
entries.after_care: Re-establish hand-cleaning routines after travel or caregiving and make it easy for household members to access soap, water and drying materials.
entries.prevention: Make hand hygiene routine before eating, during food preparation, after toilet use, and after coughing or caring for sick people.
sources: PHAC ΓÇö Clean your hands to help reduce infectious disease spread
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Oral and dental hygiene
entries.what_it_is: Oral care aims to keep the teeth and gums healthy and reduce tooth decay and gum disease. Dental pain or swelling may indicate a condition needing professional treatment.
entries.recognize: Possible reasons to seek dental advice include persistent tooth pain, bleeding gums, damaged teeth, swelling, or a sore that does not heal.
entries.get_help_fast: Arrange prompt dental care for suspected tooth infection, severe pain or swelling. If mouth or facial swelling makes breathing, swallowing, or speaking difficult, call emergency services. Do not wait for a routine dental appointment in that situation.
entries.do_now: Brush teeth gently with fluoride toothpaste and clean between the teeth regularly. Keep dental appliances clean. For persistent pain or swelling, contact a dentist rather than attempting to treat the underlying cause yourself.
entries.do_not: Do not try to drain a dental abscess, extract a tooth yourself, or substitute home remedies for treatment of an infection. Do not apply harsh disinfectants inside the mouth.
entries.after_care: Follow the dentist's plan for treatment and follow-up; note changes in pain, swelling or bleeding and report worsening symptoms.
entries.prevention: Regular brushing with fluoride toothpaste, daily cleaning between the teeth, and routine dental visits can support mouth health.
sources: Public Health Agency of Canada ΓÇö Oral health for adults
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Reading a laboratory report
entries.what_it_is: A laboratory report describes measurements or findings from a test. Results contribute information, but cannot usually be interpreted reliably without symptoms, medical history and the laboratory's own reference intervals.
entries.recognize: The report may show the test name, result, units, collection date, reference interval and a flag for values outside that interval. A flag is not a diagnosis, and an unflagged result does not rule out illness.
entries.get_help_fast: Contact the ordering clinician promptly if the report labels a result critical or requests urgent follow-up. Seek emergency care for serious new symptoms regardless of whether a report appears normal.
entries.do_now: Identify the exact test, numerical result, units, the interval printed by that laboratory, and the collection date. Ask the ordering clinician what the result means in context, whether repeat testing is needed, and what follow-up timeline applies.
entries.do_not: Do not use unrelated online reference ranges to diagnose yourself; do not compare values from different laboratories without checking units and methods. Do not change a medication because of an isolated lab value without professional direction.
entries.after_care: Keep the report and written explanation with the date. Record planned repeat tests or appointments and ask how results will be communicated.
entries.prevention: Before a test, follow the preparation instructions provided by the laboratory or clinician; disclose medicines or supplements that may affect results.
sources: MedlinePlus ΓÇö How to Understand Your Lab Results
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Understanding children's growth charts
entries.what_it_is: Child growth charts show how height, length, weight or other measurements compare with age-appropriate growth references. The pattern across measurements is generally more informative than one number.
entries.recognize: A child's measurement must be interpreted with age, sex, measurement method and the appropriate chart. An isolated percentile cannot confirm a medical problem.
entries.get_help_fast: Ask a pediatric healthcare professional about unexpected changes in a child's growth pattern, feeding concerns, or weight changes. A child who seems acutely ill needs assessment for symptoms rather than relying on a growth chart.
entries.do_now: Record measured values with the measurement date, units and the child's age. Use the growth charts recommended by the child's healthcare team and ask them to explain the pattern over time.
entries.do_not: Do not invent a percentile from memory, apply an adult BMI threshold to a young child, or diagnose growth failure from one measurement. Do not change a child's feeding plan solely because of an isolated chart point.
entries.after_care: Bring past measurements and growth records to visits; agree with the child's clinician on whether follow-up measurement is needed.
entries.prevention: Follow regular child health visits and discuss nutrition, feeding and health concerns with the child's care team.
sources: Canadian Paediatric Society ΓÇö WHO Growth Charts
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Keeping a safer medication list
entries.what_it_is: A medication list helps healthcare professionals see the medicines and health products a person is using, so they can discuss directions, possible interactions and changes.
entries.recognize: A useful list includes prescribed and non-prescribed products, vitamins and supplements, the product name, strength from the label, the prescribed directions, and the date last checked.
entries.get_help_fast: Contact a pharmacist or prescribing clinician when instructions conflict, a medicine has been changed, or side effects are suspected. Severe allergic-reaction symptoms or difficulty breathing require emergency help.
entries.do_now: Copy each medicine's exact name and label instructions into a dated list, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements. Keep allergies and past significant reactions nearby. Bring the list or containers to healthcare appointments and confirm questions with a pharmacist.
entries.do_not: Do not invent doses, merge tablets into an unlabeled container, stop prescribed therapy solely because a list seems confusing, or share someone else's prescription.
entries.after_care: Reconcile the list after each clinic or pharmacy visit and remove outdated items only after confirming the actual treatment plan.
entries.prevention: Try to keep one up-to-date list accessible for emergency consultations and share it with professionals responsible for your medicines.
sources: Health Canada ΓÇö Using medications safely
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Questions about children's liquid medicines
entries.what_it_is: Liquid medicines for children can have different formulations and concentrations. The correct instructions depend on the specific product and the child's circumstances and must come from the label or a qualified professional.
entries.recognize: Before a dose is given, confirm the child's identity, medicine name, product concentration, prescription or label instructions, and supplied measuring device. Different brand names may contain the same active ingredient.
entries.get_help_fast: If an accidental overdose or wrong medicine is suspected, contact poison control immediately; for serious breathing problems, collapse, or anaphylaxis symptoms, contact emergency services. Ask a pharmacist before giving a dose if the label is unclear.
entries.do_now: Check the package and ask the pharmacist to demonstrate the proper oral measuring syringe or other supplied device. Follow the label exactly; record medicine administration so caregivers do not duplicate it. Ask about allergy history and interactions.
entries.do_not: Do not use a household spoon, guess a millilitre amount, substitute concentrations without advice, give adult products to a young child unless explicitly directed, or double up on products with the same active ingredient.
entries.after_care: Keep the product in its original child-resistant container and out of children's reach. Follow up if the child's symptoms are not improving as expected or if unexpected reactions appear.
entries.prevention: Review the label whenever a product is refilled or changes formulation; coordinate dosing records among caregivers.
sources: Health Canada ΓÇö Safe use of medication for children
Health Canada ΓÇö Acetaminophen and children
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Everyday eating using Canada's Food Guide
entries.what_it_is: Canada's Food Guide provides general healthy-eating advice about food variety, preparation and habits. It is educational guidance, not an individualized medical diet.
entries.recognize: Everyday meals can include vegetables and fruits, whole grains, protein foods, and water as the preferred drink. Needs can differ with age, allergies and medical conditions.
entries.get_help_fast: Ask a registered dietitian or healthcare professional before making major dietary changes for a medical condition, significant food allergy, pregnancy-related concerns or a child's special nutritional needs. This chapter does not diagnose an eating or nutritional problem.
entries.do_now: Use the food guide plate as a flexible planning tool: roughly half vegetables/fruits, a quarter whole grains and a quarter protein foods. Choose plant proteins more often if suitable, use food labels and consider budget and culture.
entries.do_not: Do not treat the general plate model as a prescription or override medically required diets, allergy precautions, feeding restrictions, or clinician advice.
entries.after_care: Choose practical changes that can be sustained; ask a qualified clinician or dietitian for advice if nutrition affects treatment or growth.
entries.prevention: Build routines around a variety of minimally processed foods, accessible water and meals that suit cultural and household needs.
sources: Health Canada ΓÇö Healthy eating recommendations
Health Canada ΓÇö Make healthy meals with Canada's food guide plate
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Preparing for a health appointment
entries.what_it_is: Preparing a short account of symptoms, medicines, concerns and questions can make a healthcare visit more useful and improve understanding of a follow-up plan.
entries.recognize: Before a visit, note what changed, when symptoms began, important test results, current medicines, allergies and the main questions you want answered.
entries.get_help_fast: Seek prompt medical care if symptoms are suddenly severe or worsening; appointment preparation must never delay emergency help. If a laboratory report is flagged critical or an instruction is unclear, ask the responsible clinician directly.
entries.do_now: Write a brief symptom timeline, bring medication and family-history lists, record questions in priority order, and ask for plain-language explanations. Confirm what to do next, which symptoms require urgent help, and how results will be delivered.
entries.do_not: Do not conceal relevant symptoms or treatment changes out of embarrassment. Do not rely on an AI-generated visit summary as a substitute for the clinician's actual instructions.
entries.after_care: Before leaving, confirm any follow-up date, referrals, medication changes or repeat tests. Keep written instructions and check whom to call if the plan is unclear.
entries.prevention: Maintain an up-to-date list of medicines, allergies and key diagnoses so future appointments require less reconstruction.
sources: MedlinePlus ΓÇö Make the most of your doctor visit
MedlinePlus ΓÇö How to Understand Your Lab Results
Health Canada ΓÇö Using medications safely
entries.author: Jeff Robinson

entries.title: Blood clot in the lung (pulmonary embolism)
entries.what_it_is: A blood clot — usually from a deep vein in the leg — that travels to the lungs and blocks blood flow. It can strain the heart and lower the body's oxygen, and can be life-threatening.
entries.recognize: Sudden breathlessness; sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in; fast breathing or a racing heart; coughing (sometimes with blood); light-headedness or collapse. A swollen, tender calf on one side (a deep vein clot) often comes first. Risk rises after surgery, long immobility or long flights, with the contraceptive pill or pregnancy, with cancer, or after a previous clot.
entries.get_help_fast: Sudden breathlessness or chest pain — especially with a swollen, painful calf, coughing up blood, or feeling faint — call your local emergency number now (for example 911 in Canada and the US, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the UK).
entries.do_now: Call emergency services. Keep still and rest, stay with the person, and be ready to say when it started. Do not dismiss breathlessness that came on suddenly as 'just anxiety'.
entries.do_not: Don't 'wait and see' with sudden breathlessness, don't drive yourself to hospital, and don't start extra blood thinners or aspirin on your own unless emergency staff tell you to.
entries.after_care: After hospital, take blood thinners exactly as prescribed, keep follow-up blood tests, and report any bleeding, new breathlessness or chest pain straight away.
entries.prevention: Move and walk on long trips, stay hydrated, get up and about after surgery as advised, and tell doctors about any past clot before operations or before starting the contraceptive pill.

entries.title: Cauda equina syndrome (spinal emergency)
synonyms: nerve compression at base of spine
entries.what_it_is: Compression of the bundle of nerves at the base of the spine, often from a large slipped disc. It is a surgical emergency: delay can cause permanent loss of bladder, bowel and sexual function and leg weakness.
entries.recognize: New numbness between the legs or around the back passage (the 'saddle' area); losing the feeling of needing to pass urine, trouble starting or stopping the stream, or leaking; new numbness or weakness in one or both legs; new loss of bowel control — usually with back and leg pain.
entries.get_help_fast: Numbness between the legs or around the back passage, or new trouble passing or controlling urine or stool together with back or leg pain — go to emergency care now. This is time-critical.
entries.do_now: Go to the nearest emergency department now — do not wait to see if it settles. Note exactly when the saddle numbness or bladder changes started, as timing guides treatment.
entries.do_not: Don't wait overnight to 'see if it eases', don't rely on painkillers to mask it, and don't let a routine back-pain appointment delay emergency assessment when saddle or bladder symptoms are present.
entries.after_care: After surgery, follow the spinal team's movement and physiotherapy plan and keep urology and bladder/bowel follow-up appointments.
entries.prevention: There is no sure way to prevent it, but anyone with back pain should know the red flags — saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, leg weakness — and act fast if they appear.

entries.title: Twisted testicle (testicular torsion)
entries.what_it_is: The testicle twists on its cord and cuts off its own blood supply. It is an emergency — the testicle can usually be saved only if treated within about six hours.
entries.recognize: Sudden, severe pain in one testicle, often with swelling, a testicle that sits higher or at an odd angle, nausea or vomiting, and sometimes lower belly pain. Most common in teenagers and young men, but it can happen at any age, including newborns.
entries.get_help_fast: Sudden testicle pain — or sudden lower belly pain with nausea or vomiting in a boy or young man — go to emergency care now. Every hour counts.
entries.do_now: Go to the nearest emergency department immediately. Do not eat or drink, in case surgery is needed. Do not wait for the pain to ease.
entries.do_not: Don't wait to see if the pain settles, don't apply heat, and don't eat or drink in case an operation is needed.
entries.after_care: After surgery, rest as advised, support the area, watch the wound for signs of infection, and keep the follow-up appointment.
entries.prevention: It usually can't be prevented, but fixing both testicles during surgery lowers the chance of a repeat; remember that sudden testicle pain always needs same-hour care.

entries.title: Flesh-eating infection (necrotising fasciitis)
entries.what_it_is: A rare but very fast, deep infection that destroys the tissue under the skin. It can spread within hours and is life-threatening without urgent surgery and antibiotics.
entries.recognize: Pain far worse than the wound or skin looks; spreading redness, swelling and warmth; skin that turns dusky, purple or blistered; fever and feeling very unwell; sometimes a crackling feel under the skin. It can start from a small cut, graze or surgical wound.
entries.get_help_fast: Pain out of proportion to a wound, redness spreading quickly, and feeling very unwell — go to emergency care now. This spreads in hours.
entries.do_now: Go to the nearest emergency department now. Mark the edge of the redness with a pen and note the time, so how fast it spreads can be seen. Do not wait.
entries.do_not: Don't wait, don't just cover and ignore a rapidly worsening wound, and don't assume that needing strong painkillers means it's getting better.
entries.after_care: After hospital, follow wound-care and rehabilitation plans closely, keep all surgical follow-up, and report any new spreading redness or fever at once.
entries.prevention: Keep wounds clean and covered, take extra care with cuts in people with diabetes or weak immunity, and seek help early whenever pain seems far worse than the wound looks.

entries.title: Tuberculosis (TB)
entries.what_it_is: A bacterial infection, usually of the lungs, spread through the air when someone with active lung TB coughs or sneezes. Not everyone infected becomes ill (latent TB). It is curable, and in most places testing and treatment are free and confidential regardless of immigration or insurance status.
entries.recognize: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks; coughing up phlegm or blood; drenching night sweats; unexplained weight loss; fever; tiredness; chest pain. It builds slowly over weeks, not days.
entries.get_help_fast: See a doctor or TB/public-health clinic soon for a cough over 3 weeks with night sweats or weight loss. Coughing up blood, severe breathlessness, or marked weight loss warrants urgent care.
entries.do_now: Go for testing (chest X-ray and sputum). Cover coughs, open windows, and limit close contact until assessed. Write down anyone you share a home with.
entries.do_not: Do not stop antibiotics early because you feel better — stopping is how drug-resistant TB develops. Do not hide the diagnosis from close contacts who may need testing.
entries.after_care: Take the full course (about 6 months) exactly as prescribed; attend monitoring for liver side effects. Close contacts are screened. You usually stop being infectious within weeks of starting treatment.
entries.prevention: Good ventilation; prompt testing of contacts; BCG vaccination where recommended; completing treatment for latent TB if advised.

entries.title: RSV and bronchiolitis in babies
entries.what_it_is: RSV is a common winter virus. In babies and young children it can inflame the small airways (bronchiolitis), causing wheezy, fast, laboured breathing. It spreads by coughs, sneezes, hands and surfaces. Most babies recover at home; the very young and premature are most at risk.
entries.recognize: Starts like a cold, then fast breathing, wheeze or crackles, a tugging-in under the ribs or at the neck, feeding less, fewer wet nappies. Danger: blue lips, long pauses in breathing, exhaustion, grunting.
entries.get_help_fast: Emergency care now for blue colour, pauses in breathing, severe effort to breathe, or a baby too breathless to feed. Same-day advice for fast breathing, poor feeding, or fewer than half the usual wet nappies.
entries.do_now: Keep the nose clear with saline drops, offer small frequent feeds, hold upright, count the breaths and watch the chest. Keep the room smoke-free.
entries.do_not: Do not give cough medicines or antibiotics (they don't help a virus). Do not expose the baby to cigarette smoke. Do not leave a struggling baby to 'sleep it off'.
entries.after_care: Recovery over 1-2 weeks; the cough can linger. Return if breathing or feeding worsens. Some babies need hospital oxygen or feeding support for a few days.
entries.prevention: Hand washing; keeping newborns away from people with colds; not smoking around babies; preventive antibody/vaccine programmes where offered.

entries.title: Norovirus (the vomiting bug)
entries.what_it_is: A very contagious virus causing sudden vomiting and diarrhoea. It spreads easily by hands, surfaces, food and tiny airborne particles from vomit, so outbreaks race through homes, schools and ships. The main danger is dehydration.
entries.recognize: Sudden onset of vomiting and watery diarrhoea, cramps, nausea, sometimes a low fever and aches. Often several people in one household fall ill within a day or two.
entries.get_help_fast: Seek care for signs of dehydration (very little urine, dizziness, sunken eyes, a drowsy child), blood in stool, a high fever, or symptoms lasting beyond a few days. Babies and the frail dehydrate fastest.
entries.do_now: Sip fluids often — water or oral rehydration salts; rest. Wash hands with soap and water. Clean soiled surfaces with a bleach-based product.
entries.do_not: Do not rely on alcohol hand gel alone (it works poorly on norovirus). Do not prepare food for others, and stay off work/school until 48 hours after symptoms stop. Avoid anti-diarrhoea drugs in children.
entries.after_care: Usually settles in 1-3 days. Keep up fluids as appetite returns; reintroduce bland food. Deep-clean and wash laundry hot after an episode.
entries.prevention: Thorough soap-and-water hand washing; isolating the ill person; careful cleaning of vomit/diarrhoea; not sharing towels.

entries.title: Malaria (fever after travel)
entries.what_it_is: A serious infection spread by mosquito bites in tropical and subtropical regions. Some types can kill within a day or two if untreated. It is one of the most important causes of fever in anyone recently back from an affected area.
entries.recognize: Fever, chills and sweats (sometimes in waves), headache, body aches, nausea — often mistaken for flu. Severe signs: confusion, drowsiness, fits, breathlessness, jaundice, very little urine.
entries.get_help_fast: Any fever within a year of travel to a malaria area — especially the first 3 months — needs same-day testing; treat confusion, drowsiness, breathlessness or fits as an emergency. Always tell staff where and when you travelled.
entries.do_now: Go for a blood test urgently (it may be repeated). Bring travel dates and any antimalarials taken. Lower fever with paracetamol.
entries.do_not: Do not assume it is 'just flu'. Do not wait to see if it passes. Do not stop prescribed antimalarials early.
entries.after_care: With prompt treatment most people recover fully. Finish the full course; follow-up confirms the parasite has cleared.
entries.prevention: Mosquito bite avoidance (nets, repellent, covering up), taking preventive tablets exactly as prescribed for the destination, and seeking advice before travel.

entries.title: Dengue (fever after travel)
entries.what_it_is: A mosquito-borne virus in tropical regions. Most people recover, but a small number enter a dangerous phase as the fever falls (days 3-7), with plasma leakage and bleeding. A second infection with a different strain carries higher risk.
entries.recognize: High fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, intense muscle and joint aches, a rash. Warning signs as fever drops: severe belly pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, restlessness, cold clammy skin.
entries.get_help_fast: Seek care for any fever after tropical travel. Go urgently for the warning signs above — the window as the fever breaks is when it turns dangerous.
entries.do_now: Rest and take plenty of fluids; use paracetamol for fever and pain; monitor closely during days 3-7.
entries.do_not: Do not take ibuprofen, aspirin or other NSAIDs — they raise bleeding risk. Do not ignore worsening belly pain or vomiting.
entries.after_care: Fever lasts 2-7 days; tiredness can linger for weeks. Keep hydrated and rest; return promptly if warning signs appear.
entries.prevention: Mosquito bite avoidance day and night; removing standing water; vaccination only where specifically recommended.

entries.title: Measles
entries.what_it_is: A highly contagious virus — one of the most infectious known. It spreads through the air and can linger in a room after an infected person leaves. It can cause serious complications (pneumonia, brain inflammation), especially in the very young, pregnant people and those with weak immunity.
entries.recognize: Several days of high fever, cough, runny nose and red sore eyes, then a blotchy rash starting at the hairline/face and spreading down. Tiny white spots inside the cheeks may appear first.
entries.get_help_fast: Phone a doctor or health line first (do not sit in a waiting room and expose others). Emergency care for breathing difficulty, drowsiness, fits, or a stiff neck with a severe headache.
entries.do_now: Isolate at home, rest, fluids, paracetamol for fever. Tell the clinic before arriving so they can protect others. Warn any pregnant or unvaccinated contacts.
entries.do_not: Do not go to crowded waiting areas unannounced. Do not assume immunity without two documented vaccine doses or past infection.
entries.after_care: Stay isolated until about 4 days after the rash appears. Watch for complications. Public health may contact you to protect others.
entries.prevention: Two doses of the MMR vaccine give strong, lasting protection and are the main way measles is controlled.

entries.title: Whooping cough (pertussis)
entries.what_it_is: A bacterial infection of the airways spread by coughs and sneezes. It causes long bouts of coughing that can end in a 'whoop' as the person gasps for air. It is most dangerous for young babies, who may stop breathing rather than whoop.
entries.recognize: Starts like a cold, then fits of coughing that worsen over 1-2 weeks, often worse at night, sometimes with vomiting after coughing or a whooping sound. Babies may go red or blue, or have breathing pauses.
entries.get_help_fast: Emergency care for a baby with breathing pauses, blue spells, or feeding difficulty. See a doctor early if whooping cough is suspected, especially around babies or in pregnancy — early antibiotics reduce spread.
entries.do_now: Keep infants away from the ill person; antibiotics early can limit spread. Small frequent fluids; calm, upright positioning during coughing fits.
entries.do_not: Do not expect cough medicines to help. Do not delay care for a young baby — they can deteriorate fast.
entries.after_care: The cough can last many weeks ('the 100-day cough'). Complete antibiotics; close contacts and babies may need preventive treatment.
entries.prevention: Vaccination in childhood and in pregnancy (which protects the newborn); boosters where recommended.

entries.title: Scabies
entries.what_it_is: A very itchy skin condition caused by tiny mites burrowing into the skin. It spreads by prolonged skin-to-skin contact, so whole households and care settings are often affected together. It is not a sign of poor hygiene.
entries.recognize: Intense itch, worse at night; a pimply rash; thin wavy burrow lines, often between fingers, wrists, armpits, waist, genitals. Itch can continue for weeks after successful treatment.
entries.get_help_fast: See a pharmacist or GP to confirm and get treatment. Urgent review if skin becomes infected (spreading redness, pus, fever) or for a crusted/severe form in someone with weak immunity.
entries.do_now: Apply the prescribed cream/lotion over the whole body as directed; treat all household and close contacts on the same day, even if they have no symptoms yet. Wash bedding and clothes hot.
entries.do_not: Do not treat only the itchy areas. Do not skip treating contacts — untreated contacts re-infect everyone.
entries.after_care: Itch may persist up to a few weeks after treatment; a second application is often advised. See a doctor if new burrows appear after treatment.
entries.prevention: Avoiding prolonged skin contact with an untreated person; treating contacts together; hot-washing or sealing bedding/clothes.

entries.title: Pattern hair loss (male and female)
entries.what_it_is: The common, gradual, inherited thinning of hair with age — a receding hairline and thinning crown in men, a widening parting in women. It is driven by genetics and hormones, is not a disease, and does not harm health.
entries.recognize: Slow thinning over months to years in a typical pattern; the scalp may show through. No scaling, scarring, or sudden patches (those suggest another cause).
entries.get_help_fast: No urgency. See a GP if loss is rapid, patchy, scarring, or comes with other symptoms (tiredness, weight change) — that may point to thyroid, iron, or another cause worth checking.
entries.do_now: Decide what you want: accepting it is a perfectly valid choice. If you want to slow it, a pharmacist or GP can discuss evidence-based options such as topical minoxidil.
entries.do_not: Do not waste money on unproven 'miracle' cures. Do not expect any treatment to work overnight — effects take months, and stopping reverses gains.
entries.after_care: If using a treatment, give it 3-6 months and review. Protect the scalp from sunburn. Support groups help if it affects confidence.
entries.prevention: There is no proven prevention for the inherited pattern; early treatment can slow it for some. Treating other causes (iron, thyroid) protects remaining hair.

entries.title: Understanding how health risks are described
entries.what_it_is: How a risk is worded changes how big it feels, even when the facts are identical. This entry explains the plain-language ideas behind the way this guide — and sources like the CDC, WHO and NHS — describe how likely something is and what to do about it.
entries.recognize: Watch for: relative risk ('doubles your risk') which sounds alarming but may be a jump from tiny to still-tiny; big round scary numbers with no timeframe; a benefit or harm given without saying 'out of how many' or 'over how long'.
entries.get_help_fast: When a number worries you, ask a clinician three things: out of how many people, over what time, and compared with what? Those turn a scary phrase into something you can weigh.
entries.do_now: Prefer natural frequencies: '2 in 1,000 people per year' is clearer than '0.2%' or 'a doubling'. Ask for both the chance something helps and the chance it harms. Separate 'how likely' from 'how serious'.
entries.do_not: Do not act on a relative change alone ('50% more') without the baseline. Do not treat a rare risk as common because it is frightening, or a common risk as rare because it is familiar.
entries.after_care: Write the real numbers down and revisit them when calm. A good source states its uncertainty and its date; be wary of anything that promises certainty.
entries.prevention: Learn to ask 'out of how many, over how long, compared to what'. Use trusted public-health sources, check the date, and match the strength of your response to the real size of the risk.

entries.title: Airway swelling / epiglottitis (throat emergency)
entries.what_it_is: Dangerous swelling at the entrance of the windpipe (often the epiglottis), which can block breathing within minutes. Causes include infection (epiglottitis), a severe allergic reaction, a burn/scald to the throat, or a swallowed foreign body. It is a time-critical emergency at any age, and especially in children.
entries.recognize: Drooling or unable to swallow saliva; a muffled 'hot-potato' voice or inability to speak; noisy, harsh breathing in (stridor); sitting upright and leaning forward (tripod) to breathe; reluctance to lie down; severe sore throat with a high fever; blue or grey lips; rising distress and effort to breathe.
entries.get_help_fast: Call emergency services now (911/999/112). Treat drooling + muffled voice + leaning forward to breathe, or any stridor at rest, as an airway emergency even without a fever.
entries.do_now: Keep the person calm and sitting upright in the position they find easiest — do not force them to lie down. Do not put anything in the mouth or try to look down the throat (it can trigger total obstruction). Loosen tight clothing. If an allergic cause is likely and an adrenaline auto-injector is available, use it. Stay with them and be ready to start CPR if they stop breathing.
entries.do_not: Do not examine the throat with a spatula or finger. Do not lay the person flat. Do not give food or drink. Do not leave them alone. Do not delay the emergency call to 'wait and see'.
entries.after_care: After emergency treatment the airway may be protected in hospital and the cause treated (antibiotics for epiglottitis, allergy care, foreign-body removal). Follow discharge advice, complete any antibiotics, and ensure contacts are vaccinated where advised (e.g. Hib).
entries.prevention: Keep childhood Hib and other vaccinations up to date. Carry and know how to use prescribed adrenaline auto-injectors for known severe allergies. Keep small objects and button batteries away from young children.

entries.title: Bowel obstruction (blocked bowel)
synonyms: no wind or stool with vomiting
entries.what_it_is: The bowel becomes blocked so food, fluid and gas cannot pass. Causes include adhesions from past surgery, a trapped hernia, a twist (volvulus), a tumour, or severe constipation. A blockage can cut off blood supply to the bowel, which is life-threatening, so it needs urgent hospital assessment.
entries.recognize: A swollen, distended, often tight belly; cramping waves of tummy pain; vomiting (which may become green/brown); and not passing any stool or wind (gas). In a strangulated hernia there may be a tender lump in the groin or at an old scar. Fever, a constant severe pain, or feeling very unwell suggests the bowel's blood supply is affected.
entries.get_help_fast: Go to the emergency department or call emergency services the same day — especially with constant severe pain, fever, a tender irreducible lump, or vomiting that won't stop. Do not wait it out at home.
entries.do_now: Stop eating and drinking (nil by mouth) in case surgery is needed. Rest in whatever position eases the pain. Note when symptoms started, the last bowel movement, and any past abdominal surgery or hernia to tell the team. Take sips only if advised by a clinician.
entries.do_not: Do not eat or drink normally. Do not take laxatives, strong painkillers that mask the picture, or 'something to settle the stomach' without advice. Do not try to push a tender groin/scar lump back in forcefully.
entries.after_care: Treatment may involve hospital fluids, a tube to decompress the stomach, and sometimes surgery. After recovery, follow advice on diet, fluids and gradual return to eating, and seek help early if it recurs.
entries.prevention: Treat constipation early with fluids, fibre and activity. Have hernias assessed before they become trapped. Attend bowel-screening and report persistent changes in bowel habit, blood, or unexplained weight loss.

entries.title: Pre-eclampsia (pregnancy high blood pressure)
entries.what_it_is: A serious condition of the second half of pregnancy (usually after 20 weeks) and the early days after birth, where raised blood pressure and strain on the organs can quickly threaten both mother and baby. It can progress to seizures (eclampsia) or HELLP syndrome. It can develop with few symptoms, so it is found partly through routine blood-pressure and urine checks.
entries.recognize: A severe or persistent headache; vision changes (blurring, flashing lights, spots); sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet; pain just below the ribs on the right; feeling very unwell, nauseous or vomiting; and a rapid increase in blood pressure. In HELLP there may be severe upper-belly pain and feeling generally awful.
entries.get_help_fast: In pregnancy or just after birth, a severe headache with visual changes, upper-belly pain, or sudden facial/hand swelling needs same-hour assessment — contact your maternity triage or labour ward, or call emergency services. A fit (seizure) in pregnancy is a 911/999 emergency.
entries.do_now: Contact maternity care immediately and have someone take you in or call an ambulance. Rest and stay calm. Note your most recent blood-pressure readings and symptoms. Do not drive yourself if you have visual symptoms or feel faint.
entries.do_not: Do not wait for your next routine appointment if you have warning symptoms. Do not dismiss a bad headache or swelling as 'normal pregnancy'. Do not take extra medication to lower blood pressure yourself without medical advice.
entries.after_care: Treatment is in hospital with blood-pressure medicines, monitoring, and sometimes early delivery — the only cure is birth of the baby and placenta. Blood pressure is watched closely for several days after delivery, as pre-eclampsia can appear or worsen postnatally. Follow-up checks are important.
entries.prevention: Attend all antenatal appointments for blood-pressure and urine checks. If you are higher risk, your team may advise low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy. Report warning symptoms promptly. Know your numbers and keep a record.
sources: UK NICE hypertension in pregnancy guidance

entries.title: Open (compound) fracture
entries.what_it_is: A broken bone where the skin is also broken — the bone may be visible or a wound sits over the break. High risk of heavy bleeding and deep infection; a surgical emergency.
entries.recognize: A wound over an obvious fracture, or bone visible through the skin, after a significant fall, crush or impact. Marked deformity, severe pain, bleeding, inability to use the limb.
entries.get_help_fast: Call your local emergency number now (911/112/999). This needs hospital assessment, antibiotics and usually surgery within hours.
entries.do_now: Keep the person still. Control bleeding with firm pressure AROUND the wound (not directly on protruding bone). Cover the wound with a clean, moist sterile dressing if available. Support/immobilise the limb in the position found. Keep them warm. Nil by mouth in case surgery is needed.
entries.do_not: Do not push the bone back in. Do not wash out or probe the wound. Do not straighten a badly deformed limb. Do not give food or drink.
entries.after_care: Follow hospital wound-care and antibiotic instructions; watch for spreading redness, fever, or increasing pain (infection).
entries.prevention: Protective equipment for high-risk activities; fall-proofing for older adults.

entries.title: Severe drug skin reaction (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN)
entries.what_it_is: A rare, life-threatening reaction — often to a new medicine — where the skin and the linings of the mouth, eyes and genitals blister and peel off in sheets.
entries.recognize: A rapidly spreading painful rash with blisters; skin peeling off in sheets; raw, sore lips, mouth, eyes or genitals; fever and feeling very unwell; usually days to a few weeks after starting a new drug.
entries.get_help_fast: Call your local emergency number now. This needs emergency hospital (often burns/ICU) care.
entries.do_now: Stop the suspected medicine if a clinician advises. Keep the person comfortable and hydrated while help comes. Bring a list of all medicines started recently.
entries.do_not: Do not keep taking the suspected drug. Do not burst blisters or apply random creams.
entries.after_care: The culprit drug (and related ones) must be recorded as a lifelong allergy and avoided. Eye and skin follow-up is often needed.
entries.prevention: Tell every prescriber about past severe drug reactions; some drugs have genetic risk tests in certain groups.

entries.title: Peritonitis / acute surgical abdomen
entries.what_it_is: Inflammation of the lining of the abdomen, often from a perforated organ (e.g. appendix, ulcer, bowel). The belly becomes rigid and extremely tender — a surgical emergency.
entries.recognize: Sudden, severe, constant abdominal pain; a hard, rigid, 'board-like' belly that is agony to move, press or release; pain worse with any movement or coughing; often fever and vomiting; the person lies very still.
entries.get_help_fast: Call your local emergency number now. This needs urgent hospital assessment and usually surgery.
entries.do_now: Keep the person still and comfortable, knees bent can ease the belly. Nil by mouth. Note when the pain started and where it began.
entries.do_not: Do not give food, drink, laxatives or strong painkillers that mask signs. Do not apply heat.
entries.after_care: Post-surgical wound and recovery care per the hospital; finish any prescribed antibiotics.
entries.prevention: Early assessment of severe or worsening abdominal pain prevents progression.

entries.title: Kidney infection (pyelonephritis)
entries.what_it_is: A urinary infection that has reached the kidney. More serious than a simple bladder infection and can progress to blood infection (sepsis) if untreated.
entries.recognize: Fever and shaking chills (rigors); pain in the back or side (flank); burning or frequent urination; nausea or vomiting; feeling very unwell. Can occur with or soon after bladder-infection symptoms.
entries.get_help_fast: Be seen the same day (urgent care or your doctor). Go to emergency care if confused, very drowsy, a very high or very low temperature, a fast heartbeat, little or no urine, or pregnant — these can signal sepsis.
entries.do_now: Drink fluids. Note your temperature and symptoms. A clinician will usually test urine and start antibiotics.
entries.do_not: Do not just wait it out or rely on cranberry/over-the-counter remedies — a kidney infection needs assessment and usually antibiotics.
entries.after_care: Finish the full antibiotic course; seek review if not improving within 48 hours. Recurrent infections should be investigated.
entries.prevention: Treat bladder infections promptly; stay well hydrated; for some people, prevention strategies from a clinician.

entries.title: Cardiac arrest — CPR
entries.what_it_is: The heart has stopped pumping, so the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Without immediate CPR, survival falls every minute. Bystander CPR can double or triple the chance of survival.
entries.recognize: Unresponsive (no reaction to shouting or shaking) AND not breathing, or only gasping/agonal breaths. May follow a collapse, drowning, electric shock, choking, overdose, or heart attack.
entries.get_help_fast: Call your local emergency number now (911/112/999), put the phone on speaker, and send someone for an AED (defibrillator). Start CPR immediately — do not wait.
entries.do_now: Push HARD and FAST in the centre of the chest, about 100-120 pushes a minute (twice a second), letting the chest come fully back up each time. If trained and willing, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 pushes; if not, keep doing continuous chest pushes (hands-only CPR). Do not stop except to use an AED. Turn on the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its spoken instructions.
entries.do_not: Do not stop to check for a pulse if unsure. Do not delay to 'make sure.' Do not be afraid to push hard — broken ribs heal, a stopped heart does not.
entries.after_care: Once the person is breathing normally, place them on their side (recovery position) and monitor until help arrives. Everyone who has had a cardiac arrest needs hospital assessment.
entries.prevention: Learn CPR and where AEDs are. Treat chest pain and known heart conditions early.

entries.title: Chemical burn to the eye
entries.what_it_is: A chemical splashed into the eye can damage the surface within minutes. Immediate, prolonged rinsing is the single most important action and can save sight.
entries.recognize: Pain, burning, redness, watering, blurred vision or a feeling something is in the eye, right after a splash of a cleaner, acid, alkali, bleach or other chemical.
entries.get_help_fast: Start rinsing immediately, then get emergency eye care. Alkalis (oven/drain cleaner, cement, bleach) are especially dangerous.
entries.do_now: Rinse the eye at once with clean lukewarm running water for at least 15-20 minutes, holding the eyelid open and letting water run from the inner corner away from the other eye. Remove contact lenses if you can. Keep rinsing on the way to hospital. Bring the chemical's container or name.
entries.do_not: Do not rub the eye. Do not use anything other than water (no neutralisers) unless told to. Do not bandage tightly before rinsing.
entries.after_care: Follow eye-unit instructions; use prescribed drops; attend review — some injuries worsen over days.
entries.prevention: Wear eye protection with chemicals; store them capped and labelled, away from children.

entries.title: Object impaled in a wound
entries.what_it_is: A penetrating object left in a wound may be plugging damaged blood vessels. Pulling it out can trigger severe, hard-to-control bleeding.
entries.recognize: An object (knife, glass, metal, stick) still embedded in a wound, with bleeding around it.
entries.get_help_fast: Call your local emergency number now. Keep the person still.
entries.do_now: Leave the object in place. Control bleeding by pressing firmly AROUND (not on) the object. Build up padding on either side of it and bandage around it to hold it still, so it cannot move or press deeper. Keep the person calm and still, lie them down, and treat for shock (keep warm).
entries.do_not: Do NOT pull the object out. Do not press directly on it. Do not push it in further.
entries.after_care: Removal and repair happen in hospital, often in surgery; follow wound-care and tetanus/antibiotic advice.
entries.prevention: Safe handling and storage of knives, tools and glass.

entries.title: Electric shock
entries.what_it_is: Electric current passing through the body can stop the heart, cause internal and surface burns, and throw the person — even when they look unharmed afterward.
entries.recognize: A person who has been shocked by mains power, an appliance, a live wire or lightning. There may be entry/exit burns, muscle pain, confusion, or collapse.
entries.get_help_fast: Make the area safe first, then call emergency services. Anyone shocked by high voltage, who has burns, chest pain, or any loss of consciousness needs hospital assessment.
entries.do_now: Do NOT touch the person while they are still in contact with the electricity — switch off the power at the fuse box or unplug it first; if you cannot, stand on something dry and use something non-conductive (dry wood) to move the source away. Once it is safe, check response and breathing: if they are unresponsive and not breathing, start CPR. Cool any burns with running water.
entries.do_not: Do not touch the person or the source until the power is off. Do not approach anyone near high-voltage or overhead power lines until the authorities confirm it is safe (stay well back).
entries.after_care: Heart-rhythm monitoring is often needed even if they feel fine; follow burn care.
entries.prevention: Maintain wiring and appliances; use RCDs; keep electrics away from water; teach children.
