field_guides.answer: If someone is unresponsive or breathing slowly or irregularly after possible opioid use, call 911 or the local emergency number immediately. Give naloxone using the instructions on the kit, and provide rescue breaths or CPR as trained or directed by emergency dispatch. If there is no improvement after 2–3 minutes, another naloxone dose may be needed. Stay with them; the overdose can return when naloxone wears off. Are they awake and breathing normally right now?
field_guides.source: Ontario Ministry of Health — naloxone overdose response (2026)
field_guides.title: Possible opioid overdose

field_guides.answer: Someone who cannot be woken, is vomiting while very drowsy, has cold clammy skin, or has slow or irregular breathing may have alcohol poisoning. Call emergency services now. Stay with them and keep their airway clear; if they are breathing normally but unconscious, position them on their side as instructed by responders. Do not force them to vomit, give coffee, or leave them to sleep it off. Are they responsive and breathing normally?
phrases: drank too much alcohol and vomiting
field_guides.source: Health Canada — signs and response to substance poisoning
field_guides.title: Possible alcohol poisoning

field_guides.answer: Stopping alcohol suddenly after frequent heavy drinking can cause dangerous withdrawal, not just discomfort. Shaking, sweating and anxiety may progress; confusion, hallucinations, seizures or an irregular heartbeat require emergency care. Medical withdrawal support is safer than attempting a severe detox alone. How much and how often has the person been drinking, and when was the last drink? If severe signs are happening now, call emergency services.
field_guides.source: MedlinePlus — Alcohol withdrawal; Health Canada — substance use treatment
field_guides.title: Alcohol withdrawal

field_guides.answer: If someone has collapsed, is having a seizure, is hard to wake, or has breathing difficulty, call emergency services now. Otherwise contact a poison centre promptly; in Canada the national number is 1-844-764-7669. Keep the container or label available and tell them what was taken, approximately how much and when. Do not induce vomiting or try an unverified antidote. Is the person awake and breathing normally?
field_guides.source: Health Canada — Poison centres (1-844-POISON-X)
field_guides.title: Unknown medicine or drug poisoning

field_guides.answer: Call emergency services. Apply firm, continuous direct pressure over the bleeding wound with a clean cloth or dressing. If life-threatening limb bleeding cannot be controlled with pressure or pressure cannot be applied, a properly placed commercial tourniquet may be needed; follow its instructions or trained emergency dispatch guidance. Do not repeatedly lift the dressing to check. Keep the person warm and arrange immediate evacuation. Where is the bleeding and is pressure stopping it?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — Comprehensive First Aid & CPR Guide (2025)
field_guides.title: Major bleeding

field_guides.answer: A severed finger or limb is a medical emergency. Call emergency services, control bleeding with direct pressure and use a tourniquet for uncontrolled life-threatening limb bleeding. Wrap the detached part in clean cloth, seal it in a clean bag, and keep that bag cool against a cold pack or ice without freezing or direct ice contact. Send the part with the person to the hospital. Do not attempt to sew it back on or operate in the field.
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — Wound care and amputations (2025)
field_guides.title: Traumatic amputation

field_guides.answer: Stop exposure safely, move away from the heat, electricity or chemical, and call emergency services for a major burn, airway injury or large affected area. For a thermal burn, cool the area with cool running water if available and cover it with a clean, non-stick dressing. Do not apply ice or attempt surgery or remove clothing stuck to the burn. Keep the person from becoming cold. What caused the burn and where is it?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — Comprehensive First Aid & CPR Guide (2025)
field_guides.title: Serious burns

field_guides.answer: For a small superficial cut or scrape, first wash your hands, apply direct pressure if it is bleeding, rinse away visible dirt with clean running water, and cover it with a clean dressing. Watch for increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus or fever. Deep, gaping, dirty or animal-bite wounds need prompt assessment, including whether tetanus prevention is needed. How deep is it, and is the bleeding controlled?
field_guides.source: MedlinePlus — First aid; Canadian Red Cross — Wound care
field_guides.title: Small cuts and scratches

field_guides.answer: Limit movement, support the injured area in the position found, and do not try to force a bone or joint back into place. Cover an open wound and control bleeding with direct pressure. Seek urgent assessment for visible deformity, open fracture, numbness, poor circulation or severe pain. In the wilderness, protect the person from further injury and organize safe transport or rescue. Where is the injury and can the person move or feel their fingers or toes?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — Comprehensive First Aid & CPR Guide (2025)
field_guides.title: Suspected fracture or serious sprain

field_guides.answer: Move the person out of wind and wet conditions as safely as possible. Remove wet outer layers when shelter and dry replacement clothing are available, insulate from the ground and cover the head and body. Handle a severely cold, confused or unresponsive person gently and request rescue. Avoid rapid direct heat on limbs or giving drinks to someone not fully alert. Is the person alert, shivering and able to move?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — First Aid & CPR; wilderness medical guidance
field_guides.title: Hypothermia in the field

field_guides.answer: Confusion, collapse or altered consciousness during heat exposure can be heat stroke. Call emergency services and start rapid cooling: move to shade, remove excess clothing and cool the body with water or cold packs while arranging rescue. Do not give drinks to an unconscious person. What is the person's level of alertness, and can you start cooling immediately?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — Comprehensive First Aid & CPR Guide (2025)
field_guides.title: Severe heat illness

field_guides.answer: A severe allergic reaction involving breathing trouble, throat swelling, fainting or rapid worsening is an emergency. Call emergency services and use the person's prescribed epinephrine auto-injector immediately if available, following its instructions. Do not wait to see if symptoms pass. Help the person stay in a safe position and monitor breathing until responders arrive. Is an auto-injector available?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — First Aid & CPR Guide (2025)
field_guides.title: Severe allergic reaction

field_guides.answer: If someone cannot cough, speak or breathe, call emergency services. Follow trained first-aid and dispatcher instructions for age-appropriate choking care, and begin CPR if they become unresponsive. If they can cough effectively, encourage coughing and monitor closely. Do not blindly sweep the mouth. Is the person able to make any sound or cough?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — First Aid & CPR Guide (2025)
field_guides.title: Severe choking

field_guides.answer: A head injury with loss of consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, unusual confusion, seizure or weakness needs emergency assessment. Avoid moving the person unnecessarily if neck injury is possible. Even mild symptoms can evolve; do not return to risky activity before proper assessment. Was there a loss of consciousness, vomiting or increasing confusion?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — Comprehensive First Aid & CPR Guide (2025)
field_guides.title: Head injury

field_guides.answer: When care is far away, the priorities are scene safety, breathing, major-bleeding control, protection from cold or heat, clean wound covering, immobilizing serious injuries, communication and evacuation. Activate satellite SOS, radio or another emergency contact route if possible; record times, changes and what treatment was given. Do not attempt invasive surgery, internal procedures, or untrained wound closure in the field: these can cause hemorrhage, infection or permanent injury. What happened, where are you, and what communication or first-aid supplies do you have?
field_guides.source: Wilderness Medical Society practice guidelines; Canadian Red Cross first aid
field_guides.title: Remote-area medical emergency

field_guides.answer: We can talk about drinking without judgment. Support can include counselling, structured therapy, peer support, medication prescribed by a clinician, and supervised withdrawal when needed. If you drink heavily every day, stopping suddenly can be dangerous, so it is important to get medical advice before detox. In Ontario, ConnexOntario can help find services at 1-866-531-2600. What would you most like to change about your drinking?
field_guides.source: Health Canada — Substance use treatment and support
field_guides.title: Alcohol dependence and recovery

field_guides.answer: You deserve a practical plan without judgment. Treatment depends on the substance and your situation: for opioid use disorder, medication treatment and continuing support can reduce overdose risk, while other substances may call for different medical and counselling approaches. In Ontario, ConnexOntario is available at 1-866-531-2600. If overdose risk is possible, keep naloxone nearby and know how to call for emergency help. Are you looking for immediate safety, withdrawal support or longer-term recovery?
phrases: i want to stop using drugs
field_guides.source: Health Canada — Substance use treatment; Get help with substance use
field_guides.title: Drug use and addiction support

field_guides.answer: Muscle aches and cramps can follow exertion, dehydration or many other causes. Rest the area, avoid further strain, and drink normally if thirsty; gentle stretching may help some ordinary cramps. Severe swelling, weakness, dark urine, fever or persistent unexplained pain needs assessment. Where is the pain, how long has it lasted, and was there a recent injury or heavy exercise?
field_guides.source: MedlinePlus — First aid and general health references
field_guides.title: Muscle aches or cramps

field_guides.answer: Most mild stomach upsets can be managed by taking small, frequent sips of fluid and paying attention to hydration. Seek urgent assessment for severe abdominal pain, bloody stools, repeated vomiting, confusion, fainting or signs of dehydration, especially in infants or older adults. How long has this been happening, and are you able to keep fluids down?
field_guides.source: MedlinePlus — First aid and digestive health
field_guides.title: Stomach upset and diarrhea

field_guides.answer: A headache can have many causes, including tension, migraine and illness. A sudden unusually severe headache, a headache with neurological changes, stiff neck and fever, or one after significant head injury needs emergency assessment. For a familiar mild headache, rest and hydration may help, but I'd want to know what makes this one different. When did it begin, how severe is it, and is it your usual pattern?
field_guides.source: MedlinePlus — First aid and headache references
field_guides.title: Headaches

field_guides.answer: If a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call emergency services, send someone for an AED if available, and begin CPR immediately following your training or the emergency dispatcher's instructions. Use the AED as prompted. Keep going until help takes over, the person starts breathing normally, or you cannot continue safely.
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — first aid facts and CPR
field_guides.title: Unresponsive and not breathing normally

field_guides.answer: Sudden facial weakness, one-sided arm weakness, or a change in speech can be signs of stroke. Call 911 immediately and note when the symptoms began or the person was last known to be well. Keep them safe, avoid giving food or drink if swallowing may be impaired, and don't wait for symptoms to disappear.
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — signs and symptoms of stroke
field_guides.title: Possible stroke

field_guides.answer: New or severe chest discomfort, especially with shortness of breath, faintness, sweating or pain spreading to the arm, back or jaw, needs immediate emergency assessment. Call 911; do not drive yourself. Stop exertion, sit or rest, and follow dispatcher instructions. Is the person awake and breathing normally?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — comprehensive first aid cardiovascular emergencies
field_guides.title: Possible heart emergency

field_guides.answer: Move nearby hazards away and protect the person's head. Do not restrain them or put anything in their mouth. Time the event, watch breathing and request emergency help for a first, prolonged, repeated or injury-associated seizure, or if breathing doesn't recover. When the convulsions stop, check breathing and place them on their side if safe. Is the seizure happening now, and how long has it lasted?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — seizure first aid
field_guides.title: Seizure first response

field_guides.answer: Call emergency services and ensure rescuers are not put in danger. Once the person is safely out of the water, check breathing; if not breathing normally, start CPR following your training or dispatch instructions. Keep the person warm and arrange medical assessment even if they revive but have coughing or breathing symptoms. Did they lose consciousness or have trouble breathing?
phrases: pulled someone from water not breathing
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — water rescue and first aid
field_guides.title: Submersion or drowning

field_guides.answer: Low blood sugar can cause sweating, shaking, confusion and eventually unconsciousness. If the person is awake, able to swallow safely and has a diabetes care plan, follow their prescribed low-glucose instructions, including fast-acting carbohydrate when appropriate. Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious or unsafe-to-swallow person; call emergency services and use prescribed rescue medication if trained. Are they alert and able to swallow?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — comprehensive first aid diabetic emergencies
field_guides.title: Very low blood sugar

field_guides.answer: A rapidly worsening infection with confusion, difficult breathing, fainting, very low urine output or extreme weakness may be life-threatening. Call emergency services and describe the symptoms and their timing. Do not assume it's only a routine fever or wait for a home remedy to work.
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — severe illness first aid; MedlinePlus sepsis reference
field_guides.title: Possible serious infection or sepsis

field_guides.answer: Severe breathlessness, inability to speak normally, blue or grey lips or exhaustion while breathing needs emergency care. Call 911 and help the person use their own prescribed reliever inhaler according to their asthma plan if they have one. Keep them in a comfortable position and watch breathing. Are they able to speak in full sentences?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — comprehensive first aid breathing emergencies
field_guides.title: Severe asthma or breathing difficulty

field_guides.answer: I'm glad you told me. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 911 now and move away from anything that could be used to cause harm. In Canada, call or text 988 to speak with a trained crisis responder at any time. You don't have to manage this alone. Are you safe right now, and is there someone nearby you trust who can stay with you?
field_guides.source: Public Health Agency of Canada — 9-8-8 crisis helpline
field_guides.title: Mental health crisis

field_guides.answer: Move away from the animal, control bleeding with pressure, and gently rinse the wound with clean water if safe. Deep bites, punctures or bites from wild animals need prompt medical assessment for infection, tetanus and possible rabies prevention. If breathing problems, severe swelling or collapse occurs, call emergency services immediately. What animal caused the bite, and where is the injury?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — bite and wound first aid
field_guides.title: Animal bite or venom exposure

field_guides.answer: For a suspected severe allergic reaction, call 911 and use the prescribed EpiPen immediately. Hold the EpiPen with the orange end down, pull the blue safety release straight up, press the orange end firmly against the middle of the OUTER thigh until it clicks, and hold it there for 3 seconds. It can be given through clothing. Avoid placing fingers near the orange end. Do not reuse it. Keep emergency help coming even if the person improves; another EpiPen may be needed after 5–15 minutes if symptoms persist or return, following the device guidance. Is the person having breathing trouble or throat swelling right now?
phrases: how do i use an epipen
how to administer epinephrine auto injector
how to use an epinephrine autoinjector
field_guides.source: EpiPen Canada — Manufacturer instructions, 3-second device
field_guides.title: How to use an EpiPen auto-injector

field_guides.answer: For suspected opioid overdose, call 911 and give naloxone promptly. For a single-use nasal-spray device, remove it from the package, lay the person on their back, gently tilt the head back, place the nozzle in one nostril, and press the plunger fully ONCE. Support breathing with CPR or rescue breaths as trained and directed by dispatch. If breathing has not improved after 2–3 minutes, give another dose if available using a NEW device. Stay with the person—an overdose can return after naloxone wears off. Is the person awake and breathing normally?
phrases: how to administer naloxone to someone else
field_guides.source: Public Health Agency of Canada — How to administer naloxone
field_guides.title: How to give naloxone nasal spray

field_guides.answer: A suspected opioid overdose is an emergency: call 911. If your kit is injectable naloxone, follow the exact printed instructions and the training for YOUR kit. Canadian public-health instructions describe preparing the supplied syringe as directed and giving the kit dose into a large muscle such as the thigh or upper arm. Do not guess the volume or substitute a different concentration. Continue breathing support as trained; another kit dose may be needed after 2–3 minutes if the person still is not responding. What type and strength are printed on the naloxone kit?
field_guides.source: Public Health Agency of Canada — How to administer naloxone
field_guides.title: Injectable naloxone kit

field_guides.answer: Check the patient, product name, concentration, prescribed amount, route, timing, expiry and known allergies against the original label. For an oral liquid, use the oral syringe or marked dosing device supplied with that product; kitchen spoons are not reliable measures. Measure at eye level and record the time given so doses are not accidentally repeated. Do not guess or calculate a dose from a different-strength bottle. If the person cannot swallow safely or is unconscious, do not give it by mouth. What medicine, strength and directions are on the label?
field_guides.source: Health Canada — Acetaminophen and children; Medication safety
field_guides.title: Safely measure an oral liquid medicine

field_guides.answer: For mild pain or fever, acetaminophen or an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen may help in some circumstances, but their risks differ. Acetaminophen can injure the liver if too much is taken or it is duplicated in combination products; ibuprofen can be unsuitable with certain kidney, stomach, pregnancy or bleeding conditions. Check the actual label and ask a pharmacist or clinician about age, conditions, pregnancy, allergies and other medicines before choosing. Do not borrow someone else's prescription pain medicine. What kind of pain is it, and what medicines are available?
field_guides.source: Health Canada — Using medications safely
field_guides.title: Over-the-counter pain and fever medicines

field_guides.answer: Penicillin and other antibiotics need a known, appropriate drug and controlled manufacture. Do not try to grow mould or make injectable or oral antibiotics at home: strength, contamination and allergic reactions would be unpredictable. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, not routine viral illnesses. If you have an existing prescription but no supply, contact a pharmacist, health service, remote clinician or emergency evacuation route for a legitimate refill or alternative. Meanwhile, maintain cleanliness, cover wounds and watch for spreading redness, fever, confusion or rapid deterioration. What infection is suspected, and has a clinician prescribed anything?
field_guides.source: Health Canada — What you need to know about antimicrobials
field_guides.title: Penicillin and antibiotic use when help is remote

field_guides.answer: If ORS packets aren't available, WHO guidance describes an emergency sugar-and-salt solution: mix ONE litre of safe drinking water with SIX level teaspoons of sugar and ONE-HALF level teaspoon of salt, stirring until dissolved. Measure carefully—too much salt or too little water can be dangerous. Offer small frequent sips only to someone alert and able to swallow. Severe dehydration, blood in stool, confusion, inability to drink, or an infant becoming weak needs urgent medical assessment. Commercial ORS packets are preferable when available. Is the person able to drink and urinating normally?
field_guides.source: World Health Organization — Cholera outbreaks: oral rehydration
field_guides.title: Homemade oral rehydration solution if packets unavailable

field_guides.answer: If a limb may be broken, avoid unnecessary movement and seek rescue. If you must move the person to reach help and no commercial splint is available, Canadian Red Cross first-aid guidance describes padding with a folded blanket or towel, or using a rigid board or rolled newspaper to support the joint and bone without forcing them straight. Tie it gently so it does not cut off circulation; check warmth, colour, sensation and movement beyond the injury. An open fracture, numbness, deformity or poor blood flow needs urgent evacuation. Which limb is injured and can it be supported without moving it much?
field_guides.source: Canadian Red Cross — Comprehensive Guide for First Aid & CPR 2025, splinting
field_guides.title: Improvised support for a suspected fracture

field_guides.answer: Some simple home measures—rest, adequate fluids, nutrition, gentle skin care and stress management—can support comfort and recovery, but they don't replace the specific treatment required for infections, poisoning, severe dehydration or another emergency. Homeopathic products may rely on traditional rather than modern scientific evidence; 'natural' doesn't mean safe or effective, and herbal products can interact with medicines. Let's identify the symptom and which remedies have evidence, then separate low-risk supportive steps from treatments that require a licensed product. What condition are you trying to manage?
field_guides.source: Health Canada — Information on homeopathic products
field_guides.title: Holistic care and homeopathic claims

field_guides.answer: For routine mouth care, brush teeth gently with fluoride toothpaste for about two minutes at least twice daily, and clean between the teeth daily with floss or another appropriate tool. Limit frequent sugary snacks and drinks and replace a worn brush. Persistent gum bleeding, swelling or dental pain calls for dental assessment. Swelling with fever or trouble swallowing is urgent. Are you asking about daily prevention, a tooth problem, or mouth care without normal supplies?
field_guides.source: Public Health Agency of Canada — Oral health for adults
field_guides.title: Oral and dental hygiene

field_guides.answer: Tooth pain may come from decay, injury or infection. Rinse gently with clean water, keep the area clean, and avoid chewing on the affected side. A dental visit is needed to identify the cause; do not attempt to drill, remove a tooth, inject anesthetic or use homemade antibiotics. If facial swelling, fever, spreading redness or difficulty swallowing or breathing occurs, arrange urgent emergency care. Is there swelling, fever, trauma or a broken tooth?
field_guides.source: Public Health Agency of Canada — Oral health and dental problems
field_guides.title: Tooth pain when dental care is unavailable

field_guides.answer: For vulvar hygiene, gently wash the external area with lukewarm water and avoid fragranced products, scrubbing and douching or cleaning inside the vagina. Wear breathable, clean underwear and change out of wet clothing. Persistent itching, pain, unusual discharge or odour can have different causes and shouldn't automatically be treated as yeast or another infection. If you're asking about a penis or another type of genital care, let me know and I’ll tailor the discussion. What kind of care or symptom are you concerned about?
field_guides.source: Government of Canada — Vulvovaginal hygiene
field_guides.title: Genital and reproductive hygiene

field_guides.answer: Wash hands before and after changing menstrual products. Change disposable products regularly, and never leave a tampon in longer than the manufacturer's maximum time. Reusable pads should be washed with soap or detergent and dried completely; menstrual cups need cleaning according to their manufacturer's instructions and appropriate sanitizing between cycles. In remote areas, carry clean replacements and safe water or unscented external wipes. Avoid douching. Very heavy bleeding, fainting, severe pain or signs of infection need prompt medical assessment. Are you using pads, tampons, a cup or another product?
field_guides.source: Government of Canada — Guide to Menstrual Health
field_guides.title: Menstrual product hygiene in normal or remote conditions

field_guides.answer: Family history can help identify risks worth discussing early with a clinician, but it doesn't mean you'll develop the same illness. For each biological relative, note the relationship, condition, approximate age at diagnosis and, when known, cause and age of death. Patterns in several close relatives or illness at an unusually young age may justify earlier screening or genetic counselling. We can save the reported facts in an encrypted profile, without claiming they are confirmed. Which condition and family members are you thinking about?
field_guides.source: CDC — About Family Health History
field_guides.title: Family medical history and inherited risk

field_guides.answer: If an essential prescribed medicine is unavailable, don't substitute a homemade product or someone else's supply. Contact a pharmacist, medical service, telehealth or emergency assistance as quickly as possible; loss of insulin, breathing medicine, seizure medicine or other essential treatment may require urgent action. Keep a written list of medication names, strengths, timing, allergies and the original packaging, and plan backup supplies when possible. What medicine is missing and how long has it been since the last dose?
field_guides.source: CDC — Prescriptions and emergency health preparedness
field_guides.title: Preparing for a medicine shortage or remote care

field_guides.answer: Prioritize hand cleaning before preparing food, after toileting, and before caring for a wound. Use soap and safe running water when available; alcohol-based hand sanitizer can help when hands aren't visibly dirty, but is not a full substitute in all situations. Keep drinking water separate from water used for washing and change soiled clothing when possible. Clean small wounds with safe water rather than harsh household chemicals. What water and cleaning supplies do you have?
field_guides.source: Health Canada — Healthy home guide, handwashing
field_guides.title: Body and hand hygiene with limited supplies

field_guides.source: WHO / Red Cross emergency delivery guidance
field_guides.answer: Call your local emergency number now and keep them on the line — they can talk you through it. Wash your hands if you can. Help her into a comfortable position (often semi-sitting, or on her side). Do NOT pull the baby. As the head appears, support it gently and let it come on its own; if the cord is around the neck, gently slip it over the head. Support the body as it delivers — babies are slippery. Once born, keep the baby warm against the mother's skin and dry it; rub the back gently to help it breathe and cry. Do not pull the cord or the afterbirth — let the placenta deliver on its own and keep it with the mother. Keep both warm. If the baby does not breathe, begin rescue breaths/CPR for a newborn and tell the dispatcher. Watch the mother for heavy bleeding after birth. Keep emergency help coming the whole time.

field_guides.source: Resuscitation Council / Canadian Red Cross CPR guidance
field_guides.answer: If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call your local emergency number now (or have someone call) and get an AED if one is nearby. Start chest compressions: place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, the other hand on top, and push hard and fast — about twice per second — letting the chest come all the way back up each time. Keep going without long pauses. If you are trained and willing, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions; if not, hands-only compressions are still life-saving — don't stop. Use an AED as soon as it arrives and follow its spoken instructions. Keep going until help takes over or the person starts breathing normally. For a baby or small child, use gentler compressions (two fingers for an infant) and, if trained, include rescue breaths.

field_guides.source: St John / Red Cross first-aid guidance
phrases: about to pass out from injury
field_guides.answer: Shock is a life-threatening drop in circulation, often from heavy bleeding, major injury, severe burns, or serious infection. Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin; fast weak pulse; rapid breathing; thirst; confusion, drowsiness or fainting. Call your local emergency number now. Treat the cause you can see — control heavy bleeding with firm pressure. Lay the person down and, if there is no spinal or leg injury, raise their legs a little. Keep them warm with a coat or blanket, loosen tight clothing, and reassure them. Do not give food or drink (they may need surgery). Monitor breathing and be ready to start CPR if they stop breathing normally.

field_guides.source: Red Cross / Resuscitation Council
field_guides.answer: If someone is unconscious but breathing normally, put them in the recovery position to keep their airway open and let fluids drain. Kneel beside them, place the near arm out at a right angle, bring the far hand against their cheek, bend the far knee up and roll them toward you onto their side, resting the head on the hand so the airway stays open. Tilt the head back slightly. Call your local emergency number, keep checking that they are still breathing, and stay with them. If you suspect a spinal/neck injury, avoid twisting — keep the head and body in line — but opening the airway always comes first.

field_guides.source: Heart & Stroke / Red Cross
field_guides.answer: Call your local emergency number now — do not wait or drive yourself. Warning signs: chest pain, pressure, squeezing or heaviness that may spread to the arm(s), neck, jaw, or back; shortness of breath; cold sweat; nausea; light-headedness. Signs can be milder in women, older adults, and people with diabetes. Help the person sit, rest, and stay calm. Loosen tight clothing. If they are not allergic and a clinician hasn't told them otherwise, dispatch may advise chewing aspirin — follow the dispatcher, don't decide a dose yourself. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR and use an AED if available.

field_guides.source: Red Cross / trauma first-aid
field_guides.answer: Suspect a spine injury after any fall from height, diving injury, serious crash, or blow to the head/neck — especially with neck/back pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, or loss of movement. Call your local emergency number now. Tell the person to stay as still as possible. Do NOT move them unless they are in immediate danger (fire, water) or stop breathing. Steady the head and neck in the position found, keeping the head in line with the body. If they are unconscious but breathing, keep the airway open with minimal movement; opening the airway and breathing always come before worrying about the spine. Keep them warm and reassured until help arrives.

field_guides.source: WHO / public-health meningitis guidance
field_guides.answer: Meningitis can worsen very fast and is an emergency. Warning signs: fever, severe headache, a stiff neck, dislike of bright light, drowsiness or confusion, vomiting, and sometimes a rash of small red/purple spots that does NOT fade when pressed with a glass. In babies: high-pitched cry, floppiness or stiffness, a bulging soft spot, poor feeding, and being hard to wake. If you suspect it, call your local emergency number or get to a hospital immediately — do not wait to see if it passes. Keep the person comfortable and monitor their breathing while help comes.

field_guides.source: Canadian Paediatric Society / NHS child-fever guidance
field_guides.answer: Most childhood fevers come from infections the body can fight, and the child's overall state matters more than the exact number. Keep them comfortable and offer plenty of fluids in small sips. Seek urgent care or call your local emergency number if: a baby under 3 months has any fever; the child is very drowsy, floppy or hard to wake; has trouble breathing; has a stiff neck, a rash that doesn't fade under pressure, or a seizure; is not drinking and has far fewer wet diapers; has a fever lasting more than a few days; or you are seriously worried. Do not guess medicine doses — follow the product's weight-based chart on the label or ask a pharmacist.

field_guides.source: WHO postpartum haemorrhage guidance
field_guides.answer: Heavy bleeding after childbirth is an emergency. Call your local emergency number now. Signs of danger: soaking a pad in an hour or less, passing large clots, feeling faint, dizzy, pale, cold or clammy, or a racing heart. While waiting for help: have the mother lie down, keep her warm, and firmly but gently rub the top of the womb (just below the navel) in a circular motion to help it contract and slow the bleeding. Encourage the baby to breastfeed if able, as this helps the womb contract. Keep both warm and monitor her breathing.

field_guides.source: General triage / red-flag guidance
phrases: should I go to the hospital
field_guides.answer: Call your local emergency number now for: trouble breathing or blue lips; severe chest pain or pressure; signs of stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech); heavy bleeding that won't stop; a seizure; unconsciousness or being very hard to wake; a stiff neck with fever or a rash that doesn't fade; severe allergic reaction; thoughts of harming yourself; sudden severe pain; or a serious injury. See a clinician the same day for: a fever that won't settle or lasts several days, a wound that looks infected (spreading redness, pus, fever), dehydration, or symptoms that keep getting worse. When in doubt, it is always okay to call a nurse line or emergency number and ask.

field_guides.source: MedlinePlus / mental-health reference
phrases: cant get out of bed sad
field_guides.answer: Depression is more than feeling sad — it is a low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, and changes in sleep, appetite, energy or concentration lasting two weeks or more, sometimes with hopelessness. It is common and treatable. Things that help day to day: talking to someone you trust, a regular routine, movement, sleep and sunlight, and easing off alcohol. Effective treatments include talking therapies such as CBT and, for some people, medication a doctor prescribes. See a clinician if it lasts, worsens, or affects daily life. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call your local emergency number or 988 (US/Canada) now — you deserve support.

field_guides.source: MedlinePlus / mental-health reference
field_guides.answer: Anxiety is worry or fear strong enough to affect daily life; a panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear with a racing heart, shortness of breath, chest tightness, shaking or a sense of doom that usually peaks within minutes and passes. During a panic attack: remind yourself it will pass and is not dangerous, slow your breathing (in for 4, out for 6), and ground yourself by naming things you can see, hear and touch. Ongoing anxiety responds well to talking therapy such as CBT, lifestyle steps, and sometimes medication from a doctor. Seek care if it is frequent or limiting. New or severe chest pain or breathing trouble should be checked to rule out a physical cause.

field_guides.source: MedlinePlus / mental-health reference
field_guides.answer: Post-traumatic stress can follow a frightening or life-threatening event. Signs: reliving it (flashbacks, nightmares), avoiding reminders, feeling on edge or easily startled, and low mood or numbness, lasting more than a month. It is a normal response to abnormal events, and it is treatable — trauma-focused therapies such as CBT or EMDR help many people. Grounding, routine, support from trusted people, and limiting alcohol can help day to day. A mental-health professional can guide treatment. If you feel unsafe or have thoughts of harming yourself, reach a crisis line (988 US/Canada) or emergency services.

field_guides.source: Bereavement support reference
field_guides.answer: Grief after a loss is natural and has no fixed timeline. It can bring sadness, numbness, anger, guilt, trouble sleeping, and waves of emotion. Things that help: letting yourself feel it, talking with people who care, keeping gentle routines, and being patient with yourself. Seek support from a counsellor or doctor if grief feels unbearable, does not ease over time, or you cannot function — and urgently if you have thoughts of not wanting to live (988 US/Canada or emergency services).

field_guides.source: MedlinePlus / medication-safety reference
field_guides.answer: Your medicine label and your pharmacist are your guide. Read the medicine name, what it is for, how and when to take it, and for how long. Ask the pharmacist: what it treats, common side effects, what to avoid (foods, alcohol, other medicines), and what to do if you miss a dose. Take it exactly as prescribed, finish the course if told to, do not share medicines or take someone else's, and keep them away from children. Tell your prescriber about all other medicines, supplements, allergies, and if you are pregnant or breastfeeding. This app can explain what a medicine is for and its general reference information — but your prescriber and the label decide how much YOU take.

field_guides.source: MedlinePlus / Health Canada antibiotic reference
field_guides.answer: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections — they do not work on colds or flu, which are viral. If a doctor prescribes them, take them exactly as directed and finish the full course even if you feel better, unless your prescriber says otherwise; stopping early can let the infection return and helps bacteria become resistant. Tell your prescriber about allergies (especially to penicillin) and other medicines. Common side effects can include upset stomach or diarrhea; get urgent help for a rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing (possible serious allergy). Never take leftover or someone else's antibiotics. The right antibiotic and amount come from your prescriber and the label.

field_guides.source: MedlinePlus / medication reference
field_guides.answer: Two common over-the-counter options are acetaminophen (paracetamol / Tylenol) and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (Advil / Motrin). Acetaminophen helps pain and fever and is gentle on the stomach, but can harm the liver if you go over the label's maximum or combine products that both contain it — check other medicines for 'acetaminophen'. NSAIDs help pain, fever and inflammation but can irritate the stomach and are not right for everyone (kidney problems, ulcers, some heart conditions, later pregnancy). Follow the dosing on the product label for the person's age and weight, do not double up on products with the same ingredient, and ask a pharmacist if unsure. For a child, use the label's weight-based chart.

label.uses: Acamprosate calcium delayed-release tablets are indicated for the maintenance of abstinence from alcohol in patients with alcohol dependence who are abstinent at treatment initiation. The efficacy of acamprosate calcium delayed-release tablets in promoting abstinence has not been demonstrated in subjects who have not undergone detoxification and not achieved alcohol abstinence prior to beginning acamprosate calcium delayed-release tablets treatment. label.dosing: The recommended dose of acamprosate calcium delayed-release tablets is two 333 mg tablets (each dose should total 666 mg) taken three times daily. A lower dose may be effective in some patients. Although dosing may be done without regard to meals, dosing with meals was employed during clinical trials and is suggested in those patients who regularly eat three meals daily. Treatment with acamprosate calcium delayed-release tablets should be initiated as soon as possible after the period of alcohol withdrawal, when the patient has achieved abstinence, and should be maintained if the patient relapses. Acamprosate calcium delayed-release tablets should be used as part of a comprehensive psychosocial treatment program. Recommended dose: 666 mg (two 333 mg tablets) taken three times daily (2). […]

label.side_effects: Common adverse events that occurred in any acamprosate calcium treatment group at a rate of 3% or greater and greater than the placebo group in controlled clinical trials with spontaneously reported adverse events are: accidental injury, asthenia, pain, anorexia, diarrhea, flatulence, nausea, anxiety, depression, dizziness, dry mouth, insomnia, paresthesia, pruritus and sweating (6.1). label.pregnancy: 8.1 Pregnancy Pregnancy Category C Teratogenic effects: Acamprosate calcium has been shown to be teratogenic in rats when given in doses that are approximately equal to the human dose (on a mg/m 2 basis) and in rabbits when given in doses that are approximately 3 times the human dose (on a mg/m 2 basis). label.overdose: In all reported cases of acute overdosage with acamprosate calcium (total reported doses of up to 56 grams of acamprosate calcium), the only symptom that could be reasonably associated with acamprosate calcium was diarrhea. Hypercalcemia has not been reported in cases of acute overdose. A risk of hypercalcemia should be considered in chronic overdosage only. Treatment of overdose should be symptomatic and supportive.

label.uses: Acitretin Capsules, USP are indicated for the treatment of severe psoriasis in adults. Because of significant adverse effects associated with its use, Acitretin Capsules, USP should be prescribed only by those knowledgeable in the systemic use of retinoids. In females of reproductive potential, Acitretin Capsules, USP should be reserved for non-pregnant patients who are unresponsive to other therapies or whose clinical condition contraindicates the use of other treatments (see boxed CONTRAINDICATIONS AND WARNINGS — Acitretin Capsules, USP can cause severe birth defects). Most patients experience relapse of psoriasis after discontinuing therapy. […]
label.dosing: There is intersubject variation in the pharmacokinetics, clinical efficacy, and incidence of side effects with Acitretin Capsules, USP. A number of the more common side effects are dose-related. Individualization of dosage is required to achieve sufficient therapeutic response while minimizing side effects. Therapy with Acitretin Capsules, USP should be initiated at 25 to 50 mg per day, given as a single dose with the main meal. Maintenance doses of 25 to 50 mg per day may be given dependent upon an individual patient’s response to initial treatment. Relapses may be treated as outlined for initial therapy. When Acitretin Capsules, USP are used with phototherapy, the prescriber should decrease the phototherapy dose, dependent on the patient’s individual response (see PRECAUTIONS: General). Females who have taken TEGISON (etretinate) […]
label.boxed_warning: CONTRAINDICATIONS AND WARNINGS: Pregnancy Acitretin must not be used by females who are pregnant, or who intend to become pregnant during therapy or at any time for at least 3 years following discontinuation of therapy. Acitretin also must not be used by females who may not use reliable contraception while undergoing treatment and for at least 3 years following discontinuation of treatment. Acitretin is a metabolite of etretinate (TEGISON), and major human fetal abnormalities have been reported with the administration of acitretin and etretinate. Potentially, any fetus exposed can be affected. […]
label.do_not_use: Pregnancy Category X: (see boxed CONTRAINDICATIONS AND WARNINGS.) Acitretin is contraindicated in patients with severely impaired liver or kidney function and in patients with chronic abnormally elevated blood lipid values (see boxed WARNINGS: Hepatotoxicity, WARNINGS: Lipids and Possible Cardiovascular Effects, and PRECAUTIONS). An increased risk of hepatitis has been reported to result from combined use of methotrexate and etretinate. Consequently, the combination of methotrexate with acitretin is also contraindicated (see PRECAUTIONS: Drug Interactions). […]
label.warnings: WARNINGS (See also boxed CONTRAINDICATIONS AND WARNINGS .) Hepatotoxicity: Of the 525 subjects treated in US clinical trials, 2 had clinical jaundice with elevated serum bilirubin and transaminases considered related to treatment with acitretin. Liver function test results in these subjects returned to normal after acitretin was discontinued. Two of the 1,289 subjects treated in European clinical trials developed biopsy-confirmed toxic hepatitis. A second biopsy in one of these subjects revealed nodule formation suggestive of cirrhosis. One subject in a Canadian clinical trial of 63 subjects developed a 3-fold increase of transaminases. […]
label.interactions: Pharmacokinetic Drug Interactions (see also boxed CONTRAINDICATIONS AND WARNINGS and PRECAUTIONS: Drug Interactions): In studies of in vivo pharmacokinetic drug interactions, no interaction was seen between acitretin and cimetidine, digoxin, phenprocoumon, or glyburide. Ethanol: Clinical evidence has shown that etretinate (a retinoid with a much longer half-life, see below) can be formed with concurrent ingestion of acitretin and ethanol. In a 2-way crossover trial, all 10 subjects formed etretinate with concurrent ingestion of a single 100-mg oral dose of acitretin during a 3-hour period of ethanol ingestion (total ethanol, approximately 1.4 g per kg body weight). Many of the clinical adverse reactions reported to date with administration of acitretin resemble those of the hypervitaminosis A syndrome. Adverse Events/Postmarketing Reports: In addition to the events listed in the tables for the clinical trials, the following adverse events have been identified during postapproval use of acitretin. label.overdose: In the event of acute overdosage, acitretin must be withdrawn at once. Symptoms of overdose are identical to acute hypervitaminosis A (e.g., headache and vertigo). The acute oral toxicity (LD 50) of acitretin in both mice and rats was greater than 4,000 mg per kg. In one reported case of overdose, a 32-year-old male with Darier’s disease took 21 x 25-mg capsules (525-mg single dose). He vomited several hours later but experienced no other ill effects. […]

drug_reference.name: acyclovir

label.uses: Herpes Zoster Infections: Acyclovir is indicated for the acute treatment of herpes zoster (shingles). Genital Herpes: Acyclovir is indicated for the treatment of initial episodes and the management of recurrent episodes of genital herpes. Chickenpox: Acyclovir is indicated for the treatment of chickenpox (varicella).
label.dosing: Acute Treatment of Herpes Zoster: 800 mg every 4 hours orally, 5 times daily for 7 to 10 days. Genital Herpes: Treatment of Initial Genital Herpes: 200 mg every 4 hours, 5 times daily for 10 days. Chronic Suppressive Therapy for Recurrent Disease: 400 mg 2 times daily for up to 12 months, followed by re-evaluation. Alternative regimens have included doses ranging from 200 mg 3 times daily to 200 mg 5 times daily. The frequency and severity of episodes of untreated genital herpes may change over time. After 1 year of therapy, the frequency and severity of the patient's genital herpes infection should be re-evaluated to assess the need for continuation of therapy with acyclovir. Intermittent Therapy: 200 mg every 4 hours, 5 times daily for 5 days. Therapy should be initiated at the earliest sign or symptom (prodrome) of recurrence. […]
label.do_not_use: Acyclovir is contraindicated for patients who develop hypersensitivity to acyclovir or valacyclovir.
label.warnings: Acyclovir capsules are intended for oral ingestion only. Renal failure, in some cases resulting in death, has been observed with acyclovir therapy (see ADVERSE REACTIONS: Observed During Clinical Practice and OVERDOSAGE). Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic uremic syndrome (TTP/HUS), which has resulted in death, has occurred in immunocompromised patients receiving acyclovir therapy.
label.interactions: Drug Interactions: See CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY: Pharmacokinetics.
label.side_effects: Herpes Simplex: Short-Term Administration: The most frequent adverse events reported during clinical trials of treatment of genital herpes with acyclovir 200 mg administered orally 5 times daily every 4 hours for 10 days were nausea and/or vomiting in 8 of 298 patient treatments (2.7%). Nausea and/or vomiting occurred in 2 of 287 (0.7%) patients who received placebo. Long-Term Administration: The most frequent adverse events reported in a clinical trial for the prevention of recurrences with continuous administration of 400 mg (two 200-mg capsules) 2 times daily for 1 year in 586 patients treated with acyclovir were nausea (4.8%) and diarrhea (2.4%). […]
label.pregnancy: Pregnancy: Teratogenic Effects: Pregnancy Category B. Acyclovir administered during organogenesis was not teratogenic in the mouse (450 mg/kg/day, p.o.), rabbit (50 mg/kg/day, s.c. and IV), or rat (50 mg/kg/day, s.c.). These exposures resulted in plasma levels 9 and 18, 16 and 106, and 11 and 22 times, respectively, human levels. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. […]
label.overdose: Overdoses involving ingestion of up to 100 capsules (20 g) have been reported. Adverse events that have been reported in association with overdosage include agitation, coma, seizures, and lethargy. Precipitation of acyclovir in renal tubules may occur when the solubility (2.5 mg/mL) is exceeded in the intratubular fluid. […]

label.uses: Uses Uses: Decrease the appearance of fine lines, wrinkles, scarring and discolorations of the skin PURPOSE Purpose: Anti wrinkle
label.dosing: Directions Directions: 1. Wash the face and pat dry skin. Do not use toner before applying this product. 2. Apply 1/3 up to 2/2 of a dropper of the essence to face and neck, massaging in gently and evenly. 3. Allow the essence to dry. 4. The product may precipitate during long-term storage. However, it will not cause any quality problems. Make sure to shake well before using. 5. Reapplication to rapidly aging spots such as around the eyes and mouth is recommended. 6. After 1-2 minutes, when you feel some tension in your skin, apply moisturizer as usual. 7. For best results, apply twice a day, morning and night. 8. Single treatments are recommended at nighttime. 9. Store in a refrigerator (2-15℃) after each use.
label.warnings: Warnings: 1. For external use only. 2. Do not use on wounds and/or any inflammation of the skin. 3. Stop use and ask a doctor if you are experiencing any of the following symptoms: reddening or spotting of the skin, irritation, and/or increased sensitivity. 4. When using this product avoid contact with eyes. If irritation occurs, immediately cleanse with fresh water. 5. Keep out of reach of children. If swallowed, get medical help or contact a Poison Control Center right away.

label.uses: Cathflo ® Activase ® (Alteplase) is indicated for the restoration of function to central venous access devices as assessed by the ability to withdraw blood.
label.dosing: Cathflo ® Activase ® (Alteplase) is for instillation into the dysfunctional catheter at a concentration of 1 mg/mL. • Patients weighing ≥30 kg: 2 mg in 2 mL • Patients weighing <30 kg: 110% of the internal lumen volume of the catheter, not to exceed 2 mg in 2 mL If catheter function is not restored at 120 minutes after 1 dose of Cathflo Activase, a second dose may be instilled (see Instructions for Administration). There is no efficacy or safety information on dosing in excess of 2 mg per dose for this indication. Studies have not been performed with administration of total doses greater than 4 mg (two 2‑mg doses). label.dosing: Dosage and Administration The dose of amantadine hydrochloride may need reduction in patients with congestive heart failure, peripheral edema, orthostatic hypotension, or impaired renal function (see Dosage for Impaired Renal Function). Dosage for Prophylaxis and Treatment of Uncomplicated Influenza A Virus Illness: Adult: The adult daily dosage of amantadine hydrochloride is 200 mg (four teaspoonfuls of oral solution) as a single daily dose. The daily dosage may be split into two teaspoonfuls of oral solution twice a day. If central nervous system effects develop in once-a-day dosage, a split dosage schedule may reduce such complaints. In persons 65 years of age or older, the daily dosage of amantadine hydrochloride is 100 mg. […]
label.do_not_use: Contraindications Amantadine hydrochloride is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to amantadine hydrochloride or to any of the other ingredients in Amantadine Hydrochloride Oral Solution, USP.
label.warnings: Deaths: Deaths have been reported from overdose with amantadine hydrochloride. The lowest reported acute lethal dose was 1 gram. Acute toxicity may be attributable to the anticholinergic effects of amantadine hydrochloride. Drug overdose has resulted in cardiac, respiratory, renal or central nervous system toxicity. Cardiac dysfunction includes arrhythmia, tachycardia and hypertension (see OVERDOSAGE). Deaths due to drug accumulation (overdose) have been reported in patients with renal impairment, who were prescribed higher than recommended doses of amantadine hydrochloride for their level of renal function (see DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION; Dosage of Impaired Renal Function and OVERDOSAGE). label.uses: Pacerone is indicated for the treatment of documented, life-threatening recurrent ventricular fibrillation and life-threatening recurrent hemodynamically unstable tachycardia in adults who have not responded to adequate doses of other available antiarrhythmics or when alternative agents cannot be tolerated. label.dosing: Dosage must be individualized based on severity of arrhythmia and response. Use the lowest effective dose. Obtain baseline chest x-ray, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests, and liver aminotransferases. Correct hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia before initiating treatment. Initiate treatment with a loading dose of 800 to 1600 mg/day until initial therapeutic response occurs (usually 1 to 3 weeks). Once adequate arrhythmia control is achieved, or if side effects become prominent, reduce Pacerone tablets dose to 600 to 800 mg/day for one month and then to the maintenance dose, usually 400 mg/day. (2) Recommended Dosage: Initiate treatment with a loading dose of 800 to 1600 mg/day until initial therapeutic response occurs (usually 1 to 3 weeks). […]

Pacerone can cause pulmonary toxicity (hypersensitivity pneumonitis or interstitial/alveolar pneumonitis) that has resulted in clinically manifest disease at rates as high as 17% in some series of patients. Pulmonary toxicity has been fatal about 10% of the time. Obtain a baseline chest X-ray and pulmonary-function tests, including diffusion capacity, when Pacerone therapy is initiated. […]

label.uses: For the relief of symptoms of depression. Endogenous depression is more likely to be alleviated than are other depressive states.
label.dosing: Oral Dosage Dosage should be initiated at a low level and increased gradually, noting carefully the clinical response and any evidence of intolerance. Initial Dosage for Adults For outpatients, 75 mg of amitriptyline hydrochloride a day in divided doses is usually satisfactory. If necessary, this may be increased to a total of 150 mg per day. Increases are made preferably in the late afternoon and/or bedtime doses. A sedative effect may be apparent before the antidepressant effect is noted, but an adequate therapeutic effect may take as long as 30 days to develop. An alternate method of initiating therapy in outpatients is to begin with 50 to 100 mg amitriptyline hydrochloride at bedtime. This may be increased by 25 or 50 mg as necessary in the bedtime dose to a total of 150 mg per day. Hospitalized patients may require 100 mg a day initially. […]
label.boxed_warning: Suicidality and Antidepressant Drugs: Antidepressants increased the risk compared to placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (suicidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of major depressive disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of amitriptyline hydrochloride tablets or any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must balance this risk with the clinical need. Short-term studies did not show an increase in the risk of suicidality with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults beyond age 24; there was a reduction in risk with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults aged 65 and older. […]
label.do_not_use: Amitriptyline hydrochloride is contraindicated in patients who have shown prior hypersensitivity to it. It should not be given concomitantly with monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Hyperpyretic crises, severe convulsions, and deaths have occurred in patients receiving tricyclic antidepressant and monoamine oxidase inhibiting drugs simultaneously. When it is desired to replace a monoamine oxidase inhibitor with amitriptyline hydrochloride, a minimum of 14 days should be allowed to elapse after the former is discontinued. […]
label.warnings: Clinical Worsening and Suicide Risk Patients with major depressive disorder (MDD), both adult and pediatric, may experience worsening of their depression and/or the emergence of suicidal ideation and behavior (suicidality) or unusual changes in behavior, whether or not they are taking antidepressant medications, and this risk may persist until significant remission occurs. Suicide is a known risk of depression and certain other psychiatric disorders, and these disorders themselves are the strongest predictors of suicide. There has been a long-standing concern, however, that antidepressants may have a role in inducing worsening of depression and the emergence of suicidality in certain patients during the early phases of treatment. […]
label.interactions: Drug Interactions Topiramate Some patients may experience a large increase in amitriptyline concentration in the presence of topiramate and any adjustments in amitriptyline dose should be made according to the patient's clinical response and not on the basis of plasma levels. Drugs Metabolized by P450 2D6 The biochemical activity of the drug metabolizing isozyme cytochrome P450 2D6 (debrisoquin hydroxylase) is reduced in a subset of the caucasian population (about 7 to 10% of Caucasians are so called "poor metabolizers"); reliable estimates of the prevalence of reduced P450 2D6 isozyme activity among Asian, African and other populations are not yet available. […]

Signs and symptoms of toxicity develop rapidly after tricyclic antidepressant overdose, therefore, hospital monitoring is required as soon as possible. […]

label.pregnancy: 8.1 Pregnancy Teratogenic Effects: Pregnancy Category B. Reproduction studies have been performed in mice and rats at doses up to 2000 mg/kg (3 and 6 times the 3 g human dose, based on body surface area). There was no evidence of harm to the fetus due to amoxicillin. There are, however, no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Because animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, amoxicillin should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed.

label.dosing: Regardless of indication, amphetamine should be administered at the lowest effective dosage and dosage should be individually adjusted. Late evening doses should be avoided because of resulting insomnia. Narcolepsy Usual dose is 5 to 60 milligrams per day in divided doses depending on the individual patient response. Narcolepsy seldom occurs in children under 12 years of age; however, when it does, amphetamine sulfate tablets may be used. The suggested initial dose for patients aged 6 to 12 is 5 mg daily; daily dose may be raised in increments of 5 mg at weekly intervals until optimal response obtained. In patients 12 years of age and older, start with 10 mg daily; daily dosage may be raised in increments of 10 mg at weekly intervals until optimal response is obtained. Misuse and abuse of CNS stimulants, including amphetamine sulfate, can result in overdose and death (see OVERDOSAGE), and this risk is increased with higher doses or unapproved methods of administration, such as snorting or injection. Before prescribing amphetamine sulfate tablets, assess each patient’s risk for abuse, misuse, and addiction. Educate patients and their families about these risks, proper storage of the drug, and proper disposal of any unused drug. […]

Misuse and abuse of CNS stimulants, including amphetamine sulfate tablets, can result in overdose and death (see OVERDOSAGE), and this risk is increased with higher doses or unapproved methods of administration, such as snorting or injection. A variety of neurological toxic effects and malignant hyperpyrexia can occur, sometimes with fatal results. label.uses: To reduce the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of ampicillin capsules, ampicillin for oral suspension and other antibacterial drugs, ampicillin capsules and ampicillin for oral suspension should be used only to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by bacteria. When culture and susceptibility information are available, they should be considered in selecting of modifying antimicrobial therapy, in the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns contribute to the empiric selection of therapy. […]
label.dosing: Adults and children weighing over 20 kg: For genitourinary or gastrointestinal tract infections other than gonorrhea in men and women, the usual dose is 500 mg qid in equally spaced doses; severe or chronic infections may require larger doses. For the treatment of gonorrhea in both men and women, a single oral dose of 3.5 grams of ampicillin administered simultaneously with 1 gram of probenecid is recommended. Physicians are cautioned to use no less than the above recommended dosage for the treatment of gonorrhea. Follow-up cultures should be obtained from the original site(s) of infection 7 to 14 days after therapy. In women, it is also desirable to obtain culture test-of-cure from both the endocervical and anal canals. Prolonged intensive therapy is needed for complications such as prostatitis and epididymitis. […]
label.do_not_use: The use of Ampicillin is contraindicated in individuals with a history of serious hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) to ampicillin or to other beta-lactam antibacterial drugs. Ampicillin is also contraindicated in infections caused by penicillinase-producing organisms. Ampicillin is contraindicated in patients with a previous history of cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction associated with treatment with ampicillin.
label.warnings: WARNINGS SERIOUS AND OCCASIONALLY FATAL HYPERSENSITIVITY (ANAPHYLACTIC) REACTIONS HAVE BEEN REPORTED IN PATIENTS ON PENICILLIN THERAPY. ALTHOUGH ANAPHYLAXIS IS MORE FREQUENT FOLLOWING PARENTERAL THERAPY, IT HAS OCCURRED IN PATIENTS ON ORAL PENICILLINS. THESE REACTIONS ARE MORE LIKELY TO OCCUR IN INDIVIDUALS WITH A HISTORY OF SENSITIVITY TO MULTIPLE ALLERGENS. THERE HAVE BEEN REPORTS OF INDIVIDUALS WITH A HISTORY OF PENICILLIN HYPERSENSITIVITY WHO HAVE EXPERIENCED SEVERE REACTIONS WHEN TREATED WITH CEPHALOSPORINS. BEFORE THERAPY WITH ANY PENICILLIN, CAREFUL INQUIRY SHOULD BE MADE CONCERNING PREVIOUS HYPERSENSITIVITY REACTIONS TO PENICILLINS, CEPHALOSPORINS OR OTHER ALLERGENS. IF AN ALLERGIC REACTION OCCURS, APPROPRIATE THERAPY SHOULD BE CONSIDERED. […]
label.interactions: Drug Interactions When administered concurrently, the following drugs may interact with ampicillin. Allopurinol: Substantially increased incidence of skin rashes in patients receiving both drugs as compared to patients receiving ampicillin alone. It is not known whether this potentiation of ampicillin rashes is due to allopurinol or the hyperuricemia present in these patients. Bacteriostatic Antibiotics: Chloramphenicol, erythromycins, sulfonamides, or tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal effect of penicillins. This has been demonstrated in vitro; however, the clinical significance of this interaction is not well-documented. […]
label.side_effects: As with other penicillins, it may be expected that untoward reactions will be essentially limited to sensitivity phenomena. They are more likely to occur in individuals who have previously demonstrated hypersensitivity to penicillin and in those with a history of allergy, asthma, hay fever, or urticaria. The following adverse reactions have been reported as associated with the use of ampicillin: Infections and Infestations: Clostridioides difficile -associated diarrhea (see WARNINGS section). Gastrointestinal: glossitis, stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, enterocolitis, pseudomembranous colitis, and diarrhea. […]
label.pregnancy: Pregnancy Teratogenic Effects Reproduction studies in animals have revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus due to penicillin. There are, however, no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Because animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, penicillin should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. (See PRECAUTIONS-Drug/Laboratory Test Interactions .)
label.overdose: In case of overdosage, discontinue medication, treat symptomatically and institute supportive measures as required. In patients with renal function impairment, ampicillin-class antibiotics can be removed by hemodialysis but not by peritoneal dialysis.

label.uses: Anastrozole is an aromatase inhibitor indicated for: Adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer (1.1) First-line treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive or hormone receptor unknown locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer (1.2) Treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following tamoxifen therapy. Patients with ER-negative disease and patients who did not respond to previous tamoxifen therapy rarely responded to anastrozole (1.3) […]
label.dosing: One 1 mg tablet taken once daily (2.1) 2.1 Recommended Dose The dose of anastrozole tablet is one 1 mg tablet taken once a day. For patients with advanced breast cancer, anastrozole tablets should be continued until tumor progression. Anastrozole tablets can be taken with or without food. For adjuvant treatment of early breast cancer in postmenopausal women, the optimal duration of therapy is unknown. In the ATAC trial, anastrozole was administered for five years [see Clinical Studies (14.1)]. No dosage adjustment is necessary for patients with renal impairment or for elderly patients [see Use in Specific Populations (8.6)]. 2.2 Patients with Hepatic Impairment No changes in dose are recommended for patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic impairment. Common adverse reactions (occurring with an incidence of ≥10%) […]

Anastrozole caused embryo-fetal toxicities in rats at maternal exposure that were 9 times the human clinical exposure, based on area under the curve (AUC). […]

label.uses: Hypertension Atenolol tablets are indicated for the treatment of hypertension, to lower blood pressure. Lowering blood pressure lowers the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, primarily strokes and myocardial infarctions. These benefits have been seen in controlled trials of antihypertensive drugs from a wide variety of pharmacologic classes including atenolol. Control of high blood pressure should be part of comprehensive cardiovascular risk management, including, as appropriate, lipid control, diabetes management, antithrombotic therapy, smoking cessation, exercise, and limited sodium intake. […]
label.dosing: Hypertension The initial dose of atenolol is 50 mg given as one tablet a day either alone or added to diuretic therapy. The full effect of this dose will usually be seen within one to two weeks. If an optimal response is not achieved, the dosage should be increased to atenolol 100 mg given as one tablet a day. Increasing the dosage beyond 100 mg a day is unlikely to produce any further benefit. Atenolol may be used alone or concomitantly with other antihypertensive agents including thiazide-type diuretics, hydralazine, prazosin, and alpha-methyldopa. Angina Pectoris The initial dose of atenolol is 50 mg given as one tablet a day. If an optimal response is not achieved within one week, the dosage should be increased to atenolol 100 mg given as one tablet a day. Some patients may require a dosage of 200 mg once a day for optimal effect. […]
label.do_not_use: Atenolol tablets are contraindicated in sinus bradycardia, heart block greater than first degree, cardiogenic shock, and overt cardiac failure. (See WARNINGS .) Atenolol tablets are contraindicated in those patients with a history of hypersensitivity to the atenolol or any of the drug product’s components.
label.warnings: Cardiac Failure Sympathetic stimulation is necessary in supporting circulatory function in congestive heart failure, and beta-blockade carries the potential hazard of further depressing myocardial contractility and precipitating more severe failure. In patients with acute myocardial infarction, cardiac failure which is not promptly and effectively controlled by 80 mg of intravenous furosemide or equivalent therapy is a contraindication to beta-blocker treatment. In Patients Without a History of Cardiac Failure Continued depression of the myocardium with beta-blocking agents over a period of time can, in some cases, lead to cardiac failure. […]
label.interactions: Drug Interactions Catecholamine-depleting drugs (e.g., reserpine) may have an additive effect when given with beta-blocking agents. Patients treated with atenolol plus a catecholamine depletor should therefore be closely observed for evidence of hypotension and/or marked bradycardia which may produce vertigo, syncope, or postural hypotension. Calcium channel blockers may also have an additive effect when given with atenolol (see WARNINGS). Disopyramide is a Type I antiarrhythmic drug with potent negative inotropic and chronotropic effects. Disopyramide has been associated with severe bradycardia, asystole and heart failure when administered with beta-blockers. […]

The efficacy of atomoxetine capsules was established in seven clinical trials in outpatients with ADHD: four 6 to 9-week trials in pediatric patients (ages 6 to 18), two 10-week trial in adults, and one maintenance trial in pediatrics (ages 6 to 15) [see Clinical Studies (14)]. 1.2 Diagnostic Considerations A diagnosis of ADHD (DSM-IV) […]

label.boxed_warning: WARNING: SUICIDAL IDEATION IN CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS Atomoxetine increased the risk of suicidal ideation in short-term studies in children or adolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Anyone considering the use of atomoxetine in a child or adolescent must balance this risk with the clinical need. Co-morbidities occurring with ADHD may be associated with an increase in the risk of suicidal ideation and/or behavior. Patients who are started on therapy should be monitored closely for suicidality (suicidal thinking and behavior), clinical worsening, or unusual changes in behavior. […]
label.do_not_use: 4 CONTRAINDICATIONS • Hypersensitivity to atomoxetine or other constituents of product. (4.1) • Atomoxetine capsules use within 2 weeks after discontinuing MAOI or other drugs that affect brain monoamine concentrations. (4.2, 7.1) • Narrow Angle Glaucoma. (4.3) • Pheochromocytoma or history of pheochromocytoma.(4.4) • Severe Cardiovascular Disorders that might deteriorate with clinically important increases in HR and BP. (4.5) […]
label.warnings: 5 WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS • Suicidal Ideation – Monitor for suicidality, clinical worsening, and unusual changes in behavior. (5.1) • Severe Liver Injury – Should be discontinued and not restarted in patients with jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury. (5.2) • Serious Cardiovascular Events – Sudden death, stroke and myocardial infarction have been reported in association with atomoxetine treatment. Patients should have a careful history and physical exam to assess for presence of cardiovascular disease. […]
label.interactions: 7 DRUG INTERACTIONS • Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors. (4.2, 7.1) • CYP2D6 Inhibitors - Concomitant use may increase atomoxetine steady-state plasma concentrations in EMs. (7.2) • Antihypertensive Drugs and Pressor Agents – Possible effects on blood pressure. (7.3) • Albuterol (or other beta 2 agonists) - Action of albuterol on cardiovascular system can be potentiated. (7.4) […]

label.overdose: 10.1 Human Experience There is limited clinical trial experience with atomoxetine overdose. During postmarketing, there have been fatalities reported involving a mixed ingestion overdose of atomoxetine and at least one other drug. There have been no reports of death involving overdose of atomoxetine alone, including intentional overdoses at amounts up to 1400 mg. In some cases of overdose involving atomoxetine, seizures have been reported. […]
