You may also need imaging tests. Treatments include antibiotics, decongestants, and pain relievers. Using heat pads on the inflamed area, saline nasal sprays, and vaporizers can also help. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is osteoarthritis? Osteoarthritis, sometimes called OA, is a type of arthritis that only affects the joints, usually in the hands, knees, hips, neck, and lower back. It's the most common type of arthritis. In a healthy joint, the ends of the bones are covered with a smooth, slippery tissue called cartilage. The cartilage pads the bones and helps them glide easily when you move the joint. With osteoarthritis, the cartilage breaks down and becomes rough. Sometimes, all the cartilage wears away and the bones rub together. Bumps of extra bone called bone spurs may grow in the joint area. There is no cure for osteoarthritis. It usually gets worse slowly. But there's a lot you can do to manage the symptoms. What are the symptoms of osteoarthritis? Osteoarthritis affects people in different ways, and not everyone has pain. The most common symptoms are: Pain when you move, which often gets better with rest Stiffness, especially for the first 30 minutes after you get up from resting Swollen joints, especially after using the joint a lot Less movement in the joint than normal A joint that feels loose or unstable What causes osteoarthritis? Researchers aren't sure what causes osteoarthritis. They think that it could be caused by a combination of factors in the body and the environment. Your chance of developing osteoarthritis increases with age. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is rheumatoid arthritis? Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a form of arthritis that causes pain, swelling, and stiffness in your joints. RA is an autoimmune disease. Although it is most common in the wrist and fingers, this disease can cause your immune system to attack any joint tissue. The inflammation (swelling) that comes with RA can also affect other body parts. Inflammation could cause medical issues in your eyes, skin, heart, nerves, blood, or lungs. RA differs from osteoarthritis, a common arthritis that often comes with age. RA affects the lining of your joints and damages the tissue that covers the ends of the bones in a joint. Eventually, this might cause your joints to not work as well. There is no cure for RA, but early treatment can help you manage symptoms, reduce joint damage, and lead a productive life. Who is more likely to get rheumatoid arthritis? Rheumatoid arthritis can happen at any age, but your risk increases as you become an older adult. Your chance of developing RA can also increase if: You're a woman. Women are more likely to get RA than men. You have a family history. If a member of your family has RA, you're more likely to get the disease. You're a smoker.Smoking over a long period of time increases your risk of getting RA and how serious the disease can be. You have other medical conditions that may increase your risk of getting RA. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is gout? Gout is a common type of inflammatory arthritis. It causes pain, swelling, and redness in one or more joints. It usually happens as a flare, which can last for a week or two and then gets better. The flares often begin in your big toe or a lower limb. What causes gout? Gout happens when too much uric acid (urate) builds up in your body over a long time. Uric acid is a waste product your body makes when it breaks down purines. Purines are substances that are in your body's tissues and in many foods. When your body breaks down old cells or digests foods that contain purine, most of the uric acid that's made dissolves in your blood. Your kidneys filter the uric acid out of your blood, and it leaves your body in your urine (pee). However, sometimes your body can make too much uric acid or does not remove enough of it. Then the uric acid levels build up in your body, including in your blood. Having too much uric acid in the blood is called hyperuricemia. It does not cause health problems for everyone. But in some people, uric acid forms needle-like crystals. They can form in your joints, which causes gout. The crystals can also cause kidney stones. Calcium pyrophosphate arthritis, sometimes called pseudogout, is a related disease. It causes similar symptoms and is sometimes confused with gout. But it is caused by a buildup of calcium phosphate, not uric acid. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is hypothyroidism? Hypothyroidism, or underactive thyroid, happens when your thyroid gland doesn't make enough thyroid hormones to meet your body's needs. Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy. These hormones affect nearly every organ in your body and control many of your body's most important functions. For example, they affect your breathing, heart rate, weight, digestion, and moods. Without enough thyroid hormones, many of your body's functions slow down. But there are treatments that can help. What causes hypothyroidism? Hypothyroidism has several causes. They include: Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune disorder where your immune system attacks your thyroid. This is the most common cause. Thyroiditis, inflammation of the thyroid Congenital hypothyroidism, hypothyroidism that is present at birth Surgical removal of part or all of the thyroid Radiation treatment of the thyroid Certain medicines In rare cases, a pituitary disease or too much or too little iodine in your diet Who is at risk for hypothyroidism? See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is hyperthyroidism? Hyperthyroidism, or overactive thyroid, happens when your thyroid gland makes more thyroid hormones than your body needs. Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy. These hormones affect nearly every organ in your body and control many of your body's most important functions. For example, they affect your breathing, heart rate, weight, digestion, and moods. If not treated, hyperthyroidism can cause serious problems with your heart, bones, muscles, menstrual cycle, and fertility. But there are treatments that can help. What causes hyperthyroidism? Hyperthyroidism has several causes. They include: Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder in which your immune system attacks your thyroid and causes it to make too much hormone. This is the most common cause. Thyroid nodules, which are growths on your thyroid. They are usually benign (not cancer). But they may become overactive and make too much thyroid hormone. Thyroid nodules are more common in older adults. Thyroiditis, inflammation of the thyroid. It causes stored thyroid hormone to leak out of your thyroid gland. Too much iodine. Iodine is found in some medicines, cough syrups, seaweed and seaweed-based supplements. Taking too much of them can cause your thyroid to make too much thyroid hormone. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: If you have anemia, your blood does not carry enough oxygen to the rest of your body. The most common cause of anemia is not having enough iron. Your body needs iron to make hemoglobin. Hemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that gives the red color to blood. It carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. Anemia has three main causes: blood loss, lack of red blood cell production, and high rates of red blood cell destruction. Conditions that may lead to anemia include: Heavy periods Pregnancy Ulcers Colon polyps or colon cancer Inherited disorders A diet that does not have enough iron, folic acid or vitamin B12 Blood disorders such as sickle cell anemia and thalassemia, or cancer Aplastic anemia, a condition that can be inherited or acquired G6PD deficiency, a metabolic disorder Anemia can make you feel tired, cold, dizzy, and irritable. You may be short of breath or have a headache. Your doctor will diagnose anemia with a physical exam and blood tests. Treatment depends on the kind of anemia you have. NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is hepatitis? Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. It can damage your liver. This swelling and damage can affect how well your liver functions. Hepatitis can be an acute (short-term) infection or a chronic (long-term) infection. Some types of hepatitis cause only acute infections. Other types can cause both acute and chronic infections. What causes hepatitis? There are different types of hepatitis, with different causes: Viral hepatitis is the most common type. It is caused by one of several viruses -- hepatitis viruses A, B, C, D, and E. In the United States, A, B, and C are the most common. Alcoholic hepatitis is caused by heavy alcohol use Toxic hepatitis can be caused by certain poisons, chemicals, medicines, or supplements Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic type in which your body's immune system attacks your liver. The cause is not known, but genetics and your environment may play a role. How is viral hepatitis spread? Hepatitis A and hepatitis E usually spread through contact with food or water that was contaminated with an infected person's stool. You can also get hepatitis E by eating undercooked pork, deer, or shellfish. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and hepatitis D spread through contact with the blood of someone who has the disease. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: A kidney stone is a solid piece of material that forms in the kidney from substances in the urine. It may be as small as a grain of sand or as large as a pearl. Most kidney stones pass out of the body without help from a doctor. But sometimes a stone will not go away. It may get stuck in the urinary tract, block the flow of urine and cause great pain. The following may be signs of kidney stones that need a doctor's help: Extreme pain in your back or side that will not go away Blood in your urine Fever and chills Vomiting Urine that smells bad or looks cloudy A burning feeling when you urinate Your doctor will diagnose a kidney stone with urine, blood, and imaging tests. If you have a stone that won't pass on its own, you may need treatment. It can be done with shock waves; with a scope inserted through the tube that carries urine out of the body, called the urethra; or with surgery. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: You have two kidneys, each about the size of your fist. Their main job is to filter your blood. They remove wastes and extra water, which become urine. They also keep the body's chemicals balanced, help control blood pressure, and make hormones. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) means that your kidneys are damaged and can't filter blood as they should. This damage can cause wastes to build up in your body. It can also cause other problems that can harm your health. Diabetes and high blood pressure are the most common causes of CKD. The kidney damage occurs slowly over many years. Many people don't have any symptoms until their kidney disease is very advanced. Blood and urine tests are the only way to know if you have kidney disease. Treatments cannot cure kidney disease, but they may slow kidney disease. They include medicines to lower blood pressure, control blood sugar, and lower cholesterol. CKD may still get worse over time. Sometimes it can lead to kidney failure. If your kidneys fail, you will need dialysis or a kidney transplantation. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Your gallbladder is a pear-shaped organ under your liver. It stores bile, a fluid made by your liver to digest fat. As your stomach and intestines digest food, your gallbladder releases bile through a tube called the common bile duct. The duct connects your gallbladder and liver to your small intestine. Your gallbladder is most likely to give you trouble if something blocks the flow of bile through the bile ducts. That is usually a gallstone. Gallstones form when substances in bile harden. Gallstone attacks usually happen after you eat. Signs of a gallstone attack may include nausea, vomiting, or pain in the abdomen, back, or just under the right arm. Gallstones are most common among older adults, women, overweight people, Native Americans and Mexican Americans. Gallstones are often found during imaging tests for other health conditions. If you do not have symptoms, you usually do not need treatment. The most common treatment is removal of the gallbladder. Fortunately, you can live without a gallbladder. Bile has other ways to reach your small intestine. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a problem that affects the large intestine. It can cause abdominal cramping, bloating, and a change in bowel habits. Some people with the disorder have constipation. Some have diarrhea. Others go back and forth between the two. Although IBS can cause a great deal of discomfort, it does not harm the intestines. IBS is common. It affects about twice as many women as men and is most often found in people younger than 45 years. No one knows the exact cause of IBS. There is no specific test for it. Your doctor may run tests to be sure you don't have other diseases. These tests may include stool sampling tests, blood tests, and x-rays. Your doctor may also do a test called a sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy. Most people diagnosed with IBS can control their symptoms with diet, stress management, probiotics, and medicine. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Your stomach is an organ between your esophagus and small intestine. It is where digestion of protein begins. The stomach has three tasks. It stores swallowed food. It mixes the food with stomach acids. Then it sends the mixture on to the small intestine. Most people have a problem with their stomach at one time or another. Indigestion and heartburn are common problems. You can relieve some stomach problems with over-the-counter medicines and lifestyle changes, such as avoiding fatty foods or eating more slowly. Other problems like peptic ulcers or GERD require medical attention. You should see a doctor if you have any of the following: Blood when you have a bowel movement Severe abdominal pain Heartburn not relieved by antacids Unintended weight loss Ongoing vomiting or diarrhea NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Eczema is a term for several different types of skin swelling. Eczema is also called dermatitis. Most types cause dry, itchy skin and rashes on the face, inside the elbows and behind the knees, and on the hands and feet. Scratching the skin can cause it to turn red, and to swell and itch even more. Eczema is not contagious. The cause of eczema is unknown. It is likely caused by both genetic and environmental factors. Eczema may get better or worse over time, but it is often a long-lasting disease. People who have it may also develop hay fever and asthma. The most common type of eczema is atopic dermatitis. It is most common in babies and children, but adults can have it too. As children who have atopic dermatitis grow older, this problem may get better or go away. But sometimes the skin may stay dry and get irritated easily. Treatments may include medicines, skin creams, light therapy, and good skin care. You can prevent some types of eczema by avoiding: Things that irritate your skin, such as certain soaps, fabrics, and lotions Stress Things you are allergic to, such as food, pollen, and animals NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Psoriasis is a skin disease that causes itchy or sore patches of thick, red skin with silvery scales. You usually get the patches on your elbows, knees, scalp, back, face, palms and feet, but they can show up on other parts of your body. Some people who have psoriasis also get a form of arthritis called psoriatic arthritis. A problem with your immune system causes psoriasis. In a process called cell turnover, skin cells that grow deep in your skin rise to the surface. Normally, this takes a month. In psoriasis, it happens in just days because your cells rise too fast. Psoriasis can be hard to diagnose because it can look like other skin diseases. Your doctor might need to look at a small skin sample under a microscope. Psoriasis can last a long time, even a lifetime. Symptoms come and go. Things that make them worse include: Infections Stress Dry skin Certain medicines Psoriasis usually occurs in adults. It sometimes runs in families. Treatments include creams, medicines, and light therapy. NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is shingles? Shingles (herpes zoster) is an infection that causes a painful rash. It is caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). This is the same virus that causes chickenpox. After you have chickenpox, the virus stays in your body. It may not cause problems for many years. But as you get older, the virus may become active again and cause shingles. Is shingles contagious? Shingles is not contagious. You cannot get shingles from someone else. But you can catch chickenpox from someone with shingles if you have direct contact with fluid from their shingles rash. The risk of spreading the virus is low if the shingles rash is kept covered. People with shingles cannot spread the virus before their rash blisters appear or after the rash crusts. Who is at risk for shingles? Anyone who has had chickenpox can get shingles. But the risk of shingles goes up as you get older. Shingles is most common in people over age 50. People with weakened immune systems are at higher risk of getting shingles. This includes those who: Have immune system diseases such as HIV Have certain cancers Take medicines that weaken their immune system, such as steroids and medicines you take after an organ transplant Your immune system may be weaker when you have an infection or are stressed. This can raise your risk of shingles. It is rare, but possible, to get shingles more than once. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Chickenpox is an infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Most cases are in children under age 15, but older children and adults can get it. It spreads very easily from one person to another. The classic symptom of chickenpox is an uncomfortable, itchy rash. The rash turns into fluid-filled blisters and eventually into scabs. It usually shows up on the face, chest, and back and then spreads to the rest of the body. Other symptoms include: Fever Headache Tiredness Loss of appetite Chickenpox is usually mild and lasts 5 to 10 days. Calamine lotions and oatmeal baths can help with itching. Acetaminophen can treat the fever. Do not use aspirin for chickenpox; that combination can cause Reye syndrome. Chickenpox can sometimes cause serious problems. Adults, babies, teenagers, pregnant women, and those with weak immune systems tend to get sicker from it. They may need to take antiviral medicines. Once you catch chickenpox, the virus usually stays in your body. You probably will not get chickenpox again, but the virus can cause shingles in adults. A chickenpox vaccine can help prevent most cases of chickenpox, or make it less severe if you do get it. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is the flu? The flu, also called influenza, is a respiratory infection caused by viruses. Each year, millions of Americans get sick with the flu. Sometimes it causes mild illness. But it can also be serious or even deadly, especially for people over 65, newborn babies, and people with certain chronic illnesses. What causes the flu? The flu is caused by flu viruses that spread from person to person. When someone with the flu coughs, sneezes, or talks, they spray tiny droplets. These droplets can land in the mouths or noses of people who are nearby. Less often, a person may get flu by touching a surface or object that has flu virus on it and then touching their own mouth, nose, or possibly their eyes. What are the symptoms of the flu? Symptoms of the flu come on suddenly and may include: Fever or feeling feverish/chills Cough Sore throat Runny or stuffy nose Muscle or body aches Headaches Fatigue (tiredness) Some people may also have vomiting and diarrhea. This is more common in children. Sometimes people have trouble figuring out whether they have a cold or the flu. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) is an illness caused by a virus. This virus is a coronavirus called SARS-CoV-2. It spreads when a person who has the infection breathes out droplets and very small particles that contain the virus. On this page, you'll find links to resources on important issues such as symptoms, risks, and how you can protect yourself and your family. We also have pages on: COVID-19 testing COVID-19 vaccines Long COVID See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What are streptococcal infections? Strep is short for Streptococcus, a type of bacteria that often lives in your nose and throat. Most strep infections are mild, but some may become serious depending on your overall health. There are several types of strep. Two of them cause most of the strep infections in people: group A and group B. How do streptococcal infections spread? There are different ways that streptococcal infections may spread: Group A strep can be spread from a person who has the infection, even if they don't feel sick, when: They cough or sneeze You share a glass or utensil with them You touch something with the bacteria on it and then touch your eyes, mouth, or nose You touch their open wound or sore Group B strep can be passed to a newborn through fluids during a vaginal birth Who is more likely to get a streptococcal infection? Group A strep infections are most common in children ages 5 to 15, but adults can get them too. You may be at higher risk if you have a weakened immune system, open sores or wounds, or certain viral infections such as a cold or flu. Group B strep is most often a concern for newborns. Adults can also get group B strep infections, especially those 65 or older or who already have other health problems. What are the symptoms of streptococcal infections? Symptoms depend on the type of infection. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Ear infections are the most common reason parents bring their child to a doctor. Three out of four children will have at least one ear infection by their third birthday. Adults can also get ear infections, but they are less common. The infection usually affects the middle ear and is called otitis media. The tubes inside the ears become clogged with fluid and mucus. This can affect hearing, because sound cannot get through all that fluid. If your child isn't old enough to say "My ear hurts," here are a few things to look for: Tugging at ears Crying more than usual Fluid draining from the ear Trouble sleeping Balance difficulties Hearing problems Your health care provider will diagnose an ear infection by looking inside the ear with an instrument called an otoscope. Often, ear infections go away on their own. Your health care provider may recommend pain relievers. Severe infections and infections in young babies may require antibiotics. Children who get infections often may need surgery to place small tubes inside their ears. The tubes relieve pressure in the ears so that the child can hear again. NIH: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Conjunctivitis is the medical name for pink eye. It involves inflammation of the outer layer of the eye and inside of the eyelid. It can cause swelling, itching, burning, discharge, and redness. Causes include: Bacterial or viral infection Allergies Substances that cause irritation Contact lens products, eye drops, or eye ointments Pink eye usually does not affect vision. Infectious pink eye can easily spread from one person to another. The infection will clear in most cases without medical care, but bacterial pink eye needs treatment with antibiotic eye drops or ointment. NIH: National Eye Institute See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is osteoporosis? Osteoporosis is a disease in which your bones become weak and are likely to fracture (break). The disease can develop when your bone mineral density and bone mass decrease. It can also happen if the structure and strength of your bones change. Osteoporosis is called a "silent" disease because it doesn't usually cause symptoms. You may not even know you have the disease until you break a bone. This could happen with any bone, but it's most common in the bones of your hip, vertebrae in the spine, and wrist. What causes osteoporosis? Your bones are made of living tissue. To keep them strong, your body breaks down old bone and replaces it with new bone. Osteoporosis develops when more bone is broken down than replaced. You lose bone mass and changes happen in the structure of your bone tissue. This can happen as you get older. Other risk factors can also lead to the development of osteoporosis or increase your chance of developing the disease. Who is more likely to develop osteoporosis? Anyone can develop osteoporosis, but you are more likely to develop it if you have one or more risk factors: Your sex. Osteoporosis is more common in women, especially after menopause (postmenopausal). Your age. Your risk increases as you get older. It is most common in people over age 50. Your body size. It is more common in people who are slim and thin boned. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Epilepsy is a brain disorder that causes people to have recurring seizures. The seizures happen when clusters of nerve cells, or neurons, in the brain send out the wrong signals. People may have strange sensations and emotions or behave strangely. They may have violent muscle spasms or lose consciousness. Epilepsy has many possible causes, including illness, brain injury, and abnormal brain development. In many cases, the cause is unknown. Doctors use brain scans and other tests to diagnose epilepsy. It is important to start treatment right away. There is no cure for epilepsy, but medicines can control seizures for most people. When medicines are not working well, surgery or implanted devices such as vagus nerve stimulators may help. Special diets can help some children with epilepsy. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a type of movement disorder. It happens when nerve cells in the brain don't produce enough of a brain chemical called dopamine. Sometimes it is genetic, but most cases do not seem to run in families. Exposure to chemicals in the environment might play a role. Symptoms begin gradually, often on one side of the body. Later they affect both sides. They include: Trembling of hands, arms, legs, jaw and face Stiffness of the arms, legs and trunk Slowness of movement Poor balance and coordination As symptoms get worse, people with the disease may have trouble walking, talking, or doing simple tasks. They may also have problems such as depression, sleep problems, or trouble chewing, swallowing, or speaking. There is no specific test for PD, so it can be difficult to diagnose. Doctors use a medical history and a neurological examination to diagnose it. PD usually begins around age 60, but it can start earlier. It is more common in men than in women. There is no cure for PD. A variety of medicines sometimes help symptoms dramatically. Surgery and deep brain stimulation (DBS) can help severe cases. With DBS, electrodes are surgically implanted in the brain. They send electrical pulses to stimulate the parts of the brain that control movement. NIH: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is Alzheimer's disease? Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia among older people. Dementia is a brain disorder that seriously affects thinking and memory skills. If you have AD, it can impair your ability to reason or learn new skills until it becomes difficult to complete daily activities. AD begins slowly over many years. It first involves the parts of the brain that control thought, memory, and language. It may be mistaken for normal memory changes with aging. However, AD is not a normal part of aging. The brain changes from the disease lead to symptoms that get worse over time. What are the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease? People with AD may have trouble remembering recent events or the names of people they know. Behavior may vary from person to person and day to day. AD progresses in stages. Late-onset AD occurs in adults aged 65 and older, which is when most people develop the disease. Early-onset AD happens before age 65, which is not common. Some symptoms of AD can include: Getting lost in familiar places Repeating the same question Not recognizing family members Having trouble speaking, reading, or writing Not taking care of yourself, such as not bathing or eating poorly In AD, over time, symptoms get worse. Later on, people with AD may become anxious or aggressive or wander away from home. Eventually, they need total care. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is heart failure? Heart failure means that your heart can't pump enough oxygen-rich blood to meet your body's needs. Heart failure doesn't mean that your heart has stopped or is about to stop beating. But without enough blood flow, your organs may not work well, which can cause serious problems. Heart failure can affect one or both sides of your heart: With right-sided heart failure, your heart is too weak to pump enough blood to your lungs to get oxygen. With left-sided heart failure, your heart can't pump enough oxygen-rich blood out to your body. This happens when the left side of your heart becomes either: Too weak to pump enough blood. Too thick or stiff to relax and fill with enough blood. Left-sided heart failure is more common than right-sided heart failure. What causes heart failure? Heart failure can start suddenly after a medical condition or injury damages your heart muscle. But in most cases, heart failure develops slowly from long-term medical conditions. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What is atrial fibrillation (AFib)? Atrial fibrillation, also known as AFib or AF, is one of the most common types of arrhythmias. Arrhythmias are problems with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat. They can cause your heart to beat too slowly, too fast, or in an irregular way. If you have AFib, your heart beats irregularly and sometimes much faster than normal. Also, your heart's upper and lower chambers do not work together as they should. When this happens, the lower chambers do not fill completely or pump enough blood to your lungs and body. This can cause symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, and a pounding heartbeat. AFib may happen in brief episodes, or it may be a permanent condition. It's very important to treat it, since AFib can put you at risk for stroke and other heart conditions. What causes atrial fibrillation (AFib)? AFib is most often caused by changes to the heart's tissue or the electrical signaling that helps the heartbeat. These changes can happen due to different conditions and factors, such as high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, congenital heart defects, infections, and aging. Sometimes the cause is unknown. Who is more likely to develop atrial fibrillation (AFib)? Anyone can develop AFib, but there are certain things that raise your risk for it: Aging. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is a blood clot that forms in a vein deep in the body. Most deep vein clots occur in the lower leg or thigh. If the vein swells, the condition is called thrombophlebitis. A deep vein thrombosis can break loose and cause a serious problem in the lung, called a pulmonary embolism. Sitting still for a long time can make you more likely to get a DVT. Some medicines and disorders that increase your risk for blood clots can also lead to DVTs. Common symptoms are: Warmth and tenderness over the vein Pain or swelling in the part of the body affected Skin redness Treatment includes medicines to ease pain and inflammation, break up clots and keep new clots from forming. Keeping the affected area raised and applying moist heat can also help. If you are taking a long car or plane trip, take a break, walk or stretch your legs and drink plenty of liquids. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: What are hemorrhoids? Hemorrhoids are swollen, inflamed veins around your anus or the lower part of your rectum. There are two types: External hemorrhoids, which form under the skin around your anus Internal hemorrhoids, which form in the lining of your anus and lower rectum What causes hemorrhoids? Hemorrhoids happen when there is too much pressure on the veins around the anus. This can be caused by: Straining during bowel movements. Sitting on the toilet for long periods of time. Chronic constipation or diarrhea. A low-fiber diet. Weakening of the supporting tissues in your anus and rectum. This can happen with aging and pregnancy. Frequently lifting heavy objects. What are the symptoms of hemorrhoids? The symptoms of hemorrhoids depend on which type you have: With external hemorrhoids, you may have: Anal itching One or more hard, tender lumps near your anus Anal pain, especially when sitting Too much straining, rubbing, or cleaning around your anus may make your symptoms worse. For many people, the symptoms of external hemorrhoids go away within a few days. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Your thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland in the front of your neck. It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy. These hormones affect nearly every organ in your body and control many of your body's most important functions. For example, they affect your breathing, heart rate, weight, digestion, and moods. Thyroid diseases cause your thyroid to make either too much or too little of the hormones. Some of the different thyroid diseases include: Goiter, an enlargement of the thyroid gland Hyperthyroidism, which happens when your thyroid gland makes more thyroid hormones than your body needs Hypothyroidism, which happens when your thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormones Thyroid cancer Thyroid nodules, lumps in the thyroid gland Thyroiditis, swelling of the thyroid To diagnose thyroid diseases, your health care provider may use a medical history, physical exam, and thyroid tests. In some cases, your provider may also do a biopsy. Treatment depends on the problem, how severe it is, and what your symptoms are. Possible treatments may include medicines, radioiodine therapy, or thyroid surgery. Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
phrases: high cholesterol in children and teens
conditions_ref.answer: What is cholesterol? Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in the body. The liver makes cholesterol, and it is also in some foods, such as meat and dairy products. The body needs some cholesterol to work properly. But if your child or teen has high cholesterol (too much cholesterol in the blood), it can stick to the walls of their arteries and narrow or even block the arteries. This can put your child or teen at risk of coronary artery disease and other heart diseases. What causes high cholesterol in children and teens? Three main factors contribute to high cholesterol in children and teens: An unhealthy diet, especially one that is high in saturated fats A family history of high cholesterol, especially when one or both parents have high cholesterol Having obesity Some diseases, such as diabetes, kidney disease, and certain thyroid diseases, can also cause high cholesterol in children and teens. What are the symptoms of high cholesterol in children and teens? There are usually no signs or symptoms that your child or teen has high cholesterol. How do I know if my child or teen has high cholesterol? There is a blood test to measure cholesterol levels. The test gives information about: Total cholesterol. This is a measure of the total amount of cholesterol in your blood. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

conditions_ref.source: MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine, public domain)
conditions_ref.answer: Sciatica is a symptom of a problem with the sciatic nerve, the largest nerve in the body. It controls muscles in the back of your knee and lower leg and provides feeling to the back of your thigh, part of your lower leg, and the sole of your foot. When you have sciatica, you have pain, weakness, numbness, or tingling. It can start in the lower back and extend down your leg to your calf, foot, or even your toes. It's usually on only one side of your body. Causes of sciatica include: A ruptured intervertebral disk Narrowing of the spinal canal that puts pressure on the nerve, called spinal stenosis An injury such as a pelvic fracture. In many cases no cause can be found. Sometimes sciatica goes away on its own. Treatment, if needed, depends on the cause of the problem. It may include exercises, medicines, and surgery. See a clinician for diagnosis and a plan; this is general reference, not a diagnosis.

Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, a medical EMERGENCY. Classic signs: pain that starts near the navel then moves to the lower-right abdomen, worsening over hours, with nausea, loss of appetite and low fever. RED FLAGS — go to an emergency department urgently; it can burst if untreated. Do not eat, drink, or take laxatives/painkillers that could mask it while seeking care.

Cellulitis is a bacterial skin infection causing an area of skin that is red, warm, swollen and tender, often spreading, sometimes with fever. It usually needs antibiotics from a clinician. RED FLAGS — seek urgent care for rapidly spreading redness, severe pain out of proportion, fever, or red streaks, which can signal a serious, fast-spreading infection.

Diverticulitis is inflammation or infection of small pouches (diverticula) in the colon wall, causing pain usually in the lower-left abdomen, fever, and changes in bowel habits. Mild cases may be managed with a clinician's guidance; some need antibiotics or hospital care. RED FLAGS — severe pain, high fever, or vomiting need urgent care (risk of abscess or perforation).

A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or upper small intestine, often from H. pylori infection or long-term use of anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), causing burning upper-belly pain, often related to meals. A clinician can diagnose and treat it. RED FLAGS — vomiting blood, black tarry stools, or sudden severe abdominal pain are emergencies (bleeding or perforation).

Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas, often from gallstones or heavy alcohol use, causing severe upper-abdominal pain that may radiate to the back, nausea and vomiting. Acute pancreatitis is a medical emergency needing hospital care. RED FLAGS — severe constant abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, or fever: seek emergency care.

Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils, usually from a viral or bacterial infection, causing a sore throat, painful swallowing, swollen tonsils (sometimes with white patches), and fever. Many cases are viral and settle with rest and fluids; bacterial strep may need antibiotics (see the strep throat entry). RED FLAGS — difficulty breathing, drooling, inability to swallow, or a muffled voice need urgent care.

Vertigo is a false sensation that you or the room is spinning. A common cause is BPPV, where tiny inner-ear crystals are displaced, triggering brief spinning with head movement. Many cases are benign and treatable with specific repositioning manoeuvres a clinician can teach. RED FLAGS — vertigo with a severe headache, weakness, slurred speech, double vision, or trouble walking could be a stroke: seek emergency care.

Carpal tunnel syndrome is pressure on a nerve at the wrist, causing numbness, tingling and weakness in the thumb and first fingers, often worse at night or with repetitive hand use. Rest, wrist splints, and ergonomic changes help; some cases need a clinician's treatment or surgery. See a doctor if symptoms persist or the hand weakens.

Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the tissue along the sole, causing stabbing heel pain that's worst with the first steps in the morning. It usually improves with stretching, supportive footwear, rest, and calf/foot exercises over weeks to months. See a clinician if it doesn't improve or the pain is severe.

Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition causing widespread muscle pain and tenderness, fatigue, poor sleep, and 'brain fog'. Its cause isn't fully understood and there's no single test; it's diagnosed clinically after excluding other causes. Management focuses on gentle exercise, sleep, stress management, and treatments a clinician may advise. See a doctor for assessment.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten (in wheat, barley, rye) that damages the small intestine, causing diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss, fatigue and nutrient deficiencies — though some have few gut symptoms. It's diagnosed with blood tests and often a biopsy BEFORE starting a gluten-free diet. Treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet. See a doctor for testing — don't go gluten-free first, as it affects the tests.

Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) is chronic immune-driven inflammation of the gut, causing recurring abdominal pain, diarrhoea (sometimes bloody), urgency, weight loss and fatigue. It's different from IBS (there's real inflammation and damage). It needs specialist diagnosis and ongoing treatment. RED FLAGS — heavy rectal bleeding, severe pain, high fever, or signs of dehydration need urgent care.

Glaucoma is damage to the optic nerve, usually from high pressure in the eye, that can slowly steal peripheral vision — often with no early symptoms, which is why regular eye exams matter. Treatment (drops, laser, or surgery a specialist provides) can halt further loss. RED FLAGS — sudden eye pain, redness, headache, nausea and blurred vision/halos can be acute glaucoma, an emergency.

A cataract is clouding of the eye's lens, developing slowly with age, causing blurry, dim or yellowed vision, glare, and poor night vision. It's common and treatable with a routine surgery that replaces the lens once it affects daily life. See an eye-care professional for assessment; it isn't an emergency but shouldn't be ignored.

Bell's palsy is sudden weakness or drooping of one side of the face from inflammation of a facial nerve, often improving over weeks. BECAUSE facial droop can also signal a STROKE, treat sudden facial droop as an emergency until a clinician confirms otherwise — especially if there's also arm weakness, slurred speech, or it affects more than the face. Early treatment can help Bell's palsy, so seek care promptly.

A transient ischaemic attack ('mini-stroke') is a brief episode of stroke-like symptoms — face droop, arm weakness, speech trouble — that resolves, but it is a major WARNING of a possible full stroke soon. CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES even if symptoms go away; urgent assessment and treatment can prevent a disabling stroke. Remember FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call.

A pulmonary embolism is a blood clot that travels to the lungs — a life-threatening EMERGENCY. Signs: sudden shortness of breath, sharp chest pain worse on breathing, rapid heartbeat, coughing (sometimes blood), often after a leg clot (DVT), surgery, immobility or a long flight. CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES immediately.

Skin cancer includes common, usually-treatable types and melanoma, which is more dangerous. Watch moles with the ABCDE signs: Asymmetry, irregular Borders, uneven Colour, Diameter over ~6mm, and Evolving/changing. See a doctor promptly about any new, changing, bleeding or non-healing skin spot. Early detection is highly treatable; protect skin from UV to prevent it.

Angina is chest pain or pressure from reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, usually due to coronary artery disease (narrowed arteries). It's often triggered by exertion or stress and eases with rest. It's a warning sign of heart disease that needs medical assessment. RED FLAGS — chest pain that is new, severe, lasts more than a few minutes, occurs at rest, or comes with sweating, nausea, or breathlessness may be a HEART ATTACK: call emergency services now.

A stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked (clot) or a vessel bursts (bleed), damaging brain tissue fast. Risk factors include high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, and high cholesterol — most are controllable. Prevention centres on managing these with a doctor. RED FLAGS — act F.A.S.T.: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services immediately. Every minute counts.

Varicose veins are enlarged, twisted veins (usually in the legs) when valves weaken and blood pools, causing bulging veins, aching, heaviness, and swelling. They're common and often cosmetic, but can cause discomfort. Exercise, elevating the legs, and compression stockings help; procedures exist for severe cases. See a doctor if a vein becomes hard, red, and painful (possible clot) or skin breaks down.

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so blood sugar runs high; it often starts in childhood or young adulthood. It requires lifelong insulin. Symptoms of onset: excessive thirst, frequent urination, weight loss, fatigue. RED FLAGS — very high sugar with vomiting, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, or confusion can be diabetic ketoacidosis, a medical emergency — seek care immediately.

Obesity and metabolic syndrome (a cluster of high blood pressure, high blood sugar, excess waist fat, and abnormal cholesterol) raise the risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes. Management focuses on sustainable changes in eating and activity, sleep, and, where a doctor advises, medications or other treatments. Work with a healthcare professional on a realistic, supportive plan rather than extreme diets.

Cirrhosis is advanced scarring of the liver from long-term damage (alcohol, viral hepatitis, or fatty liver), which impairs its function. Early on there may be few symptoms; later signs include fatigue, easy bruising, swelling, and yellowing (jaundice). It needs medical management and removing the cause. RED FLAGS — vomiting blood, black stools, confusion, or severe abdominal swelling need urgent care.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is a build-up of fat in the liver, linked to obesity, diabetes, and high cholesterol; it's often found incidentally and usually has no symptoms. It can progress to inflammation and scarring. Management is weight loss, controlling blood sugar and cholesterol, and limiting alcohol, guided by a doctor. See a clinician for monitoring if you have risk factors.

A hernia is when an organ or tissue pushes through a weak spot in the muscle wall — commonly in the groin or abdomen, causing a bulge that may ache, especially with lifting. Many are managed with monitoring or surgical repair. RED FLAGS — a hernia that becomes suddenly painful, hard, red, or can't be pushed back in, especially with vomiting, can be 'strangulated' — a surgical emergency.

Constipation means infrequent or difficult bowel movements, often from low fibre, dehydration, inactivity, or some medications. Usually it improves with more fibre, fluids, activity, and sometimes a clinician-advised laxative. RED FLAGS — see a doctor for new constipation with weight loss, blood in the stool, severe pain, or a marked change in bowel habits, especially over age 50.

Gastroenteritis ('stomach flu') is inflammation of the gut, usually from a virus, causing vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps, and sometimes fever, typically lasting a few days. The main treatment is preventing dehydration with small frequent sips of fluids/oral rehydration. RED FLAGS — signs of dehydration (little urine, dizziness), blood in stool, high fever, severe pain, or symptoms in a baby/older adult need medical care.

Food poisoning comes from eating food contaminated with germs or toxins, causing nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and cramps, usually within hours to a couple of days. Most cases resolve with rest and fluids. RED FLAGS — high fever, bloody diarrhoea, signs of dehydration, symptoms lasting over 3 days, or illness in pregnancy, infants, or the elderly need medical attention; some toxins act fast and seriously.

Lactose intolerance is difficulty digesting the sugar in dairy, causing bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea after milk products. It's not an allergy. Management is limiting lactose, using lactose-free products, or lactase supplements. See a doctor to distinguish it from other gut conditions if symptoms are severe or include weight loss or blood.

Colorectal cancer develops in the colon or rectum, often from polyps over years. Early disease may have no symptoms, which is why SCREENING (e.g., colonoscopy or stool tests from the recommended age) saves lives. Warning signs: change in bowel habits, blood in stool, unexplained weight loss, or persistent abdominal discomfort. See a doctor promptly about these and ask about screening.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women (and can affect men). Warning signs include a new lump, skin or nipple changes, or unusual discharge. SCREENING (mammograms from the recommended age) and prompt evaluation of changes improve outcomes greatly. See a doctor about any new breast lump or change — most are not cancer, but all deserve assessment.

Prostate cancer is common in older men and often grows slowly. Early disease usually has no symptoms; later it may cause urinary changes. Screening (PSA blood test and exam) is a decision to discuss with a doctor based on age and risk. See a doctor about urinary changes or a family history; many prostate cancers are very treatable.

Lung cancer is strongly linked to smoking (and radon/pollution). Warning signs: a persistent or changing cough, coughing blood, chest pain, breathlessness, or unexplained weight loss. Screening (low-dose CT) is recommended for certain long-term smokers. Not smoking is the biggest prevention. See a doctor promptly about a persistent cough or coughing blood.

The most common skin cancers (basal and squamous cell) usually appear as a new or changing growth, sore that won't heal, or scaly patch, often on sun-exposed skin. They're usually very treatable when caught early and rarely spread (squamous can). See a doctor about any new, changing, or non-healing skin spot, and protect your skin from UV.

Lupus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, causing fatigue, joint pain, a facial 'butterfly' rash, and flares affecting skin, joints, kidneys, and other organs. It varies widely and needs specialist diagnosis and ongoing care. See a doctor for persistent unexplained joint pain, rashes, and fatigue, especially with sun sensitivity.

Multiple sclerosis is an immune condition that damages the protective covering of nerves, causing varied symptoms — numbness, weakness, vision problems, balance issues, fatigue — that may come and go or progress. It needs specialist diagnosis (MRI) and long-term management. See a doctor about new unexplained neurological symptoms like vision loss, numbness, or weakness.

A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury from a blow or jolt, causing headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, or feeling 'foggy'. Most recover with physical and mental rest and a gradual return to activity. RED FLAGS — worsening or severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, weakness, slurred speech, unequal pupils, or increasing drowsiness/confusion need EMERGENCY care (possible brain bleed).

Cluster headaches cause excruciating pain around one eye, in bouts ('clusters') over weeks, often with a watering eye and blocked nostril on that side. They're rare but intensely painful and have specific treatments a doctor can provide. See a doctor for diagnosis; seek urgent care for the 'worst headache of your life' or a sudden thunderclap headache (different, dangerous causes).

Peripheral neuropathy is damage to the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, often from diabetes, causing numbness, tingling, burning, or weakness, usually starting in the feet/hands. Managing the cause (e.g., blood sugar) and specific treatments help. See a doctor for persistent numbness or burning, and protect numb feet from unnoticed injuries.

Bipolar disorder involves episodes of depression and of elevated mood (mania/hypomania) with high energy, reduced need for sleep, and impulsive behaviour. It's a treatable medical condition, usually with a combination of medication and therapy guided by a mental-health professional. If you or someone has thoughts of self-harm or suicide, seek help immediately (call a crisis line or emergency services).

Obsessive-compulsive disorder causes unwanted, distressing thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) done to ease anxiety, which can take over daily life. It's treatable, especially with a specific therapy (exposure and response prevention) and sometimes medication. See a mental-health professional; it is not a personality flaw.

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition involving ongoing inattention, impulsivity, and/or hyperactivity that affects daily functioning, in children and adults. It's diagnosed by a professional and managed with behavioural strategies, support, and sometimes medication. See a clinician for assessment if symptoms significantly affect school, work, or relationships.

Eating disorders (such as anorexia, bulimia, and binge-eating disorder) are serious mental-health conditions involving disturbed eating and body image, with real physical dangers. They are treatable, and early help improves recovery. If you or someone is struggling, reach out to a doctor or an eating-disorder helpline. RED FLAGS — fainting, chest pain, very low heart rate, or signs of severe malnutrition need urgent medical care.

Insomnia is ongoing trouble falling or staying asleep despite the chance to, leaving you tired by day. Good 'sleep hygiene' (regular schedule, limiting screens/caffeine, a dark cool room) and a specific therapy (CBT-I) are first-line. See a doctor if it's chronic, or with loud snoring/pauses (possible sleep apnoea), or linked to low mood or anxiety.

A food allergy is an immune reaction to a food (commonly peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, egg, milk), ranging from hives and stomach upset to life-threatening anaphylaxis. Management is strict avoidance and carrying prescribed emergency adrenaline (an auto-injector) if at risk. RED FLAGS — trouble breathing, throat tightness, swelling, or faintness is anaphylaxis: use the auto-injector if prescribed and call emergency services immediately.

Hives are raised, itchy welts that appear suddenly, often from an allergic trigger, infection, or unknown cause, and usually fade within hours to days. Antihistamines and avoiding triggers help. RED FLAGS — hives WITH swelling of the lips/tongue/throat, trouble breathing, or faintness can be anaphylaxis — use an adrenaline auto-injector if prescribed and call emergency services.

Acne is a common skin condition where pores clog with oil and dead cells, causing pimples, blackheads, and sometimes painful cysts, especially in teens. Gentle skincare and over-the-counter or prescribed treatments usually control it; avoid picking (scarring). See a doctor/dermatologist for severe, scarring, or persistent acne.

Rosacea is a chronic condition causing facial redness, flushing, visible vessels, and sometimes bumps, often triggered by heat, alcohol, spicy food, or sun. Identifying triggers, gentle skincare, sun protection, and clinician-prescribed treatments help. See a doctor for diagnosis and if the eyes are affected (burning, grittiness).

Fungal skin infections (athlete's foot, ringworm, jock itch) cause itchy, red, scaly, sometimes ring-shaped rashes, thriving in warm moist areas. Over-the-counter antifungal creams usually clear them; keep the area clean and dry. See a doctor if it spreads, affects nails or scalp, doesn't improve, or you have diabetes or a weak immune system.

Cold sores are small painful blisters around the lips caused by the herpes simplex virus, which stays dormant and reactivates with stress, illness, or sun. They usually heal in 1–2 weeks; antiviral creams or tablets can shorten attacks if started early. Avoid contact (kissing, sharing) while active, especially with babies and people with weak immunity.

The common cold is a mild viral infection of the nose and throat causing a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, cough, and sometimes mild fever, resolving in about a week. Rest, fluids, and symptom relief help; antibiotics don't work on viruses. See a doctor if symptoms are severe, last beyond ~10 days, or come with high fever or breathing trouble.

Tuberculosis is a serious bacterial infection usually affecting the lungs, causing a persistent cough (sometimes with blood), fever, night sweats, and weight loss over weeks. It's contagious and needs a specific, lengthy course of antibiotics from a doctor — and public-health follow-up. See a doctor urgently for a cough lasting over 2–3 weeks, especially with blood, fevers, or weight loss.

Sexually transmitted infections (such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV, herpes, HPV) often have NO symptoms, so regular testing matters if you're sexually active. Possible signs: unusual discharge, sores, burning when urinating, or pelvic pain. Most are treatable and many curable — early testing and treatment prevent complications and spread. See a clinician or sexual-health clinic for testing; use protection.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia is a common, non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate in older men, squeezing the urethra and causing a weak stream, frequent urination (especially at night), and trouble emptying. Lifestyle steps, medications, or procedures a doctor offers help. RED FLAGS — a sudden complete inability to urinate is an emergency; blood in urine needs prompt assessment.

Erectile dysfunction is difficulty getting or keeping an erection, which becomes more common with age but can also signal underlying heart, vascular, diabetes, or psychological issues — so it's worth assessing. Lifestyle changes and clinician-prescribed treatments are effective. See a doctor, especially since ED can be an early warning of heart or blood-vessel disease.

Menopause is the natural end of menstrual periods (around the early 50s), with the transition (perimenopause) bringing hot flashes, sleep and mood changes, and irregular periods. It also affects bone and heart health long-term. Many symptoms can be managed with lifestyle measures and, where appropriate, clinician-guided hormone or non-hormone therapy. See a doctor for bothersome symptoms or any bleeding after menopause (needs evaluation).

Polycystic ovary syndrome is a common hormonal condition causing irregular periods, excess hair growth or acne, and difficulty with weight, and is linked to insulin resistance and fertility challenges. Management (lifestyle, and treatments a doctor tailors) addresses symptoms and long-term risks like diabetes. See a doctor for irregular periods with these features.

Endometriosis is when tissue like the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, causing painful, sometimes heavy periods, pelvic pain, pain with sex, and fertility problems. It's often under-diagnosed for years. It needs medical assessment; treatments range from pain management and hormones to surgery. See a doctor for severe period pain that disrupts your life — it is not something to just endure.

Fibroids are common non-cancerous growths of the uterus that can cause heavy or prolonged periods, pelvic pressure, and sometimes fertility issues — though many cause no symptoms. Options range from monitoring to medication or procedures. See a doctor for heavy bleeding (which can cause anaemia), pelvic pressure, or fertility concerns.

A vaginal yeast infection is a common fungal overgrowth causing itching, irritation, and thick white discharge. Over-the-counter or prescribed antifungals usually clear it. See a doctor if it's a first episode (to confirm), recurrent, during pregnancy, or if symptoms differ (discharge with odour or a different colour may be another infection needing different treatment).

Tension-type headache is the most common headache — a dull, tight, band-like pressure on both sides, often from stress, poor posture, or fatigue, without the nausea or light sensitivity of migraine. Rest, hydration, stress management, and occasional over-the-counter pain relief help. See a doctor for frequent headaches, or urgent care for a sudden severe or 'worst-ever' headache.

Gum disease starts as gingivitis (red, swollen, bleeding gums from plaque) and can progress to periodontitis, which damages the bone and can loosen teeth. Good brushing and flossing and regular dental cleanings prevent and treat early disease. See a dentist for bleeding gums, persistent bad breath, or loose teeth; gum health is also linked to overall health.

Haemorrhoids are swollen veins around the anus/rectum causing itching, discomfort, and bright-red bleeding on wiping, often from straining or constipation. Fibre, fluids, not straining, and over-the-counter treatments usually help. RED FLAGS — see a doctor for significant or dark bleeding, a change in bowel habits, or if you're over 50, to rule out other causes; never assume rectal bleeding is 'just piles'.

Generalized anxiety disorder is persistent, excessive worry that's hard to control, with restlessness, poor concentration, muscle tension, and sleep trouble, affecting daily life. It's common and very treatable with therapy (like CBT), lifestyle measures, and sometimes medication. See a doctor or mental-health professional; if you ever have thoughts of self-harm, seek help immediately via a crisis line or emergency services.

Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from a gallstone blocking its outlet, causing steady severe pain in the upper-right abdomen, often after fatty meals, with nausea and sometimes fever. It usually needs prompt medical care and often surgery. RED FLAGS — severe persistent pain, fever, or yellowing of skin/eyes need urgent assessment.

New or worsening breathlessness and wheezing in adults can come from asthma, COPD, heart failure, infection, or a clot — causes that are managed very differently, so it needs a medical assessment rather than guesswork. RED FLAGS — severe breathlessness, blue lips, chest pain, or inability to speak in full sentences is an emergency: call emergency services.

Dehydration is when the body loses more fluid than it takes in — from heat, illness, vomiting, or diarrhoea — causing thirst, dark urine, dizziness, headache, and tiredness. Sip fluids or oral rehydration solution. RED FLAGS — confusion, fainting, a fast heartbeat, very little or no urine, or sunken eyes (especially in babies and the elderly) mean severe dehydration needing urgent care.

Lyme disease is a bacterial infection from the bite of an infected tick, often starting with a spreading 'bull's-eye' rash, fever, fatigue, and aches; untreated it can affect joints, the heart, and nerves. Early antibiotics from a doctor are very effective. Remove ticks promptly and see a doctor about a tick bite with a rash or flu-like symptoms. RED FLAGS — facial droop, severe headache with neck stiffness, or heart palpitations need prompt care.

Mononucleosis ('mono') is usually caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, common in teens/young adults, causing severe fatigue, sore throat, swollen glands, and fever lasting weeks. It's managed with rest and fluids. RED FLAGS — avoid contact sports while the spleen may be enlarged (risk of rupture); seek care for severe abdominal pain, trouble breathing/swallowing, or dehydration.

Measles is a highly contagious viral illness with high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic rash, preventable by vaccination (MMR). It can cause serious complications (pneumonia, encephalitis). If you suspect measles, call ahead before going to a clinic to avoid spreading it. RED FLAGS — trouble breathing, high persistent fever, confusion, or dehydration need urgent care; infants and the immunocompromised are at highest risk.

Whooping cough is a very contagious bacterial infection causing severe coughing fits, sometimes with a 'whoop,' lasting weeks; it's dangerous for babies. Vaccination (DTaP/Tdap) prevents it, and early antibiotics reduce spread. RED FLAGS — in infants, pauses in breathing, blue colour, or poor feeding are emergencies; see a doctor early for a prolonged severe cough, especially around newborns.

RSV is a common respiratory virus — a mild cold in most, but in infants and older adults it can cause bronchiolitis or pneumonia with wheezing and breathing trouble. Most recover with fluids and rest. RED FLAGS — in a baby: fast or labored breathing, flaring nostrils, ribs pulling in, blue lips, or poor feeding need urgent care.

Hand, foot and mouth disease is a common, usually mild childhood viral illness causing fever, mouth sores, and a rash/blisters on the hands and feet. It clears in about a week with fluids and comfort care; keeping hydrated is the main concern. RED FLAGS — signs of dehydration (very little urine, no tears), a stiff neck, or a child who is very drowsy need medical care.

Croup is a viral infection in young children causing a distinctive barking cough and sometimes a harsh sound breathing in (stridor), usually worse at night. Mild cases ease with calm and humid or cool air. RED FLAGS — stridor at rest, struggling to breathe, blue colour, drooling, or a child unable to speak/drink need emergency care.

Malaria is a serious, sometimes fatal parasitic infection from mosquito bites in affected tropical regions, causing cycles of fever, chills, sweats, headache, and body aches, often 1–4 weeks after exposure. It is a medical EMERGENCY. If you develop a fever during or after travel to a malaria area, seek care urgently and mention the travel — prompt testing and treatment are critical. Preventive medication and bite protection matter before travel.

Preeclampsia is a pregnancy complication of high blood pressure and signs of organ stress (often after 20 weeks), which can be dangerous for mother and baby. Warning signs: severe headache, vision changes, upper-right belly pain, sudden swelling, or breathlessness. RED FLAGS — these symptoms in pregnancy need urgent assessment; untreated preeclampsia can progress to seizures (eclampsia). Keep all prenatal appointments where blood pressure is checked.

Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar that develops in pregnancy, usually found on routine screening, raising risks for mother and baby if uncontrolled. It's managed with diet, activity, monitoring, and sometimes medication under medical care, and usually resolves after birth (with higher future diabetes risk). Attend prenatal care and screening; follow the care plan.

Mastitis is inflammation/infection of breast tissue, common in breastfeeding, causing a red, painful, swollen area, often with fever and flu-like feelings. Continuing to breastfeed/empty the breast, rest, and fluids help; a doctor may prescribe antibiotics. RED FLAGS — high fever, a firm painful lump that may be an abscess, or worsening despite care need prompt medical attention.

Bacterial vaginosis is an imbalance of normal vaginal bacteria causing thin greyish discharge with a fishy odour, more than itching. It's common and treated with antibiotics a clinician prescribes. See a doctor to confirm (it's often confused with a yeast infection, which is treated differently), especially in pregnancy, as untreated BV can raise some risks.

Postpartum depression is more than the short-lived 'baby blues' — persistent sadness, hopelessness, anxiety, or difficulty bonding with the baby lasting beyond two weeks after birth. It's common and treatable with support, therapy, and sometimes medication. Reach out to a doctor — it is not a failing. RED FLAGS — thoughts of harming yourself or the baby need immediate help: call a crisis line or emergency services now.

Prostatitis is inflammation or infection of the prostate, causing pelvic/groin pain, painful or frequent urination, and sometimes fever. Bacterial cases need antibiotics from a clinician; chronic cases are managed over time. RED FLAGS — high fever, chills, or inability to urinate need urgent care (possible acute infection or retention).

Polymyalgia rheumatica causes aching and marked morning stiffness in the shoulders, neck, and hips, usually in people over 50. It responds well to treatment a doctor prescribes. Importantly, it can be linked to giant cell arteritis — RED FLAGS: a new severe headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, or sudden vision change need URGENT care to prevent vision loss.

Raynaud's is when small blood vessels in the fingers/toes overreact to cold or stress, turning them white then blue then red, with numbness. Most cases are mild (primary) and managed by keeping warm and avoiding triggers. See a doctor if it's severe, one-sided, causes sores, or appears with other symptoms (it can sometimes signal an underlying condition).

Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition that attacks moisture-producing glands, causing persistent dry eyes and dry mouth, sometimes with fatigue and joint pain. It's managed with moisture replacement and treatments a specialist advises, and needs monitoring. See a doctor for persistent dryness, as it can affect teeth and, rarely, other organs.

Psoriatic arthritis is joint inflammation that occurs in some people with psoriasis, causing painful, swollen joints, sometimes with 'sausage' fingers/toes and nail changes. Early treatment from a rheumatologist helps prevent joint damage. See a doctor for joint pain and swelling, especially with a history of psoriasis.

Ankylosing spondylitis is inflammatory arthritis mainly of the spine and pelvis, causing chronic back pain and stiffness that is worse with rest and better with movement, often starting in young adults. Exercise and treatments from a rheumatologist help. See a doctor for inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness over 30 minutes, improves with activity) rather than assuming it's mechanical.

Sickle cell disease is an inherited disorder where red blood cells are misshapen, blocking blood flow and causing episodes of severe pain ('crises'), anaemia, and infection risk. It needs lifelong specialist care, hydration, and prompt treatment of crises. RED FLAGS — a severe pain crisis, chest pain/breathlessness, fever, or stroke symptoms are emergencies.

Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause fatigue, pale skin, a sore tongue, and — if advanced — numbness/tingling and memory/balance problems from nerve effects. Causes include low intake (e.g., vegan diets) or poor absorption (pernicious anaemia). It's diagnosed with a blood test and treated with B12 replacement. See a doctor for persistent fatigue or new neurological symptoms rather than self-dosing.

Vitamin D deficiency is common, especially in low-sunlight climates, and can cause fatigue, bone/muscle aches, and, long-term, weaker bones. It's confirmed with a blood test and corrected with sunlight, diet, and supplements a clinician recommends. Ask your doctor about testing if you have risk factors rather than taking high doses unsupervised.

A kidney infection is a UTI that has reached the kidney, causing fever, chills, back/flank pain, nausea, and painful urination — more serious than a bladder infection. It needs prompt antibiotics from a clinician. RED FLAGS — high fever, vomiting, confusion, or being unable to keep fluids down need urgent care; it can lead to sepsis if untreated.

Pleurisy is inflammation of the lining around the lungs, causing sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, often from an infection. Because chest pain has many serious causes, it needs assessment. RED FLAGS — severe breathlessness, chest pain with sweating/nausea (possible heart attack), or coughing blood need emergency care; don't assume chest pain is 'just' pleurisy.

Pericarditis is inflammation of the sac around the heart, causing sharp chest pain that often eases leaning forward and worsens lying down or breathing in, sometimes after a viral illness. It needs medical assessment to confirm and to exclude a heart attack. RED FLAGS — severe or crushing chest pain, breathlessness, or fainting need emergency evaluation.

Peripheral artery disease is narrowing of the arteries (usually in the legs) from atherosclerosis, causing cramping leg pain with walking that eases with rest, cold or discoloured feet, and slow-healing sores. It signals widespread vascular risk. Managing risk factors (smoking, diabetes, cholesterol) is key. RED FLAGS — sudden severe leg pain, coldness, and pallor can be an arterial blockage emergency; non-healing foot sores need prompt care.

A stye is a small, painful red lump on the eyelid from a blocked, infected oil gland. Warm compresses several times a day usually clear it within a week or so; don't squeeze it. See a doctor if it doesn't improve, affects vision, spreads to the eyelid/face (possible cellulitis), or keeps recurring.

Dry eye is when the eyes don't make enough quality tears, causing grittiness, burning, redness, and sometimes blurry vision or watering. Causes include screen use, age, and some medications. Artificial tears, screen breaks, and addressing causes help. See an eye-care professional if it's persistent, painful, or affecting vision.

Age-related macular degeneration damages the central retina, blurring or distorting central vision (faces, reading) while side vision is spared, usually in older adults. Early detection and, for some types, treatment can slow it. RED FLAGS — sudden distortion (straight lines looking wavy) or rapid central vision loss needs prompt eye-care assessment. Don't smoke; get regular eye exams.

Hearing loss can be gradual (age, noise exposure) or sudden, and may come from wax, infection, noise damage, or nerve changes.
