Protect hearing from loud noise and get tested if you're struggling to follow conversations. RED FLAGS — SUDDEN hearing loss in one ear is a medical urgency (prompt treatment can help); hearing loss with dizziness, pain, or discharge needs assessment.

Tinnitus is ringing, buzzing, or hissing in the ears without an external source, often linked to hearing loss, noise exposure, or earwax. It's common and usually not dangerous, and sound therapy and managing hearing help. See a doctor if it's one-sided, pulsing (in time with your heartbeat), or comes with hearing loss or dizziness, which need evaluation.

Laryngitis is inflammation of the voice box, usually from a virus or overuse, causing hoarseness or voice loss, often with a cold. Resting the voice, fluids, and humidity help; most cases clear in a week or two. See a doctor if hoarseness lasts more than ~3 weeks, or with trouble breathing/swallowing or coughing blood — persistent hoarseness needs evaluation.

Ménière's disease is an inner-ear disorder causing episodes of spinning vertigo (often with nausea), fluctuating hearing loss, ringing, and ear fullness. It's managed with diet (low salt), lifestyle changes, and treatments a specialist advises. See a doctor for recurring vertigo with ear symptoms; sudden hearing loss or neurological symptoms need urgent assessment.

Contact dermatitis is an itchy, red, sometimes blistering rash where skin touched an irritant or allergen (soaps, metals like nickel, plants like poison ivy, cosmetics). Avoiding the trigger, gentle skincare, and treatments for flares help. See a doctor if it's widespread, severe, infected, or not improving; identify and avoid the cause.

Impetigo is a contagious bacterial skin infection, common in children, causing red sores that ooze and form honey-coloured crusts, often around the nose and mouth. It's treated with antibiotic cream or tablets a clinician prescribes; keep it clean and covered to limit spread. See a doctor to confirm and treat, and keep children home until no longer contagious.

Warts are harmless skin growths caused by HPV, common on hands and feet (plantar warts), that often resolve on their own over months to years. Over-the-counter salicylic-acid treatments or clinic procedures can speed removal. See a doctor if they spread, bleed, are painful, are on the face/genitals, or if you have diabetes or a weak immune system.

Tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon from overuse or injury, causing pain, tenderness, and sometimes swelling near a joint (common in the elbow, shoulder, wrist, knee, and Achilles). Rest, ice, gentle stretching/strengthening, and activity modification usually help over weeks. See a doctor if pain is severe, follows a 'pop' (possible tear), or doesn't improve.

Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa (a fluid-filled cushion near a joint), causing pain and tenderness with movement, commonly at the shoulder, elbow, hip, or knee, often from repetitive pressure. Rest, ice, and avoiding the aggravating activity help. RED FLAGS — a hot, red, very swollen joint with fever could be an infected bursa needing urgent care.

Frozen shoulder is painful progressive stiffness of the shoulder that limits movement, going through freezing, frozen, and thawing phases over months to a couple of years; it's more common in diabetes and after shoulder immobilization. Physiotherapy and treatments a clinician advises help recovery. See a doctor for persistent shoulder pain and stiffness.

Low back pain is extremely common, usually mechanical (muscle/ligament or disc-related) and improving within weeks with staying active, gentle movement, and heat; prolonged bed rest is NOT advised. RED FLAGS — seek urgent care for back pain with leg weakness/numbness, loss of bladder/bowel control, saddle numbness, fever, unexplained weight loss, or after major trauma.

A sprain (stretched/torn ligament) or strain (muscle/tendon) causes pain, swelling, and bruising after a twist or overstretch. First aid is R.I.C.E. (rest, ice, compression, elevation) and gradual return to movement. RED FLAGS — inability to bear weight or use the limb, severe swelling/deformity, or numbness may mean a fracture or serious tear and need assessment/X-ray.

A herniated ('slipped') disc is when the soft centre of a spinal disc pushes out and can press on a nerve, causing back pain and radiating pain, numbness, or weakness down an arm or leg (e.g., sciatica). Most improve over weeks with activity, physio, and time. RED FLAGS — progressive weakness, or loss of bladder/bowel control or saddle numbness, is an emergency (cauda equina) needing immediate care.

Schizophrenia is a serious mental-health condition affecting how a person thinks, feels, and perceives reality, which can include hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking. It is treatable, and early treatment (medication and support from a mental-health team) improves outcomes. Reach out to a doctor or mental-health service. RED FLAGS — thoughts of harming oneself or others, or an acute break from reality, need urgent/emergency help.

Panic disorder involves recurring panic attacks — sudden intense fear with racing heart, chest tightness, shortness of breath, dizziness, and a sense of doom — and worry about future attacks. Attacks peak within minutes and aren't dangerous themselves, but the symptoms overlap with heart problems, so a first episode should be medically checked. It's very treatable with therapy (CBT) and sometimes medication.

Substance use disorder is a treatable medical condition — not a moral failing — where use of alcohol or drugs becomes compulsive and harmful despite consequences. Help ranges from counselling and support groups to medical treatment and, for some substances, medically supervised withdrawal. Reach out to a doctor or a helpline. RED FLAGS — stopping alcohol or benzodiazepines suddenly can be dangerous; and signs of overdose are a medical emergency — call for help.

A hiatal hernia is when part of the stomach pushes up through the diaphragm, often causing reflux/heartburn symptoms; many are small and need no treatment beyond managing reflux. Larger ones occasionally need repair. See a doctor for persistent reflux; RED FLAGS — sudden severe chest/abdominal pain, vomiting, or inability to swallow could signal a trapped hernia needing urgent care.

Sepsis is the body's extreme, life-threatening response to an infection, where it starts injuring its own organs. It is a TIME-CRITICAL EMERGENCY. Warning signs: a known or suspected infection PLUS confusion/slurred speech, extreme shivering or muscle pain, passing little/no urine, severe breathlessness, fast heartbeat, or skin that is mottled, very pale, or bluish. RED FLAGS — call emergency services immediately and say you are worried about sepsis; early antibiotics and fluids save lives.

Meningitis is inflammation of the lining around the brain and spinal cord, often from infection; bacterial meningitis is a life-threatening EMERGENCY. Warning signs: severe headache, stiff neck, fever, sensitivity to light, confusion, and — a danger sign — a rash that does NOT fade when pressed with a glass. RED FLAGS — these symptoms need emergency care immediately; do not wait. Some types are vaccine-preventable.

Testicular torsion is a surgical EMERGENCY where a testicle twists and loses its blood supply, causing sudden severe testicle pain, swelling, and often nausea/vomiting, most common in teens. RED FLAGS — sudden severe testicular pain needs emergency care within HOURS; delay can cost the testicle. Do not wait to see if it passes.

An aortic aneurysm is a bulge in the body's main artery; a rupture or dissection (tear) is a catastrophic EMERGENCY. Warning signs: sudden severe tearing chest or back/abdominal pain, fainting, or a pulsing feeling in the abdomen. RED FLAGS — call emergency services immediately. Risk rises with age, smoking, and high blood pressure; large aneurysms are repaired electively, so known risk factors warrant screening with a doctor.

A pneumothorax (collapsed lung) is air in the space around the lung, causing sudden sharp chest pain and breathlessness, sometimes after injury or in tall thin young people spontaneously. RED FLAGS — severe breathlessness, a fast heartbeat, and worsening distress (tension pneumothorax) is an emergency — call for help. Even smaller ones need medical assessment.

Guillain-Barré syndrome is a rare condition where the immune system attacks the nerves, causing weakness and tingling that typically starts in the feet/legs and spreads upward over days, often after an infection. RED FLAGS — rapidly spreading weakness, or any trouble breathing or swallowing, is an EMERGENCY (it can paralyze breathing muscles). Seek urgent care for progressive weakness.

ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) is a progressive disease of the motor nerves, causing worsening muscle weakness, wasting, twitching, and problems with speech, swallowing, and eventually breathing. It needs specialist diagnosis and care. See a doctor for persistent unexplained weakness, muscle wasting, or twitching, especially if progressive.

Essential tremor is a common movement disorder causing rhythmic shaking, usually of the hands, worse with action (holding a cup, writing), often running in families — it is NOT Parkinson's. It can be managed with lifestyle measures and medication a doctor may prescribe. See a doctor to distinguish it from Parkinson's and other causes, and if it affects daily tasks.

Restless legs syndrome is an uncomfortable urge to move the legs, usually in the evening/at rest, relieved by movement, which disrupts sleep. It can be linked to iron deficiency, pregnancy, kidney disease, or some medications. Lifestyle steps, treating iron deficiency, and medication help. See a doctor to check for underlying causes (like low iron).

Trigeminal neuralgia causes sudden, severe, electric-shock-like face pain, often triggered by touch, chewing, or wind, from irritation of a facial nerve. It is very treatable with specific medications or procedures a specialist provides. See a doctor for severe facial pain — ordinary painkillers rarely work and the right treatment can transform it.

Addison's disease (adrenal insufficiency) is when the adrenal glands make too little cortisol, causing fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, salt craving, and skin darkening. An 'adrenal crisis' is life-threatening. RED FLAGS — severe weakness, vomiting, confusion, and very low blood pressure (adrenal crisis) need emergency steroids and care. See a doctor for persistent unexplained fatigue, weight loss, and dizziness.

Cushing's syndrome results from too much cortisol (often from long-term steroid medication), causing weight gain in the face/trunk, a round face, easy bruising, purple stretch marks, high blood pressure, and high blood sugar. It needs medical evaluation to find the cause. See a doctor; never stop prescribed steroids suddenly, which is dangerous.

Low testosterone can cause low energy, reduced libido, erectile problems, mood changes, and loss of muscle, and becomes more common with age and certain conditions. It is diagnosed with morning blood tests (often repeated) and treated only when truly low and symptomatic, under medical supervision. See a doctor rather than using unregulated 'boosters'; testosterone therapy has risks and needs monitoring.

Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection of the female reproductive organs, often from untreated STIs, causing lower-abdominal/pelvic pain, abnormal discharge, fever, and pain with sex or urination. Prompt antibiotics prevent serious complications (chronic pain, infertility, ectopic pregnancy). RED FLAGS — severe pain, high fever, or vomiting need urgent care. See a clinician quickly for these symptoms.

Ovarian cysts are fluid-filled sacs on an ovary — very common and usually harmless, often resolving on their own, though they can cause pelvic pain, bloating, or irregular periods. RED FLAGS — sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain with nausea/vomiting could be a ruptured cyst or ovarian torsion (an emergency). See a doctor for persistent pelvic pain; most cysts just need monitoring.

Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) means periods heavy enough to disrupt life or cause anaemia (soaking through protection hourly, large clots, fatigue). Causes include fibroids, hormonal issues, and others. It is very treatable. See a doctor — heavy bleeding is not something to just endure, and it can cause iron-deficiency anaemia; sudden very heavy bleeding or bleeding with dizziness/fainting needs urgent care.

Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe, persistent pregnancy vomiting (far beyond normal morning sickness) that causes dehydration and weight loss and may need hospital treatment. RED FLAGS — inability to keep ANY fluids down, very dark/little urine, dizziness, or weight loss in pregnancy need prompt medical care (IV fluids and anti-nausea treatment). Don't tough it out — it's treatable.

Leukemia is a cancer of blood-forming cells, causing fatigue, frequent infections, easy bruising/bleeding, pale skin, bone pain, and swollen glands. It ranges from acute (fast) to chronic. Early diagnosis matters. See a doctor promptly for unexplained persistent fatigue, bruising/bleeding, repeated infections, or night sweats and weight loss; a simple blood test is the first step.

Lymphoma is a cancer of the lymphatic (immune) system, classically causing painless swollen lymph nodes (neck, armpit, groin), night sweats, fever, unexplained weight loss, and fatigue. Many types are highly treatable. See a doctor about a lymph node that is persistently enlarged (over a few weeks), hard, or growing, especially with night sweats or weight loss.

Seborrheic dermatitis is a common, chronic skin condition causing flaky, greasy, red or scaly patches on the scalp (dandruff), face (eyebrows, sides of the nose), and chest. It flares and settles and isn't contagious. Medicated shampoos and gentle skincare usually control it. See a doctor if it's severe, widespread, or not responding.

Scabies is an intensely itchy rash caused by tiny mites burrowing in the skin, worse at night, often between the fingers, wrists, and waist; it spreads by close contact. It needs a prescribed treatment (cream or tablets), and all close contacts and bedding/clothing must be treated/washed at the same time. See a clinician to confirm and treat.

Head lice are tiny insects that live on the scalp causing itching; they spread by head-to-head contact and are common in children — NOT a sign of poor hygiene. Treat with a recommended lice treatment and wet-combing, and check/treat household contacts and bedding. See a pharmacist/doctor if treatments fail or the scalp is infected (sore, crusted, swollen glands).

Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition where patches of skin lose their pigment, becoming white, often symmetrically. It isn't harmful or contagious but can affect wellbeing; sun protection of pale patches matters, and treatments can help restore some colour. See a dermatologist to discuss options and to check for associated autoimmune conditions (e.g., thyroid).

Hair loss has many causes — male/female pattern (genetic), stress or illness (temporary shedding), thyroid or iron issues, autoimmune (alopecia areata, causing round bald patches), and some medications. Pattern loss has treatments; reversible causes can be corrected. See a doctor for sudden, patchy, or rapid hair loss, or loss with other symptoms, to find the cause.

Fungal nail infection makes a nail thick, discoloured, and brittle, usually on the toes. It is stubborn; mild cases may respond to topical treatment, but clearing it often needs oral antifungals a doctor prescribes (with monitoring). See a doctor to confirm it's fungal (not another nail problem) and discuss treatment, especially if you have diabetes or circulation problems.

Blepharitis is chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins, causing red, itchy, crusty eyelids and gritty eyes, often linked to oil-gland problems or dandruff. Warm compresses and daily eyelid hygiene usually control it (it tends to recur). See an eye-care professional if it's severe, affects vision, or doesn't improve with lid care.

A corneal abrasion is a scratch on the surface of the eye, causing pain, tearing, light sensitivity, and a feeling of something in the eye, often after a scratch or foreign body. Don't rub it; most heal in a day or two. RED FLAGS — significant pain, vision changes, a possible embedded object, or a chemical/high-speed injury need prompt eye-care; infection is a risk, so see a clinician for anything beyond a minor scratch.

Uveitis is inflammation inside the eye, causing a red, painful, light-sensitive eye with blurred vision, sometimes linked to autoimmune disease or infection. RED FLAGS — a painful red eye with light sensitivity and vision change needs PROMPT eye-care assessment; untreated uveitis can threaten vision. Don't treat it as simple conjunctivitis.

Swimmer's ear (otitis externa) is infection/inflammation of the ear canal, causing itch, pain (especially when the ear is tugged), and discharge, common after water exposure. It's treated with prescribed ear drops; keep the ear dry. See a doctor for diagnosis and drops; severe pain, spreading redness, fever, or diabetes warrant prompt care.

TMJ disorders affect the jaw joint and muscles, causing jaw pain, clicking, difficulty chewing, and headaches, often linked to clenching/grinding or stress. Most improve with jaw rest, soft foods, gentle stretches, stress management, and sometimes a dental night guard. See a dentist or doctor if pain is persistent, the jaw locks, or chewing is limited.

Nasal polyps are soft, noncancerous growths in the nose/sinuses from chronic inflammation, causing a persistently blocked/runny nose, reduced smell, and sinus pressure, often with asthma or allergies. Treatments (nasal steroids, and sometimes surgery) a clinician provides help. See a doctor for a persistently blocked nose or loss of smell that doesn't resolve.

Mumps is a contagious viral infection causing painful swelling of the salivary glands (puffy cheeks/jaw), fever, and headache, preventable by the MMR vaccine. Most recover with rest and fluids. RED FLAGS — severe headache with stiff neck, testicular pain/swelling, or abdominal pain can signal complications needing care. Isolate to avoid spreading it.

Rubella is a usually-mild contagious viral illness with a rash and swollen glands, preventable by MMR — but it is DANGEROUS in pregnancy, where it can cause serious birth defects. Anyone who may be pregnant and exposed, or with a rash, should contact a doctor. Confirm MMR vaccination, especially before pregnancy.

Scarlet fever is a strep infection with a fine, sandpaper-like red rash, sore throat, fever, and a 'strawberry' tongue, mainly in children. It's treated with antibiotics, which also prevent complications. See a doctor for diagnosis and antibiotics; untreated strep can rarely affect the heart/kidneys, so don't skip treatment.

Tetanus is a serious infection from bacteria entering a wound (classically a deep/dirty puncture), causing painful muscle stiffness and spasms, including 'lockjaw.' It's vaccine-preventable. After a dirty or puncture wound, clean it and check whether your tetanus shot is up to date — get a booster if it's been over 5–10 years or you're unsure. RED FLAGS — muscle stiffness/spasms after a wound is an emergency.

Rabies is an almost-always-fatal viral infection spread by the bite/scratch of an infected animal (dogs, bats, raccoons, foxes) — but it is PREVENTABLE if treated promptly after exposure, before symptoms start. RED FLAGS — after any bite/scratch from a wild or unknown animal, or waking to a bat in the room, wash the wound well and seek medical care IMMEDIATELY for post-exposure treatment. Once symptoms appear it is nearly always fatal.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne tropical viral illness causing high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle/joint aches, and rash. Most recover, but a minority develop severe dengue. RED FLAGS — warning signs a few days in (severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums/nose, blood in vomit/stool, extreme fatigue) need urgent care. Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs with suspected dengue; see a doctor, especially after travel.

HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system; untreated it can progress to AIDS, but with modern treatment people live long, healthy lives and become non-infectious to partners ('undetectable = untransmittable'). Early flu-like symptoms may occur, but many have none — so testing is key. Prevention includes condoms, PrEP (preventive medication), and clean injecting equipment. Get tested if at risk; after a possible exposure, PEP started within 72 hours can prevent infection.

Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory condition where clusters of immune cells (granulomas) form in organs — most often the lungs and lymph nodes — causing cough, breathlessness, fatigue, and sometimes skin/eye involvement. Many cases resolve on their own; others need treatment a specialist provides. See a doctor for persistent cough, breathlessness, or unexplained fatigue with swollen glands.

Overactive bladder causes a sudden urgent need to urinate, frequency, and sometimes leakage, from the bladder muscle contracting too often. It's common and treatable with bladder training, pelvic-floor exercises, fluid/caffeine adjustments, and medication. See a doctor to rule out infection or other causes, especially with pain, blood in the urine, or sudden onset.

A rotator cuff tear is damage to the shoulder tendons, from injury or wear, causing shoulder pain (often worse at night), weakness, and trouble lifting the arm. Partial tears often improve with physio; some need surgery. See a doctor for shoulder weakness after a fall/injury or pain that doesn't improve; early assessment guides whether repair is needed.

A meniscus tear is a tear of the knee's cartilage cushion, often from a twist, causing pain, swelling, and sometimes catching or 'locking' of the knee. Many are managed with rest, physio, and strengthening; some need a procedure. RED FLAGS — a knee that is locked and won't straighten, or gives way, warrants prompt assessment. See a doctor for persistent knee pain/swelling after a twist.

An ACL tear is a knee-ligament injury, often from a sudden pivot/landing, typically with a 'pop,' rapid swelling, and instability. Treatment ranges from physio/rehab to surgical reconstruction depending on activity and instability. See a doctor/sports-medicine clinician for a knee that swells quickly after a twist or gives way — early assessment guides treatment.

Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine, most often appearing in growing children/teens; mild curves just need monitoring, moderate ones may need a brace, and severe ones may need surgery. Most cases aren't painful. See a doctor if you notice uneven shoulders/hips or a rib hump, or for back pain with a curve; early detection in growing children matters.

Seasonal affective disorder is depression that recurs seasonally, usually in the darker winter months, with low mood, low energy, oversleeping, and carbohydrate cravings. Light therapy, getting daylight/activity, and the usual depression treatments help. See a doctor if it recurs each year or affects your life. If you ever have thoughts of self-harm, seek help immediately.

Autism spectrum disorder is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference affecting communication, social interaction, and sensory processing, with a wide range of strengths and support needs. It is not an illness to be 'cured'; diagnosis and tailored supports help people thrive. See a clinician for assessment if a child (or adult) has persistent differences in communication, social interaction, or sensory needs that affect daily life.

nutrition.summary: For the first six months, breast milk (or infant formula when that isn't possible) gives a baby everything they need — no other food or water is required.
nutrition.energy: Feed on demand, following the baby's hunger and fullness cues rather than a fixed schedule; most newborns feed 8–12 times a day.
key_nutrients: Breast milk (ideal — also passes on antibodies) or iron-fortified infant formula
No cow's milk as a drink, no water, no juice, no solids yet
nutrition.hydration: Milk provides all the fluid a baby needs; extra water can be dangerous for young infants.
nutrition.safety: Always hold the baby for feeds (never prop a bottle); prepare formula exactly per instructions; sterilise bottles; never add cereal to bottles.
nutrition.supplements: A daily vitamin D supplement is advised for breastfed and partly breastfed babies (formula is already fortified).
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Few wet nappies, poor feeding, not gaining weight, a sunken soft spot, floppiness or drowsiness — seek care promptly.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: Around six months, alongside continued milk, babies start solid foods — beginning with iron-rich foods and gradually widening variety and texture.
nutrition.energy: Milk is still the main source of nutrition this year; solids are added in increasing amounts as the baby learns to eat.
key_nutrients: Iron-rich first foods (well-cooked egg, meat/poultry purée, lentils, iron-fortified cereal)
Soft vegetables and fruits, then mashed and soft finger foods
Introduce common allergens (egg, peanut as smooth butter/thinned, dairy) one at a time, early, unless advised otherwise
nutrition.hydration: Small sips of water with meals are fine from a cup; milk remains the main drink.
nutrition.safety: NO honey before 12 months (botulism risk). Avoid choking hazards (whole nuts, grapes/round foods uncut, hard raw veg, popcorn). No added salt or sugar. Cow's milk can be used in cooking but not as the main drink before 12 months. Always supervise eating.
nutrition.supplements: Continue daily vitamin D for breastfed/partly breastfed babies.
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Choking, persistent refusal to eat, poor weight gain, or a reaction to a new food (swelling, widespread rash, breathing trouble — this is an emergency).
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: Toddlers eat family foods in small portions, learning to enjoy a variety of tastes and textures — appetite naturally varies day to day.
nutrition.energy: Offer three small meals plus 2–3 healthy snacks; a toddler portion is roughly the size of their own hand.
key_nutrients: Varied family foods: vegetables, fruit, grains, protein (meat, fish, eggs, beans), dairy
Whole milk is usual from 12 months; move toward lower-fat milks from about age 2 if growth is good
Limit juice (small amounts, with meals); avoid sugary drinks
nutrition.hydration: Water and milk are the best drinks; limit juice to a small amount.
nutrition.safety: Still avoid choking hazards (cut grapes/tomatoes lengthways, no whole nuts, no hard sweets). Keep added salt and sugar low. Let the child decide HOW MUCH to eat — you decide what's offered; avoid pressure, which worsens fussiness.
nutrition.supplements: A daily vitamin D supplement is often advised, especially with limited sun or limited diet.
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Poor weight gain or weight loss, extreme food refusal, choking episodes, or signs of iron deficiency (pale, very tired, craving non-foods).
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: School-age children thrive on regular balanced meals built around vegetables, fruit, whole grains, protein, and dairy — with room for activity and treats in moderation.
nutrition.energy: Three meals plus healthy snacks; let hunger guide amounts. Energy needs rise with growth and activity.
key_nutrients: Half the plate vegetables and fruit; whole grains; lean protein (meat, fish, eggs, beans, nuts if no allergy); calcium foods (dairy or fortified alternatives) for growing bones
Oily fish about weekly for omega-3; iron-rich foods
nutrition.hydration: Water as the main drink; milk for calcium; limit sugary and fizzy drinks.
nutrition.safety: Build a positive, pressure-free relationship with food. Encourage breakfast, family meals, and daily active play. Limit ultra-processed snacks and sugary drinks rather than banning foods outright.
nutrition.supplements: A daily vitamin D supplement is advised through winter in many regions (and year-round for some).
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Faltering growth, excessive or very restricted eating, constant tiredness/pallor, or a worrying relationship with food or body image.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: Teenagers have high energy and nutrient needs during the growth spurt — the priority is enough good food, strong bones, and a healthy relationship with eating.
nutrition.energy: Appetite rises with growth; regular meals plus snacks support school, sport, and development. Under-eating during these years can affect growth, periods, and bone strength.
key_nutrients: Plenty of energy from balanced meals; protein for growth; calcium + vitamin D for peak bone mass (this is the key window)
Iron is especially important for teenage girls (periods) — red meat, beans, fortified cereals with vitamin-C foods to absorb it
nutrition.hydration: Water is best; limit energy drinks and high-caffeine drinks; limit sugary drinks.
nutrition.safety: Support a healthy relationship with food and body — avoid diet talk and calorie-counting pressure; these years carry eating-disorder risk. Athletes need extra fuel, not restriction.
nutrition.supplements: A daily vitamin D supplement is commonly advised, especially in winter.
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Rapid weight loss or gain, skipping meals, secrecy or distress around eating, periods stopping, fainting, or over-exercising — reach out for support.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: For most adults, healthy eating is simple and flexible: mostly vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and good protein, with fewer ultra-processed foods — built into a pattern you can keep.
nutrition.energy: Match energy to your activity. Health is about overall pattern and how you feel, not a single number on the scale.
key_nutrients: Fill half the plate with vegetables and fruit; choose whole grains; include lean protein (fish, poultry, beans, lentils, eggs, nuts); use healthy oils
Oily fish ~weekly for omega-3; plenty of fibre; calcium and vitamin D for bones
nutrition.hydration: Water is the best everyday drink; limit sugary drinks; keep alcohol within low-risk limits (and some weeks with none).
nutrition.safety: Reduce salt, added sugar, and ultra-processed foods rather than chasing fads. Small, consistent changes beat crash diets. Plant-forward patterns suit most people.
nutrition.supplements: Many adults benefit from a vitamin D supplement in winter; vegans need reliable B12.
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, or new digestive symptoms deserve a check — and support is available if eating or weight feels out of control.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: In later years, the aim shifts toward protecting muscle, bone, and strength — enough protein and energy matter more than cutting back, and appetite often needs a little help.
nutrition.energy: Appetite and thirst can fade, so regular, appealing, nourishing meals matter. Unintended weight loss is a warning sign, not a goal.
key_nutrients: Protein at each meal to protect muscle (eggs, fish, dairy, beans, meat)
Calcium + vitamin D for bones and fewer falls; vitamin B12 (absorption drops with age); fibre and fluids to prevent constipation
Nourishing, easy-to-eat foods if appetite is small — full-fat versions and fortified meals can help
nutrition.hydration: Drink regularly even without thirst — older adults dehydrate easily; aim for pale urine.
nutrition.safety: Watch for dental, chewing, or swallowing problems; make eating social where possible; review medicines that affect appetite. Soft textures help if swallowing is hard.
nutrition.supplements: A daily vitamin D supplement is widely advised; B12 may be needed if low.
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Unintentional weight loss, poor appetite, difficulty swallowing, recurrent falls, or signs of dehydration — see a clinician.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: In pregnancy, the focus is a balanced diet plus a few key nutrients and some food-safety care — you don't need to 'eat for two', but quality matters.
nutrition.energy: Energy needs rise modestly, mainly in later pregnancy; steady, balanced meals support you and the baby.
key_nutrients: Folic acid/folate before and in early pregnancy (reduces neural-tube defects); iron (for increased blood volume); calcium + vitamin D; iodine; omega-3
Plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains, protein, and dairy
nutrition.hydration: Drink water regularly; limit caffeine; avoid alcohol entirely.
nutrition.safety: Food safety: avoid unpasteurised dairy, undercooked meat/eggs, pâté, and high-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel); wash produce; take care with listeria risks. Avoid alcohol; limit caffeine.
nutrition.supplements: A folic acid supplement is advised before conception and in the first trimester; many are also advised vitamin D (and sometimes iron if low).
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Severe vomiting with dehydration, bleeding, severe headache with vision changes or swelling, reduced baby movements, or one-sided pelvic pain — seek care promptly/urgently.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: While breastfeeding, eat a normal balanced diet with a little extra energy and fluids — there's no long list of forbidden foods for most mothers.
nutrition.energy: Breastfeeding uses extra energy, so appetite often rises; eat to appetite with nourishing foods rather than dieting hard in the early months.
key_nutrients: Balanced meals with protein, whole grains, vegetables, fruit, and dairy or fortified alternatives
Keep up calcium, iron, and omega-3; vegans need reliable B12
nutrition.hydration: Drink to thirst — keep a drink to hand at feeds; this alone meets most needs.
nutrition.safety: Limit alcohol (and time feeds away from drinking if you do); moderate caffeine (it passes into milk). Continue the baby's vitamin D. Watch for foods that seem to upset the baby, but routine restriction isn't needed.
nutrition.supplements: Continue a vitamin D supplement for the baby; mothers may continue their own as advised.
nutrition.when_to_see_care: If the baby isn't gaining weight or has few wet nappies, or you have a red painful breast with fever (mastitis), seek care.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

nutrition.summary: Good hydration supports energy, concentration, digestion, and temperature control — needs vary with age, heat, activity, and illness.
nutrition.energy: Let thirst and urine colour guide you (pale straw is the aim). Needs rise in heat, exercise, pregnancy, breastfeeding, and illness with fever/vomiting/diarrhoea.
key_nutrients: Water is the best everyday choice; milk and diluted drinks count
Older adults and young children dehydrate fastest — offer fluids regularly
nutrition.hydration: Increase fluids in hot weather, during exercise, and when unwell; use oral rehydration for vomiting/diarrhoea.
nutrition.safety: Very young children and older adults are most at risk. Don't give large amounts of plain water to infants under 6 months.
nutrition.when_to_see_care: Signs of dehydration — dry mouth, little/dark urine, dizziness, sunken eyes, drowsiness, or no wet nappies in a baby — need prompt care, urgently if severe.
nutrition.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain nutrition guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Face a bright light or use a phone torch. Have the person tilt the head back and open wide and say 'aaah'. If needed, gently press the middle of the tongue down with a clean spoon handle (not too far back — it triggers gagging). Look at the back of the throat and the tonsils on each side.
look_for: Redness of the throat or tonsils
White or yellow patches or pus on the tonsils
Tonsils swollen or touching in the middle
Grey coating
Ulcers or blisters
Swollen tender glands in the neck (feel just under the jaw)
One-sided bulging (pushes the tonsil toward the middle)
red_flags: Can't swallow their own saliva, or drooling
Muffled 'hot-potato' voice
Noisy breathing (a harsh sound breathing in) or struggling to breathe
Can't open the mouth, or severe one-sided swelling
Stiff neck with fever
examination.photo: Good light, mouth wide, tongue pressed down, photo of the back of the throat and each tonsil.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Look at the outer ear and behind it. Gently pull the ear and press the small flap at the front (tragus) — note if that causes pain. You usually can't see the eardrum without an otoscope, so go by pain, discharge, hearing, and the outside.
look_for: Pain when the ear is pulled or the front flap is pressed
Discharge or fluid from the ear canal
Redness or swelling of the outer ear
Swelling or redness behind the ear that pushes it forward
Reduced hearing on that side
red_flags: Swelling/redness behind the ear pushing it out (possible mastoiditis)
Severe pain with high fever and feeling very unwell
Sudden facial weakness on that side
Stiff neck with fever
examination.photo: Photo of the outer ear and the area behind it from the side.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: In good light, compare both eyes. Look at the white, the coloured part, and the pupil. Check if the pupils are equal and shrink to light. Ask about pain, vision change, and light sensitivity.
look_for: Redness — all over (often infection/irritation) vs around the coloured part (more concerning)
Discharge: watery, or sticky/pus
Pupils unequal, or one not reacting to light
A cloudy or hazy coloured part
Yellow whites (jaundice)
Eyelid swelling or a lump
red_flags: Painful red eye with blurred vision or halos around lights
Sudden loss of vision, or a curtain/shadow over vision
A pupil that is fixed/unequal with a severe headache or vomiting
Eye injury with something embedded
Marked eyelid swelling with fever and the eye pushed forward
examination.photo: Photo straight on in good light, and a close-up of the affected eye.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: In good light, look at the whole area and a bit beyond it. Note colour, whether it's raised, blistered, or flat, how far it spreads, and whether it's warm or tender. For redness, draw a line at the edge with a pen so you can tell if it spreads.
look_for: Flat vs raised vs blistered
Spreading redness that is warm and tender (possible cellulitis)
A rash that does NOT fade when a glass is pressed on it (do the glass test)
Blisters in a band on one side (possible shingles)
Honey-coloured crusts (possible impetigo)
Pus-filled lump (abscess)
Target/bullseye shape
red_flags: A rash that doesn't fade under pressure (glass test) — especially with fever
Rapidly spreading redness, severe pain out of proportion, or skin going dusky/black
Widespread blistering or skin peeling
Swelling of the lips/tongue/face with the rash, or any breathing trouble
examination.photo: Photo in natural light with something for scale (a coin), plus one close-up and one wider shot showing spread.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Compare the spot with the person's other moles and look for the ABCDE changes. A photo next to a ruler, repeated over weeks, helps show change.
look_for: A — Asymmetry (one half unlike the other)
B — Border irregular or blurred
C — Colour uneven or several colours
D — Diameter larger than ~6 mm (a pencil eraser)
E — Evolving: changing in size, shape, colour; itching, bleeding, or crusting
The 'ugly duckling' — one spot that looks different from all the others
red_flags: A mole that is changing, bleeding, or crusting
A new dark streak under a nail
A sore that won't heal
examination.photo: Photo in good natural light, straight on, with a ruler or coin beside it for scale; repeat the same way in a few weeks to compare.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Have the person lie flat with knees slightly bent and relaxed. With a warm flat hand, press gently in each of the four quarters, watching the face for pain. Note where it hurts most, whether it's soft or hard/rigid, and whether pressing in and quickly letting go hurts more (rebound).
look_for: Where the pain is worst (upper/lower, left/right)
Soft vs hard/rigid ('board-like')
A tender spot in the lower right (possible appendicitis)
Pain worse when you quickly release the press (rebound)
A pulsating mass in the middle (do NOT press hard — seek care)
Bloating/distension
red_flags: A rigid, board-like, very tender belly
Severe constant pain, or pain with a pulsating mass
Vomiting blood, or black/tarry stools
Pain with fainting, pale clammy skin, or a racing heart
No gas or stool passing with vomiting
examination.photo: Not usually photographed — describe the location and feel. Photograph only visible swelling, bruising, or skin changes.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Watch the chest rise and fall for a full 30–60 seconds while the person is at rest and unaware (counting makes people change it). Note the rate, whether they can speak full sentences, any wheeze or noisy breathing, and whether the skin between/under the ribs sucks in (recession — important in children).
look_for: Breaths per minute at rest (adults ~12–20)
Can they speak full sentences, or only a few words?
Wheeze (whistle out) or stridor (harsh sound in)
Ribs/neck muscles pulling in with each breath (recession)
Blue tinge to lips or fingertips
Sitting forward, refusing to lie flat
red_flags: Can only speak a few words, or silent chest
Blue lips or face
Ribs sucking in, grunting, or a baby struggling to feed
Stridor (harsh noise breathing in) at rest
Oxygen level under 92% if measured
examination.photo: A short video of the chest/ribs while breathing can show rate and recession better than a photo.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Act FAST: F — ask them to smile; A — ask them to raise both arms and hold; S — ask them to repeat a simple sentence; T — time: if any are abnormal, note the time symptoms started and call emergency services now.
look_for: Face: does one side droop or is the smile uneven?
Arms: does one arm drift down or can't be raised?
Speech: slurred, strange, or unable to speak?
Also: sudden numbness one side, sudden confusion, sudden severe headache, sudden vision loss
red_flags: ANY face, arm, or speech abnormality — call emergency services immediately and note the start time. Do not give food, drink, or medicine.
examination.photo: Record a short video of the smile, arm-raise, and speech if it helps responders — but do not delay calling for help.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Check the mouth (moist or dry), the eyes (normal or sunken), and urine (amount and colour). Pinch the skin on the back of the hand or belly and let go — it should spring back quickly. Press a fingernail for 5 seconds and release — colour should return within ~2 seconds. In babies, check the soft spot and the number of wet nappies.
look_for: Dry mouth and lips
Sunken eyes (or sunken soft spot in a baby)
Little urine, dark in colour, or few/no wet nappies
Skin pinch stays tented instead of springing back
Nail colour takes over 2 seconds to return
Drowsiness, irritability, or dizziness on standing
red_flags: No urine/wet nappy for many hours
Very drowsy, floppy, or hard to wake
Sunken eyes with skin that stays pinched
Fast breathing, cold mottled hands/feet
Can't keep any fluids down
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Compare with the other side. Look for deformity, swelling, bruising, and open wounds. Check the fingers/toes beyond the injury: are they warm, pink, with normal feeling and movement? Check a pulse beyond the injury if you can. Don't move a suspected broken bone more than needed.
look_for: Visible deformity (bent, rotated, shorter than the other side)
Swelling and bruising
Bone showing or a wound over the break (open fracture)
Fingers/toes beyond the injury cold, pale, blue, or numb
Can't move or bear weight at all
red_flags: Bone through the skin, or a wound over the break
Limb/digit cold, pale, blue, or numb, or no pulse beyond the injury
Suspected neck, back, hip, or thigh injury — do not move; call for help
Severe bleeding that won't stop
examination.photo: Photo comparing both sides, plus a close-up of any deformity or wound (cover a wound first; photograph through the dressing if needed).
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Using flat fingertips, gently feel in small circles: under the jaw and down the sides of the neck, in front of and behind the ears, above the collarbones, in the armpits, and in the groin. Compare both sides. Note size, whether they're tender, soft or hard, and whether they move.
look_for: Tender, soft, mobile glands (often infection)
Hard, fixed, painless, or steadily growing glands
A single gland bigger than ~2 cm or growing over weeks
Glands above the collarbone (always worth checking)
Night sweats, weight loss, or fever alongside
red_flags: A hard, fixed, painless, growing lump
A lump above the collarbone
Any lump with night sweats, weight loss, or unexplained fever
examination.photo: Photo of any visible swelling, with a finger or coin for scale.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

examination.how: Check for a stiff neck (can they comfortably touch the chin to the chest?), dislike of bright light, drowsiness/confusion, and a rash. Do the GLASS TEST: press the side of a clear glass firmly on any rash — a meningococcal rash does NOT fade under pressure.
look_for: Stiff neck — can't bring chin to chest
Dislike of bright light
Drowsiness, confusion, or hard to wake
A rash that does NOT fade when pressed with a glass
In babies: high-pitched cry, bulging soft spot, floppiness, refusing feeds
red_flags: Stiff neck with fever and headache, a non-fading rash, drowsiness, or a fitting/very unwell person — seek emergency care now (don't wait for a rash).
examination.photo: If a non-fading rash is present, photograph it with the glass pressed on it — but do not delay seeking help.
examination.source: HIVE Doctor original guide (general public-domain clinical guidance, re-expressed)

vitals_reference.name: Temperature
vitals_reference.note: Measured in °C. (100.4°F = 38°C; 103°F = 39.4°C.) A fever with confusion, fast breathing, a non-fading rash, or a very unwell child needs urgent care.

vitals_reference.name: Oxygen (SpO₂)
vitals_reference.note: On a finger pulse oximeter. Under 92% (or a drop of ≥3–4% from normal) needs urgent assessment. Cold fingers, nail polish, and movement can give false low readings.

vitals_reference.name: Heart rate
vitals_reference.note: Adult resting range ~60–100. Children run faster. A fast or very slow pulse with chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, or feeling very unwell needs urgent care.

vitals_reference.name: Breathing rate
vitals_reference.note: Adult resting range ~12–20. Children breathe faster. Fast breathing with fever or confusion can signal serious infection; very slow breathing with drowsiness is an emergency.

vitals_reference.name: Blood pressure (systolic)
vitals_reference.note: Top (systolic) number. A reading ≥180, or with chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, vision change, weakness, or confusion, needs urgent care. A single high reading should be rechecked calmly.

vitals_reference.name: Blood sugar (glucose)

bands.label: Very high — review, esp. if unwell

vitals_reference.note: In mmol/L (×18 ≈ mg/dL, so 4 mmol/L ≈ 72 mg/dL). Under 4 mmol/L (72 mg/dL): give fast sugar now if awake and able to swallow. Very high with vomiting, deep breathing, or drowsiness in diabetes can be ketoacidosis — an emergency.

anatomy.title: Anatomical position, planes & regions
anatomy.overview: Anatomy is described from the 'anatomical position': standing, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms forward. Directions and planes give everyone a shared map of the body.

structures.name: Directional terms
structures.detail: Superior/inferior (up/down), anterior/posterior (front/back), medial/lateral (toward/away from midline), proximal/distal (near/far from the trunk), superficial/deep.

structures.name: Planes
structures.detail: Sagittal (left/right), coronal/frontal (front/back), transverse/axial (top/bottom).

structures.name: Abdominal regions
structures.detail: Nine regions, or four quadrants (RUQ, LUQ, RLQ, LLQ) used to locate belly pain.

structures.name: Body cavities
structures.detail: Cranial (brain), thoracic (heart/lungs), abdominal, and pelvic cavities.

anatomy.normal: A shared reference frame; no 'normal/abnormal' — it's the language the rest of anatomy uses.
common_problems: Mislocating pain — e.g., appendicitis pain is classically RLQ; gallbladder RUQ.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Bones & the skeleton
anatomy.overview: The adult skeleton has 206 bones. It supports the body, protects organs, anchors muscles for movement, stores calcium, and makes blood cells in the marrow.

structures.name: Axial skeleton
structures.detail: Skull, spine (cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacrum, coccyx), ribs (12 pairs), sternum — protects brain, cord, heart, lungs.

structures.name: Appendicular skeleton
structures.detail: Shoulder girdle, arms (humerus, radius, ulna, hand), pelvis, legs (femur, tibia, fibula, foot) — for movement.

structures.name: Bone types
structures.detail: Long (femur), short (wrist), flat (skull, ribs), irregular (vertebrae).

structures.name: Bone structure
structures.detail: Hard outer cortical bone, spongy inner trabecular bone, and marrow (blood-cell factory).

anatomy.normal: Bones are dense and non-tender, aligned and symmetrical left-to-right; a limb matches its opposite in length and shape.
common_problems: Fractures (breaks), osteoporosis (thinning/fragile bone), osteoarthritis (joint wear), scoliosis (spine curve), bone infection, bone tumours.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Joints, ranges & movements
anatomy.overview: Joints are where bones meet. Most movement happens at freely-moving (synovial) joints, cushioned by cartilage and lubricated by fluid, held by ligaments and moved by muscles.

structures.name: Joint types
structures.detail: Ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip — move all directions), hinge (elbow, knee — bend/straighten), pivot (neck rotation), gliding (wrist), saddle (thumb).

structures.name: Support tissues
structures.detail: Cartilage (smooth cushion), ligaments (bone-to-bone), tendons (muscle-to-bone), bursae (friction-reducing sacs), joint capsule + synovial fluid.

structures.name: Movements
structures.detail: Flexion/extension (bend/straighten), abduction/adduction (away/toward midline), rotation, circumduction, pronation/supination (palm down/up), inversion/eversion (sole in/out), dorsiflexion/plantarflexion (foot up/down).

anatomy.normal: Smooth, pain-free movement through a full expected range, equal to the other side, without swelling, heat, locking, or instability.
common_problems: Sprains (ligament), strains (muscle/tendon), dislocations, arthritis (osteo/rheumatoid/gout), bursitis, tendinitis, torn cartilage, frozen shoulder.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Muscles & movement
anatomy.overview: Over 600 skeletal muscles move the body by contracting and pulling on bones across joints. Muscles work in pairs — one shortens (agonist) while its partner relaxes (antagonist). There are also smooth muscle (organs) and cardiac muscle (heart).

structures.name: How it works
structures.detail: A muscle attaches at an origin (fixed) and insertion (moving) point; contracting shortens it and moves the insertion toward the origin.

structures.name: Major upper-body
structures.detail: Deltoids (shoulder), pectorals (chest), biceps/triceps (arm), trapezius & lats (back), rotator cuff (shoulder stability), abdominals, erector spinae (spine).

structures.name: Major lower-body
structures.detail: Gluteals (hip), quadriceps (knee extend), hamstrings (knee bend), gastrocnemius/soleus (calf), hip flexors, adductors.

structures.name: Muscle types
structures.detail: Skeletal (voluntary), smooth (involuntary — gut, vessels), cardiac (heart).

anatomy.normal: Muscles are symmetrical, with normal bulk and tone, full strength against resistance, and no wasting, twitching, or fixed weakness.
common_problems: Strains/tears, cramps, tendinitis, muscle wasting, myositis, rhabdomyolysis (breakdown), neuromuscular disease, fibromyalgia (widespread pain).
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Heart & blood vessels
anatomy.overview: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump that drives blood through two circuits: to the lungs for oxygen, and to the body to deliver it. It beats about 60–100 times a minute at rest.

structures.name: Chambers
structures.detail: Right atrium & ventricle (pump blood to the lungs), left atrium & ventricle (pump oxygen-rich blood to the body — the left ventricle is the strongest).

structures.name: Valves
structures.detail: Tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic — one-way doors that stop backflow; their closing makes the 'lub-dub'.

structures.name: Vessels
structures.detail: Arteries carry blood away from the heart (high pressure), veins return it, capillaries exchange oxygen/nutrients. The aorta is the main artery; coronary arteries feed the heart itself.

structures.name: Electrical system
structures.detail: The SA node sets the rhythm; signals spread to make the chambers beat in order.

structures.name: Pulse points
structures.detail: Radial (wrist), carotid (neck), brachial (arm), femoral (groin), pedal (foot).

anatomy.normal: A regular pulse 60–100/min at rest, blood pressure around 120/80, warm well-perfused limbs, no chest pain, breathlessness, or swelling.
common_problems: Heart attack (blocked coronary artery), angina, heart failure, arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation), valve disease, high blood pressure, aneurysm, DVT/PE, peripheral arterial disease.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Airway & lungs
anatomy.overview: The respiratory system brings air in, exchanges oxygen for carbon dioxide in the lungs, and breathes the waste out. The diaphragm does most of the work of breathing.

structures.name: Upper airway
structures.detail: Nose/mouth, pharynx (throat), larynx (voice box with the epiglottis that guards the airway).

structures.name: Lower airway
structures.detail: Trachea (windpipe) → two bronchi → smaller bronchioles → alveoli (tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens).

structures.name: Lungs
structures.detail: Right lung (3 lobes), left lung (2 lobes, smaller — the heart sits there), wrapped in pleura.

structures.name: Muscles
structures.detail: Diaphragm (main), intercostals between the ribs; accessory neck muscles when struggling.

anatomy.normal: Quiet, effortless breathing ~12–20/min at rest, full sentences, no wheeze or noisy breathing, oxygen ≥95%, both sides of the chest moving equally.
common_problems: Asthma, COPD, pneumonia, bronchitis, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax (collapsed lung), pleurisy, lung cancer, croup (children).
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Gut & digestion
anatomy.overview: The digestive tract is a ~9-metre tube that breaks food down, absorbs nutrients, and removes waste, helped by the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.

structures.name: Upper tract
structures.detail: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach (acid + churning) → small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum — most absorption).

structures.name: Lower tract
structures.detail: Large intestine/colon (water absorption) → rectum → anus.

structures.name: Accessory organs
structures.detail: Liver (processes nutrients, makes bile, detoxifies — RUQ), gallbladder (stores bile), pancreas (digestive enzymes + insulin).

structures.name: Appendix
structures.detail: Small pouch at the start of the large intestine (RLQ) — can become inflamed (appendicitis).

anatomy.normal: Comfortable eating and swallowing, no persistent pain, regular bowel habit, no blood in stool, stable weight, no jaundice.
common_problems: Reflux/GERD, gastritis/ulcers, appendicitis, gallstones, pancreatitis, hepatitis, IBS/IBD, diverticulitis, bowel obstruction, coeliac, GI bleeding, colorectal cancer.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Brain, cord & nerves
anatomy.overview: The nervous system is the body's control and communication network. The brain and spinal cord (central nervous system) process information; nerves (peripheral) carry signals in and out.

structures.name: Brain regions
structures.detail: Cerebrum (thought, movement, senses — in lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital), cerebellum (balance/coordination), brainstem (breathing, heart rate, consciousness).

structures.name: Spinal cord
structures.detail: Runs in the spine; relays signals and handles reflexes. Damage affects function below the level.

structures.name: Nerves
structures.detail: 12 cranial nerves (face/head), spinal nerves to the body; sensory (in), motor (out), and autonomic (automatic — heart, gut).

structures.name: Protection
structures.detail: Skull, vertebrae, meninges (membranes), and cerebrospinal fluid.

anatomy.normal: Clear thinking, normal speech, equal strength and sensation on both sides, steady balance, equal reactive pupils, normal coordination.
common_problems: Stroke/TIA, seizures, migraine, meningitis, concussion/head injury, Parkinson's, dementia, MS, neuropathy, Bell's palsy, Guillain-Barré, brain tumour.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Glands & hormones
anatomy.overview: The endocrine system is a set of glands that release hormones into the blood to control slow, body-wide processes — metabolism, growth, stress, reproduction, and blood sugar.

structures.name: Pituitary
structures.detail: 'Master gland' at the brain's base — directs other glands.

structures.name: Thyroid
structures.detail: Neck gland setting metabolic rate (energy, temperature, weight).

structures.name: Adrenals
structures.detail: Atop the kidneys — stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline), salt/water balance.

structures.name: Pancreas (islets)
structures.detail: Insulin and glucagon — control blood sugar.

structures.name: Gonads
structures.detail: Ovaries/testes — sex hormones.

structures.name: Parathyroids
structures.detail: Calcium balance.

anatomy.normal: Stable energy, weight, temperature tolerance, mood, and blood sugar; normal growth and periods.
common_problems: Diabetes, hypo/hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency (Addison's)/excess (Cushing's), PCOS, pituitary disorders.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Kidneys & bladder
anatomy.overview: The urinary system filters the blood, removes waste and extra water as urine, and balances salts, fluid, and blood pressure.

structures.name: Kidneys
structures.detail: Two bean-shaped organs (flank/back) filtering blood into urine and controlling fluid, salts, and blood pressure.

structures.name: Ureters
structures.detail: Tubes carrying urine from each kidney to the bladder.

structures.name: Bladder
structures.detail: Muscular storage sac that signals when full.

structures.name: Urethra
structures.detail: Tube that carries urine out (longer in males, passing the prostate).

anatomy.normal: Passing urine comfortably several times a day, pale-yellow, no blood, no burning, good control, no flank pain.
common_problems: UTI, kidney infection, kidney stones, chronic kidney disease, incontinence, retention, bladder/kidney cancer, enlarged prostate (affects flow).
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Skin, hair & nails
anatomy.overview: The skin is the body's largest organ — a waterproof barrier that protects, senses touch, controls temperature, and makes vitamin D.

structures.name: Epidermis
structures.detail: Thin outer layer — barrier and pigment (melanin).

structures.name: Dermis
structures.detail: Deeper layer with nerves, blood vessels, sweat and oil glands, hair roots, collagen.

structures.name: Subcutaneous fat
structures.detail: Insulation and cushioning beneath.

structures.name: Appendages
structures.detail: Hair, nails, sweat glands, sebaceous (oil) glands.

anatomy.normal: Intact, even-toned for the person, no spreading redness, non-healing sores, or changing moles; warm and well-perfused.
common_problems: Eczema, psoriasis, cellulitis, abscess, shingles, impetigo, hives, fungal infections, skin cancer/melanoma, pressure sores.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Lymph nodes, spleen & defence
anatomy.overview: The lymphatic system drains fluid from tissues, filters it through lymph nodes, and is central to the immune defence against infection.

structures.name: Lymph nodes
structures.detail: Small filters clustered in the neck, armpits, groin, chest, and abdomen — swell when fighting infection.

structures.name: Spleen
structures.detail: LUQ organ that filters blood and supports immunity (can be injured/enlarged).

structures.name: Thymus & marrow
structures.detail: Make and train immune cells.

structures.name: Tonsils/adenoids
structures.detail: Immune tissue guarding the throat.

anatomy.normal: Nodes usually not felt, or small, soft, mobile, and briefly tender with a nearby infection; no drenching night sweats or unexplained weight loss.
common_problems: Reactive swollen glands (infection), glandular fever, lymphoma, leukaemia, enlarged/ruptured spleen, immune deficiency.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Eyes, ears, nose & tongue
anatomy.overview: The special senses gather information about the world: sight, hearing and balance, smell, and taste.

structures.name: Eye
structures.detail: Cornea and lens focus light onto the retina; the iris sets pupil size; the optic nerve carries images to the brain.

structures.name: Ear
structures.detail: Outer ear → eardrum → middle-ear bones → cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance).

structures.name: Nose
structures.detail: Smell receptors high in the nose; also warms and filters air.

structures.name: Tongue
structures.detail: Taste buds (sweet, salt, sour, bitter, umami) and helps speech and swallowing.

anatomy.normal: Clear vision, equal reactive pupils, normal hearing and balance, normal smell and taste.
common_problems: Conjunctivitis, glaucoma, retinal detachment, ear infections, hearing loss, vertigo (inner ear), sinus problems, loss of smell/taste.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Female reproductive anatomy
anatomy.overview: The adult female reproductive system produces eggs and sex hormones, supports menstruation, and carries a pregnancy. (Educational/clinical reference.)

structures.name: Ovaries
structures.detail: Two glands that release an egg each cycle and make oestrogen and progesterone.

structures.name: Fallopian tubes
structures.detail: Carry the egg toward the uterus; usual site of fertilisation (and of ectopic pregnancy if it implants there).

structures.name: Uterus (womb)
structures.detail: Muscular organ whose lining builds up and sheds each month, and where a pregnancy grows; the cervix is its neck.

structures.name: Vagina & vulva
structures.detail: The vagina connects the cervix to the outside; the vulva is the external genital area.

structures.name: Menstrual cycle
structures.detail: ~21–35 days: lining thickens, an egg is released (ovulation ~mid-cycle), then the lining sheds (period) if no pregnancy.

structures.name: Breasts
structures.detail: Glandular tissue for milk, plus ducts and fat.

anatomy.normal: Regular-for-the-person cycles, no bleeding between periods/after sex/after menopause, no new breast lump or nipple change, no severe pelvic pain.
common_problems: Period problems, endometriosis, PCOS, fibroids, ovarian cysts, PID, ectopic pregnancy, menopause symptoms, cervical/uterine/ovarian/breast cancer.
Bleeding after menopause, or a new breast lump, should always be checked.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: Male reproductive anatomy
anatomy.overview: The adult male reproductive system makes sperm and sex hormones and delivers them. It overlaps with the urinary tract (shared urethra). (Educational/clinical reference.)

structures.name: Testes
structures.detail: Two glands in the scrotum that make sperm and testosterone; kept cooler than body temperature.

structures.name: Epididymis & vas deferens
structures.detail: Store and carry sperm.

structures.name: Prostate
structures.detail: Gland below the bladder surrounding the urethra; adds fluid to semen and can enlarge with age and affect urine flow.

structures.name: Penis & urethra
structures.detail: The urethra carries both urine and semen; erectile tissue fills with blood for an erection.

structures.name: Seminal vesicles
structures.detail: Add most of the fluid in semen.

anatomy.normal: Comfortable, symmetrical testes with no new lump; a normal urine stream; no pain, discharge, or blood in urine/semen.
common_problems: Testicular torsion (sudden severe pain — emergency) or lump (needs checking), epididymitis, prostatitis, enlarged prostate (BPH), erectile problems, STIs, testicular/prostate cancer.
anatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original anatomy reference (standard public-domain anatomy, re-expressed)

anatomy.title: The heart — chambers, valves & vessels
anatomy.overview: The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump about the size of a fist, sitting slightly left of centre behind the breastbone.

structures.name: Four chambers
structures.detail: Two upper atria (receiving) and two lower ventricles (pumping). The right side sends blood to the lungs; the left side (thicker) sends it to the body.

structures.name: Four valves
structures.detail: Tricuspid and mitral (between atria and ventricles) and pulmonary and aortic (exits). They keep blood moving one way.

structures.name: Coronary arteries
structures.detail: Supply the heart muscle itself; a blockage causes a heart attack.

structures.name: Conduction system
structures.detail: The SA node sets the pace; signals travel to the AV node and through the ventricles to coordinate each beat.

anatomy.title: The brain — major regions
anatomy.overview: The brain is the control centre, protected by the skull and cushioned in cerebrospinal fluid.

structures.name: Cerebrum
structures.detail: The large wrinkled part; its lobes handle thinking, movement, sensation, vision, language and personality.

structures.name: Cerebellum
structures.detail: At the back/base; coordinates balance and fine movement.

structures.name: Brainstem
structures.detail: Connects to the spinal cord and controls automatic functions — breathing, heart rate, blood pressure.

structures.name: Limbic system
structures.detail: Deep structures (hippocampus, amygdala) for memory and emotion.

anatomy.title: The lungs — airways & air sacs
anatomy.overview: Two lungs fill most of the chest; air reaches them through a branching tree of airways.

structures.name: Trachea & bronchi
structures.detail: The windpipe divides into two main bronchi, then smaller and smaller branches (bronchioles).

structures.name: Alveoli
structures.detail: Hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves.

structures.name: Pleura
structures.detail: A double membrane around each lung that lets it glide as you breathe.

structures.name: Diaphragm
structures.detail: The dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that drives breathing.

anatomy.title: The kidney — nephrons & filtration
anatomy.overview: Two bean-shaped kidneys filter the blood, balance fluids and salts, and make urine.

structures.name: Nephron
structures.detail: The filtering unit — about a million per kidney. Each has a glomerulus (filter) and a tubule (fine-tunes what's kept or excreted).

structures.name: Cortex & medulla
structures.detail: The outer cortex and inner medulla house the nephrons and collecting ducts.

structures.name: Renal pelvis & ureter
structures.detail: Collect urine and carry it to the bladder.

anatomy.title: The liver — the body's chemical plant
anatomy.overview: The liver is the largest internal organ, in the upper right abdomen, doing hundreds of jobs.

structures.name: Lobules
structures.detail: Functional units of liver cells (hepatocytes) that process blood from the gut.

structures.name: Key jobs
structures.detail: Filters toxins and drugs, makes bile for digestion, stores glucose as glycogen, makes clotting proteins, and processes fats and proteins.

structures.name: Bile ducts & gallbladder
structures.detail: Bile drains to the gallbladder (storage) and into the intestine to help absorb fats.

anatomy.title: Stomach & intestines
anatomy.overview: The gut is a long muscular tube that breaks down food, absorbs nutrients, and forms waste.

structures.name: Stomach
structures.detail: A muscular bag that churns food and adds acid and enzymes.

structures.name: Small intestine
structures.detail: Duodenum, jejunum, ileum — most nutrient absorption happens here across a vast lining of villi.

structures.name: Large intestine (colon)
structures.detail: Absorbs water and salts and forms stool; home to the gut microbiome.

anatomy.title: The eye
anatomy.overview: The eye focuses light onto light-sensing cells and sends signals to the brain.

structures.name: Cornea & lens
structures.detail: The clear front (cornea) and the adjustable lens bend light to focus it.

structures.name: Retina
structures.detail: The light-sensing layer at the back; rods (dim light) and cones (colour) convert light to nerve signals.

structures.name: Optic nerve
structures.detail: Carries the signals to the brain's visual cortex.

structures.name: Pupil & iris
structures.detail: The iris adjusts the pupil to control how much light enters.

anatomy.title: The ear — hearing & balance
anatomy.overview: The ear turns sound into nerve signals and helps you keep your balance.

structures.name: Outer & middle ear
structures.detail: The ear canal funnels sound to the eardrum; three tiny bones amplify it.

structures.name: Cochlea
structures.detail: A fluid-filled spiral where hair cells convert vibrations into nerve signals.

structures.name: Vestibular system
structures.detail: Semicircular canals sense head movement for balance.

anatomy.title: Blood — what it's made of
phrases: red cells white cells platelets plasma
anatomy.overview: Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, heat and immune cells, and removes waste.

structures.name: Red blood cells
structures.detail: Carry oxygen using haemoglobin; low numbers = anaemia.

structures.name: White blood cells
structures.detail: Fight infection — several types for different threats.

structures.name: Platelets
structures.detail: Cell fragments that start clots to stop bleeding.

structures.name: Plasma
structures.detail: The liquid (mostly water) carrying proteins, salts, nutrients and clotting factors.

anatomy.title: The spine & spinal cord
anatomy.overview: The spine supports the body and protects the spinal cord, the main nerve highway.

structures.name: Vertebrae
structures.detail: 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (chest), 5 lumbar (low back), then the sacrum and coccyx.

structures.name: Discs
structures.detail: Cushions between vertebrae; a 'slipped' (herniated) disc can press on a nerve.

structures.name: Spinal cord & nerve roots
structures.detail: Carries signals between brain and body; nerve roots branch out at each level.

anatomy.title: The pancreas
anatomy.overview: The pancreas sits behind the stomach and has two jobs — digestion and blood-sugar control.

structures.name: Exocrine part
structures.detail: Makes digestive enzymes released into the intestine.

structures.name: Islets of Langerhans
structures.detail: Make insulin (lowers blood sugar) and glucagon (raises it).

anatomy.title: Immune organs — spleen, thymus, nodes, marrow
phrases: spleen thymus lymph nodes bone marrow
anatomy.overview: The immune system is spread through several organs that make, train and deploy defence cells.

structures.name: Bone marrow
structures.detail: Makes blood and immune cells.

structures.name: Thymus
structures.detail: Trains T-cells (most active in childhood).

structures.name: Lymph nodes
structures.detail: Filter lymph and trap germs — they swell when fighting infection.

structures.name: Spleen
structures.detail: Filters blood, recycles old red cells, and stores immune cells.

anatomy.title: Thyroid & parathyroid glands
anatomy.overview: A butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that sets the body's metabolic pace, with four tiny glands behind it controlling calcium.

structures.name: Thyroid
structures.detail: Makes thyroid hormones (T3/T4) that regulate metabolism, energy, and temperature.

structures.name: Parathyroids
structures.detail: Four small glands that release parathyroid hormone to keep blood calcium in range.

anatomy.title: Adrenal glands
anatomy.overview: Two small glands sitting on top of the kidneys that make hormones for stress, salt/water balance, and metabolism.

structures.name: Cortex (outer)
structures.detail: Makes cortisol (stress/metabolism), aldosterone (salt/water), and some sex hormones.

structures.name: Medulla (inner)
structures.detail: Makes adrenaline and noradrenaline for the 'fight-or-flight' response.

anatomy.title: Pituitary gland & hypothalamus
anatomy.overview: At the base of the brain, this duo links the nervous and hormonal systems and directs many other glands.

structures.name: Hypothalamus
structures.detail: Monitors the body and signals the pituitary; controls temperature, hunger, thirst, and the body clock.

structures.name: Pituitary ('master gland')
structures.detail: Releases hormones that control the thyroid, adrenals, growth, reproduction, and water balance.

anatomy.title: Bladder & urethra
anatomy.overview: The bladder stores urine; the urethra carries it out. Muscles and sphincters give you control.

structures.name: Bladder
structures.detail: A muscular, stretchy sac that stores urine and contracts to empty.

structures.name: Sphincters
structures.detail: Rings of muscle that hold urine in until you choose to go.

structures.name: Urethra
structures.detail: The tube out; longer in males (passing through the prostate), shorter in females.

anatomy.title: The breast
anatomy.overview: Breasts contain milk-producing glands, ducts, fat, and connective tissue, overlying the chest muscles.

structures.name: Lobules & ducts
structures.detail: Lobules make milk; ducts carry it to the nipple.

structures.name: Fat & connective tissue
structures.detail: Give shape and support; proportion varies by person and age.

structures.name: Lymph nodes
structures.detail: Nearby (especially in the armpit) — important in breast-cancer spread.

anatomy.title: Mouth, teeth & salivary glands
anatomy.overview: The mouth starts digestion with chewing and saliva, and is key to speech.

structures.name: Teeth
structures.detail: Incisors cut, canines tear, molars grind; adults have 32 (including wisdom teeth).

structures.name: Salivary glands
structures.detail: Release saliva to moisten food and begin starch breakdown.

structures.name: Tongue
structures.detail: Moves food, holds taste buds, and shapes speech.

anatomy.title: Throat, larynx & vocal cords
anatomy.overview: The throat (pharynx) is a shared path for air and food; the larynx (voice box) protects the airway and produces voice.

structures.name: Pharynx
structures.detail: Routes food to the oesophagus and air to the larynx.

structures.name: Epiglottis
structures.detail: A flap that covers the airway when you swallow, preventing choking.

structures.name: Vocal cords
structures.detail: Vibrate as air passes to make voice.

anatomy.title: Nose & sinuses
anatomy.overview: The nose warms, moistens, and filters air and houses smell; the sinuses are air-filled spaces in the skull.

structures.name: Nasal passages
structures.detail: Lined with mucous membranes and tiny hairs that trap particles.

structures.name: Sinuses
structures.detail: Hollow spaces that lighten the skull and add resonance; can become blocked/infected.

structures.name: Olfactory area
structures.detail: Smell receptors high in the nose.

anatomy.title: The shoulder
anatomy.overview: The shoulder is the body's most mobile joint, trading stability for a huge range of motion.

structures.name: Ball-and-socket joint
structures.detail: The upper-arm bone sits in a shallow socket of the shoulder blade.

structures.name: Rotator cuff
structures.detail: Four muscles/tendons that hold the joint in place and move the arm — commonly injured.

structures.name: Labrum
structures.detail: A rim of cartilage deepening the socket.

anatomy.title: The knee
anatomy.overview: The knee is a hinge joint bearing great loads, stabilized by ligaments and cushioned by cartilage.

structures.name: Ligaments (ACL/PCL/MCL/LCL)
structures.detail: Stabilize the joint; the ACL is a common sports injury.

structures.name: Menisci
structures.detail: Two C-shaped cartilage cushions that absorb shock.

structures.name: Cartilage
structures.detail: Smooth surface that lets the joint glide; wears in osteoarthritis.

anatomy.title: The hip
anatomy.overview: The hip is a deep, stable ball-and-socket joint connecting the leg to the pelvis, built for weight-bearing.

structures.name: Ball-and-socket
structures.detail: The femur head fits deep into the pelvis socket (acetabulum).
