structures.name: Cartilage & labrum
structures.detail: Cushion and deepen the joint.

structures.name: Common issues
structures.detail: Arthritis and fractures (especially in older adults) often affect the hip.

anatomy.title: Hand & wrist
anatomy.overview: The hand's many small bones, joints, tendons, and nerves allow precise, powerful movement.

structures.name: Bones
structures.detail: 8 carpal (wrist) bones, 5 metacarpals (palm), and 14 phalanges (fingers).

structures.name: Carpal tunnel
structures.detail: A wrist passage for the median nerve — compression causes carpal tunnel syndrome.

structures.name: Tendons
structures.detail: Run from forearm muscles to move the fingers.

anatomy.title: Foot & ankle
anatomy.overview: The foot's 26 bones and arches support the body and absorb shock when walking.

structures.name: Arches
structures.detail: Distribute weight and act as springs.

structures.name: Plantar fascia
structures.detail: A band along the sole; inflammation causes plantar fasciitis.

structures.name: Achilles tendon
structures.detail: Connects the calf to the heel — powerful but prone to injury.

anatomy.title: Major blood vessels
anatomy.overview: A network of vessels carries blood from the heart to the body and back.

structures.name: Arteries
structures.detail: Carry oxygen-rich blood away from the heart under high pressure (aorta is the largest).

structures.name: Veins
structures.detail: Return blood to the heart; have valves to prevent backflow.

structures.name: Capillaries
structures.detail: Tiny vessels where oxygen, nutrients, and waste exchange with tissues.

anatomy.title: Cranial nerves & peripheral nerves
anatomy.overview: Nerves carry signals between the brain/spinal cord and the body.

structures.name: Cranial nerves
structures.detail: 12 pairs from the brain controlling senses and head/neck functions (e.g., the facial and optic nerves).

structures.name: Peripheral nerves
structures.detail: Carry motor commands out and sensory signals in.

structures.name: Autonomic nerves
structures.detail: Run automatic functions (heart rate, digestion) without conscious control.

anatomy.title: Diaphragm & abdominal wall
anatomy.overview: The diaphragm drives breathing; the abdominal wall protects organs and supports the trunk.

structures.name: Diaphragm
structures.detail: A dome muscle that contracts to pull air in; the main breathing muscle.

structures.name: Abdominal wall
structures.detail: Layered muscles that protect organs, aid breathing, and stabilize the spine.

structures.name: Weak points
structures.detail: Natural gaps where hernias can occur (groin, navel).

anatomy.title: Abdominal lining & mesentery
anatomy.overview: A smooth membrane lines the abdomen and suspends the gut, letting organs glide.

structures.name: Peritoneum
structures.detail: The lining of the abdominal cavity; its inflammation (peritonitis) is serious.

structures.name: Mesentery
structures.detail: A fold that anchors the intestines and carries their blood vessels and nerves.

anatomy.title: The gut microbiome
anatomy.overview: Trillions of microbes in the gut aid digestion, make some vitamins, and train the immune system.

structures.name: What it does
structures.detail: Ferments fibre, produces vitamins (like K and some B), and crowds out harmful germs.

structures.name: Balance
structures.detail: Antibiotics, diet, and illness can disrupt it, affecting digestion and immunity.

physiology.how_it_works: The body constantly holds its internal conditions — temperature, blood sugar, fluid, salts, pH, oxygen, blood pressure — within narrow safe ranges. Sensors detect a change, a control centre compares it to a 'set point', and effectors (muscles, glands, organs) push it back. Most control is by NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: a rise triggers a response that lowers it, and vice-versa, like a thermostat.
physiology.timing: Continuous, second-to-second.
physiology.why_it_matters: Illness is often homeostasis failing or being overwhelmed. Many emergencies are a value pushed far out of range (very low oxygen, very low/high sugar, very high temperature). The engine reasons by asking: which balance is off, and how far?
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: A master clock in the brain (the suprachiasmatic nucleus), set mainly by light, runs a ~24-hour cycle that times nearly everything. Darkness raises melatonin (sleep signal); morning light stops it and lifts cortisol to wake and energise. Body temperature, blood pressure, hormone release, alertness, and digestion all follow this daily wave.
physiology.timing: 24-hour cycle. Cortisol peaks early morning; melatonin rises in the evening and peaks ~2–4 am; core temperature is lowest ~4–5 am and highest early evening; blood pressure usually dips at night; alertness dips mid-afternoon and in the pre-dawn hours.
physiology.why_it_matters: Timing matters clinically: heart attacks and strokes cluster in the morning (as BP and clotting rise); asthma often worsens overnight; fever naturally runs higher in the evening; blood sugar can rise before waking ('dawn effect'). Shift work and jet lag disrupt the clock and affect sleep, mood, and metabolism.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Sleep cycles through light sleep, deep (slow-wave) sleep, and REM (dreaming) roughly every 90 minutes. Deep sleep repairs the body and consolidates memory and immunity; REM supports learning and mood. Adults need ~7–9 hours; children and teens need more.
physiology.timing: ~90-minute cycles through the night; deep sleep dominates early night, REM lengthens toward morning.
physiology.why_it_matters: Poor or short sleep worsens concentration, mood, immunity, blood sugar control, blood pressure, and pain. Insomnia, sleep apnoea (breathing pauses), and shift work are common and treatable causes of daytime problems.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: The body holds core temperature near 37°C. When hot, blood vessels in the skin widen and sweating cools by evaporation; when cold, vessels narrow and shivering makes heat. The brain's hypothalamus is the thermostat. In infection, it deliberately raises the set point — that's a FEVER, which helps fight infection.
physiology.timing: Follows the daily rhythm (lowest pre-dawn, highest early evening); a fever often spikes in the evening.
physiology.why_it_matters: Heat stroke (cooling fails — an emergency) and hypothermia (heat loss wins) are both dangerous. A fever is a response, not a disease; how unwell the person is matters more than the number.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: After eating, the pancreas releases INSULIN, which moves glucose from the blood into cells for energy or storage, lowering blood sugar. When fasting, it releases GLUCAGON, which frees stored glucose to keep levels up. The two balance blood sugar in a safe range (~4–7 mmol/L fasting).
physiology.timing: Rises after meals, falls between; can rise before waking (the 'dawn phenomenon').
physiology.why_it_matters: In diabetes this control fails — too little insulin or resistance to it. Too LOW (under 4 mmol/L) is an urgent, treat-now problem (confusion, collapse); very HIGH with vomiting and deep breathing can be ketoacidosis — an emergency.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Blood pressure is set by how hard the heart pumps and how tight the vessels are. Fast sensors (baroreceptors in the neck/aorta) adjust heart rate and vessel tone second-to-second; the kidneys control it over hours-to-days by managing salt and water (the renin-angiotensin system).
physiology.timing: Usually dips at night and rises in the morning.
physiology.why_it_matters: Too high over years damages the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes silently; a sudden drop causes fainting; a very high reading with symptoms (chest pain, breathlessness, vision/speech change) signals organ strain — an emergency.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: The body keeps water and salts (sodium, potassium) in balance. When fluid is low, the brain triggers thirst and releases ADH, telling the kidneys to save water (urine gets darker and scanter). When there's plenty, the kidneys pass more dilute urine.
physiology.timing: Needs rise with heat, exercise, pregnancy, breastfeeding, fever, vomiting, and diarrhoea.
physiology.why_it_matters: Dehydration (losses outpace intake) causes dizziness, dark/low urine, and — if severe — drowsiness and shock, fastest in babies and older adults. Salt imbalances can cause confusion, weakness, or dangerous heart rhythms.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Blood is kept slightly alkaline (pH ~7.35–7.45). The lungs adjust it fast by changing how much carbon dioxide (an acid) is breathed out; the kidneys adjust it slowly by handling bicarbonate and acids.
physiology.timing: Lungs respond in minutes (breathing rate), kidneys over hours-to-days.
physiology.why_it_matters: Serious illness often shifts pH: fast deep breathing can be the body blowing off acid (as in diabetic ketoacidosis or sepsis). Very slow breathing lets acid build up. Breathing rate is a key clue the engine watches.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

phrases: how oxygen gets to the body
physiology.how_it_works: Oxygen crosses from the lungs' air sacs into the blood, binds to haemoglobin in red cells, and is carried to tissues; carbon dioxide (waste) travels back and is breathed out. The heart drives the circuit; breathing rate and depth adjust to demand.
physiology.timing: Breathing speeds within seconds of exertion or low oxygen.
physiology.why_it_matters: Anaemia (low haemoglobin), lung disease, or heart failure reduce oxygen delivery — causing breathlessness and fatigue. An oxygen level under 92% signals the system is failing and needs urgent care.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Metabolism is how the body turns food into energy and building blocks. After eating (fed state), it stores energy (as glycogen and fat). Between meals (fasting state), it releases stored energy to keep going. A baseline rate (basal metabolism) keeps organs running even at rest.
physiology.timing: Shifts with each meal and fast; basal rate runs continuously and follows the daily rhythm.
physiology.why_it_matters: Thyroid hormones set the pace (over- or under-active thyroid speeds or slows it). Starvation, illness, and some conditions shift the balance — unexplained weight loss or gain can be a clue.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: A threat triggers a fast nerve surge of adrenaline (racing heart, fast breathing, wide pupils, energy released) and a slower rise of cortisol. This is protective for short bursts.
physiology.timing: Adrenaline acts in seconds; cortisol over minutes-to-hours and follows the daily rhythm (highest in the morning).
physiology.why_it_matters: Sustained stress raises blood pressure and blood sugar and disturbs sleep, mood, and the gut. A panic attack is this system firing without a real threat — intense but not dangerous — and can mimic heart or lung emergencies, which is why a first episode is checked.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Defence has two arms: INNATE immunity acts immediately (skin barrier, inflammation, white cells that engulf invaders); ADAPTIVE immunity is slower but specific (antibodies and memory cells that recognise a germ next time — the basis of vaccines).
physiology.timing: Innate responds in minutes-to-hours; adaptive over days, with lasting memory.
physiology.why_it_matters: Fever, swollen glands, and tiredness are the immune system at work. Too weak a response (immune deficiency) means frequent/severe infection; an overactive one causes allergies and autoimmune disease.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Injury or infection triggers inflammation — redness, heat, swelling, and pain — as blood flow and immune cells rush in to clean up and start repair. Healing then rebuilds tissue (clotting, new tissue, remodelling over weeks).
physiology.timing: Inflammation within minutes-to-hours; healing over days-to-weeks (longer for bone).
physiology.why_it_matters: Helpful short-term, harmful when chronic (as in arthritis). Spreading redness, increasing pain, pus, or fever can mean infection is winning — a reason to seek care.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Pain is a protective alarm. Sensors detect damage or threat and send signals up the nerves and spinal cord to the brain, which interprets them. Pain can be sharp and local (tissue damage), or burning/tingling (nerve), or deep and hard to localise (organs — 'referred' pain can be felt elsewhere, e.g., heart pain in the arm/jaw).
physiology.timing: Near-instant for acute pain; can persist and change if it becomes chronic.
physiology.why_it_matters: Where, how, and what pattern pain takes is a major clue the engine uses — e.g., migrating belly pain for appendicitis, crushing chest pain spreading to the arm for the heart.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.topic: How the body changes with age
physiology.how_it_works: The body changes across life: rapid growth and development in childhood and the teens, a long stable adulthood, then gradual decline — muscle and bone slowly reduce, senses dull, the heart and vessels stiffen, the immune response and healing slow, and thirst and temperature sense blunt in later years.
physiology.timing: A lifelong arc; most decline is gradual from mid-life onward.
physiology.why_it_matters: The same illness looks different by age: children compensate then crash fast; older adults may show infection as confusion or falls rather than fever. The engine weighs age — babies and older adults are higher-risk.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: In females, a roughly monthly hormone cycle thickens the womb lining, releases an egg (ovulation ~mid-cycle), and sheds the lining (a period) if there's no pregnancy. If fertilised, the egg implants and pregnancy hormones sustain it; the body adapts over ~40 weeks. In males, sperm and testosterone are produced continuously.
physiology.timing: ~21–35 day female cycle; pregnancy ~40 weeks; male production is continuous.
physiology.why_it_matters: Timing drives fertility and explains symptoms (cycle-related pain, pregnancy sickness). Bleeding after menopause, or one-sided pain with a positive pregnancy test, are red flags the engine escalates.
physiology.source: HIVE Doctor original physiology reference (standard public-domain physiology, re-expressed)

physiology.how_it_works: Food is broken down mechanically (chewing, stomach churning) and chemically (enzymes and acid) into small molecules — sugars, amino acids, fatty acids — that cross the gut lining into the blood and lymph. The liver processes much of what's absorbed; the colon reclaims water and forms stool.
physiology.timing: Hours — stomach emptying ~2–4h, full transit ~1–3 days.
physiology.why_it_matters: Problems here cause malnutrition, reflux, bloating, or diarrhoea/constipation.

physiology.how_it_works: The diaphragm contracts to pull air into the lungs. In the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out, driven by differences in gas concentration. Breathing rate is tuned mainly by CO2 levels sensed in the brainstem.
physiology.timing: Continuous; ~12–20 breaths/min at rest.
physiology.why_it_matters: Failure shows as breathlessness, low oxygen, or dangerous CO2 build-up.

physiology.how_it_works: Each beat has the atria fill and contract, then the ventricles contract (systole) to eject blood, then relax (diastole) to refill. An electrical signal from the SA node coordinates the timing; valves snap shut to make the 'lub-dub' sounds.
physiology.timing: ~60–100 beats/min at rest.
physiology.why_it_matters: Rhythm or pump problems cause palpitations, fainting, or heart failure.

physiology.how_it_works: Blood is filtered in the glomerulus; the tubule then reabsorbs most of the water, salts and glucose the body needs and secretes wastes, producing urine. Hormones (ADH, aldosterone) fine-tune water and salt to control blood pressure and balance.
physiology.timing: The kidneys filter the body's blood volume many times a day.
physiology.why_it_matters: Failing filtration causes waste build-up, swelling, and blood-pressure and electrolyte problems.

physiology.how_it_works: A cut triggers vessels to narrow, platelets to plug the gap, and a cascade of clotting factors to weave a fibrin mesh that stabilises the clot. The body later dissolves the clot as the wound heals.
physiology.timing: Platelet plug in minutes; stable clot in ~5–10 min.
physiology.why_it_matters: Too little clotting causes bleeding; too much causes dangerous clots (DVT, stroke, heart attack).

physiology.how_it_works: A nerve cell fires an electrical impulse down its length; at the gap (synapse) to the next cell it releases chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) that pass the signal on. Myelin insulation speeds the impulse.
physiology.timing: Milliseconds.
physiology.why_it_matters: Disruptions underlie numbness, weakness, seizures, and many brain conditions.

physiology.how_it_works: Glands release hormones into the blood to act on distant organs. Most are controlled by negative feedback: when the target level is reached, the signal to make more shuts off. The brain's hypothalamus and pituitary direct many glands.
physiology.timing: Seconds (adrenaline) to days (thyroid).
physiology.why_it_matters: Too much or too little of a hormone causes conditions like thyroid disease or diabetes.

physiology.how_it_works: The innate immune system responds fast and generally; the adaptive system learns a specific germ and makes antibodies and memory cells, so a second exposure is cleared quickly. Vaccines teach this memory safely using a harmless piece or copy of a germ.
physiology.timing: Days to build a first response; memory lasts years.
physiology.why_it_matters: It's why we recover from and resist infections, and why vaccination prevents disease.

physiology.how_it_works: A nerve signal triggers calcium release inside the muscle fibre; protein filaments (actin and myosin) ratchet past each other to shorten the muscle, using energy (ATP). Muscles pull on bones across joints to create movement.
physiology.timing: Milliseconds to contract.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains cramps, weakness, and fatigue, and why electrolytes and energy matter.

physiology.how_it_works: Cells break down glucose and other fuels, mostly using oxygen in the mitochondria, to make ATP — the body's energy currency. Without enough oxygen, cells switch to a less efficient path that produces lactic acid.
physiology.timing: Continuous.
physiology.why_it_matters: It's why oxygen and fuel (food) are essential, and why tissues die when blood flow is cut off.

physiology.how_it_works: Sound waves vibrate the eardrum; three tiny bones amplify them into the fluid-filled cochlea, where hair cells convert the vibrations into nerve signals the brain interprets as sound.
physiology.timing: Instant.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains hearing loss (damaged hair cells or blocked/stiff bones) and why loud noise is harmful.

physiology.how_it_works: Light passes through the cornea and lens, which focus it onto the retina; rods and cones convert light to signals sent via the optic nerve to the brain, which assembles the image.
physiology.timing: Instant.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains blurriness (focusing errors), colour vision, and night vision.

physiology.how_it_works: Fluid and sensors in the inner ear detect head position and movement; combined with vision and sensors in muscles/joints, the brain keeps you balanced.
physiology.timing: Continuous.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains dizziness and vertigo when the system is disturbed.

physiology.how_it_works: Smell receptors in the nose and taste buds on the tongue detect chemicals; the brain blends them into flavour. Most 'taste' is actually smell.
physiology.timing: Instant.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains why food is bland with a blocked nose and why smell loss matters.

physiology.how_it_works: Bone is living tissue constantly broken down by one cell type and rebuilt by another, guided by load, calcium, vitamin D, and hormones. A fracture heals through clot, soft callus, hard callus, then remodelling.
physiology.timing: Healing weeks to months; renewal lifelong.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains osteoporosis (breakdown outpaces building) and why weight-bearing exercise strengthens bone.

physiology.how_it_works: Minerals like sodium, potassium, and calcium carry electrical charge that drives nerve signals and muscle contractions; the kidneys and hormones keep them in tight ranges.
physiology.timing: Continuous.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains cramps, weakness, and dangerous heart rhythms when levels are off (from dehydration, vomiting, or kidney issues).

physiology.topic: How the liver processes drugs & toxins
physiology.how_it_works: The liver chemically changes drugs, alcohol, and wastes into forms the body can remove, and clears them via bile or the kidneys. Its capacity is limited and shared across substances.
physiology.timing: Minutes to hours per substance.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains why alcohol and some drug combinations are dangerous, and why liver disease changes how medicines act.

physiology.how_it_works: A reflex (like pulling off a hot stove) travels from a sensor to the spinal cord and straight back to muscles, skipping the brain for speed; the brain is informed after.
physiology.timing: Fractions of a second.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains protective reactions and why doctors test reflexes to check nerve function.

physiology.how_it_works: Experiences strengthen connections between brain cells; short-term memories can consolidate into long-term storage, especially during sleep, involving the hippocampus.
physiology.timing: Seconds to a lifetime.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains why sleep and repetition aid learning, and what's lost in dementia.

physiology.how_it_works: Bone marrow continuously produces red cells, white cells, and platelets from stem cells, tuned by signals (e.g., low oxygen boosts red-cell production).
physiology.timing: Red cells live ~120 days; constant renewal.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains anaemia, infection-fighting, and why marrow problems (or chemo) affect all blood cells.

physiology.how_it_works: Most of the body is water, split between inside cells and outside (blood and tissue fluid). Salts and proteins pull water across membranes, and the kidneys and thirst keep the total balanced.
physiology.timing: Continuous.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains swelling (oedema), dehydration, and why salt and kidney function affect fluid.

physiology.how_it_works: Growth hormone and, in puberty, sex hormones drive the body's growth and maturation, including the growth spurt and development of adult features, until growth plates in bones close.
physiology.timing: Years.
physiology.why_it_matters: Explains childhood growth monitoring and the changes of adolescence.

microanatomy.scale: whole body → organ → tissue → CELL → organelle

layers.detail: A thin oily barrier controlling what enters and leaves the cell.
The jelly interior where reactions happen and organelles sit.
The control centre holding DNA (the genetic instructions).
The 'power plants' that make energy (ATP) — plentiful in busy cells like heart and muscle.
Build and fold proteins.
Packages and ships proteins.
Recycling and clean-up units.

microanatomy.function: The cell is the smallest living unit; trillions of specialised cells build every tissue and organ.
microanatomy.clinical: Many diseases start at the cell: too little energy (mitochondrial problems), uncontrolled division (cancer), or cell death from lost blood supply (a heart attack is heart-muscle cells dying).
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: organ surface → epithelial sheet → epithelial cells

layers.detail: Covers surfaces and lines cavities, glands, and vessels — a barrier and a gateway.
Squamous (flat — for exchange, e.g. air sacs), cuboidal, columnar (tall — lining the gut), and glandular (secreting).
Tightly joined cells sitting on a basement membrane; they renew quickly.

microanatomy.function: Protection, absorption, secretion, and filtration happen at epithelial surfaces.
microanatomy.clinical: Most cancers (carcinomas) arise from epithelium. Barrier breakdown lets in infection.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: body framework → connective tissue → fibres + cells + matrix

layers.detail: Supports, binds, and protects — the body's scaffolding and packing.
Loose/fatty tissue, dense fibrous (tendons, ligaments), cartilage, bone, and blood (a fluid connective tissue).
Cells scattered in a matrix of fibres (collagen, elastin) and ground substance.

microanatomy.function: Holds the body together, cushions, stores energy (fat), and (as blood) transports.
microanatomy.clinical: Collagen disorders weaken joints and vessels; cartilage wear causes osteoarthritis.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: muscle → fascicle → muscle fibre → myofibril → actin/myosin

layers.detail: Skeletal (voluntary, striped), cardiac (heart, striped, automatic), smooth (organs/vessels, automatic).
A long muscle cell packed with myofibrils.
Repeating units (sarcomeres) of the proteins actin and myosin.
Myosin pulls on actin (powered by ATP and triggered by calcium), shortening the fibre.

microanatomy.function: Generates movement, pumps blood, and moves contents through organs.
microanatomy.clinical: Loss of blood supply kills muscle (heart attack); breakdown releases contents (rhabdomyolysis); nerve/calcium problems cause weakness or cramps.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: nervous system → nerve → neuron + glia → synapse

layers.detail: The signalling cell: dendrites receive, the cell body processes, the axon sends signals.
A fatty insulating sheath on many axons that speeds signals.
The gap where one neuron passes a chemical message (neurotransmitter) to the next.
Support cells that feed, insulate, and protect neurons.

microanatomy.function: Carries fast electrical/chemical signals for sensation, movement, and thought.
microanatomy.clinical: Losing myelin slows signals (as in MS); blocked blood supply kills neurons (stroke); neurons mostly don't regrow, so damage can be lasting.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: aorta → artery → ARTERIOLE → CAPILLARY → venule → vein

layers.detail: Thick, muscular, elastic vessels carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure.
The smallest arteries — their muscular walls tighten or relax to control blood flow and blood pressure.
One-cell-thick vessels where oxygen, nutrients, and waste are exchanged with tissues.
Collect blood and return it to the heart at low pressure; veins have valves to stop backflow.
Most vessels have three coats: intima (inner endothelium), media (muscle/elastic), adventitia (outer support).
The single-cell inner lining of every vessel — controls clotting, tone, and leakiness.

microanatomy.function: Delivers oxygen/nutrients to every cell and removes waste; arterioles set blood pressure, capillaries do the exchange.
microanatomy.clinical: Arteriole tone drives blood pressure; capillary leak causes swelling; endothelial damage starts atherosclerosis and clots; a blocked vessel starves the tissue beyond it.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: blood → plasma + cells → red cells / white cells / platelets

layers.detail: The fluid (mostly water) carrying proteins, salts, nutrients, and waste.
Carry oxygen on haemoglobin; made in the bone marrow.
The immune defenders (several types) that fight infection.
Cell fragments that plug leaks and start clotting.

microanatomy.function: Transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, heat, and immune cells; clots to stop bleeding.
microanatomy.clinical: Low red cells = anaemia; abnormal white cells = leukaemia/infection; too few platelets = easy bleeding; too much clotting = DVT/stroke.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: heart → chambers → myocardium → cardiac muscle cells

layers.detail: Four-chambered pump with valves and its own coronary blood supply.
Endocardium (inner lining), myocardium (the thick muscle), epicardium/pericardium (outer covering).
Heart-muscle tissue that contracts as one coordinated unit.
Cardiomyocytes — branching, striped cells joined by 'intercalated discs' that pass the electrical signal cell-to-cell; packed with mitochondria.

microanatomy.function: Coordinated contraction of cardiomyocytes pumps blood around the body.
microanatomy.clinical: A blocked coronary artery starves a patch of myocardium and the cells die — a heart attack. Scarred or stretched muscle causes heart failure and arrhythmias.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: lungs → lobes → bronchioles → alveoli → alveolar cells

layers.detail: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles branch like a tree.
~300 million tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries — the exchange surface.
Ultra-thin cells across which oxygen and CO₂ diffuse.
Make surfactant, a soap-like film that keeps the sacs from collapsing.

microanatomy.function: Oxygen crosses the thin alveolar wall into capillary blood; CO₂ crosses out to be breathed away.
microanatomy.clinical: Fluid or pus in the alveoli (pneumonia, heart failure) blocks exchange; too little surfactant collapses sacs; destroyed walls = emphysema/COPD.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: kidney → cortex/medulla → nephron → glomerulus + tubule cells

layers.detail: Filters blood into urine; ~1 million filtering units each.
The working unit: a filter (glomerulus) plus a long tubule.
A tuft of capillaries that filters fluid out of the blood.
Line the tubule and reclaim water, salts, and nutrients while passing waste on as urine.

microanatomy.function: Filters waste and balances water, salts, acid, and blood pressure, drop by drop.
microanatomy.clinical: Damaged glomeruli leak protein/blood; lost nephrons = chronic kidney disease; a blocked, infected kidney is an emergency.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.topic: Gut wall — sliced to the cell
microanatomy.scale: gut tube → wall layers → mucosa → lining cells

layers.detail: From inside out: mucosa (lining), submucosa, muscularis (the moving muscle), serosa (outer).
Finger-like folds of mucosa that hugely increase the absorbing surface.
Absorbing cells on the villi that take up digested nutrients.
Mucus-making goblet cells, hormone cells, and immune cells guarding the gut.

microanatomy.function: Muscle layers push food along while the mucosa digests and absorbs it.
microanatomy.clinical: Flattened villi = malabsorption (coeliac); inflamed mucosa = IBD; a full-thickness break = perforation (an emergency); mucosal cells can turn cancerous.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: skin → epidermis → dermis → subcutis → skin cells

layers.detail: Thin outer barrier of stacked keratinocytes, renewing from the bottom up.
Pigment cells that give skin colour and protect against UV.
Tough collagen layer holding nerves, vessels, glands, and hair roots.
Fat layer for insulation and cushioning.

microanatomy.function: A self-renewing waterproof barrier that senses, protects, and regulates temperature.
microanatomy.clinical: Barrier loss = eczema/infection; melanocytes can turn into melanoma; deep burns destroy all layers and need specialist care.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

layers.detail: Hard cortical shell over spongy inner bone, with marrow inside.
Rings of mineralised bone around a central vessel — the repeating unit.
Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts break it down, osteocytes maintain it — constantly remodelling.
Makes blood cells and stores fat.

microanatomy.function: Living, remodelling tissue that supports the body, stores calcium, and makes blood.
microanatomy.clinical: When breakdown outpaces building, bone thins (osteoporosis) and fractures easily; marrow problems affect blood cells.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.topic: Skeletal muscle — sliced to the cell

layers.detail: Bundles (fascicles) of muscle fibres wrapped in connective tissue, attached by tendons.
A single long muscle cell with many nuclei.
Chains of sarcomeres — the contracting units.
Overlapping actin and myosin filaments that slide to shorten the muscle.

microanatomy.function: Converts chemical energy into pulling force to move the skeleton.
microanatomy.clinical: Tears, overuse (tendinitis), breakdown (rhabdomyolysis), and nerve or calcium problems all show as weakness, pain, or cramps.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

microanatomy.scale: nerve → neuron → axon → synapse → next cell

layers.detail: The neuron holds a charge difference across its membrane, ready to fire.
A trigger flips the charge and a wave races down the axon.
Insulated gaps let the signal 'jump' and travel faster.
At the end, neurotransmitters cross the gap to excite or calm the next cell.

microanatomy.function: Fast, precise signalling underlies every sensation, movement, and thought.
microanatomy.clinical: Nerve compression, demyelination, or chemical imbalance disrupt signals — numbness, weakness, pain, seizures, or mood changes.
microanatomy.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

dosing_reference_policy.title: Dosing — clinical reference & indication only
dosing_reference_policy.statement: Dosing shown here is a MEDICAL INDICATION AND REFERENCE drawn from the official drug label (FDA label via openFDA, US public domain) — the same information a clinician looks up. It is NOT a real-world dosing guide and must NOT be used to self-treat. Doses depend on the individual: diagnosis, age, weight, kidney/liver function, pregnancy, allergies, other medicines, and the specific product. ONLY follow the directions given by your own doctor or pharmacist and the directions on your medicine’s label.
dosing_reference_policy.intended_use: A point-of-reference for clinicians (who routinely look up label dosing) and an indication for patients to RAISE WITH their prescriber — never a substitute for a prescription or professional judgment. Personalized dosing based on a patient’s medical records remains the responsibility of the treating prescriber using the full chart.
dosing_reference_policy.source: Dose values come only from official drug labels (openFDA / DailyMed, US public domain); no dose is written from memory.
dosing_reference_policy.interactions_note: See the Medication Safety Reference (hive_med_safety) for known serious interactions and duplicate-ingredient flags to raise with a professional.

harm_reduction.title: HIVE Doctor — Overdose Prevention & Harm Reduction Reference
harm_reduction.policy: This section exists to SAVE LIVES: to recognize and respond to overdose, to flag deadly combinations and the tolerance trap, and to connect people to help and to specialized harm-reduction services. It deliberately does NOT give recreational doses for illicit or street drugs — street supply is contaminated and unpredictable (fentanyl is widespread), so no amount is 'safe', and a number gives false confidence. For substance-specific safer-use guidance, use the specialized services listed here. Nothing here is a substitute for emergency care or a clinician.
universal_rules: If someone is unresponsive, breathing slowly/irregularly, or not breathing — call 911 (or local emergency) now. Give naloxone if opioids are possible; start rescue breaths/CPR as directed.
NEVER use alone. If you use, have someone with you or use a 'never use alone' phone line so someone can call help.
The TOLERANCE TRAP kills: after any break (days clean, detox, jail, illness, a new batch), your old 'usual amount' can be a fatal dose. Restart far lower than before.
NEVER mix depressants: opioids + benzodiazepines + alcohol + other sedatives stack up and stop breathing. Most overdose deaths involve a mix.
Assume illicit drugs may contain fentanyl or other potent adulterants. Use fentanyl test strips, and carry naloxone — it reverses opioid overdose.
Good Samaritan laws in many places protect you from certain charges when you call 911 for an overdose. Calling is the right move.

resources.name: Emergency
resources.note: Unresponsive, not breathing, seizure, chest pain — call now.

resources.name: Poison Control (US)
resources.note: 24/7 expert advice on overdose, interactions, exposures.

resources.name: DanceSafe
resources.note: Evidence-based harm reduction, drug checking, substance info.

resources.name: TripSit
resources.note: Harm-reduction info, a combinations chart, and live help.

resources.name: PsychonautWiki
resources.note: Detailed, referenced substance and interaction information.

resources.name: Canada — local harm reduction / 811
resources.note: Naloxone kits, supervised services, and advice.

overdose_guides.class: Opioids (heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, morphine, methadone, etc.)
overdose_signs: Slow, shallow, or stopped breathing (the thing that kills)
Unresponsive, limp, gurgling or snoring sounds
response: Give naloxone (nasal or injectable) per the kit; repeat every 2–3 minutes if no response.
Give rescue breaths; start CPR if not breathing and you're trained/directed.
Put them in the recovery position; stay — overdose can return as naloxone wears off.
key_dangers: Mixing with benzodiazepines or alcohol greatly raises the risk (and naloxone does not reverse those).
Tolerance loss after any break is a leading cause of fatal overdose.
overdose_guides.note: Carry naloxone if you or someone near you uses opioids — it's free in many places and reverses opioid overdose.

response: Recovery position to protect the airway from vomit.
Do not leave them to 'sleep it off' if breathing is abnormal or they can't be roused.
Naloxone won't reverse these, but give it anyway if opioids might also be involved.
key_dangers: Combining with opioids or other depressants stops breathing.
Stopping heavy alcohol or benzodiazepine use SUDDENLY can cause dangerous withdrawal and seizures — medical help is needed to stop safely.
GHB has a very narrow margin and a steep overdose curve.
overdose_guides.note: Alcohol/benzo withdrawal can be life-threatening — never quit heavy use cold turkey without medical support.

overdose_signs: Very high body temperature (overheating), heavy sweating
response: Call 911 — stimulant overdose can cause heart attack, stroke, or fatal overheating.
Move to a cool place, remove excess clothing, cool them down, offer sips of water if alert (MDMA overheating).
Keep them calm; protect from injury during a seizure.
Do not assume it will pass — chest pain or seizure is an emergency.
key_dangers: Overheating and dehydration (especially MDMA at events) — but also DON'T over-drink water, which can be fatal with MDMA.
Hidden heart conditions; mixing stimulants strains the heart.
Contamination with fentanyl or other substances.
overdose_guides.note: There's no reversal drug for stimulants — cooling, calming, and emergency care are the response.

overdose_signs: Unresponsive or unable to move/protect airway ('k-hole')
Dangerously high blood pressure or heart rate (PCP)
response: Call 911 if unresponsive, vomiting while out, having a seizure, or with chest pain.
Keep the environment calm and safe; reduce stimulation.
key_dangers: Loss of coordination/consciousness leads to choking or injury.
Severe psychological distress needs calm support and, if unsafe, medical help.
overdose_guides.note: For a difficult psychological experience, a calm, safe setting and reassurance help; seek medical help if there's danger to self or others.

safer_use.title: Safer use & infection prevention (needle exchange / supervised consumption basics)
safer_use.intent: The core public-health harm-reduction practices that needle-exchange and supervised consumption services provide — they dramatically cut overdose deaths, HIV, hepatitis C, and serious infections. This is infection-prevention and connection to services, not a guide on how much to use.
principles: Use a NEW, STERILE needle/syringe every single time. Never reuse your own and never share — sharing spreads HIV and hepatitis C.
Never share ANY equipment: needles, cookers, filters, water, ties, pipes, or straws. Hepatitis C survives on equipment and spreads easily.
Get free sterile supplies and sharps containers from a needle-exchange / harm-reduction program; many also give out naloxone and fentanyl test strips.
Use a supervised consumption site where available — trained staff, clean supplies, and someone present to reverse an overdose. These sites have never had an on-site death.
Wash hands and clean the skin with an alcohol swab before injecting, to prevent abscesses and bloodstream infections.
Use your own clean water; do not lick needles or equipment.
Rotate sites and avoid damaged skin; never inject into a red, swollen, or painful area.
Dispose of used needles in a sharps container or a rigid sealed container — return them to the exchange; never leave them loose.
Do not use alone; carry naloxone; use fentanyl test strips; and remember the tolerance trap after any break.
infection_warning_signs: Abscess: a red, hot, swollen, painful lump at an injection site — see a clinician; it may need draining or antibiotics.
Spreading redness, red streaks, fever, or feeling very unwell — possible serious bloodstream infection; seek care urgently.
Endocarditis (heart-valve infection): fever, chills, night sweats, breathlessness, and fatigue after injecting — a medical EMERGENCY.
A wound that will not heal, or numbness or coldness in a limb after a missed injection — get medical help.
safer_use.testing_note: Where drug-checking services exist (at many harm-reduction sites and some events), use them — they can detect fentanyl and other adulterants before use. Fentanyl test strips are a simple at-home option.
safer_use.getting_help: Needle exchanges and supervised consumption sites also connect people to HIV/HCV testing, wound care, naloxone, and — whenever wanted — treatment and support. Asking about treatment is always available and never required to get clean supplies.

interactions.title: HIVE Doctor — Medication Interaction & Food Reference
interactions.policy: This layer helps people who take several medications or see more than one prescriber spot POSSIBLE interactions and food effects, and brings them to a pharmacist/doctor. It is a reference, not a clearance to combine or skip anything. A pharmacist seeing your FULL list (including over-the-counter drugs, supplements, and herbal products) is the single best check — pharmacists do this free. Never start, stop, or change a dose based on this list alone. Interaction facts here are qualitative (from FDA label class warnings and standard references), not dosing.

med_tracker.intent: The app can hold a private list of what you take — type each medication (and OTC drugs, vitamins, and supplements) in, or tell HIVE Doctor. The list is stored locally on your device only. HIVE Doctor then flags any known interaction PAIRS among your list, plus food cautions, so you can show your pharmacist.
med_tracker.privacy: Your medication list stays in your browser's local storage on this device. It is not uploaded, not shared, and not visible to anyone else. Clearing your browser data removes it.
med_tracker.how: Add each item by its generic name if you can (e.g., 'warfarin', 'ibuprofen', 'sertraline'). The checker matches on generic and common brand names and reports pairs to review. An empty result does NOT mean 'no interactions exist' — only that none are in this reference; still confirm with a pharmacist.
med_tracker.disclaimer: Not a substitute for a pharmacist's review or your doctor's advice. If you ever have severe symptoms after a dose (trouble breathing, swelling, chest pain, severe bleeding, confusion), seek emergency care.

pairs.effect: Raises bleeding risk markedly — NSAIDs irritate the stomach and affect platelets on top of the blood thinner. Watch for black/tarry stools, unusual bruising, or blood in urine. Ask your prescriber before combining; acetaminophen is often preferred for pain.

Vitamin K–rich foods can reduce warfarin's effect. You don't have to avoid greens — keep your intake STEADY week to week rather than swinging, and tell the clinic managing your INR. (This applies to warfarin, not the newer blood thinners.)
Two blood-affecting drugs together sharply raise bleeding risk. Only combine if a doctor specifically directs it.

Combining serotonergic drugs can cause SEROTONIN SYNDROME — agitation, fast heartbeat, high temperature, tremor, sweating, and confusion, which can be life-threatening. MAOIs must not be combined with SSRIs/SNRIs at all. Seek urgent care for these symptoms.
SSRIs/SNRIs plus NSAIDs or blood thinners raise bleeding risk (especially stomach bleeding). Watch for black stools; ask about stomach protection or acetaminophen instead.

MAOIs plus tyramine-rich foods can cause a dangerous blood-pressure spike (hypertensive crisis) — severe headache, chest pain. A strict diet is required; follow the specific list your prescriber gives.

These blood-pressure drugs raise potassium; adding potassium supplements or salt substitutes (often potassium chloride) can push it too high, affecting the heart rhythm. Ask before using salt substitutes.
The 'triple whammy' — an ACE/ARB + a diuretic + an NSAID — can injure the kidneys, especially in older adults or when dehydrated. Use NSAIDs sparingly and stay hydrated; prefer acetaminophen.

Grapefruit blocks an enzyme (CYP3A4) that clears some statins (simvastatin, lovastatin, and atorvastatin most), raising drug levels and the risk of muscle damage. Avoid grapefruit with those; check which statin you take.
These raise statin levels and the risk of serious muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) — watch for severe muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine. Dose limits or a pause may be needed; ask your prescriber.

Metformin is usually paused around procedures using IV contrast dye (kidney stress can raise the rare risk of lactic acidosis), and heavy alcohol adds to that risk. Tell the imaging team you take metformin.

BOXED-WARNING combination: opioids plus benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other sedatives stack up and can stop breathing — profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. This is a leading cause of overdose. Only combine if a doctor specifically manages it; discuss naloxone.
Multiple sedating drugs together cause heavy drowsiness and impair breathing, driving, and balance (fall/accident risk, especially in older adults).
Calcium, iron, antacids, and coffee reduce levothyroxine absorption. Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach and separate it from these by about 4 hours.
Calcium, iron, antacids, and dairy bind these antibiotics and block absorption, so they don't work. Separate the antibiotic from them by 2-4 hours (check your specific drug's instructions).
Raises the risk of high potassium (dangerous for the heart). Needs blood-level monitoring; avoid extra potassium.
Some PPIs (omeprazole, esomeprazole) may reduce clopidogrel's anti-clotting effect. If you need stomach protection, pantoprazole or an H2-blocker is often preferred — ask your prescriber.
These can raise digoxin levels or lower potassium, causing toxicity (nausea, vision changes, dangerous heart rhythms). Digoxin needs careful monitoring.
These raise lithium levels toward toxicity (tremor, confusion, vomiting, unsteadiness). Lithium has a narrow safe range and needs blood monitoring; avoid adding NSAIDs without advice.
Alcohol with metronidazole/tinidazole can cause a 'disulfiram' reaction — flushing, pounding headache, nausea, and vomiting. Avoid alcohol during and for a few days after the course.
ED drugs plus nitrates (heart chest-pain medicines, or 'poppers') can cause a sudden, dangerous drop in blood pressure. Never combine. Tell emergency staff if you've taken an ED drug.

grapefruit.what_it_does: Grapefruit (and grapefruit juice, also Seville oranges and pomelo) blocks an intestinal enzyme called CYP3A4 that normally breaks down many medicines. With the enzyme blocked, more of the drug reaches the blood — effectively an unplanned overdose — which can cause side effects or toxicity. The effect can last a day or more, so 'taking them at different times' does NOT avoid it.
grapefruit.affected_examples: Some statins (simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin), some blood-pressure drugs (certain calcium-channel blockers like felodipine, nifedipine), some anti-anxiety/sleep drugs (buspirone, some benzodiazepines), certain immune-suppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), some heart-rhythm drugs (amiodarone), and others. Not all drugs in a class are affected.
grapefruit.advice: Check each medicine's label or ask your pharmacist whether to avoid grapefruit. When in doubt, keep grapefruit off the menu while on a flagged drug.
grapefruit.source: FDA consumer guidance on grapefruit–drug interactions

take_with_food: Many iron supplements can upset the stomach — taking with a little food helps absorption is lower; follow the label
take_on_empty_stomach: Levothyroxine — 30-60 min before breakfast, with water
Some antibiotics work best empty (e.g., certain penicillins) — check the label
Bisphosphonates (alendronate) — first thing, with plain water, stay upright 30-60 min
food_timing.note: These are general label patterns. Your exact medicine's leaflet, or your pharmacist, gives the right instruction for YOUR version.

chapters.title: Pharmacy & Clinical Pharmacology
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational reference; specific doses only from a current label/pharmacist.
chapters.source: Written for HIVE Doctor from standard pharmacology/pharmacy-practice references (educational). No dose numbers from memory — specific dosing cites a current label.
chapters.overview: A working pharmacy reference: what pharmacists actually do, how medicines move through and act on the body, the principles behind dosing, how to read a prescription, the major drug classes, over-the-counter self-care, special populations, interactions and adverse reactions, adherence counselling, antimicrobial stewardship, vaccines, compounding, and medication-error prevention. It is built to help a professional work faster and a patient understand their treatment. It gives the PRINCIPLES and the reasoning; exact dose numbers always come from the specific product's current label or the pharmacist, because a number written from memory can be wrong and dangerous.

sections.heading: What pharmacists do (scope & services)
sections.body: Pharmacists are medication experts, not just dispensers. Core work: verifying and dispensing prescriptions, checking for interactions/allergies/duplications/dosing errors, and counselling patients. Expanded services (varying by jurisdiction) now commonly include: medication therapy management and comprehensive medication reviews; prescribing or adapting for minor ailments (e.g., cold sores, UTIs, pink eye, shingles, contraception) and extending/renewing chronic prescriptions; administering vaccines and injections; point-of-care testing (blood pressure, blood glucose, A1c, strep, INR, lipids); smoking-cessation programs; naloxone distribution and opioid-agonist therapy support; travel health and prescribing; compounding; and deprescribing reviews for older adults. In hospitals, clinical pharmacists dose and monitor high-risk drugs (anticoagulants, antibiotics, chemotherapy), run stewardship programs, and join ward rounds. The pharmacist is often the most accessible health professional — no appointment needed — and medication reviews are usually free.

sections.heading: How drugs move through the body (pharmacokinetics / ADME)
sections.body: Pharmacokinetics is 'what the body does to the drug,' summarised as ADME. ABSORPTION: how the drug gets into the blood (affected by route, food, gut pH, formulation). Oral drugs face FIRST-PASS METABOLISM — the liver may inactivate much of a dose before it reaches circulation, which is why some drugs need far higher oral than IV doses, or a non-oral route. DISTRIBUTION: how the drug spreads into tissues (protein binding, fat vs water solubility, ability to cross the blood-brain barrier or placenta). METABOLISM: mostly in the liver via cytochrome P450 enzymes (notably CYP3A4, CYP2D6) — this is why one drug (or grapefruit) that inhibits or induces an enzyme can raise or lower another drug's level. EXCRETION: mostly via the kidneys (so kidney function drives dosing of renally-cleared drugs) and partly bile/gut. HALF-LIFE (the time for blood level to halve) sets dosing frequency and how long a drug lingers; it takes about 4-5 half-lives to reach STEADY STATE on regular dosing, and about the same to clear after stopping.

sections.heading: How drugs act (pharmacodynamics)
sections.body: Pharmacodynamics is 'what the drug does to the body.' Most drugs act on RECEPTORS, enzymes, ion channels, or transporters. An AGONIST activates a receptor (mimics the natural signal); an ANTAGONIST (blocker) occupies it and prevents activation; a partial agonist does a bit of both. POTENCY is how much drug is needed for an effect; EFFICACY is the maximum effect achievable — a potent drug is not necessarily more effective. The DOSE-RESPONSE relationship means effect rises with dose up to a ceiling, while side effects may keep rising. The THERAPEUTIC INDEX is the gap between an effective dose and a toxic one; narrow-index drugs (warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin, some anticonvulsants, aminoglycosides) need careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring. TOLERANCE (needing more for the same effect) and DEPENDENCE develop with some drugs; this underlies the opioid tolerance trap and withdrawal syndromes.

sections.heading: Dosing principles (the reasoning, not the numbers)
sections.body: Dosing is individualised, and the actual numbers belong to the label and the prescriber — but the logic is consistent. LOWEST EFFECTIVE DOSE for the shortest needed time is the default, especially for opioids, steroids, and sedatives. TITRATION: many drugs are started low and increased gradually to balance effect against side effects. LOADING vs MAINTENANCE: a larger first dose (loading) can reach a working level faster for drugs with long half-lives, then a smaller maintenance dose sustains it. WEIGHT- or BODY-SURFACE-BASED dosing is used in children and for chemotherapy. RENAL and HEPATIC ADJUSTMENT: doses of drugs cleared by the kidney or liver are reduced when those organs are impaired. THERAPEUTIC DRUG MONITORING measures blood levels for narrow-index drugs. TAPERING: some drugs (steroids, many antidepressants, benzodiazepines, some blood-pressure and seizure drugs, opioids) must be reduced gradually, never stopped abruptly. MISSED DOSE rules vary by drug — the label or pharmacist gives the right action; doubling up is often wrong and sometimes dangerous.

sections.heading: Routes & dosage forms (and why the form matters)
sections.body: The same drug behaves differently by form. ORAL immediate-release (IR) acts and clears quickly; EXTENDED-RELEASE (ER/XR/SR/CR) releases slowly for once/twice-daily dosing — crushing or splitting an ER tablet can dump the whole dose at once and cause overdose, so ER forms are usually swallowed whole. SUBLINGUAL/BUCCAL (under or against the cheek) bypasses first-pass metabolism for fast effect (e.g., nitroglycerin). TRANSDERMAL patches give steady levels over days (and must be removed/rotated correctly; a used fentanyl patch still holds lethal drug). INHALED delivers drug straight to the lungs with small systemic dose (asthma/COPD). INJECTABLE routes — IV (immediate, full dose), IM, and subcutaneous — are used when oral won't work or speed matters. TOPICAL, OPHTHALMIC, OTIC, RECTAL, and VAGINAL forms target locally. Liquids need a CALIBRATED oral syringe, never a kitchen spoon — a leading cause of paediatric dosing errors.

sections.heading: Reading a prescription & a label
sections.body: Prescriptions use Latin-derived shorthand (the 'sig'): OD/qd = once daily, BID = twice daily, TID = three times, QID = four times, QHS = at bedtime, PRN = as needed, PO = by mouth, PR = rectally, SL = sublingual, AC = before meals, PC = after meals, gtt = drops, stat = immediately. A complete prescription names the drug, strength, form, dose, route, frequency, duration/quantity, and refills. Auxiliary (coloured) labels flag key cautions: take with food, avoid alcohol, may cause drowsiness, avoid grapefruit, complete the course, protect from light, shake well. Dangerous abbreviations are being phased out (e.g., 'U' for units mistaken as a zero); when anything is unclear, the pharmacist confirms with the prescriber rather than guessing.

sections.heading: Major drug classes — a map
sections.body: A high-level map (mechanisms and cautions, not doses). PAIN/FEVER: acetaminophen (liver-dose ceiling), NSAIDs (stomach/kidney/heart cautions), opioids (respiratory depression, dependence). ANTIBIOTICS: penicillins/cephalosporins, macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (tendon/QT cautions), sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, metronidazole (alcohol) — each with its own spectrum and interactions. CARDIOVASCULAR: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, diuretics, statins, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, nitrates. RESPIRATORY: inhaled beta-agonists (SABA/LABA), inhaled corticosteroids, antimuscarinics, leukotriene blockers. GI: PPIs, H2-blockers, antacids, antiemetics, laxatives. ENDOCRINE: metformin and other antidiabetics, insulin, levothyroxine, corticosteroids. NEURO/PSYCH: SSRIs/SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, anticonvulsants, ADHD stimulants. ALLERGY: antihistamines (sedating vs non-sedating). Each class entry in the live drug reference carries the specific cautions.

sections.heading: Over-the-counter & self-care (what to reach for, by symptom)
sections.body: At the category level (always follow the product label for the dose): PAIN/FEVER — acetaminophen or an NSAID (ibuprofen/naproxen); acetaminophen is gentler on the stomach, NSAIDs reduce inflammation but carry stomach/kidney/heart cautions. COUGH/COLD — saline, decongestants (caution with high blood pressure), antihistamines, honey for cough in those over 1 year; most colds are viral and self-limited. ALLERGY — non-sedating antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) by day, steroid nasal sprays for ongoing symptoms. HEARTBURN — antacids for quick relief, H2-blockers or short PPI courses for frequent symptoms. CONSTIPATION — fibre and fluids first, then osmotic (PEG) or stimulant laxatives short-term. DIARRHOEA — fluids/rehydration first; loperamide for non-infectious cases. SKIN — emollients, hydrocortisone for mild eczema, antifungals. The pharmacist matches the product to the person (age, pregnancy, other meds, conditions). SEE SOMEONE for: high or persistent fever, breathing trouble, severe or one-sided pain, blood, symptoms beyond ~1 week, or a baby/young child.

sections.heading: Special populations
sections.body: PREGNANCY & LACTATION: many drugs are avoided or chosen carefully; acetaminophen is generally preferred for pain, NSAIDs are avoided especially in the third trimester, and resources like the product monograph, a pharmacist, or specialist services guide choices — never assume 'natural' means safe. PAEDIATRICS: doses are weight-based and forms matter (liquids, calibrated syringes); some adult drugs are unsafe in children (e.g., aspirin and Reye's syndrome, codeine in young children). GERIATRICS: ageing slows drug clearance, raises sensitivity, and stacks up POLYPHARMACY; 'start low, go slow,' watch for falls, confusion, and anticholinergic burden, and deprescribe where possible (Beers/STOPP criteria guide this). RENAL or HEPATIC IMPAIRMENT: dose reductions or alternative drugs are needed for organ-cleared medicines. Each of these is a reason the pharmacist reviews the full picture.

sections.heading: Adverse reactions, allergies & interactions
sections.body: An ADVERSE DRUG REACTION is any unwanted effect; a SIDE EFFECT is a predictable one. A true ALLERGY is an immune reaction (rash, hives, swelling, and — dangerously — anaphylaxis with throat swelling and breathing trouble) and must be recorded and avoided; an INTOLERANCE (e.g., nausea on an antibiotic) is unpleasant but not immune and may be manageable — distinguishing them prevents people being wrongly labelled 'penicillin-allergic' for life. INTERACTIONS can be drug-drug, drug-food (grapefruit, dairy, vitamin-K greens, tyramine, alcohol), drug-supplement (St John's wort, high-dose vitamins), or drug-disease. The HIVE Doctor interaction layer and med-tracker flag the common serious ones, but a pharmacist seeing the FULL list — prescription, OTC, supplements, herbals — is the definitive check. Report new or severe reactions; many countries have adverse-event reporting systems.

sections.heading: Adherence & counselling (getting the benefit safely)
sections.body: Roughly half of long-term medicines are not taken as prescribed, which drives treatment failure and hospital admissions. Good counselling covers the 'five rights' (right patient, drug, dose, route, time) plus: what the drug is for and what to expect, how and when to take it (with/without food, timing around other drugs), what to do about a missed dose, common and serious side effects, storage (cool, dry, out of children's reach; some need refrigeration), and safe disposal (pharmacy take-back, not the toilet). Adherence aids include blister/dosette packs, reminders, syncing refills, and simplifying regimens. The pharmacist also screens for whether a new symptom is actually a drug side effect — a 'prescribing cascade' is when a side effect is mistaken for a new illness and treated with yet another drug.

sections.heading: Antimicrobial stewardship & resistance
sections.body: Antibiotics are a shared, exhaustible resource: overuse breeds resistant bacteria that make future infections untreatable. Stewardship principles: use antibiotics only for bacterial infections (not colds, flu, or most sore throats/sinus congestion, which are viral); choose the narrowest effective agent; use the right dose and the shortest effective course; and COMPLETE the course as directed (stopping early can leave hardier survivors) while not demanding antibiotics 'just in case.' Pharmacists support stewardship by questioning unnecessary prescriptions, checking doses and durations, advising on symptomatic relief for viral illness, and counselling on resistance. Leftover antibiotics should never be saved or shared.

sections.heading: Vaccines in the pharmacy
sections.body: Pharmacists are now major vaccinators. Principles: vaccines train the immune system using inactivated, subunit, mRNA, or live-attenuated preparations; live vaccines are generally avoided in pregnancy and significant immunosuppression. COLD CHAIN is critical — most vaccines must be stored in a narrow temperature range and are ruined by freezing or heat, so handling and documentation matter. Common pharmacy-administered vaccines include influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, Tdap, HPV, and travel vaccines. Counselling covers the schedule, common mild reactions (sore arm, low fever) versus rare serious ones, and the 15-minute post-vaccination observation for anaphylaxis, for which epinephrine must be on hand.

sections.heading: Compounding & special preparations
sections.body: Compounding is preparing a customised medicine when a commercial product doesn't fit — e.g., a liquid for a child or someone who can't swallow tablets, a dye- or allergen-free version, a specific strength, a topical combination, or veterinary preparations. Non-sterile compounding (creams, capsules, suspensions) and sterile compounding (injectables, eye drops — under strict aseptic conditions) follow defined quality standards. Compounding is not the same as manufacturing and is patient-specific; beyond-use dates, documentation, and quality controls apply. Patients should use a pharmacy experienced in the specific preparation.

sections.heading: High-alert drugs & error prevention
sections.body: HIGH-ALERT medications cause disproportionate harm when misused: insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated electrolytes (especially potassium), chemotherapy, and sedatives. Error-prevention tools: independent double-checks, 'tall man' lettering to distinguish look-alike/sound-alike names (e.g., hydrOXYzine vs hydrALAZINE), barcode scanning, standardised concentrations, avoiding dangerous abbreviations, and calibrated measuring for liquids. The classic error pairs — mg vs mL confusion, missing a decimal point, a trailing zero read as ten-fold — are exactly why labels, auxiliary warnings, and pharmacist verification exist. When something looks off, the safe move is always to stop and verify, not to proceed.

sections.heading: What this chapter is and isn't
sections.body: This is professional-grade background and patient-education knowledge: how medicines and pharmacy practice work, written to help someone do their job better or understand their care. It deliberately does NOT list specific dose numbers from memory — those live in each product's current label and in the live drug reference, and the pharmacist individualises them. For any real decision — starting, stopping, combining, or dosing a medicine — the current label and a pharmacist or prescriber are the authority. Scope of pharmacist services varies by country, province, and state; check local regulations.

chapters.title: Physiotherapy (Physical Therapy)
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational reference.
chapters.source: Written for HIVE Doctor from standard clinical/professional references (educational). Evidence statements are kept honest: what is well-supported, mixed, or unproven is said plainly.
chapters.overview: Physiotherapy restores movement and function through assessment, exercise, manual therapy, and education. It is among the most evidence-supported of the hands-on professions, central to musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiorespiratory, and post-surgical recovery. This chapter covers what physios do, how they assess and reason, the main treatment tools and their evidence, the major clinical areas, red flags that send a patient to a doctor, and how to get the most from care.

sections.heading: What physiotherapists do
sections.body: Physiotherapists assess how the body moves and why it isn't moving well, then treat with active, patient-led methods. Core tools: prescribed EXERCISE (strengthening, mobility, motor control, graded loading), MANUAL THERAPY (joint mobilisation, soft-tissue work), EDUCATION and pacing, and functional retraining (walking, balance, returning to work/sport). They set measurable goals, track progress, and progress the plan. In many systems they are first-contact practitioners who can diagnose musculoskeletal problems, order or refer for imaging, and screen for serious pathology. Settings span clinics, hospitals, ICUs, sports teams, home care, and rehab units.

sections.heading: How a physio assesses and reasons
sections.body: A physio assessment is a clinical reasoning process: history (mechanism, behaviour of symptoms, aggravating/easing factors, red-flag screening, goals), then physical examination (observation, active and passive range of motion, strength, special orthopaedic tests, neurological screen, palpation, functional tasks). From this they form a working diagnosis and, crucially, identify the DRIVERS they can change (weakness, stiffness, poor control, deconditioning, fear-avoidance). Modern practice treats pain as biopsychosocial — tissue, nervous system, beliefs, sleep, stress, and load history all matter — so a good plan addresses more than the sore spot.

sections.heading: Therapeutic exercise — the core tool
sections.body: Exercise is the best-evidenced physiotherapy intervention across low-back pain, neck pain, osteoarthritis, tendinopathy, post-surgical recovery, falls prevention, and chronic disease. Principles: match load to the tissue's current capacity, then progressively increase it so tissue and the nervous system adapt (progressive overload and graded exposure). Specific approaches include strengthening, range-of-motion and mobility work, motor-control/stabilisation training, balance and gait training, and graded aerobic conditioning. 'Hurt does not always equal harm' — for many chronic conditions, tolerable discomfort during well-dosed exercise is expected and safe, and avoidance worsens outcomes.

sections.heading: Manual therapy & modalities — honest evidence
sections.body: Manual therapy (joint mobilisation/manipulation, soft-tissue techniques) can give short-term pain relief and improve movement, and works best as an ADJUNCT that makes active rehab easier — not as a standalone cure. Passive 'modalities' have mixed-to-weak evidence: ultrasound and most electrotherapy show little benefit beyond placebo for most conditions; heat/ice help comfort; TENS gives some short-term pain relief for some people; dry needling and taping have modest, variable support. The honest summary: hands-on and modalities can help symptoms in the short term, but lasting gains come from active exercise and load management, so they should not crowd it out.

sections.heading: Major clinical areas
sections.body: MUSCULOSKELETAL/ORTHOPAEDIC: back and neck pain, osteoarthritis, tendinopathies, sprains/strains, post-fracture and post-surgical rehab (joint replacements, ACL). SPORTS: injury rehab, return-to-play, performance and prevention. NEUROLOGICAL: stroke, spinal cord injury, Parkinson's, MS — retraining movement and function. CARDIORESPIRATORY: post-op breathing, COPD and cardiac rehab, ICU early mobilisation, airway clearance. PAEDIATRIC, GERIATRIC (falls, frailty, balance), WOMEN'S/PELVIC HEALTH (incontinence, prolapse, pregnancy-related pain), and VESTIBULAR (BPPV repositioning, dizziness) are established subspecialties.

sections.heading: Red flags — when a physio refers on
sections.body: A good physio screens for serious causes that need a doctor, not rehab. Spinal red flags: new bladder/bowel incontinence or retention, saddle (groin) numbness, progressive leg weakness (possible cauda equina — an EMERGENCY); night pain, unexplained weight loss, fever, or a cancer history with new back pain; significant trauma. General: calf swelling/pain suggesting a clot, chest pain or breathlessness, unremitting or rapidly worsening pain, or neurological signs that are spreading. Finding these and redirecting the patient is part of competent physiotherapy.

sections.heading: Getting the most from physiotherapy
sections.body: Outcomes depend heavily on doing the prescribed home program — the clinic visit is a small fraction of the week. Practical guidance for patients: be clear about your goals and daily demands; expect to be an active participant, not a passive recipient; ask what each exercise is for and how much soreness is acceptable; keep load progressing rather than staying comfortable; and give it weeks, since tissue adaptation is slow. For professionals and students: set measurable goals, re-assess objectively, and progress or change the plan when it stalls.

sections.heading: Training, regulation & scope
sections.body: Physiotherapists hold a university degree (increasingly a clinical doctorate) and are licensed/registered and regulated in most countries, with protected title and continuing-education requirements. Scope increasingly includes first-contact diagnosis, imaging referral, and in some jurisdictions limited prescribing and injection therapy. Related roles: physiotherapy/physical-therapist assistants, athletic therapists/trainers, kinesiologists, and occupational therapists (who focus on daily-living function and adaptation) — a patient is often best served by the right combination.

chapters.title: Massage Therapy
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational reference.
chapters.source: Written for HIVE Doctor from standard clinical/professional references (educational). Evidence statements are kept honest: what is well-supported, mixed, or unproven is said plainly.
chapters.overview: Massage therapy is the manual manipulation of soft tissue for relaxation, pain relief, and recovery. It has solid evidence as a comfort and short-term pain measure and as an adjunct to rehabilitation, with clear safety precautions. This chapter covers techniques, what the evidence does and doesn't support, indications, contraindications, and regulation.

sections.heading: What massage therapists do
sections.body: Registered/licensed massage therapists assess soft tissue and apply hands-on techniques to muscle, fascia, and connective tissue to reduce pain and tension, improve circulation and mobility, and promote relaxation. A session typically includes a brief history and consent, treatment tailored to goals, and self-care advice. In regulated jurisdictions they keep clinical records and screen for contraindications.

sections.heading: Main techniques
sections.body: SWEDISH/RELAXATION: gliding (effleurage), kneading (petrissage), friction, tapping — general relaxation and circulation. DEEP TISSUE: slower, firmer work on deeper layers for chronic tension. TRIGGER-POINT therapy: sustained pressure on tender 'knots' that can refer pain. MYOFASCIAL RELEASE: sustained stretch of the fascial network. SPORTS massage: pre/post-event and recovery-focused. Others: lymphatic drainage (for specific swelling conditions, under guidance), prenatal (with positioning precautions), and modality blends. Pressure should be communicated and adjusted — effective work need not be agonising.

sections.heading: What the evidence supports
sections.body: Best-supported: short-term relief of musculoskeletal pain (low-back, neck, shoulder), reduced muscle tension, lower stress/anxiety and improved sleep, and recovery/comfort after exercise. As an ADJUNCT it can make exercise and rehab more tolerable. Weaker or unproven claims: 'flushing out toxins,' correcting structural misalignment, curing disease, or lasting cure of chronic pain from massage alone — benefits are generally short-term, so massage works best combined with active care. DOMS (post-massage soreness) can occur and is usually mild and brief.

sections.heading: Contraindications & cautions
sections.body: Avoid or get medical clearance first for: a suspected or known blood clot/DVT (do NOT massage a swollen, painful calf — dislodging a clot is dangerous), acute infection or fever, over open wounds, fresh fractures, acute flare of inflammatory disease, uncontrolled bleeding disorders or high-dose blood thinners (bruising risk), certain cancers or over tumours/lymph-node areas without oncology guidance, and advanced heart failure. Relative cautions: pregnancy (positioning and certain areas), osteoporosis (gentle pressure), fragile skin, recent surgery, and neuropathy (reduced pain feedback). A competent therapist screens for these every visit.

sections.heading: Regulation & choosing a therapist
sections.body: Regulation varies widely: some regions license/register massage therapists with set training hours, exams, and a protected title; others have little oversight. Choose a regulated/licensed practitioner where available, expect a health history and consent, and raise any of the conditions above. Massage complements but does not replace medical care, physiotherapy's active rehab, or investigation of an undiagnosed problem.

chapters.title: Chiropractic
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational reference; balanced on evidence and risks.
chapters.source: Written for HIVE Doctor from standard clinical/professional references (educational). Evidence statements are kept honest: what is well-supported, mixed, or unproven is said plainly.
chapters.overview: Chiropractic focuses on the spine and musculoskeletal system, primarily using spinal manipulation. The evidence picture is mixed: reasonable support for some back and neck pain and certain headaches as part of a broader plan, little support for treating non-musculoskeletal disease, and specific safety considerations — especially for high-velocity neck manipulation. This chapter presents it even-handedly.

sections.heading: What chiropractors do
sections.body: Chiropractors assess and treat musculoskeletal complaints, most characteristically with SPINAL MANIPULATION (a high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust, often producing a 'pop' from joint gas release) and mobilisation. Many also use soft-tissue work, exercise prescription, and lifestyle advice, and order/interpret imaging. Practice philosophies vary: evidence-informed chiropractors work much like manual-therapy musculoskeletal clinicians; a minority hold traditional 'subluxation' beliefs claiming spinal adjustments treat general disease, which is not supported by evidence.

sections.heading: What the evidence supports — and doesn't
sections.body: Reasonable evidence: spinal manipulation gives modest, mostly short-term relief for acute and chronic LOW-BACK PAIN and NECK PAIN, and for some tension-type and cervicogenic headaches — broadly comparable to other active treatments and best combined with exercise.
