NOT supported: using manipulation to treat asthma, ear infections, colic, high blood pressure, or other non-musculoskeletal diseases, or the idea that routine 'maintenance' adjustments prevent illness. Guidelines generally place manipulation as one option within a plan centred on staying active and exercise, not as a lifelong dependency.

sections.heading: Risks & safety
sections.body: Common after manipulation: temporary soreness, stiffness, or headache, usually mild and short-lived. The serious concern is high-velocity NECK (cervical) manipulation and a rare association with VERTEBRAL ARTERY injury/dissection leading to stroke; whether manipulation causes it or an early dissection presents as neck pain that prompts the visit is debated, but the signal warrants caution. Reasonable safeguards: be wary of neck manipulation if you have risk factors; seek emergency care for the 5 Ds and 3 Ns (dizziness, drop attacks, diplopia/visual changes, dysarthria, dysphagia, plus numbness, nausea, nystagmus) or sudden severe 'unlike any other' neck pain/headache after manipulation. Avoid manipulation over osteoporosis, fracture, infection, inflammatory spondyloarthropathy, cancer, or significant neurological deficit.

sections.heading: When to see a doctor instead
sections.body: Manipulation is not the answer for possible cauda equina syndrome, which shows as bladder or bowel changes, numbness around the saddle area, or progressive leg weakness and is an EMERGENCY. Nor is it appropriate for a suspected fracture, infection, cancer, inflammatory arthritis, or any progressive neurological sign. A responsible chiropractor screens for these before treating and refers on promptly. Symptoms outside the muscles and joints, such as chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, sudden severe headache, or new weakness or speech change, need medical assessment, not adjustment. Sudden neck pain with dizziness, double vision or difficulty speaking after neck manipulation requires emergency care.

sections.heading: Regulation & choosing care
sections.body: Chiropractors are licensed and regulated in many countries with a defined training program. Choosing well: look for an evidence-informed practitioner who emphasises active exercise and a time-limited plan with clear goals, explains risks and obtains consent (especially for neck manipulation), avoids open-ended 'maintenance' packages and disease claims, and refers when red flags appear. Patients can decline neck manipulation and request mobilisation or soft-tissue techniques instead.

chapters.title: Psychiatry & Psychotherapy
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational reference. Not a substitute for assessment; crisis resources included.
chapters.source: Written for HIVE Doctor from standard clinical/professional references (educational). Evidence statements are kept honest: what is well-supported, mixed, or unproven is said plainly.
chapters.overview: Mental-health care spans psychiatry (medical diagnosis and medication), psychology and psychotherapy (talking therapies), and allied roles. This chapter maps who does what, the main diagnoses and treatments, how the major therapies and drug classes work, safety and crisis care, and how to navigate the system. It is educational; diagnosis and medication are individual clinical decisions.

sections.heading: Who's who in mental-health care
sections.body: PSYCHIATRIST: a medical doctor who diagnoses, can prescribe and manage medication, and treats complex/severe illness (often also does therapy). PSYCHOLOGIST: a doctoral-level specialist in assessment and psychotherapy (prescribes only in a few jurisdictions). PSYCHOTHERAPIST/COUNSELLOR: trained in talking therapies (regulation varies). CLINICAL SOCIAL WORKER, PSYCHIATRIC NURSE, and PEER-SUPPORT workers round out teams. Primary-care doctors handle much common mental illness and refer when needed. Matching the problem to the right professional — and often a combination — is the key navigation skill.

sections.heading: The major conditions (map)
sections.body: MOOD: major depression, persistent depressive disorder, bipolar disorder. ANXIETY: generalised anxiety, panic disorder, phobias, social anxiety. TRAUMA/STRESS: PTSD, acute stress. OBSESSIVE-COMPULSIVE and related. PSYCHOTIC: schizophrenia and related (hallucinations, delusions, disorganisation). NEURODEVELOPMENTAL: ADHD, autism spectrum. EATING disorders. SUBSTANCE-USE disorders. PERSONALITY disorders. Diagnosis uses criteria (DSM-5-TR/ICD-11) applied to a careful history — there is no blood test; symptoms, duration, and impact define the picture, and overlap is common.

sections.heading: How the main psychotherapies work
sections.body: CBT (cognitive behavioural therapy): identifies and reshapes unhelpful thought-behaviour cycles; strong evidence across depression and anxiety disorders. BEHAVIOURAL ACTIVATION and EXPOSURE therapy: re-engaging with activity and facing feared situations gradually — core for depression, phobias, OCD (ERP), and PTSD. DBT (dialectical behaviour therapy): skills for emotion regulation and distress tolerance, strong for self-harm and borderline personality. ACT, interpersonal therapy, psychodynamic therapy, EMDR (for trauma), and family/systemic therapy each have their niches. Common factors — a trusting therapeutic relationship, clear goals, and consistent practice — predict much of the benefit across methods.

sections.heading: Psychiatric medication classes (how they work)
sections.body: ANTIDEPRESSANTS: SSRIs and SNRIs (first-line for depression/anxiety; take weeks to work; taper to stop; watch early-weeks agitation and, rarely, increased suicidal thoughts in youth), plus older TCAs and MAOIs (dietary/interaction cautions). ANXIOLYTICS: benzodiazepines (fast but habit-forming and sedating — short-term/limited use; serotonergic options preferred long-term). MOOD STABILISERS: lithium (narrow therapeutic index, needs blood monitoring), certain anticonvulsants. ANTIPSYCHOTICS: for psychosis, bipolar, and augmentation (metabolic and movement side effects to monitor). STIMULANTS/non-stimulants for ADHD. Medication is individualised by a prescriber; the live drug reference carries the specific cautions and no dose numbers are given from memory here.

sections.heading: Safety, crisis & emergencies
sections.body: Take seriously and act on: thoughts or plans of suicide or self-harm, intent to harm others, psychosis with loss of touch with reality, mania with dangerous behaviour, and serious medication reactions (e.g., serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, lithium toxicity). If someone is in immediate danger, contact emergency services. CRISIS RESOURCES: in the US and Canada call or text 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline); elsewhere use local crisis lines and emergency numbers. For substance crises, Poison Control (US 1-800-222-1222) and SAMHSA (US 1-800-662-4357) help. A safety plan, removing means, and not being alone are protective steps.

sections.heading: Lifestyle, social & integrative factors
sections.body: Evidence-supported foundations that amplify treatment: regular physical activity (meaningful antidepressant/anxiolytic effect), sleep regulation, reduced alcohol and drugs, social connection, and structure/routine. Nutrition, mindfulness and meditation, and nature exposure have modest supporting evidence as adjuncts. These complement — not replace — therapy and medication for moderate-to-severe illness. Stigma, cost, and access are real barriers; low-cost options include primary care, community mental-health programs, group therapy, guided self-help, and reputable digital CBT programs.

sections.heading: Navigating care & getting the most
sections.body: Start with a primary-care doctor or a crisis line if urgent. Be specific about symptoms, duration, and impact; ask about both therapy and medication options and their trade-offs; expect antidepressants to take weeks and therapy to take several sessions; and don't stop medication abruptly. For students and professionals: screen for risk every contact, document safety plans, watch for medical mimics (thyroid, anaemia, medication effects, substance use), and coordinate between prescriber and therapist. Recovery is usually gradual and non-linear, and combined therapy-plus-medication often outperforms either alone for moderate-to-severe conditions.

chapters.title: Acupuncture & Traditional Chinese Medicine
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational reference; evidence-balanced.
chapters.source: Written for HIVE Doctor from standard clinical/professional references (educational). Evidence statements are kept honest: well-supported, mixed, or unproven is stated plainly. Complementary approaches are presented as adjuncts, never replacements for needed medical care.
chapters.overview: Acupuncture inserts fine needles at defined points; it sits within Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) alongside herbal medicine, cupping, moxibustion, and tui na. The chapter explains the traditional framework and the modern scientific view, where evidence is reasonable versus weak, safety, and herb-drug interaction cautions.

sections.heading: What practitioners do
sections.body: Acupuncturists insert thin, sterile, single-use needles at specific points on the body and leave them in place for a short time. The needles may be stimulated by hand, by heat (moxibustion), or by a mild electrical current (electroacupuncture). Practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine may also use herbal formulas, cupping, gua sha, dietary therapy and tui na massage, guided by a traditional assessment that includes examination of the pulse and tongue. A first visit usually includes a full health history, and a course of several sessions is typical before judging whether it is helping.

sections.heading: Two frameworks: traditional and modern
sections.body: TRADITIONAL: TCM describes health as balanced 'qi' flowing through meridians, with points chosen to rebalance it — a pre-scientific model whose concepts (qi, meridians) have no demonstrated physical basis. MODERN: research suggests needling can modulate the nervous system — local effects, spinal and brain pain-processing, and release of endorphins and other mediators. Much of acupuncture's measured benefit also includes strong non-specific effects (expectation, attention, relaxation, the ritual), shown by trials where 'sham' needling often performs nearly as well as 'real' point selection. Both framings can be stated honestly: something physiological happens, but not necessarily via meridians.

sections.heading: What the evidence supports
sections.body: Most supportive: chronic pain conditions (low-back and neck pain, knee osteoarthritis, tension and migraine headache prophylaxis) and chemotherapy-induced and post-operative nausea/vomiting — here acupuncture modestly outperforms no treatment, though often only marginally over sham, and is a reasonable option as part of a plan. Weak/unproven: infertility, smoking cessation, weight loss, allergies, and most internal diseases. It should be an ADJUNCT for symptom relief, not a substitute for diagnosis or disease-modifying treatment.

sections.heading: Safety & cautions
sections.body: With trained practitioners and single-use sterile needles, serious harm is rare. Common minor effects: bruising, soreness, minor bleeding, lightheadedness. Rare but serious: pneumothorax (collapsed lung) from deep needling near the chest, infection from non-sterile technique, and nerve or organ injury. Cautions: bleeding disorders or anticoagulants, pregnancy (some points avoided), and pacemakers (electroacupuncture). Insist on single-use needles and a regulated practitioner.

sections.heading: Chinese herbal medicine — the real risk area
sections.body: Herbal formulas carry the biggest hazards in TCM: inconsistent potency, contamination (heavy metals, undeclared pharmaceuticals), direct toxicity (some herbs cause liver or kidney injury — e.g., historical aristolochic-acid nephropathy), and HERB-DRUG INTERACTIONS (effects on blood thinners, sedatives, and liver enzymes). 'Natural' is not 'safe.' Anyone taking prescription medicine, pregnant, or with liver/kidney disease should clear herbal products with a pharmacist or doctor first, and buy only from regulated, tested sources.

sections.heading: Regulation & choosing care
sections.body: Acupuncturists are licensed or regulated in many jurisdictions, with defined training requirements, although standards vary from place to place. Some physicians and physiotherapists also practise medical acupuncture or dry needling. Choose a regulated practitioner who uses single-use needles, tell them about every medicine you take, any bleeding disorder, pregnancy, or implanted device such as a pacemaker, and keep your medical team informed. Treat acupuncture as one tool for relieving symptoms within evidence-based care, and never as a reason to delay the diagnosis of a serious problem.

chapters.overview: 'Holistic' care treats the whole person — body, mind, lifestyle, and context. This chapter separates the well-supported lifestyle foundations of health from complementary modalities of varying evidence, flags the real safety issues (supplements, interactions, delayed care), and gives a framework for weighing any unconventional therapy.

sections.heading: What 'holistic' and 'integrative' mean
sections.body: HOLISTIC care considers the whole person and root causes, not just an isolated symptom — a principle good conventional medicine shares. COMPLEMENTARY therapies are used alongside standard care; ALTERNATIVE means instead of it (the risky choice). INTEGRATIVE medicine deliberately combines evidence-based conventional care with complementary approaches that have reasonable support, within one plan. The distinction that matters most for safety is complementary-alongside versus alternative-instead-of.

sections.heading: The evidence-based foundations (the real 'holistic' wins)
sections.body: The strongest 'whole-person' levers are lifestyle, and they are genuinely powerful: regular physical activity, a predominantly whole-food diet, adequate sleep, not smoking, limited alcohol, stress management, and social connection together prevent and improve a large share of chronic disease — cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, many cancers, depression, and more. Any holistic plan should build on these first, because their evidence dwarfs that of most supplements and specialty modalities.

sections.heading: Mind-body approaches
sections.body: There is reasonable evidence for mind-body approaches as ADJUNCTS for stress, pain and wellbeing. They include mindfulness meditation and mindfulness-based stress reduction, yoga and tai chi (which also improve balance and strength), breathing techniques, biofeedback and guided relaxation. These methods are low-risk and can meaningfully help anxiety, chronic pain, blood pressure and sleep when practised consistently over weeks. They complement, and do not replace, treatment for significant illness. People with a history of trauma or psychosis should learn meditation with an experienced teacher, since intensive practice occasionally stirs up distress.

sections.heading: Supplements & natural products — benefits and real risks
sections.body: Some have defined roles (e.g., correcting a documented deficiency — iron, B12, vitamin D; folate in pregnancy; specific evidence-based uses). But the category is loosely regulated, so products vary in potency and purity, may be contaminated or adulterated, and many health claims are unproven. Key dangers: INTERACTIONS (St John's wort speeds metabolism of many drugs and can cause serotonin syndrome; high-dose fish oil, vitamin E, ginkgo, and garlic add bleeding risk with anticoagulants; grapefruit-like enzyme effects), liver toxicity (some weight-loss and bodybuilding products, kava, high-dose green-tea extract), and false reassurance. Tell your pharmacist and doctor everything you take; more is not better, and fat-soluble vitamins and minerals can reach toxic levels.

sections.heading: Modalities to approach critically
sections.body: Some popular modalities lack credible evidence or rest on implausible mechanisms: homeopathy (ultra-diluted preparations — no effect beyond placebo), detox/cleanse programs and colonic irrigation (no benefit, some harm), ear candling, most 'energy healing,' iridology, and many 'alternative' cancer cures. The honest position: a low-risk, inexpensive practice someone finds relaxing can be fine as a complement, but it should never replace effective treatment, be used to justify stopping prescribed medicine, or cost large sums on disease-cure promises.

sections.heading: A framework for weighing any therapy
sections.body: Ask: (1) What's the claim and the proposed mechanism — is it plausible? (2) What's the evidence quality — randomised trials and reviews, or testimonials? (3) What's the risk — direct harm, interactions, cost, and the opportunity cost of delaying effective care? (4) Is it complementary (alongside) or alternative (instead of)? (5) Does the provider make absolute cure claims, discourage conventional care, or require large up-front payments (red flags)? The biggest danger of complementary medicine is rarely the therapy itself — it's delaying or abandoning treatment that works. Keep your medical team informed of everything.

sections.heading: Integrative care done well
sections.body: Reputable integrative practice uses complementary methods that have reasonable evidence, such as acupuncture or mind-body therapy for pain, nutrition and exercise programmes, and massage for comfort, explicitly ALONGSIDE standard diagnosis and treatment, with everything coordinated and documented. It emphasises prevention, the patient's own participation and the therapeutic relationship, while holding itself to the same standards of evidence and safety as the rest of medicine. Warning signs of poor practice are advice to stop prescribed treatment, promises of cure, expensive proprietary supplements sold by the practitioner, and reluctance to communicate with your doctor.

chapters.title: Experimental & Emerging Therapies
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational reference. Experimental means unproven; access is through trials and specialists, not self-treatment.
chapters.source: Written for HIVE Doctor from standard clinical/professional references (educational). Evidence statements are kept honest: well-supported, mixed, or unproven is stated plainly. Complementary approaches are presented as adjuncts, never replacements for needed medical care.
chapters.overview: A tour of therapies at the frontier — how experimental medicine is tested, what's genuinely emerging across fields (gene and cell therapy, immunotherapy, mRNA, psychedelics, neurotech, regenerative medicine, AI), and how to tell real innovation from predatory 'miracle cures.' Nothing here is a protocol to attempt alone; experimental care belongs in regulated trials and specialist hands.

sections.heading: How new treatments are proven (the trial pipeline)
sections.body: A therapy moves from lab to clinic through stages: preclinical (cells, animals), then human trials — PHASE 1 (small; safety and dose), PHASE 2 (does it work, and side effects), PHASE 3 (large randomised comparison against standard care), then regulatory approval, then PHASE 4 (real-world monitoring). RANDOMISATION, blinding, and controls exist because the placebo effect and natural recovery fool uncontrolled observation. 'Promising in mice' or 'a Phase 1 result' is a long way from proven. This pipeline is the single most useful lens for judging any 'breakthrough' headline.

sections.heading: Gene & cell therapy
sections.body: Among the most transformative frontiers. GENE THERAPY adds, replaces, or silences genes (approved examples exist for some inherited blindness, spinal muscular atrophy, and certain blood disorders). CRISPR gene EDITING has produced approved treatment for sickle-cell disease and is in trials broadly. CAR-T and other CELL therapies re-engineer a patient's immune cells against cancers (approved for several blood cancers; solid tumours are harder). Real, but costly, complex, and not without serious risks — delivered only in specialist centres.

sections.heading: Immunotherapy & precision oncology
sections.body: Cancer care has shifted toward harnessing the immune system and targeting tumour biology. CHECKPOINT INHIBITORS release immune brakes so T-cells attack tumours (major gains in melanoma, lung, and others), at the cost of immune-related side effects. TARGETED therapies hit specific mutations identified by tumour genomic testing. The theme is PRECISION — matching treatment to the individual tumour's molecular profile rather than one-size-fits-all.

sections.heading: mRNA & next-generation vaccines/biologics
sections.body: mRNA technology (proven at scale in COVID-19 vaccines) instructs cells to make a target protein and is now in trials for other infections and for personalised CANCER vaccines. Monoclonal antibodies and other biologics continue to expand across autoimmune disease, migraine, cholesterol, and more. These are platform technologies — once established, they can be rapidly redirected to new targets.

sections.heading: Psychedelic-assisted therapy
sections.body: Psilocybin, MDMA, and ketamine (ketamine/esketamine already used for treatment-resistant depression) are in trials for depression, PTSD, and addiction, paired with structured psychotherapy. Early results are encouraging but preliminary, and these are powerful drugs with real risks used under medical supervision in controlled settings — not a DIY approach. Legal status and access vary and are evolving; outside approved programs, unsupervised use is unsafe.

sections.heading: Neurotechnology & devices
sections.body: DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION is established for Parkinson's and in trials for OCD and depression; transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is approved for some depression. BRAIN-COMPUTER INTERFACES (restoring communication/movement after paralysis), advanced prosthetics, retinal implants, and closed-loop devices for epilepsy are advancing quickly. Regenerative medicine (tissue engineering, stem-cell repair) and bioprinting remain mostly experimental outside a few niches.

sections.heading: AI & digital health
sections.body: Artificial intelligence is emerging in diagnostics (imaging, pathology, retinal and skin screening), risk prediction, drug discovery, and workflow. It augments clinicians rather than replacing judgement, and brings its own issues — validation, bias, privacy, and accountability. Digital therapeutics (validated app-based CBT and disease-management programs) are a related, more mature frontier. HIVE's own deterministic, no-hallucination reference design fits this caution: tools should be verifiable and safe, not black boxes.

sections.heading: Telling innovation from quackery
sections.body: Legitimate experimental care: runs through registered clinical trials (e.g., listed on trial registries), has ethics/regulatory oversight, discloses risks and uncertainty, usually doesn't charge patients large sums to participate, and reports results openly. RED FLAGS of predatory 'miracle cures': cure-all claims across unrelated diseases, 'secret' or 'suppressed' science, testimonials instead of data, large cash-only up-front fees (common in unproven stem-cell and 'alternative cancer' clinics abroad), pressure to act now, and advice to abandon conventional treatment. For patients: real access to experimental therapy comes through a specialist and a trial, not a sales page. For students/professionals: match every claim to its trial-pipeline stage before believing it.

chapters.title: The Care Team — Who to See for What
chapters.review_status: UNVERIFIED — educational navigation reference.

chapters.overview: A practical map of health professionals and how to navigate care — so a patient (or a student, or someone without easy access) knows who does what, who to see first, and when to escalate. Scope and titles vary by country/province/state.

sections.heading: Your front door: primary care
sections.body: Family doctors, nurse practitioners and physician assistants handle most health needs, coordinate referrals, manage long-term conditions and know your whole picture, so they are usually the right first stop for anything that is not an emergency. Pharmacists are the most accessible health professionals: they give walk-in advice about medicines, can prescribe for many minor ailments in some places, give vaccines and offer screening checks. For problems that are urgent but not emergencies, walk-in or urgent-care clinics and telehealth services bridge the gap. Chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of stroke, heavy bleeding or collapse go straight to emergency care.

sections.heading: Medical specialists (a quick index)
sections.body: Heart — cardiologist; lungs — respirologist/pulmonologist; gut/liver — gastroenterologist; kidneys — nephrologist; hormones/diabetes — endocrinologist; brain/nerves — neurologist; mental health — psychiatrist; bones/joints surgery — orthopaedic surgeon; joints/autoimmune — rheumatologist; skin — dermatologist; cancer — oncologist; blood — haematologist; women's health — gynaecologist/obstetrician; urinary/male — urologist; ear-nose-throat — otolaryngologist; eyes — ophthalmologist (medical/surgical) vs optometrist (vision/exams); children — paediatrician; infections — infectious-disease specialist; allergy/immune — allergist/immunologist. Most require a referral from primary care.

sections.heading: Allied health & therapies
sections.body: Movement/rehab — physiotherapist, occupational therapist, chiropractor, athletic therapist, kinesiologist; soft tissue — massage therapist; speech/swallow — speech-language pathologist; hearing — audiologist; feet — podiatrist/chiropodist; nutrition — registered dietitian; teeth — dentist/hygienist, with oral surgeons and orthodontists; vision aids — optometrist/optician; mental health — psychologist, counsellor/psychotherapist, social worker; complementary — acupuncturist and others (see those chapters). Many are direct-access (no referral).

sections.heading: Where to go, by urgency
sections.body: EMERGENCY (call emergency services / go to the ER): chest pain, stroke signs (FAST), severe breathing trouble, anaphylaxis, major bleeding or trauma, sudden severe 'worst-ever' headache, seizure, suspected cauda equina, suicidal crisis with intent. URGENT (same-day: urgent care, pharmacist, telehealth, or doctor): high fever, suspected infection, moderate injuries, medication reactions, worsening chronic conditions. ROUTINE (book primary care): ongoing or non-alarming symptoms, screening, chronic-disease management, referrals. When unsure, a nurse line, pharmacist, or telehealth triage can direct you — and this book's red-flag notes throughout point to when to escalate.

sections.heading: Care when access is hard
sections.body: For people without a regular doctor or easy access: community health centres and free/low-cost clinics, pharmacist services (advice, many minor-ailment prescriptions, vaccines), nurse telephone lines (e.g., 811 in much of Canada), telehealth, public-health units, student/occupational health, and emergency departments for true emergencies (which cannot turn away emergencies). Patient-assistance programs and generic medicines lower drug costs. This brain is built partly for exactly this gap — reliable, plain-language knowledge when a professional isn't immediately reachable — while still pointing clearly to when in-person care is essential.

chapters.title: Emergency & First Aid
chapters.overview: The time-critical knowledge: how to recognize a true emergency and what to do in the first minutes before help arrives. This chapter is action-first — the don't-miss emergencies, the core first-aid skills, and the clear line for when to call emergency services. When in doubt in a real emergency, call your local emergency number.

sections.heading: The first-minute approach (DRS-ABC)
sections.body: A simple, ordered approach saves lives. DANGER: make sure the scene is safe for you first. RESPONSE: check if the person responds to voice or touch. SHOUT for help / call emergency services (or send someone). AIRWAY: open it (head-tilt, chin-lift); clear obvious obstruction. BREATHING: look, listen, feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. CIRCULATION: if not breathing normally, start CPR. This DRS-ABC sequence works for most collapses; the sections below drill into the big ones.

sections.heading: CPR & choking
sections.body: CARDIAC ARREST (no normal breathing, unresponsive): call emergency services, start CPR — push hard and fast in the centre of the chest about 100–120 compressions per minute, allowing full recoil; use an AED as soon as one is available (it guides you). Hands-only CPR is effective if untrained in rescue breaths. CHOKING (can't breathe, speak, or cough): give firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then abdominal thrusts (Heimlich); alternate until it clears or the person collapses (then start CPR). For infants, use back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts.

sections.heading: Heart attack & stroke — recognize fast
sections.body: HEART ATTACK: chest pressure/pain (may spread to arm, jaw, back), shortness of breath, sweating, nausea — call emergency services immediately; chewing aspirin may help if advised and not allergic. STROKE — use FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Note the time symptoms started (it determines treatment). Both are TIME-CRITICAL — 'time is muscle' and 'time is brain.' Do not drive yourself; do not wait to see if it passes.

sections.heading: Severe bleeding, shock & burns
sections.body: SEVERE BLEEDING: apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth; keep pressing and add more cloth rather than removing soaked ones; a tourniquet high on a limb is a last resort for life-threatening limb bleeding. SHOCK (pale, cold, clammy, rapid weak pulse, confusion): lay them down, keep warm, call for help. BURNS: cool with running cool (not ice-cold) water for 20 minutes, remove tight items, cover loosely; never pop blisters or apply butter/creams. Large, deep, facial, or airway burns need emergency care.

sections.heading: Anaphylaxis, seizures & diabetic emergencies
sections.body: ANAPHYLAXIS (swelling of lips/throat, difficulty breathing, widespread hives, collapse after an allergen): use an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) immediately into the outer thigh and call emergency services — it is the only effective treatment; a second dose may be needed. SEIZURE: protect from injury, cushion the head, do NOT restrain or put anything in the mouth, time it, and call for help if it lasts over 5 minutes, repeats, or is a first seizure. DIABETIC low blood sugar (shaky, confused, sweating): give fast sugar if conscious and able to swallow; if unconscious, recovery position and call for help.

sections.heading: Unconscious but breathing, and when to call
sections.body: If someone is UNCONSCIOUS BUT BREATHING normally, place them in the RECOVERY POSITION (on their side, airway open) and monitor until help arrives. CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES for: no/abnormal breathing, chest pain, stroke signs, severe bleeding, anaphylaxis, a first or prolonged seizure, major trauma, suspected spinal injury (don't move them unless in danger), severe burns, poisoning/overdose (also contact Poison Control), or any rapidly worsening condition. When unsure, call — dispatchers coach you through what to do.

chapters.title: Cardiology (Heart & Circulation)
chapters.overview: How the heart and blood vessels work, what goes wrong, and how it is found and managed. Covers the common presentations a clinician sees daily — chest pain, high blood pressure, rhythm problems, heart failure — with the red flags that make it an emergency. Educational; diagnosis and treatment are individual medical decisions.

sections.heading: How the heart works
sections.body: The heart is a two-sided pump: the right side sends blood to the lungs for oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body. Its own muscle is fed by the CORONARY arteries. An electrical system (SA node → AV node → ventricles) sets the rhythm, and valves keep blood moving one way. Blood pressure is the force in the arteries; the heart rate and output, vessel tone, and blood volume set it. Most heart disease is a problem of the plumbing (blocked arteries), the pump (weak muscle), the rhythm (electrical), or the valves.

sections.heading: Chest pain & coronary disease
sections.body: Narrowing of the coronary arteries (atherosclerosis) causes ANGINA (chest pressure on exertion, relieved by rest) and, when an artery blocks, a HEART ATTACK (myocardial infarction). RED FLAGS — chest pressure/pain lasting more than a few minutes, or with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to the arm/jaw/back, is a medical EMERGENCY: call emergency services. Not all chest pain is cardiac (muscle, reflux, anxiety, lung causes), but new, severe, or exertional chest pain should be assumed cardiac until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: High blood pressure (hypertension)
sections.body: Often symptomless ('the silent killer'), sustained high blood pressure damages arteries and raises the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, and heart failure. It is diagnosed on repeated readings, confirmed with home or ambulatory monitoring. Management: lifestyle first (less salt, weight loss, activity, less alcohol, stopping smoking) and medication when needed, individualized by a clinician. RED FLAG — a very high reading with chest pain, severe headache, vision change, breathlessness, or neurological symptoms (hypertensive emergency) needs urgent care.

sections.heading: Rhythm problems (arrhythmias)
sections.body: The heart can beat too fast, too slow, or irregularly. ATRIAL FIBRILLATION (irregular, often fast) is the most common and raises STROKE risk, so it is often treated with blood thinners plus rate/rhythm control. Other arrhythmias range from benign extra beats to dangerous ventricular rhythms. Symptoms: palpitations, dizziness, breathlessness, or fainting. RED FLAGS — fainting, chest pain, or severe breathlessness with palpitations, or a very fast or very slow pulse with symptoms, need urgent assessment. Diagnosis uses an ECG and monitors.

sections.heading: Heart failure & valves
sections.body: HEART FAILURE means the heart cannot pump efficiently enough for the body's needs, causing breathlessness (worse lying flat), fatigue, and swelling of the legs/abdomen. It is managed with medication, fluid and salt control, and treating the cause; it is a chronic condition needing monitoring. VALVE disease (stenosis/narrowing or regurgitation/leak) strains the heart and may need repair or replacement. RED FLAGS — rapidly worsening breathlessness, breathlessness at rest, or sudden weight gain from fluid need prompt care.

sections.heading: Risk, tests & prevention
sections.body: Cardiovascular risk is driven by blood pressure, cholesterol (especially LDL), smoking, diabetes, obesity, inactivity, diet, family history, and age. PREVENTION is powerful: not smoking, activity, a heart-healthy diet, managing blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes, and treating risk early. Common tests: blood pressure, blood lipids and glucose, ECG, echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart), stress testing, and angiography to image the arteries. Knowing and managing your numbers is the core of cardiology for most people.

chapters.title: Respiratory Medicine (Lungs & Breathing)
chapters.overview: How breathing works and the common conditions that disrupt it — asthma, COPD, infections, and the breathlessness that can signal something serious. Practical, with the red flags that turn a cough into an emergency. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: How breathing works
sections.body: Air travels down the airways (trachea → bronchi → tiny bronchioles) to the ALVEOLI, where oxygen crosses into the blood and carbon dioxide leaves. The diaphragm and chest muscles drive the bellows action, and the brain adjusts the rate automatically. Problems arise from narrowed airways (asthma, COPD), damaged air sacs (emphysema), fluid or infection in the lungs (pneumonia), blocked blood supply (pulmonary embolism), or restricted expansion. The key symptoms are cough, breathlessness, wheeze, chest tightness, and sputum.

sections.heading: Asthma
sections.body: Asthma is reversible airway narrowing and inflammation causing episodic wheeze, cough (often at night), chest tightness, and breathlessness, triggered by allergens, exercise, cold air, smoke, or infection. It is managed with RELIEVER inhalers (open the airways) and PREVENTER inhalers (reduce inflammation), plus trigger avoidance and an action plan. RED FLAGS — a severe attack (too breathless to speak, reliever not working, lips/fingers blue, exhaustion) is an EMERGENCY: use the reliever and call emergency services. Good inhaler technique is essential and often done wrong.

sections.heading: COPD
sections.body: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (chronic bronchitis and emphysema) is largely irreversible airway damage, usually from SMOKING, causing progressive breathlessness, chronic cough, and sputum. Management: STOPPING SMOKING (the single most important step), inhalers, pulmonary rehab, vaccines, and treating flare-ups. EXACERBATIONS (worsening breathlessness, more or discoloured sputum) often need prompt treatment. RED FLAGS — severe breathlessness, confusion, or blue lips need urgent care. Oxygen is used only under medical supervision.

sections.heading: Chest infections
sections.body: Most coughs are viral (colds, bronchitis) and self-limited. PNEUMONIA (infection of the lung tissue) causes fever, productive cough, breathlessness, and chest pain, and can be serious, especially in the old, young, or frail. Influenza and COVID-19 can cause severe lung illness. RED FLAGS — breathlessness at rest, fast breathing, confusion, chest pain, blue lips, coughing blood, or a high fever that won't settle need prompt assessment. Antibiotics help bacterial infections, not viral ones (see antimicrobial stewardship in the Pharmacy chapter).

sections.heading: Breathlessness & don't-miss causes
sections.body: Sudden or severe breathlessness is a red flag for serious causes: PULMONARY EMBOLISM (a clot in the lung — sudden breathlessness, sharp chest pain worse on breathing, sometimes after immobility, surgery, or a leg clot — an EMERGENCY), PNEUMOTHORAX (collapsed lung — sudden sharp pain and breathlessness), severe asthma/COPD attacks, heart failure, and anaphylaxis. Any sudden, severe, or rapidly worsening breathlessness, or breathlessness with chest pain, coughing blood, or collapse, needs emergency care.

sections.heading: Tests, prevention & care
sections.body: Common tests: oxygen level (pulse oximetry), SPIROMETRY (breathing capacity, key for asthma/COPD), chest X-ray and CT, and blood tests. PREVENTION and self-care: never smoking (or quitting), vaccination (flu, COVID, pneumococcal), avoiding triggers and pollution, good inhaler technique, and pulmonary rehabilitation for chronic disease. Breathing exercises and staying active help. Long-term lung conditions are managed, not cured, so monitoring and an action plan matter.

chapters.title: Dermatology (Skin, Hair & Nails)
chapters.overview: The body's largest organ and the problems that bring people to the clinic: rashes, acne, infections, and the moles and skin changes that must not be missed. Covers how to think about a rash and the clear signs that mean 'get it checked.' Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: The skin & how to describe a rash
sections.body: Skin has three layers (epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat) and protects, senses, and regulates temperature. Describing a rash well is half the diagnosis: where it is and how it spread, whether it itches or hurts, flat (macule) or raised (papule), blistered, scaly, or weepy, its colour, and whether it blanches (fades) under pressure. A NON-BLANCHING rash (doesn't fade when pressed) with fever can signal meningococcal infection — a RED FLAG needing emergency care.

sections.heading: Common chronic conditions
sections.body: ECZEMA (atopic dermatitis): itchy, dry, inflamed skin, often in flexures, managed with moisturizers, trigger avoidance, and topical steroids in flares. PSORIASIS: well-defined red, scaly plaques (elbows, knees, scalp), an immune condition sometimes with joint involvement. ACNE: blocked, inflamed oil glands, treated from topical agents up to oral medication. ROSACEA: facial redness and bumps. These are controlled, not cured; a clinician matches treatment to severity, and good skincare underpins all of them.

sections.heading: Skin infections & infestations
sections.body: BACTERIAL: impetigo (crusted, contagious), CELLULITIS (spreading hot, red, tender skin with fever — needs prompt antibiotics; RED FLAG if spreading fast or very unwell). FUNGAL: ringworm, athlete's foot, thrush — itchy, scaly, treated with antifungals. VIRAL: warts, cold sores, and SHINGLES (painful band of blisters on one side — see a doctor early as antivirals help). INFESTATIONS: scabies (intense night itch, needs prescribed treatment of the person and contacts) and lice. Contagious conditions need treatment of close contacts and hygiene measures.

sections.heading: Moles & skin cancer — the don't-miss
sections.body: Skin cancer is common and highly curable when caught early. Use the ABCDE rule for moles: Asymmetry, irregular Border, uneven Colour, Diameter over ~6 mm, and Evolving (changing). RED FLAGS — a new or changing mole, a sore that won't heal, a spot that bleeds, itches, or looks different from the others ('ugly duckling'), especially in sun-damaged skin — get it checked promptly. Melanoma is the most dangerous type; non-melanoma skin cancers (basal and squamous cell) are more common and usually less aggressive but still need treatment.

sections.heading: Rashes that are emergencies
sections.body: Most rashes are benign, but some are not. RED FLAGS — a non-blanching (glass-test) rash with fever (possible meningococcal sepsis); a rash with facial/lip/tongue swelling and breathing difficulty (anaphylaxis); widespread blistering or skin peeling, especially with mouth/eye involvement or after a new medication (possible severe drug reaction like Stevens-Johnson syndrome); rapidly spreading redness with severe pain out of proportion (possible serious soft-tissue infection) — all need emergency care. When a rash comes with feeling very unwell, take it seriously.

sections.heading: Sun protection & everyday skin care
sections.body: Prevention is the best dermatology: SUN PROTECTION (broad-spectrum sunscreen, shade, clothing; avoid tanning beds) prevents most skin cancer and ageing. General care: gentle cleansing, regular moisturizing (especially for eczema-prone skin), avoiding known irritants, and not picking or over-treating. Know your skin and check it periodically, especially if you have many moles, fair skin, or a family history. See a doctor or dermatologist for anything persistent, spreading, severe, or changing.

chapters.title: Nutrition & Dietetics
chapters.overview: What the body needs to run well, how diet drives health and disease, and how to separate evidence from fad. Practical and non-faddish — the macronutrients and micronutrients, healthy patterns, special situations, and when to see a dietitian. Educational; personalized diet plans and medical nutrition therapy belong to a registered dietitian.

sections.heading: Macronutrients & energy
sections.body: Food provides energy (calories) and building blocks. CARBOHYDRATES (sugars and starches) are the main fuel — favour whole grains, legumes, fruit, and vegetables over refined sugar and white flour. PROTEIN builds and repairs tissue (meat, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes, soy). FATS are essential — favour unsaturated (olive oil, nuts, fish) over saturated and avoid trans fats. FIBRE (from plants) aids digestion, blood sugar, and cholesterol. Energy balance over time, not any single meal, drives weight; quality of food matters as much as quantity.

sections.heading: Vitamins, minerals & water
sections.body: MICRONUTRIENTS are needed in small amounts but are vital: iron (oxygen transport), calcium and vitamin D (bones), B12 and folate (blood and nerves), iodine (thyroid), and the vitamins A, C, E, K, and the B group. A varied whole-food diet usually covers them; specific groups may need supplements (vitamin D in low-sun climates, B12 for vegans, folate in pregnancy, iron for some). More is not better — fat-soluble vitamins and minerals can reach toxic levels. HYDRATION matters; water is the default drink.

sections.heading: Healthy eating patterns
sections.body: The evidence favours PATTERNS over single 'superfoods': diets rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and fish and lighter on red/processed meat, refined carbohydrates, added sugar, and ultra-processed foods (the Mediterranean-style pattern is among the best-supported) lower the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and more. Plant-forward eating, portion awareness, cooking at home, and limiting sugary drinks are high-yield. There is no one 'perfect' diet — the best is a nutritious one a person can sustain.

sections.heading: Diet & disease
sections.body: Nutrition is central to managing many conditions: DIABETES (carbohydrate quality and consistency, weight), HEART DISEASE and high cholesterol (less saturated fat and salt, more fibre), HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE (less salt — the DASH pattern), and overweight/obesity. Food allergies and intolerances (e.g., coeliac disease needing strict gluten avoidance, lactose intolerance) require specific changes. Malnutrition — under-nutrition or deficiency — is common in illness and older age and is easy to miss. Medical nutrition therapy from a dietitian is part of treating these.

sections.heading: Special life stages & situations
sections.body: Needs change across life: PREGNANCY (folate, iron, iodine, avoiding certain foods), INFANCY and childhood (growth; breastfeeding and appropriate weaning), OLDER AGE (protein and vitamin D for muscle and bone, appetite and swallowing changes), and ATHLETES (energy and protein timing). Vegetarian and vegan diets are healthy with attention to B12, iron, omega-3, and protein. Illness, surgery, and some medications change needs. These are the situations where tailored, professional advice pays off most.

sections.heading: Fads, supplements & getting real advice
sections.body: Nutrition is awash with fads and marketing. Be skeptical of 'detox' and cleanse programs (the liver and kidneys detoxify; these have no benefit), rapid-weight-loss and single-food diets, and supplements promising to cure disease. Supplements help in specific deficiencies but are not a substitute for food and can interact with medicines (tell your pharmacist). For real, personalized guidance — especially with a medical condition, pregnancy, an eating disorder, or significant weight goals — see a REGISTERED DIETITIAN, the regulated nutrition professional.

chapters.title: Nursing & Patient Care
chapters.overview: The hands-on discipline that carries most of day-to-day care: assessment and monitoring, safe medication administration, infection control, wound and pressure care, and the human side of looking after someone — in hospital or at home. Useful for carers and students alike. Educational, not a substitute for professional training.

sections.heading: What nurses do
sections.body: Nurses assess, monitor, and care for patients and coordinate much of their treatment. The work spans taking a history and VITAL SIGNS, administering medicines and treatments, wound and personal care, educating patients and families, spotting deterioration early, and advocating for the patient. Roles range from registered and licensed practical nurses to nurse practitioners (who diagnose and prescribe) and specialists (ICU, mental health, community, midwifery). Much of safe, humane healthcare rests on nursing.

sections.heading: Vital signs & spotting deterioration
sections.body: The core monitoring set: temperature, heart rate (pulse), respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and level of consciousness, plus pain and urine output. TRENDS matter more than single readings — a rising heart and breathing rate with falling blood pressure signals deterioration (early-warning scores formalize this). RED FLAGS of a deteriorating patient: new confusion, fast or laboured breathing, low oxygen, a rising or very low heart rate, low blood pressure, or markedly reduced urine — escalate for help promptly, as early action saves lives (see sepsis).

sections.heading: Safe medication administration
sections.body: Giving medicines safely follows the 'rights': the RIGHT patient, drug, dose, route, time — plus right documentation, reason, and response. Double-check high-alert drugs (insulin, anticoagulants, opioids), measure liquids with proper devices, confirm allergies, and never give a medicine you cannot identify or that looks wrong. Watch for and report side effects and errors honestly. For carers at home: keep a current medicines list, use dosette/blister packs, store safely, and ask the pharmacist about interactions and timing (see the Pharmacy chapter).

sections.heading: Infection control
sections.body: Preventing the spread of infection is foundational. HAND HYGIENE (washing or sanitizing before and after contact) is the single most effective measure. Use personal protective equipment appropriately, handle and dispose of sharps and waste safely, clean equipment and surfaces, and isolate contagious patients as indicated. Aseptic technique protects wounds, catheters, and IV lines from infection. These basics prevent healthcare-associated infections and protect both patient and carer.

sections.heading: Wound, pressure & personal care
sections.body: WOUND care keeps wounds clean and moist, protects them, and watches for infection (spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, fever — report it). PRESSURE INJURIES (bedsores) arise over bony areas from unrelieved pressure — prevent them by repositioning regularly, keeping skin clean and dry, good nutrition and hydration, and using pressure-relieving supports; check at-risk skin daily. PERSONAL care (washing, continence, mouth care, mobility) preserves dignity and prevents complications; safe moving-and-handling protects both patient and carer from injury.

sections.heading: The human side & the care team
sections.body: Good care treats the person, not just the condition: communication, dignity, consent, privacy, pain and symptom relief, emotional support, and attention to the family and carers. Nurses watch for mood, delirium, nutrition, sleep, and safety (falls), and connect patients to the wider team — doctors, pharmacists, therapists, social workers. For home carers, knowing your limits, preventing burnout, using respite and community resources, and keeping clear records and an escalation plan are part of caring well and sustainably.

chapters.title: Emergency Medicine & Prehospital Care (EMT/Paramedic)
chapters.overview: The clinical discipline of the first hours of acute illness and injury — how emergency clinicians and prehospital crews rapidly assess, prioritize, and stabilize anyone, undifferentiated, before a diagnosis is known. Goes beyond first aid into the systematic primary/secondary survey, triage, trauma and medical resuscitation, and the time-critical decisions that define EMS and the ED.

sections.heading: The primary survey (ABCDE)
sections.body: Emergency assessment is systematic and repeatable: A — Airway (patent? protect the cervical spine in trauma); B — Breathing (rate, effort, oxygen, breath sounds, treat tension pneumothorax); C — Circulation (pulse, blood pressure, control bleeding, IV access and fluids); D — Disability (conscious level by AVPU or Glasgow Coma Scale, pupils, blood glucose); E — Exposure/Environment (undress to find injuries, prevent hypothermia). Life threats are treated as they are found before moving on. The survey is repeated whenever the patient changes.

sections.heading: Triage & scene management
sections.body: When patients outnumber resources, TRIAGE sorts by severity so the most salvageable are treated first. Prehospital systems use schemes (e.g., START) sorting into immediate, delayed, minor, and deceased/expectant based on breathing, perfusion, and mental status. In the ED, triage scales (CTAS, ESI) assign urgency. Scene safety comes first — crews do not become casualties — followed by a scene size-up, mechanism of injury, and calling for appropriate resources. Communication and handover (e.g., the SBAR or MIST format) transfer critical information cleanly.

sections.heading: Trauma resuscitation
sections.body: Trauma kills by airway loss, breathing failure, and HAEMORRHAGE — the latter the leading preventable cause. Control catastrophic external bleeding first (direct pressure, tourniquet, haemostatic dressing), then ABCDE. Key concepts: the 'lethal triad' (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy), permissive hypotension in some bleeding, tranexamic acid early, and rapid transfer to definitive surgical care ('scoop and run' vs 'stay and play' judged by injury and distance). Identify and treat immediately life-threatening chest injuries (tension pneumothorax, open chest wound, massive haemothorax).

sections.heading: Medical emergencies & resuscitation
sections.body: Beyond trauma: CARDIAC ARREST (high-quality CPR, early defibrillation of shockable rhythms, treat reversible causes — the 'Hs and Ts'), acute coronary syndromes (aspirin, oxygen if hypoxic, rapid ECG and reperfusion pathway), STROKE (rapid recognition and transport to a stroke centre within the treatment window), anaphylaxis (adrenaline first), status epilepticus, severe asthma/COPD, sepsis (early recognition, fluids, antibiotics), diabetic emergencies, and overdose/poisoning (supportive care, antidotes like naloxone). Reassessment is constant.

sections.heading: Core procedures & monitoring
sections.body: The practical toolkit: airway management (positioning, adjuncts, supraglottic devices, intubation), oxygen and assisted ventilation (bag-valve-mask), vascular access and fluids, haemorrhage control, splinting and spinal precautions, and medication administration by protocol. Monitoring: pulse oximetry, ECG, capnography (end-tidal CO2 — confirms airway and tracks CPR quality), and blood glucose. Prehospital decisions run on protocols and medical direction, with destination choices (trauma centre, cardiac centre, stroke centre) that change outcomes.

sections.heading: Decisions, handover & the system
sections.body: Emergency care is high-stakes and time-compressed: clinicians act on incomplete information, weigh resuscitation against futility and advance directives/DNR orders, obtain consent (or act under implied consent when a patient cannot), and document carefully. Clean HANDOVER to the next team preserves the thread of care. The wider system — dispatch, first responders, EMS, the ED, and inpatient teams — works as a chain; the 'golden hour' concept captures why speed to definitive care matters, even as the evidence refines exactly which minutes count for which conditions.

chapters.title: Surgery & Perioperative Care
chapters.overview: The principles behind operative treatment and the care around it: how surgeons decide to operate, the anatomy and asepsis that make surgery safe, the perioperative journey (before, during, after), wound healing and complications, and the major surgical specialties. University-level background for understanding any operation.

sections.heading: Deciding to operate
sections.body: Surgery is a treatment with risks, chosen when its benefit outweighs non-operative options. Indications fall into broad groups: to remove (a tumour, an inflamed appendix), repair (a hernia, a fracture, a torn vessel), reconstruct, bypass or divert, transplant, or diagnose (biopsy). Decisions weigh the disease, the patient's fitness (comorbidities, frailty), urgency (emergency vs elective), and the patient's goals and informed consent. 'A chance to cut is not a reason to cut' — the judgment of when NOT to operate is as important as technical skill.

sections.heading: Asepsis, anatomy & the operative principles
sections.body: Safe surgery rests on ANTISEPSIS and STERILE technique (preventing infection — the advance that made modern surgery possible), detailed ANATOMY (knowing exactly what lies where), haemostasis (controlling bleeding), gentle tissue handling, and sound closure. The operating team, the surgical safety checklist (confirming patient, site, and procedure to prevent wrong-site surgery), and meticulous counts of instruments and swabs are core safety systems. Minimally invasive (laparoscopic/robotic) approaches reduce trauma and recovery for many operations.

sections.heading: Anaesthesia & the intra-operative patient
sections.body: Operations are enabled by ANAESTHESIA: general (unconscious, often with airway control and ventilation), regional (spinal, epidural, or nerve blocks numbing a region), or local. The anaesthetist keeps the patient alive and still — managing the airway, breathing, circulation, depth of anaesthesia, fluids, temperature, and pain — and manages risk from the patient's other conditions. Pre-operative assessment grades fitness (e.g., the ASA scale) and plans for difficult airways, bleeding risk, and medication (which anticoagulants to hold, diabetes management).

sections.heading: The perioperative journey
sections.body: PRE-OP: assessment, optimizing medical conditions, fasting, consent, marking the site, and prophylaxis (antibiotics for certain operations, clot prevention). INTRA-OP: the procedure under anaesthesia with monitoring. POST-OP: recovery, pain control (multimodal, opioid-sparing where possible), early mobilization, fluids and nutrition, and watching for complications. ENHANCED RECOVERY protocols (ERAS) — minimizing fasting, using regional anaesthesia, early feeding and mobilization — speed recovery and cut complications. Discharge planning starts early.

sections.heading: Wound healing & surgical complications
sections.body: Wounds heal in phases — inflammation, proliferation (new tissue and collagen), and remodelling — healing by primary intention (clean edges closed) or secondary (left to granulate). Factors that impair healing: poor blood supply, infection, diabetes, smoking, steroids, and malnutrition. Watch for COMPLICATIONS: bleeding/haematoma, infection (surgical-site infection), wound dehiscence (breakdown), clots (DVT/PE), chest infection, ileus (gut paralysis), and anastomotic leak. RED FLAGS after surgery — fever, spreading redness, severe or worsening pain, breathlessness, or a wound that opens — need prompt review.

sections.heading: The surgical specialties
sections.body: Surgery branches widely: GENERAL (abdomen, hernias, gallbladder, bowel, breast, trauma), ORTHOPAEDIC (bones and joints), CARDIOTHORACIC (heart and chest), VASCULAR, NEUROSURGERY (brain and spine), PLASTIC and reconstructive, UROLOGY, ENT (head and neck), OPHTHALMOLOGY, OBSTETRIC/GYNAECOLOGIC, PAEDIATRIC, and TRANSPLANT surgery. Each combines shared principles (asepsis, anatomy, haemostasis, perioperative care) with specialized skills and technology. Interventional radiology and endoscopy increasingly treat surgically what once needed open operations.

chapters.title: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
chapters.overview: Women's reproductive health across the lifespan: the menstrual cycle, contraception, pregnancy and birth, and the common and serious gynaecological conditions. University-level with clear red flags for the pregnancy and bleeding emergencies that must not be missed. Educational, not a substitute for obstetric/gynaecologic care.

sections.heading: The menstrual cycle & reproductive physiology
sections.body: The menstrual cycle (about 28 days, variable) is driven by a hormonal loop between the brain (GnRH, FSH, LH) and the ovaries (oestrogen, progesterone). The FOLLICULAR phase matures an egg and thickens the womb lining; OVULATION releases the egg mid-cycle; the LUTEAL phase prepares for possible pregnancy, and without it the lining sheds as a period. Understanding this underlies fertility, contraception, and the diagnosis of menstrual disorders. Menopause is the natural end of cycles, usually around the early 50s.

sections.heading: Contraception & family planning
sections.body: Methods vary in effectiveness and mechanism: long-acting reversible contraception (LARC — IUDs and implants) is the most effective and 'fit and forget'; hormonal methods (pill, patch, ring, injection) prevent ovulation and thicken cervical mucus; barrier methods (condoms — also protect against STIs); fertility awareness; sterilization (permanent); and emergency contraception after unprotected sex. Choice depends on effectiveness, health conditions (e.g., clot risk with some hormonal methods), and preference. A clinician matches the method to the person.

sections.heading: Pregnancy & antenatal care
sections.body: Pregnancy spans three TRIMESTERS over ~40 weeks. Antenatal care monitors mother and baby: confirming dates, screening (blood tests, ultrasound, genetic screening), checking blood pressure and growth, and advising on nutrition (folate), avoiding harms (alcohol, smoking, certain foods and drugs), and vaccination. Common issues: nausea, reflux, anaemia, gestational diabetes, and back pain. RED FLAGS needing urgent care: significant bleeding, severe headache with visual changes or swelling (pre-eclampsia), reduced fetal movements, severe abdominal pain, waters breaking early, or signs of preterm labour.

sections.heading: Labour, birth & the postpartum period
sections.body: Labour has stages: the cervix dilates (first stage), the baby is born (second), and the placenta is delivered (third). Births can be vaginal or by caesarean section (for the baby's or mother's safety), with pain relief options from breathing and water to epidural. The POSTPARTUM period brings recovery, breastfeeding, and bonding, but also risks: heavy bleeding (postpartum haemorrhage — an emergency), infection, clots, and mood disorders (the 'baby blues', postnatal depression, and rarely postpartum psychosis — all needing support). Newborn checks and feeding support matter.

sections.heading: Common gynaecological conditions
sections.body: Frequent problems: HEAVY or painful periods, PCOS (irregular cycles, hormonal features), ENDOMETRIOSIS (tissue like the womb lining outside it, causing pain and sometimes infertility), FIBROIDS, ovarian CYSTS, prolapse and incontinence, menopausal symptoms, and infections (thrush, bacterial vaginosis, PID, STIs). Fertility difficulties are common and investigable. Many are managed medically; some need surgery. Cervical, ovarian, endometrial, and breast cancers are screened for and investigated — hence the importance of screening programs.

sections.heading: Gynaecological & obstetric emergencies
sections.body: Do not miss: ECTOPIC PREGNANCY (a pregnancy outside the womb — one-sided pelvic pain, bleeding, and shoulder-tip pain or collapse signal rupture; an EMERGENCY), MISCARRIAGE with heavy bleeding, OVARIAN TORSION (sudden severe one-sided pain), PID (pelvic infection), PRE-ECLAMPSIA/eclampsia in pregnancy, and postpartum haemorrhage. Any pregnant person with severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, or severe headache/visual changes needs urgent assessment. Severe pelvic pain with a positive pregnancy test is an ectopic until proven otherwise.

chapters.title: Paediatrics (Child Health)
chapters.overview: How children differ from adults medically, how they grow and develop, and the common and serious childhood illnesses — plus the red flags that signal a sick child. University-level, with the recognition skills that matter most when a child cannot describe what is wrong. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Children are not small adults
sections.body: Children differ physiologically: faster heart and breathing rates (normal ranges change with age), larger heads and different airways, immature immune and organ systems, and weight-based medication dosing. They compensate for illness then deteriorate suddenly, so early recognition is vital. Assessment adapts to age — observation (the 'end of the bed' look), the Paediatric Assessment Triangle (appearance, breathing, circulation), and involving the parents, who often know first that something is wrong. Development and safeguarding are always part of the picture.

sections.heading: Growth & development
sections.body: Children follow predictable patterns of GROWTH (tracked on centile charts for weight, height, and head circumference — the trend matters more than a single point) and DEVELOPMENT across domains: gross motor, fine motor, speech and language, and social. Missing MILESTONES, or losing skills, prompts assessment. Nutrition (breastfeeding, weaning, balanced diet), sleep, and immunization underpin healthy development. Puberty brings its own physical and emotional changes. Developmental concerns (autism, ADHD, learning or motor delay) benefit from early identification and support.

sections.heading: Common childhood illnesses
sections.body: Most childhood illness is viral and self-limited: coughs, colds, ear infections, sore throats, viral rashes, gastroenteritis (where the main risk is DEHYDRATION — managed with fluids), and fevers. Common specific illnesses: croup, bronchiolitis (RSV in infants), hand-foot-and-mouth, chickenpox, and the vaccine-preventable diseases (measles, mumps, rubella, whooping cough). Asthma, eczema, and allergies are common chronic conditions. Fever itself is a symptom, not a disease; how the child looks and behaves matters far more than the number on the thermometer.

sections.heading: The sick child — red flags
sections.body: Recognizing serious illness is the core paediatric skill. RED FLAGS needing urgent/emergency care: a NON-BLANCHING rash with fever (possible meningococcal sepsis), difficulty breathing (fast breathing, chest recession, grunting, blue lips), a child who is drowsy, floppy, or hard to rouse, or inconsolable/high-pitched crying, signs of DEHYDRATION (sunken eyes, no wet nappies, no tears), a fever in a baby under 3 months, a stiff neck or dislike of light, a seizure, or a parent who feels this illness is different and serious. When a child looks very unwell, act fast.

sections.heading: Babies & the newborn
sections.body: Newborns need special attention: feeding (breast or formula) and weight, jaundice (common and usually benign but needs checking if early, deep, or prolonged), temperature, cord care, and screening (newborn exam, blood-spot, hearing). RED FLAGS in a newborn: poor feeding, lethargy, fever or low temperature, fast or laboured breathing, a bulging soft spot, persistent vomiting (especially green/bile-stained), or deep jaundice — all need prompt assessment, as babies can become seriously unwell quickly. Safe sleep (on the back, clear cot) reduces the risk of sudden infant death.

sections.heading: Safeguarding, vaccines & prevention
sections.body: Child health is also PREVENTION and PROTECTION: the immunization schedule prevents once-common deadly diseases and relies on broad uptake; injury prevention (car seats, home safety, water safety) addresses a leading cause of childhood harm; and SAFEGUARDING — recognizing and responding to possible abuse or neglect — is every clinician's duty, weighing unexplained or inconsistent injuries, developmental concerns, and the child's wellbeing. Dental care, mental health, and support for families and carers round out a child-centred approach.

chapters.title: Neurology (Brain & Nervous System)
chapters.overview: How the nervous system is organized and the major conditions that affect it — stroke, seizures, headache, Parkinson's, MS, neuropathy, and dementia — with the localizing logic neurologists use and the red flags that make a headache or weakness an emergency. University-level. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: How the nervous system is organized
sections.body: The CENTRAL nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the PERIPHERAL nerves form a signalling network. The brain's lobes have roles (frontal — movement, planning, personality; parietal — sensation; temporal — hearing, memory; occipital — vision), the cerebellum coordinates, and the brainstem runs vital functions. Neurology is largely about LOCALIZATION: the pattern of symptoms (where the weakness, numbness, or deficit is) points to where the lesion is, and the time course (sudden, over hours, or gradual) points to the cause (vascular, inflammatory, or degenerative).

sections.heading: Stroke & vascular disease
sections.body: STROKE is sudden brain injury from a blocked (ischaemic, ~85%) or burst (haemorrhagic) blood vessel — a TIME-CRITICAL EMERGENCY. Recognize with FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time). Rapid imaging distinguishes the type; ischaemic stroke may be treated with clot-busting drugs or clot retrieval within a time window, so speed to a stroke centre is everything ('time is brain'). A TIA ('mini-stroke') has the same signs but resolves — it is a serious warning requiring urgent assessment. Prevention targets blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, cholesterol, diabetes, and smoking.

sections.heading: Seizures & epilepsy
sections.body: A SEIZURE is a burst of abnormal electrical activity causing convulsions, altered awareness, or focal symptoms; EPILEPSY is a tendency to recurrent seizures. First aid: protect from injury, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, time it, and recovery position after. RED FLAGS — a seizure lasting over 5 minutes or repeating without recovery (status epilepticus) is an EMERGENCY; so is a first seizure, or one with fever, head injury, or focal signs. Diagnosis uses EEG and imaging; treatment is with anti-seizure medication and avoiding triggers. Many provoked 'seizures' (faints, low blood sugar) are not epilepsy.

sections.heading: Headache & its red flags
sections.body: Most headaches are PRIMARY and benign — tension-type (band-like, stress-related), MIGRAINE (throbbing, often one-sided, with nausea and light sensitivity, sometimes an aura), and cluster (severe, around one eye). But some signal danger. RED FLAGS — a sudden 'worst-ever' thunderclap headache (possible bleed), headache with fever and stiff neck (meningitis), with new neurological signs, after head injury, worse on lying down or straining or waking from sleep, new in someone over 50, or in pregnancy with visual changes/swelling — need urgent assessment. Pattern and company (what comes with it) distinguish benign from dangerous.

sections.heading: Movement, degenerative & inflammatory conditions
sections.body: PARKINSON'S disease causes slowness, stiffness, tremor, and balance problems from dopamine loss, managed with medication. MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS is immune damage to nerve insulation causing relapsing-remitting neurological episodes (vision loss, weakness, numbness). MOTOR NEURONE DISEASE (ALS) progressively weakens muscles. DEMENTIA (Alzheimer's and others) is progressive loss of memory and thinking. Essential tremor, dystonia, and others affect movement. Many are managed, not cured, with medication, therapy, and support — early specialist assessment guides care.

sections.heading: Nerves, spine & neuromuscular problems
sections.body: Peripheral problems: NEUROPATHY (nerve damage — numbness, tingling, weakness, often from diabetes), nerve ENTRAPMENTS (carpal tunnel), and radiculopathy (a pinched spinal nerve, e.g., sciatica). RED FLAGS — new bladder or bowel incontinence, saddle (groin) numbness, and progressive leg weakness suggest cauda equina or cord compression, an EMERGENCY. Neuromuscular conditions (myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré — ascending weakness that can threaten breathing) need prompt care. Dizziness and vertigo often come from the inner ear rather than the brain, but new neurological signs with them warrant assessment.

chapters.title: Oncology (Cancer Medicine)
chapters.overview: What cancer is, how it is found and staged, how it is treated, and the warning signs worth knowing — plus how screening and prevention cut the toll. University-level and honest about uncertainty. Educational, not a diagnosis; a cancer concern needs prompt medical assessment.

sections.heading: What cancer is
sections.body: Cancer is uncontrolled growth of the body's own cells that have accumulated genetic changes letting them divide without limit, evade normal controls, invade nearby tissue, and spread (METASTASIZE) via blood and lymph. 'Cancer' is hundreds of different diseases defined by the tissue of origin and molecular features — which is why one treatment does not fit all. BENIGN tumours grow but do not invade or spread; MALIGNANT ones do. Most cancers arise over years from a combination of inherited risk, environmental exposures (tobacco, UV, some infections, diet), and chance.

sections.heading: Warning signs & diagnosis
sections.body: Cancer often has no symptoms early, which is why screening matters, but general WARNING SIGNS worth checking include: an unexplained lump, a mole changing (ABCDE), a sore that won't heal, unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, a persistent cough or hoarseness, a change in bowel or bladder habit, unusual bleeding (in stool, urine, between periods, or coughing blood), and persistent unexplained pain. None of these means cancer — most are benign — but persistent or unexplained symptoms deserve assessment. Diagnosis uses examination, imaging, blood tests, and the definitive step: a BIOPSY examined under the microscope.

sections.heading: Staging & grading
sections.body: Once diagnosed, cancer is STAGED (how far it has spread — commonly the TNM system: Tumour size, Nodes involved, Metastases) and GRADED (how abnormal and aggressive the cells look). Stage and grade, plus the tumour's molecular markers, drive the treatment plan and prognosis — early-stage, localized cancer is often curable, while widespread disease is usually treated to control and prolong life well. Imaging (CT, MRI, PET), blood markers, and genomic testing refine the picture. This is why the same 'cancer' can mean very different things.

sections.heading: How cancer is treated
sections.body: The main modalities, often combined: SURGERY (remove localized tumour), RADIOTHERAPY (targeted radiation), and SYSTEMIC therapy — classic CHEMOTHERAPY (drugs that kill dividing cells, with side effects on normal fast-dividing tissue), plus newer TARGETED therapy (hitting specific molecular drivers), IMMUNOTHERAPY (unleashing the immune system — a major advance), and HORMONE therapy (for hormone-driven cancers like many breast and prostate). Treatment aims may be CURATIVE or PALLIATIVE (controlling disease and symptoms). Clinical trials extend options. Precision oncology increasingly matches treatment to the tumour's biology.

sections.heading: Living with cancer & supportive care
sections.body: Cancer care is more than killing tumour: managing side effects (nausea, fatigue, low blood counts and infection risk, pain), nutrition, mental health, fertility, and function; and PALLIATIVE care — which improves quality of life at any stage, not just at the end, and can be given alongside active treatment. Survivorship brings its own needs (surveillance, late effects, return to work). Honest communication about goals, prognosis, and what matters to the person guides decisions. Support for families and carers is part of good care.

sections.heading: Prevention & screening
sections.body: A large share of cancer is preventable. The biggest levers: NOT SMOKING (the single largest cause), sun protection, a healthy weight, activity, limiting alcohol and processed meat, and vaccination (HPV prevents cervical and other cancers; hepatitis B prevents liver cancer). SCREENING finds cancer (or pre-cancer) early when it is most curable — cervical (Pap/HPV), breast (mammography), bowel (stool tests/colonoscopy), and lung (low-dose CT for high-risk smokers) programs save lives. Knowing your family history and attending screening are high-yield personal steps.
