chapters.title: Gastroenterology (Digestive System)
chapters.overview: How digestion works and the common and serious conditions of the gut, liver, and pancreas — from reflux and IBS to inflammatory bowel disease, bleeding, and the don't-miss abdominal emergencies. University-level with clear red flags. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: How digestion works
sections.body: Food travels the GI tract: mouth (chewing, saliva) → oesophagus → STOMACH (acid and enzymes break food down) → SMALL INTESTINE (most digestion and absorption, aided by the PANCREAS's enzymes and the LIVER's bile) → LARGE INTESTINE/colon (water absorption, gut bacteria, forming stool) → rectum. The liver also processes nutrients and detoxifies; the gallbladder stores bile. Symptoms localize problems: swallowing trouble (oesophagus), upper pain and reflux (stomach), mid/lower pain and altered bowels (intestines), and jaundice (liver/bile).

sections.heading: Reflux, ulcers & upper-gut problems
sections.body: GORD/reflux (acid rising into the oesophagus — heartburn) is common and managed with lifestyle, antacids, and acid-reducing drugs; persistent reflux can damage the oesophagus (Barrett's). PEPTIC ULCERS (in the stomach or duodenum, often from H. pylori infection or NSAIDs) cause pain and can bleed or perforate. Gastritis, hiatus hernia, and functional dyspepsia are frequent. RED FLAGS in upper-gut symptoms: difficulty or painful swallowing, unexplained weight loss, vomiting blood or black tarry stools (bleeding), persistent vomiting, or new symptoms over age 50 — these need prompt investigation.

sections.heading: Bowel conditions
sections.body: Common lower-gut conditions: IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME (IBS — pain with altered bowel habit, no damage, managed with diet and symptom control), INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE (Crohn's and ulcerative colitis — autoimmune inflammation causing diarrhoea, bleeding, pain, and weight loss, needing specialist treatment), COELIAC disease (immune reaction to gluten), diverticular disease, haemorrhoids, and constipation. RED FLAGS: rectal bleeding, a persistent change in bowel habit (especially over 50), unexplained weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, or a family history of bowel cancer — these warrant assessment and screening for bowel cancer.

sections.heading: Liver, gallbladder & pancreas
sections.body: The LIVER can be damaged by alcohol, fatty liver disease (increasingly common with obesity), viral HEPATITIS, and others, progressing silently to CIRRHOSIS (scarring) and raising cancer risk — hence screening and vaccination. GALLSTONES can cause pain (biliary colic) or inflammation (cholecystitis) and block the bile duct (causing jaundice) or the pancreas. PANCREATITIS (severe upper-abdominal pain radiating to the back, often from gallstones or alcohol) can be life-threatening. JAUNDICE (yellow skin/eyes), dark urine, and pale stools signal a liver or bile problem needing assessment.

sections.heading: Abdominal emergencies
sections.body: The 'acute abdomen' — sudden severe abdominal pain — can be a surgical EMERGENCY. Don't miss: APPENDICITIS (pain moving to the lower right, fever), a PERFORATION (sudden severe pain with a rigid abdomen), BOWEL OBSTRUCTION (colicky pain, vomiting, distension, no stool/gas), severe PANCREATITIS, GI BLEEDING (vomiting blood or black/tarry or bloody stools — can cause shock), and ISCHAEMIC bowel. RED FLAGS: severe, worsening, or rigid-abdomen pain, pain with fever, signs of bleeding, or shock (pale, clammy, fast pulse) need emergency care. Severe pain with a tender, board-like abdomen is a surgical emergency.

sections.heading: Tests, gut health & prevention
sections.body: Investigation uses blood tests (liver function, inflammation, coeliac, anaemia), stool tests, ULTRASOUND/CT, and ENDOSCOPY (a camera into the gut — gastroscopy from above, colonoscopy from below — which can also treat and biopsy). GUT HEALTH and prevention: a fibre-rich varied diet, hydration, activity, limiting alcohol and processed meat, not smoking, a healthy weight, and attending bowel-cancer screening. The gut microbiome and diet are active research areas. Persistent digestive symptoms should be investigated rather than endlessly self-treated.

chapters.title: Endocrinology (Hormones & Metabolism)
chapters.overview: The body's chemical-messenger system and what happens when it misfires — diabetes above all, plus thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, and bone/metabolic disorders. University-level, with the metabolic emergencies that must not be missed. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: How hormones work
sections.body: The endocrine system uses HORMONES — chemical messengers released by glands into the blood — to regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction, salt and water, stress, and more. Glands (pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, gonads, parathyroids) are coordinated by FEEDBACK loops, often run by the brain's hypothalamus and pituitary ('the master gland'). Too much or too little of a hormone causes disease. Because hormones act body-wide, endocrine problems often present with vague, multi-system symptoms (fatigue, weight change, mood change) — which is why they are easy to miss and worth testing for.

sections.heading: Diabetes
sections.body: DIABETES is high blood glucose from a problem with INSULIN (which lets cells take up sugar). TYPE 1 (autoimmune loss of insulin, needing insulin for life) and TYPE 2 (insulin resistance plus relative deficiency, linked to weight and lifestyle, far more common) differ, plus gestational diabetes in pregnancy. Uncontrolled high sugar damages blood vessels over years — the heart, kidneys, eyes, nerves, and feet. Management: lifestyle, monitoring, and medication/insulin, individualized. RED FLAG emergencies — very high sugar with vomiting, deep breathing, and drowsiness (DKA, mainly type 1) and severe LOW blood sugar (shaky, confused, unconscious) both need urgent treatment.

sections.heading: Thyroid disorders
sections.body: The THYROID sets the body's metabolic pace. UNDERACTIVE (hypothyroidism — tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, low mood, dry skin; common, easily treated with hormone replacement) and OVERACTIVE (hyperthyroidism — weight loss, racing heart, anxiety, heat intolerance, tremor) are frequent, diagnosed with simple blood tests (TSH). Thyroid nodules and goitre are common and usually benign but are checked. RED FLAGS — a very overactive 'thyroid storm' (high fever, racing irregular heart, agitation) or severe hypothyroidism are rare emergencies. Thyroid disease is one of the most treatable endocrine problems once found.

sections.heading: Adrenal, pituitary & reproductive hormones
sections.body: The ADRENAL glands make cortisol (stress/metabolism) and aldosterone (salt/blood pressure) and adrenaline. Too little cortisol (Addison's) causes fatigue, weight loss, and low blood pressure, with a life-threatening 'adrenal crisis'; too much (Cushing's, often from steroid medication) causes weight gain, high sugar and blood pressure, and thin skin. The PITUITARY controls other glands; its tumours disturb hormones or vision. Reproductive-hormone disorders include PCOS, low testosterone, and menopause. Never stop long-term steroids abruptly — it can precipitate an adrenal crisis.

sections.heading: Bone & mineral, and metabolic disorders
sections.body: Calcium and bone metabolism are hormonally controlled (parathyroid hormone, vitamin D). OSTEOPOROSIS (weak, fracture-prone bones — often silent until a fracture) is common with age, especially post-menopause, and is preventable and treatable. Overactive parathyroids raise calcium (causing stones, bone pain, fatigue); low calcium or vitamin D cause their own problems. METABOLIC syndrome (central obesity, high blood pressure, high sugar and lipids) clusters cardiovascular risk. GOUT is a metabolic joint disease from high uric acid. Diet, activity, vitamin D, and weight management underpin prevention.

sections.heading: Testing, treatment & living with hormone disease
sections.body: Endocrine diagnosis relies heavily on BLOOD TESTS (hormone levels, often with dynamic/stimulation tests because single readings mislead) and imaging of glands. Treatment replaces deficient hormones (thyroxine, insulin, cortisol), blocks excess, or removes tumours. Many endocrine conditions are LIFELONG but very manageable with monitoring and medication adherence — and several (type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, osteoporosis) are strongly influenced by lifestyle, making diet, activity, and weight central. Vague, persistent symptoms like fatigue and weight change are worth a hormone check rather than being dismissed.

chapters.title: Orthopaedics & Musculoskeletal Medicine
chapters.overview: Bones, joints, muscles, tendons, and ligaments — how they are injured and diseased, how fractures are classified and heal, and the red flags that make a limb problem an emergency. University-level for recognizing and understanding MSK problems. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: The musculoskeletal system
sections.body: Bones give structure and protect organs and, at JOINTS, allow movement; they are living tissue that remodels. Joints are held by LIGAMENTS (bone to bone) and moved by MUSCLES via TENDONS (muscle to bone), cushioned by cartilage and lubricated by synovial fluid. Problems arise from injury (fracture, sprain, strain, dislocation), wear (osteoarthritis), inflammation (rheumatoid and other arthritis), infection, and tumours. The pattern — which structure, acute or chronic, with or without trauma — guides the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Fractures: types & healing
sections.body: A FRACTURE is a broken bone, classified by pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted/multi-fragment, greenstick in children), whether the skin is broken (OPEN/compound — higher infection risk, an emergency) or closed, and whether the ends have moved (displaced). Healing passes through haematoma, soft then hard callus, and remodelling, over weeks to months; children heal faster. Treatment aligns the bone (reduction) and holds it (cast, splint, or surgical fixation). RED FLAGS — open fractures, deformity with loss of pulse or sensation, or a fracture with severe swelling and pain (compartment syndrome) are emergencies.

sections.heading: Sprains, strains & soft-tissue injury
sections.body: A SPRAIN is a stretched or torn ligament (e.g., a rolled ankle); a STRAIN is an overstretched or torn muscle or tendon. Most are managed with relative rest, ice, compression, elevation, and graded return to activity (modern advice favours early controlled movement over prolonged rest). TENDINOPATHIES (tennis/golfer's elbow, Achilles, rotator cuff) come from overload and respond to progressive loading. DISLOCATIONS (a joint out of place) need prompt reduction. RED FLAGS — inability to bear weight, gross deformity, numbness, or a cold/pulseless limb need urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Arthritis & joint disease
sections.body: OSTEOARTHRITIS is 'wear-and-tear' loss of cartilage causing pain, stiffness, and reduced movement, worse with use, common with age — managed with exercise, weight control, pain relief, and sometimes joint replacement. INFLAMMATORY arthritis (rheumatoid and others — see Rheumatology) is an immune process causing swollen, warm joints and morning stiffness, needing specialist treatment. GOUT causes sudden, severe, red, hot joint attacks (often the big toe) from uric-acid crystals. A hot, swollen, acutely painful joint with fever could be a SEPTIC (infected) joint — an EMERGENCY needing urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Back & neck pain
sections.body: Back pain is extremely common and usually MECHANICAL and self-limited — staying active and avoiding prolonged bed rest speeds recovery. Nerve-root problems (sciatica from a disc) cause leg pain, numbness, or weakness. RED FLAGS that change the picture: new bladder or bowel incontinence, saddle (groin) numbness, or progressive leg weakness (possible cauda equina — an EMERGENCY); fever, night pain, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, significant trauma, or age extremes. Most back pain needs reassurance and movement, not scans; red flags need prompt assessment.

sections.heading: Assessment, imaging & rehabilitation
sections.body: MSK assessment looks, feels, and moves the part (and checks nerves and circulation). IMAGING: X-rays for bones and fractures, ultrasound and MRI for soft tissue, CT for complex fractures — but imaging is guided by the exam, not a substitute for it, and many findings are incidental. REHABILITATION (physiotherapy, graded exercise, load management) is central to recovery and prevention, often more than surgery. Bone health (calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise) and fall prevention reduce fractures, especially with osteoporosis.

chapters.title: Ophthalmology (Eyes & Vision)
chapters.overview: How the eye works and the common and sight-threatening conditions — from dry eyes and refractive error to glaucoma, cataracts, and the red flags that mean 'get eye care now.' University-level. Educational, not a diagnosis; sudden vision loss or a painful red eye needs urgent care.

sections.heading: How the eye works
sections.body: Light passes through the clear CORNEA and LENS, which focus it onto the RETINA at the back, where cells convert it to signals sent by the OPTIC NERVE to the brain. The IRIS controls how much light enters (the pupil); fluid keeps the eye pressurized. Clear vision needs each part intact and the eye the right length (refractive error — short/long sight — comes from focusing in front of or behind the retina, corrected by glasses, contacts, or surgery). Problems are grouped by where they strike: surface, lens, pressure, retina, or nerve.

sections.heading: Common eye problems
sections.body: DRY EYE (gritty, tired eyes — managed with drops and lid care), CONJUNCTIVITIS ('pink eye' — red, discharging; viral/bacterial/allergic), STYES and blepharitis (lid problems), and refractive error are everyday complaints. CATARACTS (clouding of the lens with age — blurred, dimmed vision, treated with a quick, effective lens-replacement operation) and presbyopia (needing reading glasses with age) are near-universal eventually. Floaters and mild flashes are often benign ageing changes — but a sudden shower of them needs checking (see red flags).

sections.heading: Glaucoma & the pressure diseases
sections.body: GLAUCOMA is damage to the optic nerve, usually linked to raised eye pressure, that silently steals peripheral vision — it is a leading cause of irreversible blindness, and because it is painless and gradual, regular eye checks (which measure pressure and examine the nerve) are how it is caught early. Treatment (drops, laser, surgery) halts progression but cannot restore lost vision, so detection matters. ACUTE ANGLE-CLOSURE glaucoma is different — a sudden painful red eye with blurred vision, halos, and nausea, an EMERGENCY needing immediate care.

sections.heading: Retinal & systemic eye disease
sections.body: The retina can be damaged by systemic disease — DIABETIC retinopathy (a leading cause of blindness, why diabetics need regular eye screening) and hypertensive changes — and by age (macular degeneration, affecting central vision). RETINAL DETACHMENT (the retina peeling off) is a surgical EMERGENCY: its warning signs are a sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, and a 'curtain' or shadow spreading across vision. The eye also shows signs of many general conditions, so an eye exam is a window on overall health.

sections.heading: Eye red flags — get care now
sections.body: Most eye complaints are minor, but some threaten sight or signal serious disease. SEEK URGENT EYE CARE for: sudden loss or blurring of vision, a painful red eye (especially with light sensitivity, halos, or nausea — possible acute glaucoma, uveitis, or infection), sudden floaters/flashes or a curtain over vision (possible retinal detachment), chemical splashes (irrigate immediately and get help), penetrating eye injury, or new double vision or a drooping lid with other neurological signs. Sudden painless vision loss can also signal a stroke or vascular event.

sections.heading: Eye care, testing & prevention
sections.body: Eye care is shared: OPTOMETRISTS test vision and eye health and prescribe glasses/contacts; OPHTHALMOLOGISTS are medical/surgical eye doctors; opticians fit glasses. Regular eye exams detect silent disease (glaucoma, diabetic and hypertensive changes) and update prescriptions — especially important for diabetics, those over 40, and anyone with a family history. Prevention: eye protection for hazardous work/sport, sun protection (UV), managing diabetes and blood pressure, not smoking, and good contact-lens hygiene (to avoid sight-threatening infections). Screen 'eye strain' is real but not damaging; rest and breaks help.

chapters.title: ENT (Ear, Nose & Throat / Otolaryngology)
chapters.overview: The ear, nose, throat, and related head-and-neck structures — hearing and balance, sinus and nasal problems, sore throats and tonsils, and the red flags that need urgent care. University-level. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: The ear: hearing & balance
sections.body: The ear has three parts: the OUTER (canal and eardrum), MIDDLE (tiny bones conducting sound, connected to the nose by the Eustachian tube), and INNER (the cochlea for hearing and the balance organs). Problems: EAR INFECTIONS (middle-ear otitis media — common in children, painful; outer-ear 'swimmer's ear'), wax blockage, TINNITUS (ringing), and HEARING LOSS (conductive — a blockage, or sensorineural — nerve/cochlea, often age-related or noise-induced). VERTIGO (a spinning sensation) often comes from the inner ear (BPPV, labyrinthitis, Ménière's). Sudden hearing loss or vertigo with neurological signs needs urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Nose & sinuses
sections.body: The nose warms, filters, and humidifies air and houses smell. Common problems: the common COLD, ALLERGIC RHINITIS (hay fever — sneezing, itch, blocked/runny nose), SINUSITIS (blocked, infected sinuses causing facial pain/pressure and congestion — usually viral and self-limited, occasionally bacterial), NASAL POLYPS (soft growths causing blockage and loss of smell), a DEVIATED septum, and NOSEBLEEDS (usually from the front, controlled by leaning forward and pinching the soft part for 10–15 minutes). RED FLAGS: a persistently blocked nose on one side, blood-stained discharge, or facial numbness warrant assessment.

sections.heading: Throat, tonsils & voice
sections.body: Most SORE THROATS are viral and settle in a week; bacterial (strep) throats may need antibiotics. TONSILLITIS (inflamed tonsils with fever and pain) is common in children. The LARYNX (voice box) gives voice; LARYNGITIS causes hoarseness, usually viral. RED FLAGS: difficulty breathing or swallowing, drooling, a muffled 'hot potato' voice, severe one-sided throat pain with trismus (a possible abscess — quinsy), a hoarse voice persisting beyond 3 weeks (needs assessment to exclude cancer, especially in smokers), or a neck lump that persists. Difficulty breathing or swallowing is an emergency.

sections.heading: Head & neck: lumps, glands & nerves
sections.body: The head and neck hold lymph nodes, salivary glands, the thyroid, and major nerves and vessels. Swollen LYMPH NODES usually mean infection and settle, but a hard, fixed, painless, or persistent (over a few weeks) node — especially with weight loss, night sweats, or in a smoker/drinker — needs assessment to exclude cancer or lymphoma. Salivary-gland swelling (stones, infection, mumps) and facial-nerve problems (Bell's palsy — sudden one-sided facial droop, but stroke must be excluded) also present here. A persistent neck lump is a 'see someone' sign.

sections.heading: ENT red flags & emergencies
sections.body: Seek urgent/emergency care for: difficulty breathing or stridor (noisy breathing), difficulty swallowing or drooling, severe uncontrolled nosebleed, sudden hearing loss, vertigo with new neurological signs, a foreign body or caustic substance in the ear/nose/throat, and signs of a deep neck or sinus infection spreading (severe pain, swelling, fever, eye involvement). A persistent (3+ weeks) hoarse voice, mouth ulcer, throat pain, or neck lump — particularly with smoking/alcohol use — needs assessment to rule out head-and-neck cancer. Early assessment of these signs saves lives and function.

sections.heading: Hearing protection & everyday ENT care
sections.body: Prevention and self-care: protect hearing from loud noise (ear protection, volume limits — noise damage is permanent and cumulative), do not poke cotton buds into ears (wax is usually self-clearing; drops soften it), manage allergies, stay hydrated and use saline for nasal/sinus symptoms, and stop smoking (a major cause of head-and-neck cancer and hearing/voice problems). Most ENT complaints are minor and self-limited, but the red flags above — breathing/swallowing trouble, persistent lumps or hoarseness, sudden hearing loss — always warrant prompt care.

chapters.title: Infectious Disease & Immunology
chapters.overview: How infections work, how the immune system fights them, and the principles of prevention and treatment — from everyday infections to sepsis, antimicrobial resistance, vaccination, and the immune disorders. University-level, with the red flags of serious infection. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Pathogens & how infection spreads
sections.body: Infections are caused by BACTERIA, VIRUSES, FUNGI, and PARASITES, each needing different treatment (antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses). They spread by routes: respiratory (droplets/airborne — colds, flu, COVID, TB), faecal-oral (contaminated food/water — gastroenteritis), blood/body fluid (hepatitis, HIV), sexual, vector-borne (mosquitoes — malaria, dengue), and direct contact. Understanding the route guides prevention — hand hygiene, safe food and water, safe sex, vaccination, and vector control each break specific chains of transmission.

sections.heading: How the immune system works
sections.body: Defence has two arms: INNATE immunity (immediate, general — skin barriers, inflammation, and cells that engulf invaders) and ADAPTIVE immunity (specific, with memory — B cells make ANTIBODIES and T cells kill infected cells and coordinate the response). After infection or VACCINATION, memory cells give faster, stronger protection next time — the basis of immunity. Fever and inflammation are the body fighting, not the enemy. The system is finely balanced: too weak (immunodeficiency) invites infection; misdirected, it causes allergy and autoimmune disease.

sections.heading: Common infections & their course
sections.body: Most infections are mild and self-limiting (colds, many sore throats, viral gastroenteritis) and need supportive care — rest, fluids, and time — not antibiotics. Bacterial infections (some chest, urine, skin, and throat infections) may need antibiotics. Recognizing which is which, and not demanding antibiotics for viral illness, protects you and preserves the drugs' power. Localized infections (UTI, cellulitis, abscess) have characteristic features; the key question is always whether it is staying local and mild or becoming systemic and severe.

sections.heading: Serious infection & sepsis
sections.body: The danger is when infection overwhelms the body. SEPSIS is the body's extreme, organ-damaging response to infection — a TIME-CRITICAL EMERGENCY. RED FLAGS (a known/suspected infection PLUS any of): new confusion or slurred speech, extreme shivering or muscle pain, passing little or no urine, severe breathlessness, a fast heart rate, or skin that is mottled, pale, or bluish. Call emergency services and say you are worried about sepsis — early antibiotics and fluids save lives. MENINGITIS (headache, stiff neck, fever, a non-blanching rash) is another not-to-miss emergency.

sections.heading: Vaccines & antimicrobial resistance
sections.body: Two public-health pillars. VACCINATION trains immunity safely without the disease, has eradicated or controlled once-deadly illnesses, and protects the vulnerable through herd immunity — its benefits vastly outweigh the small risks. ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE is a growing crisis: overusing antibiotics breeds resistant bacteria that make infections untreatable. Everyone's part: take antibiotics only when truly needed, as directed, and complete the course; get vaccinated; and practise good hygiene. Stewardship preserves these life-saving drugs for the future (see the Pharmacy chapter).

sections.heading: Immune disorders & the immunocompromised
sections.body: When immunity misfires: ALLERGY (overreaction to harmless things — from hay fever to life-threatening ANAPHYLAXIS, which needs immediate adrenaline), AUTOIMMUNE disease (the immune system attacking the body — type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, thyroid disease), and IMMUNODEFICIENCY (too little immunity — inherited, or from HIV, chemotherapy, or immune-suppressing drugs). The IMMUNOCOMPROMISED are vulnerable to infections that healthy people shrug off, so fever or illness in them is treated seriously and urgently. Protecting them includes vaccination of those around them.

chapters.title: Rheumatology (Joints, Autoimmune & Connective Tissue)
chapters.overview: The immune and inflammatory diseases of joints, muscles, and connective tissue — rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, gout, and the others — how they differ from wear-and-tear, and the red flags of serious disease. University-level. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Inflammatory vs mechanical
sections.body: Rheumatology deals with INFLAMMATORY and AUTOIMMUNE conditions, distinct from mechanical wear (osteoarthritis). The clue is the pattern: inflammatory joint pain is typically worse with REST and in the MORNING (prolonged morning stiffness), eases with movement, and the joints are swollen, warm, and tender — whereas mechanical pain worsens with use and eases with rest. Many rheumatic diseases are SYSTEMIC, affecting skin, eyes, lungs, kidneys, and blood vessels, not just joints. Blood tests (inflammatory markers, autoantibodies) and imaging support diagnosis.

sections.heading: Rheumatoid & inflammatory arthritis
sections.body: RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS is a chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the joint lining, causing symmetrical swelling, pain, and prolonged morning stiffness (often the small joints of hands and feet), and, untreated, joint damage and deformity — plus systemic effects. Early diagnosis and disease-modifying treatment (DMARDs, biologics) now prevent much of the damage, so prompt referral matters. Other inflammatory arthritides include PSORIATIC arthritis (with the skin condition), ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS (spine stiffness in younger adults), and reactive arthritis.

sections.heading: Gout & crystal arthritis
sections.body: GOUT is caused by uric-acid crystals depositing in joints, triggering sudden, severe attacks of a red, hot, exquisitely painful joint (classically the big toe), often at night. It is linked to diet, alcohol, certain drugs, and kidney function, and managed with attack treatment and long-term urate-lowering therapy plus lifestyle. PSEUDOGOUT is a similar crystal arthritis in older people. A single acutely hot, swollen joint always needs to exclude SEPTIC arthritis (joint infection — an emergency) before assuming gout.

sections.heading: Lupus & connective-tissue disease
sections.body: SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that can affect almost any organ — joints, skin (a classic 'butterfly' facial rash, photosensitivity), kidneys, blood, and more — with a relapsing course, mostly in younger women. Related conditions include Sjögren's (dry eyes and mouth), scleroderma (skin and organ thickening), and inflammatory muscle disease. VASCULITIS (inflamed blood vessels) can be serious and multi-system. These need specialist diagnosis and immune-modulating treatment, with monitoring for organ involvement.

sections.heading: Soft-tissue & regional rheumatism
sections.body: Common non-joint rheumatology: FIBROMYALGIA (widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep, and tenderness without inflammation — managed with exercise, pacing, sleep, and sometimes medication), POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA (shoulder/hip girdle pain and stiffness in older adults, responding dramatically to steroids), and regional problems (bursitis, tendinopathy). An important linked emergency is GIANT CELL (temporal) ARTERITIS — new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, and visual symptoms in an older person — which can cause sudden blindness and needs urgent steroids.

sections.heading: Diagnosis, treatment & living with rheumatic disease
sections.body: Diagnosis combines the history and examination with blood tests (inflammatory markers like ESR/CRP, autoantibodies such as rheumatoid factor and ANA) and imaging — but tests support, not replace, clinical judgement (autoantibodies can be positive in healthy people). Treatment ranges from anti-inflammatories to DMARDs and biologics that modify the immune response, alongside physiotherapy, exercise, and self-management. Many rheumatic diseases are LIFELONG but increasingly well-controlled; early specialist treatment prevents damage. RED FLAGS: a hot swollen joint with fever (septic arthritis) or new temporal-arteritis symptoms need urgent care.

chapters.title: Urology & Kidney Medicine (Nephrology)
chapters.overview: The kidneys and urinary tract — how they clean the blood and balance the body, and the common and serious problems: infections, stones, prostate disease, incontinence, and kidney failure. University-level, with the red flags that need urgent care. Educational, not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: How the kidneys & urinary tract work
sections.body: The two KIDNEYS filter the blood, removing waste and excess water as urine while balancing salts, acid, and blood pressure, and making hormones (for red blood cells and vitamin D). Urine drains via the ureters to the BLADDER, stored until passed through the urethra. Problems divide into: filtering failure (kidney disease), blockage or stones, infection, bladder/continence problems, and prostate disease in men. Symptoms localize the problem — flank pain (kidney/stone), burning and frequency (bladder/infection), poor stream (prostate).

sections.heading: Urinary infections & stones
sections.body: URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS (UTIs) are common (especially in women), causing burning, frequency, urgency, and sometimes blood in the urine; most are simple and treated with antibiotics. RED FLAG — a UTI with fever, flank pain, vomiting, or feeling very unwell suggests a KIDNEY infection (pyelonephritis) or urosepsis, needing prompt care. KIDNEY STONES cause sudden, severe, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, often with blood in the urine and nausea; small stones pass with fluids and pain relief, larger ones need procedures. Stones with fever and a blocked kidney are an emergency.

sections.heading: Kidney disease & failure
sections.body: CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE is gradual, often silent loss of kidney function, commonly from diabetes and high blood pressure — detected by blood (eGFR) and urine (protein) tests, which is why those conditions are monitored. Advanced disease causes fatigue, swelling, and toxin build-up, and may need dialysis or transplant. ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY is a sudden drop in function (from dehydration, severe illness, obstruction, or drugs) — often reversible if caught early. Protecting kidneys means controlling blood pressure and diabetes, staying hydrated, and avoiding kidney-harming drug combinations (see interactions).

sections.heading: Prostate & male urology
sections.body: The PROSTATE commonly enlarges with age (benign prostatic hyperplasia — BPH), causing a weak stream, frequency, urgency, and night-time urination, managed with medication or surgery. PROSTATE CANCER is common and often slow-growing; PSA testing and examination guide assessment, with nuanced decisions about screening and treatment. PROSTATITIS (infection/inflammation) causes pelvic pain and urinary symptoms. ERECTILE dysfunction can signal vascular disease. RED FLAG — sudden inability to pass urine (acute retention — a painful, distended bladder) is an emergency needing urgent drainage.

sections.heading: Bladder, continence & red flags
sections.body: INCONTINENCE (leakage) has types — stress (on coughing/exercise), urge (overactive bladder), and overflow — and is common, treatable, and not an inevitable part of ageing (pelvic-floor exercises, bladder training, medication, and sometimes surgery help). RED FLAGS across urology: BLOOD IN THE URINE (visible or found on testing) always needs investigation to exclude bladder or kidney cancer, especially in smokers and older adults; so do a sudden inability to pass urine, severe flank pain with fever, and testicular pain (see testicular torsion — an emergency).

sections.heading: Tests, prevention & kidney health
sections.body: Investigation uses urine tests (infection, blood, protein), blood tests (kidney function — eGFR, electrolytes), and imaging (ultrasound, CT for stones, cystoscopy to view the bladder). PREVENTION and kidney health: control blood pressure and diabetes (the leading causes of kidney disease), stay well hydrated, do not smoke, maintain a healthy weight, use salt and protein sensibly, be cautious with NSAIDs and nephrotoxic combinations, and treat UTIs promptly. Pelvic-floor exercises protect continence. Regular checks matter most for those with diabetes, high blood pressure, or a family history of kidney disease.

chapters.title: Whole-Body Anatomy: The Layers
chapters.overview: The body from the outside in, one layer at a time: surface regions, skeleton, muscles, organs, circulation, and nerves. Each layer has its own labelled diagram, so anyone can locate a structure, describe where a symptom is, and understand what lies beneath. The shared map behind every other chapter.

sections.heading: Layer 1 — surface regions & the language of location
sections.body: Clinicians describe location with a shared vocabulary so that 'where' is never ambiguous. The body divides into the head, neck, thorax (chest), abdomen, pelvis, and the upper and lower limbs. Directional terms pin things down: ANTERIOR (front) and POSTERIOR (back); SUPERIOR (toward the head) and INFERIOR (toward the feet); MEDIAL (toward the midline) and LATERAL (away from it); PROXIMAL (nearer the trunk) and DISTAL (further along a limb); SUPERFICIAL and DEEP. Left and right always mean the PATIENT'S left and right. Describing a symptom this way — 'right lower abdomen', 'lateral side of the left knee' — is the first step in working out what structure is involved.

sections.heading: Layer 2 — the skeleton
sections.body: An adult has about 206 bones forming the AXIAL skeleton (skull, spine, ribs, sternum — protecting the brain, spinal cord, heart, and lungs) and the APPENDICULAR skeleton (the limbs and the shoulder and pelvic girdles that attach them). Bone is living tissue: it stores calcium, houses the marrow that makes blood cells, and constantly remodels in response to load. The spine has cervical (7), thoracic (12), and lumbar (5) vertebrae above the sacrum and coccyx. Joints range from immovable (skull sutures) to freely movable synovial joints (shoulder, hip, knee). Bone pain after injury, deformity, or inability to bear weight suggests a fracture.

sections.heading: Layer 3 — the muscles
sections.body: More than 600 skeletal muscles move the skeleton by contracting across joints, attached to bone by tendons. They work in opposing pairs (biceps bends the elbow, triceps straightens it). Major groups: the deltoid and rotator cuff at the shoulder; pectorals and the back muscles (trapezius, latissimus) on the trunk; the abdominal 'core'; gluteals at the hip; quadriceps and hamstrings at the thigh; and the calf muscles. Two other muscle types work unseen: SMOOTH muscle in the gut, vessels, and airways, and CARDIAC muscle in the heart. Strains, tears, cramps, and weakness arise here; muscle pain with dark urine after extreme exertion or a crush injury is an emergency (rhabdomyolysis).

sections.heading: Layer 4 — the organs
sections.body: Inside the cavities sit the organs. The SKULL holds the brain. The THORAX holds the heart (slightly left of centre, behind the breastbone) between the two lungs. Below the diaphragm, the ABDOMEN holds the liver and gallbladder (upper right), stomach and spleen (upper left), pancreas (deep, central), the kidneys (toward the back, either side of the spine), and the coiled small and large intestines; the appendix sits in the lower right. The PELVIS holds the bladder, rectum, and reproductive organs. Knowing what lies under a painful spot is why the abdominal region map is useful — though pain can also be 'referred' and felt away from its source (heart pain in the arm or jaw, gallbladder pain in the right shoulder).

sections.heading: Layer 5 — circulation & lymph
sections.body: The heart pumps blood through two loops: to the lungs to collect oxygen, then out through the AORTA and arteries to every tissue, returning through the veins. Arteries carry blood under pressure (a pulse can be felt where one runs near the surface — wrist, neck, groin, foot); veins have valves and rely on muscle movement to return blood, which is why immobility risks clots in the deep leg veins (DVT). Capillaries are where exchange happens. Alongside runs the LYMPHATIC system, draining tissue fluid through lymph nodes (clustered in the neck, armpits, and groin) that filter it and mount immune responses — which is why nodes swell during infection.

sections.heading: Layer 6 — the nervous system
sections.body: The CENTRAL nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord (running inside the spine); the PERIPHERAL nervous system is the 31 pairs of spinal nerves and the cranial nerves that branch out to every part. Sensory nerves carry information in; motor nerves carry commands out; the autonomic system runs heart rate, digestion, and other automatic functions. Each spinal nerve root supplies a strip of skin (a dermatome) and a set of muscles, so the pattern of numbness or weakness localizes a problem: a pinched lumbar root sends pain down the leg (sciatica); the median nerve trapped at the wrist numbs the thumb-side fingers (carpal tunnel). Long nerves fail first in neuropathy, so symptoms often start in the feet.

chapters.title: Self-Checks & Home Monitoring
chapters.overview: What a person can safely check on themselves or a family member at home — skin, lumps, pulse, blood pressure, breathing, hydration, vision, and the quick emergency screens — with what is normal, what is not, and exactly when a finding needs a professional. These are awareness checks, not diagnoses: they tell you when to get seen sooner.

sections.heading: How to self-check sensibly
sections.body: A self-check is for noticing CHANGE and deciding when to seek care — not for diagnosing yourself. Learn your own normal, check at a regular interval rather than obsessively, use good light and a mirror, compare the two sides of the body, and write down or photograph what you find so you can tell whether it changes. A normal self-check never overrides a symptom: if something feels wrong, get it assessed even if your check seemed fine. And an abnormal finding is a reason to see someone, not a reason to panic — most lumps, moles, and odd readings turn out to be benign.

sections.heading: Feeling for lumps: neck, armpit, groin, breast, testicle
sections.body: Use the flat pads of your fingers in small, gentle circles, comparing both sides. LYMPH NODES (neck, under the jaw, armpits, groin): small, soft, mobile, tender nodes during an infection are normal and settle within a few weeks. See a doctor for a node that is hard, fixed, painless, growing, or still there after 3 weeks, especially with night sweats or weight loss. BREAST/CHEST (everyone, including men): feel in a spiral out to the armpit and look in a mirror for changes in shape, skin dimpling, or nipple change. TESTICLES: after a warm shower, roll each gently between thumb and fingers — a hard lump, swelling, or heaviness needs prompt assessment, and SUDDEN severe testicular pain is an emergency (possible torsion).

sections.heading: The monthly skin check
sections.body: Once a month, in good light, check the whole skin surface with a full-length and a hand mirror: scalp (part the hair), face, ears, neck, chest, back, arms, palms, nails, buttocks, legs, soles, and between the toes. Look for anything NEW, CHANGING, or different from your other moles (the 'ugly duckling'), using ABCDE: Asymmetry, irregular Border, uneven Colour, Diameter over about 6 mm, Evolving. Also note any sore that will not heal, or a spot that bleeds, itches, or crusts. Photograph moles next to a ruler to track them. Anything that fits these warnings should be shown to a doctor promptly.

sections.heading: Pulse, breathing, temperature & blood pressure at home
sections.body: PULSE: two fingers on the thumb side of the wrist, count 30 seconds and double it — a resting adult is typically about 60–100 beats a minute, and you should note whether it is regular. BREATHING: count breaths for a full minute at rest — roughly 12–20 for an adult; children breathe faster the younger they are. TEMPERATURE: about 38°C (100.4°F) or above is a fever. BLOOD PRESSURE: sit quietly for 5 minutes, back supported, arm at heart level, cuff on bare skin, no talking; take two readings a minute apart and record them. Trends over days matter more than one reading — the graph tool is built for this. Get urgent help for a very fast or very slow pulse with dizziness, chest pain, or breathlessness, or for breathing that is laboured.

sections.heading: Quick screens: stroke, dehydration, circulation, sepsis
sections.body: FAST for stroke — Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. DEHYDRATION — dry mouth, dark and scanty urine, dizziness on standing, and in babies no wet nappies or a sunken soft spot. CAPILLARY REFILL — press a fingernail until it blanches and release; colour should return within about 2 seconds. THE GLASS TEST — press a clear glass on a rash; a rash that does NOT fade with fever is an emergency. CALF — a hot, swollen, painful calf (especially one-sided, after immobility) could be a clot and needs same-day assessment. SEPSIS — an infection plus confusion, extreme shivering, breathlessness, mottled skin, or passing no urine means call for help now.

sections.heading: Vision, hearing, balance & mood
sections.body: VISION: cover each eye in turn and read something familiar; use the Amsler grid for central vision — wavy or missing lines need prompt eye assessment, and sudden vision loss is an emergency. HEARING: difficulty following conversation in noise, or needing the volume higher than others, is worth a hearing test; sudden hearing loss in one ear is urgent. BALANCE: being unable to stand from a chair without using your hands, or a new tendency to fall, deserves review. MOOD: low mood or loss of interest most days for two weeks or more, or persistent worry that disrupts life, is a health problem worth raising — and thoughts of self-harm need help straight away (call or text 988 in the US and Canada, or local emergency services).

sections.heading: Home tests and the screening you should not skip
sections.body: Reliable home monitoring includes blood-pressure cuffs, glucose meters for people with diabetes, peak-flow meters for asthma, thermometers, pulse oximeters (less accurate on darker skin and cold fingers), and pregnancy tests. Follow the device instructions, and treat a surprising result as a prompt to recheck and then ask a professional. Self-checks complement, and never replace, organized SCREENING — cervical, breast, and bowel screening, blood-pressure and diabetes checks, eye tests, and dental checks find problems before any self-check could. Keep a simple record of readings and dates to bring to appointments.

chapters.title: Radiology & Medical Imaging
chapters.overview: How the body is pictured — X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and nuclear imaging — what each is good at, what it costs in radiation and time, and how to read a report sensibly. Imaging answers a specific clinical question; it does not replace the examination, and it often finds harmless things nobody was looking for.

sections.heading: X-rays (plain radiographs)
sections.body: X-rays pass through the body and are absorbed in proportion to density: bone appears white, air black, and soft tissue shades of grey. They are fast, cheap, and widely available — the first test for suspected fractures, chest infection, heart size, and bowel obstruction. Limits: soft tissues overlap and are poorly distinguished, and small or hairline fractures (the scaphoid in the wrist, stress fractures, some hip fractures) can be invisible at first. The radiation dose from a single limb or chest film is very small, comparable to days of natural background exposure.

sections.heading: CT (computed tomography)
sections.body: CT rotates an X-ray source around the patient and reconstructs cross-sectional slices, showing organs, vessels, and bone in fine detail within seconds. It is the workhorse of emergency medicine: head injury and stroke (to exclude bleeding), major trauma, suspected pulmonary embolism, kidney stones, and the acute abdomen. Iodinated contrast dye outlines vessels and organs but can stress the kidneys and occasionally triggers allergy, so kidney function and allergy history are checked. The radiation dose is substantially higher than plain X-ray, so CT is used when the answer changes management.

sections.heading: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
sections.body: MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not ionizing radiation, to produce images with superb soft-tissue contrast — the best test for the brain, spinal cord, joints, ligaments, and many tumours. Scans are slow (20–60 minutes), noisy, and enclosed, which some people find difficult. The magnet makes some implants and metal fragments dangerous, so everyone is screened beforehand for pacemakers, aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, and metal in the eyes. Gadolinium contrast is used selectively and avoided in severe kidney failure.

sections.heading: Ultrasound
sections.body: Ultrasound builds a live image from reflected high-frequency sound, with no radiation at all — which makes it the standard for pregnancy and for children. It excels at fluid-filled and soft structures: gallstones, the kidneys and bladder, the pelvic organs, the thyroid, blood flow in vessels (Doppler, used to find leg clots), and the beating heart (echocardiography). It is portable and guides needles for biopsies and drains. Its limits are that sound does not pass through bone or gas, and image quality depends heavily on the operator and on the patient's build.

sections.heading: Nuclear medicine, mammography & bone density
sections.body: Nuclear imaging gives a small dose of a radioactive tracer and maps where it collects, showing FUNCTION rather than structure: bone scans for spread of cancer or hidden fractures, PET scans (usually combined with CT) for cancer staging, and scans of heart blood flow or thyroid activity. Mammography is a specialized low-dose X-ray for breast screening and assessment. DEXA scanning measures bone density to diagnose osteoporosis using a very small dose. Each answers a narrow question and is chosen for that purpose.

sections.heading: Reading a report, radiation sense & incidental findings
sections.body: An imaging report describes the findings and ends with an impression — the radiologist's conclusion. Phrases like 'no acute abnormality' mean nothing urgent was seen; 'clinical correlation advised' means the picture must be matched to the symptoms. Many scans reveal INCIDENTAL findings — small cysts, nodules, or disc bulges — that are common in healthy people and usually harmless; whether they need follow-up is a clinical decision, so ask rather than assume the worst. Radiation risk from diagnostic imaging is small but adds up, so the principle is to image when it changes care, and always tell staff if you might be pregnant.

chapters.title: Anaesthesia & Pain Medicine
chapters.overview: How people are kept safe, still, and pain-free through surgery, and how pain — acute and chronic — is understood and treated. Covers the types of anaesthesia, what the anaesthetist does, the risks worth knowing, and the modern approach to pain that leans on combined methods rather than opioids alone.

sections.heading: The types of anaesthesia
sections.body: GENERAL anaesthesia produces controlled unconsciousness, usually with a breathing tube or airway device and a ventilator. REGIONAL anaesthesia numbs a large area while the patient may stay awake: a SPINAL (a single injection into the fluid around the spinal cord, common for caesarean and hip surgery), an EPIDURAL (a fine tube beside the spinal covering, used in labour and after major surgery), or a nerve BLOCK for a limb. LOCAL anaesthesia numbs a small area for minor procedures. SEDATION relaxes and dulls awareness without full unconsciousness. The choice depends on the operation, the patient's health, and preference.

sections.heading: What the anaesthetist does
sections.body: The anaesthetist is a doctor who stays with the patient throughout, managing the airway, breathing, circulation, depth of anaesthesia, fluids, temperature, and pain, and responding instantly to any change. Before surgery they assess fitness and risk (often summarized by the ASA grade from 1, healthy, to 5, critically ill), examine the airway, review medicines and allergies, and agree the plan. During surgery they monitor oxygen level, heart rhythm, blood pressure, and exhaled carbon dioxide continuously. Afterwards they oversee recovery and the first stage of pain control.

sections.heading: Preparing: fasting, medicines & what to tell them
sections.body: Fasting before anaesthesia prevents stomach contents entering the lungs; typical guidance is no food for about 6 hours and clear fluids until about 2 hours before, but follow the instructions you are given. Tell the team about every medicine and supplement (blood thinners, diabetes medicines, and some weight-loss injections need specific plans), allergies, previous problems with anaesthesia in you or your family, loose teeth, sleep apnoea, heart or lung disease, pregnancy, and smoking or alcohol and drug use. Honest information here directly improves safety.

sections.heading: Risks & what recovery feels like
sections.body: Modern anaesthesia is very safe for healthy people. Common, short-lived effects are nausea, sore throat, shivering, drowsiness, and confusion in older adults. Less common are dental damage, nerve irritation after a block, and headache after a spinal. Rare but serious events include severe allergy, breathing complications, awareness under anaesthesia, and malignant hyperthermia, an inherited reaction to certain agents — which is why family history matters. Risk rises with emergency surgery, frailty, obesity, and serious heart or lung disease. Do not drive or sign important documents for 24 hours afterwards.

sections.heading: Understanding and treating acute pain
sections.body: Pain is a signal processed by the nervous system, shaped by tissue injury, inflammation, attention, and emotion. Acute pain after injury or surgery is treated with MULTIMODAL analgesia: combining simple painkillers, anti-inflammatories where safe, local anaesthetic techniques, and opioids only when needed and for the shortest time, alongside ice, elevation, movement, and reassurance. Good pain control lets people breathe deeply, move, and recover faster. Pain that is severe, escalating, or out of proportion after an injury or operation is a warning sign that needs review.

sections.heading: Chronic pain
sections.body: Pain lasting more than about three months often stops being a reliable signal of damage: the nervous system becomes sensitized, so pain persists or spreads even after tissues heal. It is real, common, and frequently accompanied by poor sleep and low mood. The best-supported approach is combined: graded activity and physiotherapy, pain education, psychological methods such as CBT, sleep and mood treatment, selected medicines for nerve pain, and occasionally injections or procedures. Long-term opioids help few people and carry real harms. The goal shifts from eliminating pain to restoring function and quality of life.

chapters.title: Dentistry & Oral Health
chapters.overview: Teeth, gums, and the mouth: how decay and gum disease develop and are prevented, what dental pain means, how dental emergencies are handled, and how the mouth connects to general health. Practical for families and anyone without easy access to a dentist.

sections.heading: Teeth and their structure
sections.body: Adults have up to 32 teeth — incisors and canines for cutting and tearing, premolars and molars for grinding — following 20 baby teeth that appear from about six months and are replaced between roughly six and twelve years. Each tooth has a crown covered in ENAMEL (the hardest tissue in the body, with no nerves), a layer of sensitive DENTINE beneath, and a central PULP containing nerves and blood vessels. The root is anchored in the jawbone by the periodontal ligament, surrounded by the gum (gingiva).

sections.heading: Tooth decay
sections.body: Decay happens when bacteria in dental plaque turn sugars into acid that dissolves enamel. Early decay is painless and can be halted or reversed with fluoride and less frequent sugar. Once it reaches dentine the tooth becomes sensitive to sweet, hot, and cold; when it reaches the pulp it causes severe, lingering toothache, and infection can spread to form an abscess at the root. Prevention: brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, clean between the teeth, limit how OFTEN sugar is eaten or drunk, and have regular check-ups. Fillings, root-canal treatment, and crowns repair progressively deeper damage.

sections.heading: Gum disease
sections.body: GINGIVITIS is inflammation of the gums from plaque: red, swollen gums that bleed on brushing. It is reversible with thorough cleaning. Left alone it can progress to PERIODONTITIS, where the bone and ligament supporting the teeth are destroyed, causing receding gums, bad breath, loose teeth, and eventually tooth loss — it is the main cause of tooth loss in adults and is often painless. Smoking and poorly controlled diabetes greatly increase the risk, and severe gum disease in turn makes diabetes harder to control. Treatment is professional cleaning below the gum line plus daily home care.

sections.heading: Dental pain & emergencies
sections.body: A KNOCKED-OUT adult tooth: hold it by the crown, rinse briefly if dirty, push it back into the socket if you can or keep it in milk, and see a dentist within the hour — do not replant baby teeth. A dental ABSCESS causes throbbing pain, swelling, and sometimes fever; it needs dental treatment, not just antibiotics. RED FLAGS needing emergency care: swelling spreading to the eye, under the jaw, or down the neck, difficulty swallowing, breathing, or opening the mouth, or bleeding that will not stop after 20 minutes of firm pressure. Jaw pain with chest symptoms can be cardiac.

sections.heading: The mouth, the jaw & oral cancer
sections.body: Common mouth problems include ulcers (usually healing within two weeks), thrush, dry mouth from medicines, cold sores, teeth grinding, and jaw-joint (TMJ) pain. An ulcer, lump, or red or white patch that has not healed after THREE WEEKS must be examined, because oral cancer is far more treatable when caught early; tobacco, alcohol, and HPV are the main risks. Dentists screen for it at routine check-ups. Wisdom teeth often cause recurrent gum infection and may need removal. A persistently dry mouth raises decay risk and deserves a review of medicines.

sections.heading: Oral health through life
sections.body: Children: start brushing when the first tooth appears, supervise until about seven, avoid sugary drinks in bottles, and consider fissure sealants and fluoride varnish. Pregnancy: gums bleed more easily and dental care is safe and worthwhile. Older adults: dry mouth, receding gums, and dentures need attention, and denture wearers still need mouth checks. Some heart conditions and medicines, including bone-strengthening drugs and blood thinners, affect dental treatment, so always tell the dentist your full medical history. Where a dentist is hard to reach, prevention at home carries most of the benefit.

chapters.title: Haematology (Blood & Clotting)
chapters.overview: The blood itself: what the cells do, how a blood count is read, anaemia and its causes, bleeding and clotting disorders, blood thinners, blood cancers, and transfusion. The full blood count is the most commonly ordered test in medicine, and this chapter explains what it is telling you.

sections.heading: What blood is made of
sections.body: Blood is cells suspended in plasma. RED cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; WHITE cells defend against infection (neutrophils against bacteria, lymphocytes directing immunity, others handling allergy and parasites); PLATELETS start clots. All are made in the bone marrow from stem cells and replaced continuously — red cells live about four months, platelets about ten days. Plasma carries clotting proteins, antibodies, salts, hormones, and nutrients. Problems arise when a cell line is too low, too high, or abnormal, or when clotting is out of balance.

sections.heading: Reading a full blood count
sections.body: The full blood count (FBC or CBC) reports haemoglobin, the size of red cells (MCV), the white-cell count with its subtypes, and the platelet count. Low haemoglobin is anaemia; the MCV then points to the cause — small cells suggest iron deficiency, large cells suggest B12 or folate deficiency or alcohol. A high white count usually means infection or inflammation; a very high or very abnormal one needs urgent review. Low platelets cause bruising and bleeding. Results are read against the laboratory's reference range and, above all, against the person and the trend over time.

sections.heading: Anaemia
sections.body: Anaemia means too little haemoglobin to carry oxygen well, causing tiredness, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, and pallor. It is a FINDING, not a final diagnosis: the cause must be found. Common causes are iron deficiency (from heavy periods, pregnancy, poor intake, or hidden bleeding from the gut — which is why unexplained iron deficiency in adults, especially men and post-menopausal women, needs investigation), B12 or folate deficiency, chronic disease, kidney disease, and inherited conditions such as thalassaemia and sickle cell disease. Treatment replaces what is missing and deals with the cause.

sections.heading: Bleeding and clotting disorders
sections.body: Clotting is a balance. Too LITTLE clotting causes easy bruising, nosebleeds, heavy periods, and prolonged bleeding — from low platelets, inherited conditions such as von Willebrand disease and haemophilia, liver disease, or medicines. Too MUCH clotting causes deep vein thrombosis (a swollen, painful leg) and pulmonary embolism (sudden breathlessness and chest pain — an emergency), with risks including immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogen-containing medicines, and inherited tendencies. Unexplained bruising with a rash of tiny red-purple spots, or bleeding that will not stop, needs urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Blood thinners
sections.body: Anticoagulants prevent and treat clots and reduce stroke risk in atrial fibrillation. WARFARIN needs regular INR blood tests and is affected by many medicines and by vitamin K in food. The newer direct oral anticoagulants need no routine monitoring but depend on kidney function and must be taken reliably. ANTIPLATELET drugs such as aspirin act differently and are used mainly for arteries. All raise bleeding risk: seek urgent help for black or bloody stools, blood in urine or vomit, a severe headache, or any significant head injury while taking them. Always tell every clinician and dentist, and never stop them without advice.

sections.heading: Blood cancers & transfusion
sections.body: LEUKAEMIA is cancer of blood-forming cells, LYMPHOMA of the lymphatic system, and MYELOMA of antibody-making plasma cells. Warning features include persistent tiredness, repeated infections, unexplained bruising or bleeding, drenching night sweats, weight loss, bone pain, and painless enlarged lymph nodes — none specific, but worth a blood test when they persist. Treatments now include chemotherapy, targeted drugs, immunotherapy, and stem-cell transplant, with outcomes far better than a generation ago. TRANSFUSION replaces red cells, platelets, or plasma; blood is matched by ABO and Rh group, and donated blood is rigorously screened.

chapters.title: Plastic, Cosmetic & Reconstructive Surgery
chapters.overview: Surgery that restores or changes form: reconstruction after injury, cancer, or birth differences, and cosmetic procedures chosen to alter appearance — rhinoplasty, eyelid and facelift surgery, breast surgery, liposuction and body contouring, and the non-surgical injectables and lasers. Covers what each involves, realistic results, real risks, how to choose a surgeon, and the warning signs afterwards.

sections.heading: Reconstructive vs cosmetic, and choosing a surgeon
sections.body: RECONSTRUCTIVE surgery restores function and form — after burns, trauma, cancer (for example breast reconstruction), or congenital differences such as cleft lip — and is medical treatment. COSMETIC (aesthetic) surgery changes a normal feature by choice. The same specialty does both. Titles are loosely protected in many places, so 'cosmetic surgeon' can be used by doctors with little surgical training: check that the surgeon is a certified specialist in plastic surgery with the national college or board, operates in an accredited facility with a qualified anaesthetist, shows their own results, and explains risks and alternatives without pressure or time-limited discounts. A good surgeon sometimes says no.

sections.heading: Facial surgery: rhinoplasty, eyelids, facelift
sections.body: RHINOPLASTY reshapes the bone and cartilage of the nose for appearance, breathing, or both (with septoplasty for a deviated septum). Bruising settles in weeks but swelling, especially at the tip, takes up to a year to resolve fully, and a meaningful minority of patients need revision surgery. BLEPHAROPLASTY removes excess eyelid skin and fat; sometimes it improves vision as well as appearance. A FACELIFT repositions deeper facial tissue and removes lax skin; risks include bleeding under the skin, facial-nerve injury, and scarring. OTOPLASTY pins prominent ears. Results depend on anatomy and healing as much as on technique.

sections.heading: Breast surgery
sections.body: AUGMENTATION uses saline or silicone implants; implants are not lifetime devices and may need replacement, can form a tight scar capsule (capsular contracture), can rupture, and textured implants carry a rare risk of an implant-associated lymphoma, so new swelling or a lump years later needs assessment. REDUCTION relieves neck, back, and shoulder pain and is among the highest-satisfaction operations. MASTOPEXY lifts without changing volume much. RECONSTRUCTION after mastectomy uses implants or the patient's own tissue. Chest surgery for gynaecomastia and gender-affirming chest surgery use related techniques. All can affect sensation and breastfeeding.

sections.heading: Liposuction & body contouring
sections.body: LIPOSUCTION removes fat through thin tubes after infiltrating fluid containing local anaesthetic and adrenaline (the tumescent technique). It reshapes; it is not a treatment for obesity and does not improve health markers or loose skin. Risks include contour irregularity, fluid shifts, clots, local-anaesthetic toxicity, and rarely organ injury. ABDOMINOPLASTY (tummy tuck) removes skin and tightens the abdominal wall, with a long scar and a real clot risk. Fat transfer to the buttocks (the 'Brazilian butt lift') has had the highest death rate of any cosmetic operation, from fat entering large veins. Non-surgical fat reduction (cooling devices) gives modest change.

sections.heading: Injectables, lasers & other non-surgical treatments
sections.body: BOTULINUM TOXIN relaxes the muscles that crease the skin; the effect appears in days and lasts roughly three to four months. Dermal FILLERS, mostly hyaluronic acid, restore volume for months to over a year and can be dissolved with an enzyme. The serious filler risk is injection into a blood vessel, which can cause skin death or blindness — severe pain, blanching, or any visual change after filler is an emergency. Lasers, peels, and microneedling resurface skin, with burns, scarring, and pigment change as risks, higher in darker skin. These are medical procedures: the injector's training and the product's source both matter.

sections.heading: Risks, recovery & red flags
sections.body: Every operation carries the general risks of bleeding, infection, clots, scarring, anaesthesia, and an imperfect or asymmetric result. Smoking and nicotine sharply raise wound-healing problems and should stop well before surgery. Follow instructions on garments, activity, and wound care. RED FLAGS after any procedure: increasing pain, spreading redness, pus or fever (infection); one side suddenly swollen and tight (bleeding); a hot, swollen calf, or sudden breathlessness or chest pain (clot — an emergency); skin turning dusky or black; or confusion and a racing heart. Surgery abroad adds risks of poor follow-up, long flights soon after surgery, and resistant infections.

sections.heading: Expectations, body image & consent
sections.body: The best predictor of satisfaction is a specific, realistic goal held for the person's own reasons. Surgery does not reliably fix relationships, careers, or low mood. BODY DYSMORPHIC DISORDER — distressing preoccupation with a flaw others barely see — is common among people seeking cosmetic procedures; surgery rarely helps it and often worsens it, whereas psychological treatment works, so reputable surgeons screen for it. Informed consent means understanding the likely result, the risks, the alternatives including doing nothing, the full cost of revisions, and having time to reflect. Cosmetic surgery in under-18s is generally limited to specific indications.

chapters.title: Pigmentation, Scars & Cosmetic Dermatology
chapters.overview: Skin colour and its disorders — dark patches, light patches, and uneven tone — plus scars, and the cosmetic treatments used for them. Explains what causes each, what actually works, why darker skin needs a more careful approach, and the real dangers of unregulated skin-lightening products.

sections.heading: How skin colour works
sections.body: Skin colour comes mainly from MELANIN, made by melanocytes in the base of the epidermis and passed to surrounding cells. Everyone has a similar number of melanocytes; differences in colour reflect how much and what type of melanin they make. Melanin protects against ultraviolet damage, and sun exposure increases it (tanning). The FITZPATRICK scale describes six skin types from I (always burns, never tans) to VI (deeply pigmented, rarely burns); it predicts sun sensitivity and how skin responds to lasers, peels, and inflammation. Pigment sitting in the epidermis responds to treatment far better than pigment that has dropped into the dermis.

sections.heading: Dark patches: melasma, post-inflammatory marks & sun spots
sections.body: MELASMA causes symmetrical brown patches on the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip, driven by sunlight and hormones (pregnancy, the contraceptive pill); it is chronic and relapses with sun. POST-INFLAMMATORY HYPERPIGMENTATION is the dark mark left after acne, eczema, a burn, or a procedure, commoner and longer-lasting in darker skin; it fades over months if the cause is controlled. SOLAR LENTIGINES ('age spots') come from cumulative sun. Any single dark patch that is new, changing, irregular, or on the palm, sole, or under a nail must be checked for melanoma before it is treated cosmetically.

sections.heading: Light patches: vitiligo and others
sections.body: VITILIGO is autoimmune loss of melanocytes producing sharply defined milk-white patches, often around the eyes, mouth, hands, and body folds; it is not contagious, can be associated with thyroid disease, and is treated with prescription creams, light therapy, and newer targeted creams, with sun protection for the white skin. PITYRIASIS ALBA gives faint pale patches on children's cheeks and settles on its own. PITYRIASIS VERSICOLOR is a harmless yeast overgrowth causing fine scaly pale or brown patches on the trunk, treated with antifungals. Pale marks can also follow inflammation or injury. Loss of sensation in a pale patch needs medical assessment.

sections.heading: What works for uneven pigment
sections.body: Daily broad-spectrum SUNSCREEN is the foundation: without it nothing else lasts, and visible light matters too in darker skin, where tinted sunscreens help. Evidence-based topical agents include hydroquinone (by prescription, in limited courses), azelaic acid, retinoids, vitamin C, niacinamide, and tranexamic acid; combinations work better than single agents and improvement takes two to three months. Chemical peels and lasers can help selected cases but can also WORSEN pigmentation, particularly in Fitzpatrick types IV to VI, so they need an experienced practitioner and a test area. Treating the underlying acne or eczema prevents new marks.

sections.heading: The dangers of skin-lightening products
sections.body: Many unregulated lightening creams, soaps, and injections sold online and in shops contain undeclared MERCURY (which damages the kidneys and nervous system and can harm an unborn child), high-strength HYDROQUINONE (which with long use can cause a paradoxical blue-black darkening called ochronosis), or potent STEROIDS (which thin the skin and cause stretch marks, acne, visible vessels, and with heavy use hormonal suppression). Glutathione injections for lightening are unproven and unsafe. Buy only regulated products with full ingredient lists, and treat any product promising rapid whitening as a warning sign.

sections.heading: Scars, keloids & stretch marks
sections.body: A scar matures over 12 to 18 months, fading from red to pale. A HYPERTROPHIC scar is raised but stays within the wound's edges and often improves; a KELOID grows beyond them, is commoner in darker skin and on the chest, shoulders, and earlobes, and tends to recur after removal. Options include silicone gel or sheets, pressure, steroid injections, laser, and surgery combined with other treatment. Acne scars respond to microneedling, lasers, and fillers. STRETCH MARKS are dermal tears from rapid growth, pregnancy, or steroid use; they fade from purple to silver, and no cream reliably prevents or removes them.

sections.heading: Hair removal, tattoos & who should treat you
sections.body: LASER hair removal targets pigment in the follicle, works best on dark hair, gives long-term reduction rather than guaranteed permanence, and needs the correct laser type for darker skin to avoid burns and pigment change. Tattoo removal needs multiple laser sessions and may leave ghosting or scarring. Sudden excess facial or body hair in a woman, especially with irregular periods, deserves a hormonal check. For pigment and laser work, see a dermatologist or a properly supervised clinic, expect a diagnosis before treatment, and be wary of anyone who treats a pigmented lesion without examining it first.

chapters.title: Genital, Intimate & Gender-Affirming Surgery
chapters.overview: A factual guide to operations on the genitals: reconstructive and gender-affirming surgery (phalloplasty, metoidioplasty, vaginoplasty), cosmetic genital procedures (labiaplasty, 'vaginal rejuvenation', penile enlargement), hymen surgery, and circumcision. Sets out what each is, what the evidence supports, the risks, and where the law and medical bodies have drawn lines.

sections.heading: Normal variation comes first
sections.body: Genital appearance varies enormously in size, shape, colour, and symmetry, and almost all of it is normal. Most people seeking cosmetic genital surgery have anatomy within the normal range, often after comparing themselves with pornography or edited images. Pain, itching, bleeding, a new lump, discharge, or difficulty with urination or sex are medical symptoms that deserve assessment in their own right. Before any elective procedure, a good clinician shows the range of normal, asks what is driving the request, screens for body-image disorders and coercion, and explains that surgery on sensitive tissue can permanently change sensation.

sections.heading: Phalloplasty, metoidioplasty & penile surgery
sections.body: PHALLOPLASTY constructs a penis from a flap of the patient's own tissue, commonly from the forearm or thigh, for transgender men or after cancer, trauma, or congenital conditions. It is staged over many months and may include lengthening the urethra and later an erectile implant; urethral narrowing and leaks (fistulas) are common and often need further surgery. METOIDIOPLASTY creates a smaller phallus from hormonally enlarged clitoral tissue with fewer stages. For erectile dysfunction that has not responded to other treatment, PENILE IMPLANTS are effective with high satisfaction. Peyronie's disease (a painful curve from scar tissue) has medical and surgical treatments.

sections.heading: Penile enlargement: what the evidence says
sections.body: Most men who seek enlargement are of normal size. No pill, cream, or supplement enlarges the penis. Traction devices produce small gains at best with months of daily use; vacuum pumps help erections, not size. Surgical options — cutting the suspensory ligament, or injecting fat or filler for girth — give modest or unpredictable results with real risks of deformity, lumps, scarring, loss of sensation, and erectile problems, and professional urology bodies do not recommend them for cosmetic reasons in men with normal anatomy. Injecting non-medical substances such as oils or silicone causes severe, disfiguring reactions. Counselling is often what helps most.

sections.heading: Vaginoplasty, labiaplasty & 'vaginal rejuvenation'
sections.body: VAGINOPLASTY constructs a vagina — for transgender women (usually by penile inversion) or for people born without one — and requires lifelong dilation and follow-up. Repair of PROLAPSE or childbirth injury is reconstructive surgery with clear benefit. LABIAPLASTY reduces the inner labia; it can relieve genuine physical discomfort, but risks include scarring, chronic pain, and altered sensation, and it is not recommended under 18 because the anatomy is still developing. Laser and radiofrequency 'vaginal rejuvenation' devices are marketed for laxity, dryness, and incontinence, but regulators including the US FDA have warned that safety and effectiveness are not established and burns and scarring have occurred. Pelvic-floor physiotherapy is the proven first treatment for laxity and leakage.

sections.heading: The hymen and hymen surgery
sections.body: The hymen is a thin rim of tissue at the vaginal opening that varies widely in shape and stretch. It can stretch or tear from sport, tampons, or examinations, may remain intact after intercourse, and often does not bleed at first intercourse; many people are born with very little. It therefore cannot prove or disprove virginity, and the World Health Organization has called for an end to 'virginity testing' as unscientific and harmful. HYMENOPLASTY stitches the remnants to recreate a membrane; it has no medical benefit and does not guarantee bleeding. It and virginity testing are criminal offences in the United Kingdom, and some other countries restrict them. Anyone feeling pressured or afraid should be offered confidential support and safeguarding help. A rare imperforate hymen that blocks menstrual flow is different and needs a simple corrective operation.

sections.heading: Circumcision
sections.body: Male circumcision removes the foreskin. Medical reasons include a tight foreskin that will not retract and causes problems (phimosis), recurrent infection, and certain skin conditions; it is also performed for religious and cultural reasons. Benefits such as fewer urinary infections in infancy and a lower risk of some sexually transmitted infections are real but modest in low-risk settings, and the main risks are bleeding, infection, and taking too much or too little skin. It should be done with proper pain relief by a trained practitioner. Female genital cutting has no health benefit, causes lifelong harm, and is illegal in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and many other countries.

sections.heading: Deciding, recovery & warning signs
sections.body: Gender-affirming genital surgery follows assessment under recognized standards of care, with attention to fertility preservation and long-term follow-up. For any intimate surgery, ask the surgeon how many they perform, their complication and revision rates, and what recovery truly involves — typically weeks without sex, exercise, or sometimes sitting comfortably. Seek urgent help afterwards for heavy bleeding, increasing pain or swelling, fever, foul discharge, wounds opening, tissue turning dark, or being unable to pass urine. Sexual function and sensation should be discussed honestly before surgery, because changes can be permanent.
