chapters.title: Bowel Care, Constipation, Enemas & Continence
chapters.overview: Practical bowel management: what normal is, how to treat constipation step by step, how laxatives, suppositories, and enemas work and how to use them safely, bowel preparation for procedures, stoma basics, and the symptoms that must not be self-treated. Useful for carers and anyone managing a long-term bowel problem.

sections.heading: What normal looks like
sections.body: Normal bowel frequency ranges from three times a day to three times a week; what matters is a change from your own pattern and how easy stools are to pass. The Bristol Stool Chart describes seven types, from separate hard lumps (type 1) to entirely liquid (type 7); types 3 and 4 — a soft, formed sausage — are the easiest to pass. Stool is normally brown. Black, tarry stool can mean bleeding higher in the gut (iron tablets and bismuth also darken it); bright red blood usually comes from lower down; pale, greasy, floating stool suggests poor fat absorption. A persistent change in habit lasting more than a few weeks deserves assessment.

sections.heading: Treating constipation: the stepwise ladder
sections.body: Start with the basics: enough fluid, more fibre from food increased gradually, daily movement, responding promptly to the urge, unhurried time on the toilet after a meal, and a footstool to raise the knees above the hips. Review medicines that constipate — opioids, iron, some antidepressants, antacids, and others. If that is not enough, an OSMOTIC laxative (such as macrogol or lactulose) draws water into the stool; a STIMULANT laxative (senna, bisacodyl) is added if needed; and a suppository or enema is used for stool stuck low in the rectum. Bulk-forming fibre supplements need plenty of fluid and are avoided when someone is already blocked or on opioids. Use the product label for doses.

sections.heading: Enemas and suppositories: types and safe use
sections.body: A SUPPOSITORY (glycerin or bisacodyl) is placed in the rectum and works within about 15 to 60 minutes. An ENEMA delivers liquid: small-volume micro-enemas and saline or phosphate enemas soften and stimulate; oil-retention enemas lubricate hard stool. Technique: lie on the LEFT side with knees bent, lubricate the tip, insert it gently pointing toward the navel, squeeze slowly, never force against resistance, and hold as long as the label advises. Phosphate enemas can cause dangerous salt disturbances in young children, frail older adults, and people with kidney or heart disease, so follow age limits exactly. Do not use plain tap water, soap, or home mixtures.

sections.heading: When not to use an enema or laxative
sections.body: Do NOT self-treat, and seek medical advice, if there is severe or worsening abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen hard abdomen, inability to pass wind (possible bowel obstruction), fever, rectal bleeding of unknown cause, recent bowel or rectal surgery, or a known inflammatory bowel flare. Repeated or daily enemas irritate the rectum, upset the body's salts, and can weaken normal function. Colonic irrigation and 'detox' or coffee enemas have no proven health benefit and have caused burns, bowel perforation, infection, and dangerous salt imbalance. In children, constipation is treated with oral laxatives under guidance; enemas are a last resort.

sections.heading: Bowel preparation and impaction
sections.body: Before a colonoscopy or bowel surgery the colon is emptied with a strong oral preparation taken in split doses with clear fluids; a clean bowel is what makes the test reliable, so follow the timing instructions exactly and ask about diabetes medicines and blood thinners. FAECAL IMPACTION is a hard mass of stool stuck in the rectum, common in frail or immobile people and those on opioids; a classic sign is liquid stool leaking around the blockage, mistaken for diarrhoea. It is treated with high-dose osmotic laxatives, suppositories, or enemas under clinical guidance, followed by a regular regimen to prevent recurrence.

sections.heading: Continence, stomas and regular bowel programmes
sections.body: Bowel leakage is common, under-reported, and treatable: firming the stool, pelvic-floor and sphincter exercises, scheduled toileting, skin protection, and specialist assessment for nerve or muscle damage all help. People with spinal cord injury or neurological disease often use a planned BOWEL PROGRAMME — a regular time, a suppository or digital stimulation, and sometimes transanal irrigation taught by a specialist nurse. A STOMA (colostomy or ileostomy) brings the bowel to the skin surface into a bag; a healthy stoma is moist and red, and one that turns dark or black, stops working with pain and vomiting, or bleeds heavily needs urgent review.

sections.heading: Red flags that need a doctor
sections.body: See a doctor promptly for: a change in bowel habit lasting more than three to four weeks, especially over the age of 50; blood in or on the stool; black tarry stools; unexplained weight loss or tiredness with anaemia; a persistent feeling of incomplete emptying; new constipation with back pain, leg weakness, numbness around the back passage, or loss of bladder control (possible spinal emergency); severe pain with a swollen abdomen and vomiting; or constipation alternating with diarrhoea. Long-term need for laxatives is common and usually safe with the right agent, but the cause should have been looked for first.

chapters.title: Geriatrics & Healthy Ageing
chapters.overview: Medicine for older adults, where illness presents differently, several conditions coexist, and the goal is function and quality of life as much as cure. Covers frailty, falls, confusion, medicines in later life, continence, nutrition, and planning ahead.

sections.heading: Why older adults are different
sections.body: Ageing reduces the reserve of every organ, so a small insult — an infection, a new medicine, dehydration — can tip a stable person into crisis. Illness often presents atypically: a urinary infection or pneumonia may show only as new confusion, a fall, or 'not being themselves', and a heart attack may cause breathlessness or fatigue rather than chest pain. Several conditions and many medicines usually coexist, so each decision is weighed against the whole person. The priorities shift toward independence, comfort, and what matters most to the individual.

sections.heading: Frailty and the geriatric giants
sections.body: FRAILTY is a state of reduced strength and resilience — weight loss, weakness, slow walking, exhaustion, low activity — that predicts falls, hospital admission, and slow recovery. It is not inevitable and can be improved with resistance exercise, adequate protein, and medicine review. Classic 'geriatric giants' cluster with it: instability and falls, immobility, incontinence, impaired memory, and the harms of medicines. A comprehensive geriatric assessment looks at medical, functional, mental, and social needs together and produces a single coordinated plan.

sections.heading: Falls
sections.body: A fall in an older person is a symptom to investigate, not an accident to dismiss. Causes combine: weak legs and poor balance, medicines that sedate or lower blood pressure, a drop in blood pressure on standing, poor vision, foot problems, alcohol, heart-rhythm problems, and hazards at home. Prevention that works includes strength-and-balance exercise, medicine review, vision checks, safe footwear, good lighting, and removing trip hazards. After a fall, inability to get up, hip or groin pain with a shortened turned-out leg, a head injury (especially on blood thinners), or new confusion needs urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Delirium, dementia and depression
sections.body: DELIRIUM is sudden confusion developing over hours to days, fluctuating, with poor attention; it is a medical emergency caused by infection, medicines, dehydration, pain, constipation, or surgery, and it is usually reversible if the cause is found. DEMENTIA develops over months to years with steadily worsening memory, language, and daily function. DEPRESSION in later life may look like apathy, poor memory, or physical complaints. They overlap and are easily confused. Any SUDDEN change in thinking or alertness should be treated as delirium until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Medicines in later life
sections.body: Older bodies clear medicines more slowly and are more sensitive to them, and each added medicine raises the risk of interactions, falls, and confusion. POLYPHARMACY is common and often includes medicines started for a side effect of another (a prescribing cascade). Particular caution applies to sedatives and sleeping tablets, strong anticholinergic drugs, anti-inflammatories, and anything lowering blood pressure or sugar too far. DEPRESCRIBING — stopping medicines whose harms now outweigh their benefits, one at a time and under supervision — is good medicine. A full review at least yearly, with every pill and supplement on the table, is worthwhile.

sections.heading: Nutrition, continence, senses and staying well
sections.body: Unintended weight loss, poor appetite, and dehydration are common and worsen frailty; protein at each meal, regular fluids, dental care, and treating swallowing problems matter. Incontinence is treatable and should be raised, not hidden. Correcting hearing and vision reduces isolation, falls, and cognitive decline. Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, shingles, COVID-19), staying physically and socially active, and managing blood pressure protect independence. Loneliness is a genuine health risk. Carers need support too: their own health often fails first.

sections.heading: Planning ahead
sections.body: Advance care planning lets a person record what matters to them and who should speak for them if they cannot: a power of attorney for personal care or health-care proxy, an advance directive, and conversations with family and clinicians about treatments they would or would not want, including resuscitation. These discussions are best had early, while the person can lead them, and revisited as health changes. Driving safety, safe housing, finances, and protection from abuse or exploitation belong in the same conversation. Planning is not giving up; it keeps the person in charge.

chapters.title: Palliative & End-of-Life Care
chapters.overview: Care focused on comfort, dignity, and quality of life for people with serious illness — alongside treatment or instead of it. Covers what palliative care is, symptom control, what dying usually looks like, supporting families, and grief.

sections.heading: What palliative care is — and is not
sections.body: Palliative care relieves suffering — physical, emotional, social, and spiritual — for people with serious illness and supports their families. It is appropriate from diagnosis, can be given alongside treatment aimed at cure or control, and is not limited to cancer or to the last days. HOSPICE care is palliative care for the final months, when the focus is entirely on comfort. Studies show that early palliative care improves quality of life and mood. Asking for it is not giving up; it is asking for an extra layer of expert support.

sections.heading: Controlling symptoms
sections.body: PAIN is treated by matching the medicine to its type and severity, given regularly rather than waiting for pain to return, with extra doses for breakthrough pain; opioids used properly for serious illness are safe and effective, and addiction is rarely the problem, though constipation almost always is and needs a laxative from the start. BREATHLESSNESS is eased by positioning, a fan to the face, calm, and low-dose opioids. NAUSEA, anxiety, agitation, and noisy secretions each have specific treatments. Mouth care, skin care, and attention to fears and unfinished business matter as much as medicines.

sections.heading: Honest conversations and choices
sections.body: Good care depends on honest, kind conversations: what the person understands about their illness, what they hope for and fear, what trade-offs they would accept, and where they want to be cared for. Prognosis is uncertain and is usually given as a range — days to weeks, weeks to months. Decisions may include stopping treatments that no longer help, declining resuscitation, and choosing home, hospice, or hospital. Where medical assistance in dying is lawful, people may ask about it and are entitled to accurate information. The person's own values lead.

sections.heading: What dying usually looks like
sections.body: In the last days most people sleep more, eat and drink little, and become less responsive; forcing food or fluids does not help and can cause distress. Breathing changes, with pauses and sometimes a rattling sound from secretions that usually troubles listeners more than the person. Hands and feet cool and may mottle; urine output falls. Restlessness or confusion can occur and is treatable. Hearing is thought to persist, so keep talking and touching. Most deaths with good palliative care are peaceful. Knowing these changes in advance spares families a great deal of fear.

sections.heading: Supporting family and carers
sections.body: Caring for a dying person is exhausting and often lonely. Carers need clear information about what to expect, a number to call at any hour, help with equipment and personal care, respite, and permission to rest. Children should be told the truth in simple words and included as far as they wish. After a death at home there is no need to rush: call the palliative team or doctor as arranged. Practical matters — the medical certificate, registering the death, and funeral arrangements — follow in their own time.

sections.heading: Grief and bereavement
sections.body: Grief is the normal response to loss and has no fixed stages or timetable; it comes in waves and may include sadness, anger, guilt, relief, numbness, poor sleep, and physical symptoms. Most people adjust with the support of family and friends. Seek help when grief remains overwhelming and disabling many months on, when there is prolonged inability to function, heavy use of alcohol or drugs, or any thoughts of self-harm — in the US and Canada call or text 988. Bereavement support groups, counselling, and the family doctor all help, and anniversaries often reopen the wound.

chapters.title: Sexual & Reproductive Health
chapters.overview: Sexually transmitted infections, testing and prevention, contraception and emergency contraception, fertility, sexual function, and consent. Frank, non-judgemental, and practical about when to get tested and where.

sections.heading: Sexually transmitted infections
sections.body: Common STIs include chlamydia and gonorrhoea (often with no symptoms, sometimes discharge, burning on urination, pelvic or testicular pain), syphilis (a painless sore, then a rash that can include the palms and soles, then silent damage years later), genital herpes (recurrent painful blisters), HPV (genital warts and several cancers), trichomoniasis, hepatitis B, and HIV. Because many cause no symptoms, people pass them on unknowingly, and untreated infections can cause infertility, chronic pain, pregnancy complications, and serious illness. Most are easily treated or well controlled once found.

sections.heading: Testing: when and how
sections.body: Get tested if you have symptoms, a new partner, more than one partner, a partner with an STI, or simply as a routine check when sexually active. Tests are simple — a urine sample or self-taken swab, and a blood test — but each infection has a WINDOW PERIOD before it shows, so a test too soon after exposure may need repeating. Tell the clinic which kinds of sex you have so the right sites are tested. Treatment should include current partners, and you should avoid sex until treatment is complete. Sexual health clinics are confidential.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.body: Condoms, used consistently, greatly reduce the risk of most STIs and of pregnancy. VACCINES prevent HPV and hepatitis B. For HIV, PrEP (a preventive medicine taken before exposure) is highly effective, PEP started within 72 hours after a possible exposure can prevent infection, and a person on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV sexually. Regular testing, honest conversations with partners, and clean injecting equipment complete the picture. Cervical screening detects HPV-related changes long before they become cancer.

sections.heading: Contraception and emergency contraception
sections.body: Long-acting reversible methods — hormonal and copper IUDs and the implant — are the most effective because they do not rely on daily action. The pill, patch, ring, and injection are effective when used correctly; combined methods containing oestrogen are unsuitable for some people, including those with certain migraines, clot risks, or who smoke over 35. EMERGENCY contraception after unprotected sex is time-critical: the copper IUD is the most effective and can be fitted within five days, and emergency pills work best the sooner they are taken. Vasectomy and tubal surgery are permanent options.

sections.heading: Fertility and pregnancy planning
sections.body: Most couples conceive within a year of regular unprotected sex. Seek assessment after 12 months of trying, or after 6 months if the woman is 35 or older, or sooner with irregular periods, known problems, or previous pelvic infection. Causes are shared roughly equally between female factors, male factors, and combined or unexplained. Before conception: folic acid, a review of medicines, vaccination status, stopping smoking and alcohol, and control of long-term conditions. Unplanned pregnancy options — continuing, adoption, or abortion where lawful — deserve unbiased, prompt information.

sections.heading: Sexual function and wellbeing
sections.body: Sexual difficulties are common and usually treatable. ERECTILE dysfunction may be an early sign of blood-vessel disease or diabetes and merits a health check as well as treatment. Low desire, pain with sex, vaginal dryness (especially after menopause), difficulty with orgasm, and premature ejaculation all have physical, psychological, and relationship contributors, and many medicines affect sexual function. Pain with sex, bleeding after sex, or a new lump or sore should be examined. Sex therapy, pelvic-floor physiotherapy, hormonal treatment, and medicines each have a place.

sections.heading: Consent, safety and where to get help
sections.body: Consent must be freely given, informed, specific, and can be withdrawn at any time; a person who is asleep, unconscious, or incapacitated by alcohol or drugs cannot consent, and neither can someone below the legal age. After sexual assault, medical care is available whether or not the police are involved: emergency contraception, PEP for HIV, STI prevention, treatment of injuries, and forensic evidence collection, which is best done early but still worthwhile later. Sexual-assault centres and crisis lines provide confidential support, and none of what happened is the survivor's fault.

chapters.title: Sleep Medicine
chapters.overview: How sleep works, how much is needed, and the common disorders — insomnia, sleep apnoea, restless legs, and the body-clock problems of shift work and jet lag — with treatments that work better than sleeping tablets.

sections.heading: How sleep works
sections.body: Sleep is governed by two processes: SLEEP PRESSURE, which builds the longer you are awake, and the CIRCADIAN clock, a roughly 24-hour rhythm set mainly by light. Through the night the brain cycles about every 90 minutes through light sleep, deep slow-wave sleep (physical restoration, most in the first half of the night), and REM sleep (dreaming and memory processing, most toward morning). Most adults need seven to nine hours; teenagers and children need more. Chronic short sleep impairs attention, mood, immunity, and blood-sugar control and raises accident risk.

sections.heading: Sleep habits that matter
sections.body: The foundations are a consistent wake-up time seven days a week, morning daylight, a wind-down routine, and a bedroom that is dark, quiet, and cool. Caffeine lingers for many hours, so stop by early afternoon; alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night; nicotine is a stimulant. Keep screens and work out of bed. Exercise helps, though not right before bedtime. If you cannot sleep after about twenty minutes, get up, do something quiet in dim light, and return when sleepy, so the bed stays linked with sleep.

sections.heading: Insomnia
sections.body: Insomnia is difficulty falling or staying asleep, or waking too early, with daytime consequences, at least three nights a week for three months. It is often kept going by worry about sleep itself and by habits such as long lie-ins and napping. The most effective treatment is COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY FOR INSOMNIA (CBT-I), which combines sleep restriction, stimulus control, and tackling unhelpful beliefs; it works better and lasts longer than tablets and is available in person and as digital programmes. Sleeping tablets help briefly but cause tolerance, dependence, falls, and morning impairment.

sections.heading: Obstructive sleep apnoea
sections.body: In sleep apnoea the throat repeatedly narrows or closes during sleep, causing loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, gasping or choking awakenings, unrefreshing sleep, morning headaches, and daytime sleepiness. Risk rises with excess weight, a large neck, male sex, age, alcohol, and sedatives. Untreated it raises blood pressure and the risk of heart disease, stroke, and road accidents. Diagnosis is by a sleep study, often at home. Treatment includes weight loss, avoiding alcohol and sleeping on the back, mandibular devices, and CPAP, which holds the airway open with gentle air pressure.

sections.heading: Other sleep disorders
sections.body: RESTLESS LEGS syndrome is an urge to move the legs in the evening, relieved by movement; check iron levels. NARCOLEPSY causes irresistible daytime sleep and sometimes sudden loss of muscle tone with emotion. PARASOMNIAS include sleepwalking and night terrors, mostly in children, and acting out dreams in older adults, which should be assessed because it can precede neurological disease. Nightmares are common after trauma and treatable. Excessive sleepiness despite enough time in bed always deserves assessment, especially in anyone who drives or operates machinery.

sections.heading: Shift work, jet lag and teenagers
sections.body: When the body clock and the schedule disagree, sleep suffers. SHIFT workers do best with a consistent pattern where possible, bright light during the shift, dark glasses on the way home, a dark quiet bedroom, and a protected sleep period. JET LAG eases faster with daylight exposure at the destination's daytime; travelling east is harder than west. TEENAGERS have a naturally delayed clock, so late nights and difficult mornings are partly biological; morning light, a regular wake time, and no screens in bed help. Drowsy driving is as dangerous as drink-driving: pull over and nap.

chapters.title: Toxicology & Poisoning
chapters.overview: What to do when someone has swallowed, inhaled, or touched something harmful: first actions, the dangerous household and medicine poisonings, carbon monoxide, bites and stings, and prevention. In any suspected poisoning call Poison Control (US 1-800-222-1222; in Canada 1-844-764-7669) or emergency services.

sections.heading: First actions in any poisoning
sections.body: If the person has collapsed, is having a seizure, is very drowsy, or is struggling to breathe, call emergency services. Otherwise call Poison Control straight away, even with no symptoms, and have the container ready: what it was, how much, when, and the person's age and weight. Do NOT make the person vomit and do not give salt water, milk, or home remedies unless told to. For a chemical on the skin or in the eye, rinse with running water for at least fifteen minutes. For fumes, get to fresh air. Take the container to hospital.

sections.heading: Medicine overdoses
sections.body: Some common medicines are far more dangerous in overdose than people assume. PARACETAMOL (acetaminophen) causes little at first, then severe liver damage one to three days later; an effective antidote exists but works best when started early, so every possible overdose needs assessment even if the person feels well. Aspirin, iron tablets, antidepressants, heart and blood-pressure medicines, diabetes medicines, and opioids can each be fatal, and a single adult tablet of some can kill a small child. For a suspected opioid overdose give naloxone and call for help. An intentional overdose also needs compassionate mental-health care.

sections.heading: Household and garden hazards
sections.body: Caustic cleaners (drain, oven, and toilet cleaners) burn the mouth and gullet. Laundry and dishwasher pods are dangerous to children. BUTTON BATTERIES and high-powered magnets can cause fatal internal injury within hours if swallowed — go to emergency immediately. Lamp oils and fuels can enter the lungs. Mixing bleach with ammonia or acids releases toxic gas. Antifreeze and windscreen fluid are highly poisonous and taste sweet. Nicotine liquids, cannabis edibles, and alcohol are increasingly common causes of serious poisoning in young children.

sections.heading: Carbon monoxide
sections.body: Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas from faulty or poorly ventilated furnaces, boilers, stoves, generators, vehicles, and barbecues used indoors. It causes headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, and confusion, and then collapse — often mistaken for flu, with the clue that several people or pets in the same home are unwell and symptoms improve away from the building. If suspected, get everyone into fresh air, call emergency services, and do not re-enter. Fit carbon monoxide alarms near sleeping areas and never run a generator or grill indoors or in a garage.

sections.heading: Bites, stings and plants
sections.body: Most insect stings cause only local pain and swelling; remove a bee sting by scraping, and use a cold pack. Swelling of the face or throat, widespread hives, wheeze, or faintness after a sting is anaphylaxis — give adrenaline if available and call for help. For a snakebite keep the person still with the limb immobilized at heart level, remove rings, and get to hospital; do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. Animal and human bites need thorough washing and medical review for infection, tetanus, and rabies risk. Many garden plants and wild mushrooms are toxic: call Poison Control.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.body: Keep medicines and chemicals in their original containers, locked or out of reach and sight, and never call medicine 'candy'. Use child-resistant caps but do not rely on them. Check doses carefully, especially liquids for children, and keep a written list when several people give medicines. Dispose of unused medicines through a pharmacy take-back. Store button batteries and magnets securely. Install carbon monoxide and smoke alarms. Keep the Poison Control number in your phone and on the fridge, and keep naloxone in any home where opioids are present.

chapters.title: Travel & Tropical Medicine
chapters.overview: Staying healthy abroad: preparing before the trip, vaccines, malaria and mosquito protection, food and water, altitude, long flights, and what to do about illness during and after travel.

sections.heading: Before you go
sections.body: See a travel clinic or doctor ideally six to eight weeks before departure, since some vaccines need several doses. Take enough of your regular medicines in original labelled containers, plus a copy of prescriptions, and check whether any are restricted where you are going. Arrange travel health insurance that covers medical evacuation and any pre-existing conditions, and know how to reach consular help. People who are pregnant, immunocompromised, very young or old, or who have long-term conditions need individual advice. Pack a small kit: pain relief, rehydration salts, antiseptic, dressings, and insect repellent.

sections.heading: Travel vaccines
sections.body: First make sure routine vaccines are up to date — measles, tetanus, polio, influenza. Destination-specific vaccines commonly include hepatitis A and typhoid for areas with uncertain food and water, hepatitis B, rabies for remote travel or animal contact, Japanese encephalitis, meningococcal disease, and cholera for certain settings. YELLOW FEVER vaccination is legally required for entry to some countries and must be recorded on an international certificate from an authorized centre. Requirements change, so check current official guidance for each country on the route, including transit stops.

sections.heading: Malaria and mosquito-borne infections
sections.body: Malaria is a potentially fatal parasitic infection spread by night-biting mosquitoes in much of the tropics. Prevention has four parts: awareness of risk, bite avoidance (repellent containing DEET or picaridin, long sleeves, treated bed nets, screened or air-conditioned rooms), preventive tablets chosen for the destination and the traveller, and prompt diagnosis. No method is complete, so ANY FEVER during travel or for up to a year afterwards is malaria until proven otherwise and needs a same-day blood test. Dengue, chikungunya, and Zika are spread by day-biting mosquitoes; Zika is a particular risk in pregnancy.

sections.heading: Food, water and traveller's diarrhoea
sections.body: Where sanitation is uncertain, drink bottled, boiled, or treated water, avoid ice, and prefer food that is freshly cooked and served hot; peel fruit yourself. Traveller's diarrhoea is common and usually settles in a few days; the essential treatment is replacing fluid, ideally with oral rehydration salts. Anti-diarrhoeal medicine can help for travel days but should be avoided with fever or blood in the stool. Seek care for bloody diarrhoea, high fever, persistent vomiting, signs of dehydration, or symptoms lasting more than a few days, and urgently for young children and older adults.

sections.heading: Altitude, heat, flights and accidents
sections.body: Above about 2,500 metres, ascending too fast causes ALTITUDE sickness — headache, nausea, fatigue, poor sleep; the rule is to climb gradually, and never go higher with symptoms. Worsening breathlessness at rest, confusion, or unsteadiness means descend immediately. In heat, drink regularly, rest in the hottest hours, and recognize heat exhaustion before it becomes heat stroke. On long flights, move, stretch calves, and stay hydrated to reduce clot risk. Road crashes, drowning, and injuries — not exotic infections — are the leading causes of death in travellers: wear seatbelts and helmets.

sections.heading: Illness after returning
sections.body: Tell any doctor where you have travelled, and when. Fever after travel to a malaria area is an emergency. Persistent diarrhoea, a rash, jaundice, a skin sore that will not heal, or blood in the urine after freshwater swimming in parts of Africa all need assessment. An animal bite or scratch abroad needs urgent advice about rabies treatment even after returning home, because treatment before symptoms is life-saving. Some infections appear weeks or months later, so the travel history remains relevant long after the trip ends.

chapters.title: Laboratory Tests Explained
chapters.overview: How to read the commonest blood and urine tests: what each measures, typical adult reference ranges, and what high or low results usually mean. Ranges differ between laboratories and with age, sex, and pregnancy — always read your result against the range printed on your own report, and against how you feel.

sections.heading: How to read any result
sections.body: A reference range covers the middle 95 percent of healthy people, so one in twenty healthy results falls just outside it. A value slightly out of range in a well person is often unimportant; the size of the abnormality, the trend over time, and the symptoms matter more than the flag. Units differ between countries, so never compare numbers without checking them. Results can be altered by fasting, exercise, dehydration, time of day, medicines, and supplements such as biotin. Ask what a test is for before it is taken and what will be done with the answer.

sections.heading: Full blood count
sections.body: Typical adult ranges: HAEMOGLOBIN about 120–160 g/L in women and 130–175 g/L in men; WHITE CELLS about 4–11 ×10⁹/L; PLATELETS about 150–400 ×10⁹/L. Low haemoglobin is anaemia, and the red-cell size (MCV, roughly 80–100 fL) points to the cause: small cells suggest iron deficiency, large cells suggest B12 or folate deficiency or alcohol. A raised white count usually reflects infection or inflammation; low counts raise infection risk. Low platelets cause bruising and bleeding. Very abnormal counts need prompt review.

sections.heading: Kidney function and electrolytes
sections.body: SODIUM is typically about 135–145 mmol/L and POTASSIUM about 3.5–5.0 mmol/L; potassium that is clearly high or low can disturb the heart rhythm and is treated urgently. CREATININE is a waste product cleared by the kidneys, converted into the eGFR: above 90 is normal, 60–89 mildly reduced, and persistently below 60 indicates chronic kidney disease. Urine protein (albumin-to-creatinine ratio) detects early kidney damage, especially in diabetes and high blood pressure. Dehydration, anti-inflammatory painkillers, and some blood-pressure medicines commonly shift these results.

sections.heading: Blood sugar and cholesterol
sections.body: FASTING GLUCOSE below about 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) is normal; 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or above on two occasions indicates diabetes, with the range between called prediabetes. HbA1c reflects average sugar over about three months: below 5.7% is normal, 5.7–6.4% prediabetes, and 6.5% or above diabetes. A LIPID profile reports total cholesterol, LDL ('bad'), HDL ('good'), and triglycerides; treatment decisions rest on overall cardiovascular risk — age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes — rather than on a single number, with lower LDL targets for those at higher risk.

sections.heading: Liver, thyroid and inflammation
sections.body: LIVER tests include ALT and AST (raised when liver cells are irritated — fatty liver, alcohol, viral hepatitis, medicines), ALP and GGT (bile-duct problems), bilirubin (jaundice when high), and albumin (the liver's manufacturing capacity). THYROID function starts with TSH, typically about 0.4–4.0 mU/L: a high TSH suggests an underactive thyroid and a low TSH an overactive one. CRP and ESR are non-specific markers of inflammation or infection that help track activity rather than name a cause. Mildly raised liver enzymes are very common and are usually rechecked before further tests.

sections.heading: Urine tests, vitamins and clotting
sections.body: A urine DIPSTICK screens for infection (nitrites and white cells), blood, protein, and glucose; a culture identifies the bacteria and the antibiotics that work. Blood in the urine without infection always needs follow-up. FERRITIN reflects iron stores but rises with inflammation; B12, folate, and vitamin D are checked when deficiency is suspected. The INR measures clotting time and guides warfarin dosing. PSA, tumour markers, and autoantibodies are useful only in the right clinical setting and cause false alarms when used as general screening. Home test kits vary in quality: confirm unexpected results properly.

chapters.title: Addiction Medicine & Recovery
chapters.overview: Substance use disorders as treatable medical conditions: how addiction works, alcohol, opioids, stimulants, cannabis, nicotine, and gambling, the treatments with evidence behind them, and how families can help. Complements the overdose-prevention and harm-reduction reference.

sections.heading: What addiction is
sections.body: Addiction is a chronic, relapsing condition in which use continues despite harm, with loss of control, craving, and narrowing of life around the substance or behaviour. Repeated use reshapes the brain's reward, stress, and self-control circuits, which is why willpower alone so often fails and why it is not a moral weakness. Risk is shaped by genetics, early-life adversity, mental illness, age at first use, and availability. TOLERANCE and WITHDRAWAL signal physical dependence, which can exist without addiction. Recovery is common, usually takes more than one attempt, and is helped by treatment.

sections.heading: Alcohol
sections.body: Risky drinking damages the liver, heart, brain, and gut, raises the risk of several cancers, and worsens mood and sleep. Dependence shows as needing a drink to function, morning shakes, and failed attempts to cut down. Stopping SUDDENLY after heavy daily drinking can cause dangerous withdrawal — tremor, sweating, seizures, and delirium with confusion and hallucinations — and should be medically supervised. Effective help includes brief advice, medicines that reduce craving or make drinking unpleasant, thiamine to protect the brain, psychological therapy, and mutual-aid groups.

sections.heading: Opioids
sections.body: Opioid use disorder carries a high risk of death from overdose, especially with illicit fentanyl and after any period of abstinence, when tolerance has fallen. The most effective treatment is OPIOID AGONIST THERAPY with methadone or buprenorphine, which stops withdrawal and craving, allows a stable life, and roughly halves the risk of death; it is treatment, not swapping one addiction for another, and works best continued long term. Detox alone is followed by frequent relapse and a high overdose risk. Everyone at risk, and their household, should carry naloxone.

sections.heading: Stimulants, cannabis, sedatives and nicotine
sections.body: STIMULANTS (cocaine, methamphetamine) cause heart attack, stroke, psychosis, and severe crashes in mood; treatment is mainly psychological, with contingency management — tangible rewards for negative tests — the best supported. CANNABIS use disorder affects roughly one in ten regular users, more if started in adolescence, and heavy use can trigger psychosis or cyclical vomiting. BENZODIAZEPINES and other sedatives cause dependence and must be reduced gradually, never stopped abruptly. NICOTINE is the leading preventable cause of death; nicotine replacement and prescription medicines combined with support multiply quit rates.

sections.heading: Gambling and other behavioural addictions
sections.body: Gambling disorder follows the same pattern as substance addiction — preoccupation, chasing losses, lying about it, and continuing despite serious harm — and carries a particularly high suicide risk. Online betting and gaming make it constantly available. Help includes cognitive behavioural therapy, self-exclusion schemes and bank gambling blocks, debt advice, and support for affected family members. Problematic gaming and other compulsive behaviours are assessed by the same test: loss of control and continued harm, not the number of hours alone.

sections.heading: Treatment, relapse and helping someone
sections.body: Good treatment is non-judgemental and combines medical care, psychological therapy such as motivational interviewing and CBT, treatment of co-existing depression, anxiety, or trauma, and practical help with housing, work, and relationships. RELAPSE is part of the condition, not proof of failure; the response is to re-engage and adjust the plan. Families help most by expressing concern without ultimatums or shaming, setting clear boundaries, learning about the condition, carrying naloxone where relevant, and looking after themselves. In the US the SAMHSA helpline is 1-800-662-4357; in a crisis call 988 or emergency services.

chapters.title: Critical Care & the Intensive Care Unit
chapters.overview: What happens when the body's vital systems fail and need machine and medicine support. Explains the intensive care unit, organ support, sepsis, shock, the monitors and lines at the bedside, and what families should expect and ask.

sections.heading: What intensive care is for
sections.body: Intensive care supports organs that are failing while the underlying illness is treated. People are admitted after major surgery, severe infection, serious injury, breathing failure, or when they need closer watching than a ward can give. The ratio of nurses to patients is high, often one to one, and a team of intensivists, nurses, physiotherapists, pharmacists and dietitians reviews each person every day. Intensive care buys time; it does not cure by itself. Whether it is likely to help a particular person is an honest conversation that should include their own wishes.

sections.heading: Shock and its four types
sections.body: SHOCK means the tissues are not receiving enough oxygen, and it is a medical emergency whatever the blood pressure reading. HYPOVOLAEMIC shock follows loss of blood or fluid. CARDIOGENIC shock is pump failure, as after a large heart attack. DISTRIBUTIVE shock, including sepsis and anaphylaxis, is caused by wide-open blood vessels. OBSTRUCTIVE shock is a blockage such as a large clot in the lung, a collapsed lung under tension, or fluid squeezing the heart. Early signs are a fast pulse, fast breathing, cool mottled skin, confusion and low urine output. Low blood pressure is a late sign.

sections.heading: Sepsis
sections.body: SEPSIS is a life-threatening, out-of-control response to infection that damages the body's own organs. Suspect it when someone with an infection becomes confused, breathes fast, has a racing heart, passes little urine, has mottled or ashen skin, or says they feel they are going to die. Treatment is time-critical: cultures are taken, antibiotics and fluids are given quickly, the source is controlled, and blood pressure is supported with medicines called vasopressors when fluids are not enough. Lactate in the blood is used as a marker of how starved the tissues are. Survivors often need months to recover strength and concentration.

sections.heading: Breathing support
sections.body: Oxygen can be given by simple mask, by high-flow nasal cannulae that deliver warmed humidified gas, or by non-invasive ventilation through a tight-fitting mask. When these are not enough, a tube is placed in the windpipe and a ventilator takes over the work of breathing while the person is sedated. Lung-protective ventilation uses small breaths to avoid further injury. Lying people on their front (proning) can improve oxygen levels in severe lung inflammation. A tracheostomy, a tube through the front of the neck, may be used for people who need many weeks of support.

sections.heading: Monitors, lines and machines
sections.body: The bedside can look frightening, but each device has a plain job. An arterial line measures blood pressure beat by beat and allows blood sampling. A central line in a large vein delivers strong medicines safely. A urinary catheter measures urine output hour by hour, a sensitive guide to kidney blood flow. A feeding tube provides nutrition. Kidney replacement therapy filters the blood when the kidneys stop. Alarms sound often and most do not signal danger; staff are trained to tell which matter. Families are welcome to ask what each line is for.

sections.heading: Delirium, recovery and decisions
sections.body: Delirium, a fluctuating confusion with poor attention, affects many people in intensive care and is reduced by lighter sedation, daylight, sleep, glasses and hearing aids, early movement and familiar voices. After discharge many people have weakness, poor sleep, low mood, memory gaps and frightening false memories; this is called post-intensive care syndrome and it improves with rehabilitation and follow-up. When recovery is not possible, the team should say so plainly and discuss moving the focus to comfort. A person's previously stated wishes and any advance directive guide those decisions.

chapters.title: Prehospital Care: The Paramedic & EMT Handbook
chapters.overview: How emergency medical responders think and work before the hospital: scene safety, the primary survey, triage when there are many casualties, trauma, medical emergencies, moving patients and handing over. Written so a lay rescuer understands what the crew is doing and why.

sections.heading: Scene safety and the first minute
sections.body: Responders are taught that a dead or injured rescuer helps no one. The first step is always to check for danger: traffic, fire, electricity, gas, unstable structures, violence, water and chemicals. Gloves and other protection go on before touching the patient. The crew then forms a general impression from the doorway: is this person sick or not sick, breathing or not, bleeding heavily or not? They count casualties and call for extra help early rather than late. A bystander can help most by making the scene safe, calling the emergency number and giving a clear location.

sections.heading: The primary survey
sections.body: The primary survey finds and fixes what kills first, in order. Catastrophic bleeding is controlled with firm direct pressure or a tourniquet. AIRWAY is opened and cleared. BREATHING is assessed for rate, effort and chest movement. CIRCULATION is checked by pulse, skin colour and temperature. DISABILITY is a quick check of consciousness using Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive, with pupils and blood sugar. EXPOSURE means looking for hidden injuries while keeping the person warm. Each problem is treated as it is found, before moving on. Only then comes the head-to-toe secondary survey and a history.

sections.heading: History taking under pressure
sections.body: Crews use short memory aids to gather a safe history fast. SAMPLE covers Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medicines, Past illnesses, Last food or drink, and Events leading up to the call. For pain, OPQRST asks about Onset, Provocation, Quality, Radiation, Severity and Time. Relatives, medicine boxes, medical alert jewellery and care plans in the home are all sources. Keeping an up-to-date list of medicines and conditions on the fridge door or in a phone's emergency information is one of the most useful things a household can do for a future crew.

sections.heading: Triage at a multiple-casualty incident
sections.body: When casualties outnumber rescuers, the aim changes from doing everything for one person to doing the most good for the most people. Simple triage systems sort people in seconds by whether they can walk, whether they are breathing, their breathing rate, circulation, and whether they can obey a command. The usual categories are immediate (red), delayed (yellow), minor (green) and expectant or dead (black). The walking wounded are directed to a safe area first. Triage is repeated, because people change. It is one of the hardest duties in emergency work.

sections.heading: Trauma principles
sections.body: Serious trauma care before hospital is built on a few rules: stop the bleeding, protect the airway, support breathing, keep the person warm, and get them to the right hospital quickly. Time on scene is kept short for the critically injured. The spine is protected when the mechanism or symptoms suggest injury, but spinal precautions never take priority over airway or bleeding. A broken pelvis or thigh bone can hide litres of blood loss, so binders and splints are applied early. Penetrating objects are left in place and padded. Major trauma centres improve survival for the most severe injuries.

sections.heading: Moving, monitoring and handover
sections.body: Patients are moved with equipment and technique that protect both the patient and the crew's backs. During transport the crew repeats observations, because trends matter more than single readings. At hospital, a structured handover prevents information being lost: who the patient is, what happened, what was found, what was done, and how they responded. A widely used format covers the mechanism or medical complaint, injuries or illness found, signs, and treatment given. The crew will also pass on the medicine list and the name of anyone who came with the patient.

chapters.title: Allergy & Clinical Immunology
chapters.overview: How the immune system protects, and what happens when it over-reacts, attacks the body, or fails. Covers hay fever, food allergy, anaphylaxis, drug allergy, testing, immunotherapy, and immune deficiency.

sections.heading: How immunity works
sections.body: The immune system has two arms. INNATE immunity is fast and general: skin and mucous barriers, white cells that swallow invaders, and inflammation. ADAPTIVE immunity is slower and specific: B cells make antibodies and T cells kill infected cells or direct the response, and both keep a memory so the next encounter is faster. Vaccines train this memory without the disease. Problems arise in three broad ways: the system over-reacts to harmless things (allergy), attacks the body's own tissue (autoimmunity), or is too weak (immunodeficiency).

sections.heading: Allergy, intolerance and sensitisation
sections.body: A true ALLERGY is an immune reaction, most often driven by IgE antibodies that make mast cells release histamine within minutes. Symptoms include hives, swelling, wheeze, vomiting and, at worst, anaphylaxis. An INTOLERANCE, such as lactose intolerance, does not involve the immune system and causes discomfort rather than danger. SENSITISATION means a test is positive but the person has no symptoms on exposure; it is not an allergy. This distinction matters because unnecessary avoidance, especially of foods in children, causes real harm.

sections.heading: Anaphylaxis
sections.body: ANAPHYLAXIS is a severe, rapid allergic reaction affecting the airway, breathing or circulation, usually with skin changes. Signs include throat tightness, a hoarse voice, noisy breathing, wheeze, faintness, collapse, widespread hives and swelling. The treatment is adrenaline (epinephrine) given without delay into the outer thigh from an auto-injector, following the device's own instructions, and an emergency call. The person should lie flat with legs raised, or sit up if breathing is hard, and must not stand suddenly. A second reaction can follow hours later, so hospital observation is needed even after recovery. Antihistamines are not a substitute for adrenaline.

sections.heading: Testing and diagnosis
sections.body: Diagnosis starts with the story: what was eaten or touched, how quickly symptoms began, and whether it happens every time. SKIN-PRICK tests and blood tests for specific IgE support the story but do not replace it, since false positives are common. The most reliable test for food or drug allergy is a supervised CHALLENGE, in which increasing amounts are given in a clinic equipped to treat reactions. Patch tests are used for delayed contact dermatitis, such as nickel or fragrance. Unvalidated tests, including IgG food panels and hair analysis, should be avoided.

sections.heading: Hay fever, food and drug allergy
sections.body: Allergic rhinitis is treated by reducing exposure, non-sedating antihistamines, and steroid nasal sprays used regularly with correct technique. IMMUNOTHERAPY, by injection or under the tongue, retrains the immune system over several years for pollen, dust mite and insect-venom allergy. For food allergy, strict avoidance, clear labelling habits and a written emergency plan remain central, and early introduction of peanut and egg in infancy lowers the chance of allergy developing. Many people labelled penicillin-allergic are not; formal testing can safely remove the label and widen their antibiotic choices.

sections.heading: Immune deficiency and autoimmunity
sections.body: Suspect an immune deficiency when infections are unusually frequent, severe, long-lasting or caused by unusual organisms. Primary deficiencies are inherited; secondary ones follow conditions or treatments such as HIV, chemotherapy, long-term steroids, removal of the spleen, or malnutrition. People without a working spleen need specific vaccines and prompt treatment of fever. Autoimmune diseases, in which the system attacks self, are treated with medicines that damp the response, and those medicines in turn raise infection risk, so vaccination and early review of fever matter.

chapters.title: Vaccines, Screening & Public Health
chapters.overview: Medicine for whole populations: how vaccines work and are tested, how outbreaks are tracked, what screening can and cannot do, and the social conditions that shape health more than any clinic.

sections.heading: How vaccines work
sections.body: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or weakened form of a germ so that memory cells are ready for the real thing. Types include live attenuated vaccines, inactivated vaccines, protein subunit and conjugate vaccines, toxoids, and messenger RNA or viral-vector vaccines that instruct the body's own cells to make a target protein briefly. Some need several doses or boosters to build lasting protection. Live vaccines are generally avoided in pregnancy and in people with severely weakened immunity. The schedule for a given country is set nationally and should be followed from the official source.

sections.heading: Safety, side effects and testing
sections.body: Vaccines are tested in staged trials, first for safety in small groups, then for immune response, then in large trials for protection, and they are monitored after licensing through reporting systems that can detect rare events. Common effects are a sore arm, tiredness, mild fever and aches for a day or two; these are signs of an immune response. Serious allergic reactions are rare and treatable, which is why people wait briefly after vaccination. Large studies in many countries have found no link between vaccines and autism.

sections.heading: Herd immunity and outbreaks
sections.body: When enough people are immune, a germ struggles to find the next person to infect, which protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns and people on chemotherapy. The proportion needed depends on how contagious the disease is, and for measles it is very high. The basic reproduction number describes how many people one case infects in a fully susceptible population. Outbreak control combines finding cases, tracing contacts, isolating the infectious, vaccinating around the outbreak, and clear public information.

sections.heading: Screening: benefits and harms
sections.body: SCREENING looks for disease in people without symptoms. A good programme targets an important condition with a detectable early stage, an acceptable test, and treatment that works better when started early. Every screening test produces FALSE POSITIVES that cause worry and further tests, and FALSE NEGATIVES that falsely reassure. OVERDIAGNOSIS means finding conditions that would never have caused harm. Sensitivity is the share of people with the disease whom the test detects; specificity is the share without it whom the test correctly clears. A screening result is not a diagnosis, and symptoms should never be ignored because a screen was normal.

sections.heading: What really shapes health
sections.body: Income, housing, education, work, food, clean air and water, safety and social connection influence how long and how well people live more than medical care does. These are called the social determinants of health, and they explain much of the gap in life expectancy between neighbourhoods. Prevention is described in levels: PRIMARY prevention stops disease starting, SECONDARY prevention finds it early, and TERTIARY prevention limits its damage. Effective public health measures include clean water, tobacco control, seat belts, vaccination and safe sleeping advice for babies.

sections.heading: Reading numbers about risk
sections.body: INCIDENCE counts new cases over a period; PREVALENCE counts everyone living with a condition at one time. RELATIVE risk compares two groups and can sound dramatic, while ABSOLUTE risk tells you how many people are actually affected. A treatment that halves a risk from two in a thousand to one in a thousand has a relative reduction of fifty percent and an absolute reduction of one in a thousand. The number needed to treat is how many people must take a treatment for one to benefit. Always ask for absolute numbers.

chapters.title: Medical Genetics & Genomics
chapters.overview: How traits and conditions are inherited, what genetic tests can and cannot tell you, family history, cancer genes, prenatal and newborn screening, and the practical and ethical questions that come with knowing.

sections.heading: Genes, chromosomes and variation
sections.body: Each cell nucleus holds about twenty thousand genes written in DNA and packaged into 23 pairs of chromosomes, one of each pair from each parent. A gene is an instruction for making a protein. A VARIANT is a difference in the DNA spelling; most are harmless, some change risk a little, and a few cause disease. Laboratories classify variants as benign, likely benign, of uncertain significance, likely pathogenic, or pathogenic. A variant of uncertain significance is not a diagnosis and should not drive major decisions.

sections.heading: Patterns of inheritance
sections.body: AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT conditions need only one altered copy, so each child of an affected parent has a one-in-two chance; Huntington disease is an example. AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE conditions need two altered copies, one from each carrier parent, giving a one-in-four chance in each pregnancy; cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease are examples. X-LINKED conditions, such as haemophilia, mostly affect males and are carried by females. MITOCHONDRIAL conditions pass through the mother only. Many common illnesses, including diabetes and heart disease, are MULTIFACTORIAL: many genes combine with environment.

sections.heading: Chromosome conditions
sections.body: Some conditions arise from an extra, missing or rearranged chromosome rather than a single gene. Down syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 and its chance rises with maternal age. Turner syndrome involves a single X chromosome, and Klinefelter syndrome an extra X in males. Small missing or duplicated segments, called copy-number variants, are detected by microarray testing and can cause developmental differences. Most chromosome changes arise by chance at conception and are not caused by anything the parents did.

sections.heading: Kinds of genetic test
sections.body: DIAGNOSTIC testing looks for the cause of existing symptoms. PREDICTIVE testing tells a healthy person whether they carry a family variant. CARRIER testing shows whether a couple could have a child with a recessive condition. PHARMACOGENOMIC testing predicts how a person handles certain medicines. Tests range from a single gene to panels, the whole exome, or the whole genome. Direct-to-consumer tests check a limited set of markers, miss most disease-causing variants, and can produce false alarms, so a clinical laboratory should confirm any worrying result.

sections.heading: Inherited cancer risk
sections.body: About one cancer in ten to twenty is linked to an inherited variant. Clues are cancer at a young age, the same or related cancers in several close relatives on one side of the family, more than one primary cancer in a person, and rare cancers such as male breast cancer. Variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2 raise breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer risk; Lynch syndrome raises bowel and womb cancer risk. Knowing allows earlier and more frequent screening, risk-reducing surgery or medicines, and testing of relatives.

sections.heading: Counselling, pregnancy and newborn screening
sections.body: GENETIC COUNSELLING helps people understand a result, its limits, and its meaning for relatives before and after testing. In pregnancy, screening by blood test and ultrasound estimates the chance of certain chromosome conditions; a diagnostic test such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis gives a definite answer with a small risk. NEWBORN SCREENING from a heel-prick blood spot finds treatable conditions before symptoms begin. People should consider who will be affected by a result, how they would feel about uncertain findings, and the insurance and privacy rules where they live.

chapters.title: Pathology & Laboratory Medicine
chapters.overview: The science of how disease changes tissue and how samples are turned into diagnoses: inflammation, healing, cell injury, tumours, biopsies, microbiology and the blood bank. Written so a report from the laboratory can be read with understanding.

sections.heading: How cells are injured and die
sections.body: Cells are injured by lack of oxygen, toxins, infection, immune attack, heat, cold, radiation and genetic faults. Mild injury is reversible. Severe injury leads to NECROSIS, an uncontrolled death that spills cell contents and provokes inflammation, or to APOPTOSIS, an orderly programmed death that does not. Cells also adapt: HYPERTROPHY is an increase in cell size, HYPERPLASIA an increase in number, ATROPHY a shrinking, and METAPLASIA a change from one mature cell type to another, as in the lower gullet exposed to acid.

sections.heading: Inflammation and healing
sections.body: ACUTE inflammation is the rapid response to injury: blood vessels widen and leak, white cells called neutrophils arrive, and the area becomes red, hot, swollen and painful. It usually resolves. CHRONIC inflammation lasts weeks to years, involves lymphocytes and macrophages, and causes scarring. A GRANULOMA is a tight cluster of immune cells walling off something the body cannot clear, seen in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis. Healing occurs by regeneration where cells can divide, and by fibrous scar where they cannot, as in heart muscle.

sections.heading: Tumours: benign and malignant
sections.body: A NEOPLASM is a new growth of cells that no longer obey normal controls. BENIGN tumours grow slowly, stay in one place and usually have a clear edge. MALIGNANT tumours invade neighbouring tissue and can spread to distant sites, which is METASTASIS. DYSPLASIA describes disordered cells that are not yet invasive, and CARCINOMA IN SITU is cancer confined to the layer where it arose. GRADE describes how abnormal the cells look under the microscope; STAGE describes how far the cancer has spread, commonly by tumour size, lymph nodes and metastasis.

sections.heading: From biopsy to report
sections.body: Tissue is fixed in formalin, embedded in wax, sliced thinly, stained and examined by a pathologist. A CYTOLOGY sample looks at loose cells, as in a cervical smear or a fine-needle aspirate; HISTOLOGY looks at intact tissue architecture. Special stains and IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY use antibodies to identify the cell type and markers that guide treatment. A report describes the specimen, the microscopic findings, the diagnosis, and for cancers the margins, which state whether tumour reaches the cut edge. A FROZEN SECTION gives a rapid provisional answer during an operation.

sections.heading: Microbiology
sections.body: Microbiology identifies the organism and the medicines that will work against it. A GRAM STAIN sorts bacteria quickly into two broad groups by cell-wall colour and shape. CULTURE grows the organism over one to several days, and SENSITIVITY testing shows which antibiotics inhibit it. Molecular tests detect genetic material within hours and are used for many viruses. A positive result can reflect contamination or harmless colonisation rather than infection, so results are always read alongside symptoms. Good samples taken before antibiotics start give the most useful answers.

sections.heading: The blood bank
sections.body: Blood is grouped by the ABO system and the Rh(D) factor, and a CROSSMATCH checks donor and recipient compatibility. Group O negative red cells are used in emergencies when the group is unknown. Components are given separately according to need: red cells for oxygen carriage, platelets and plasma for clotting. Transfusion reactions range from mild fever or itch to rare life-threatening incompatibility, so identity is checked at the bedside every time. Wrong blood in the wrong patient is almost always an identification error, which is why staff ask for name and date of birth repeatedly.

chapters.title: Pain Medicine
chapters.overview: Understanding and managing pain as a condition in its own right: how pain signals work, acute versus chronic pain, nerve pain, the place and risks of medicines, and the non-drug approaches with the best evidence.

sections.heading: How pain works
sections.body: Pain is an experience produced by the brain to protect the body, not a simple readout of damage. Signals from nerve endings called nociceptors travel through the spinal cord, where they can be turned up or down, to the brain, which weighs them against memory, mood, attention and threat. This is why the same injury hurts more when a person is frightened, tired or alone. In long-lasting pain the system itself can become over-sensitive, a change called CENTRAL SENSITISATION, so that pain continues after tissues have healed. That pain is real.

sections.heading: Types of pain
sections.body: NOCICEPTIVE pain comes from tissue injury or inflammation, such as a sprain or arthritis, and is usually aching or throbbing. NEUROPATHIC pain comes from damaged or diseased nerves and is described as burning, shooting, electric or pins and needles, often with numbness; sciatica, shingles pain and diabetic neuropathy are examples. NOCIPLASTIC pain arises from altered processing without clear tissue or nerve damage, as in fibromyalgia. ACUTE pain is short and has a clear cause; CHRONIC pain lasts beyond three months. Many people have a mixture.

sections.heading: Assessing pain
sections.body: A good assessment asks where the pain is, what it feels like, what makes it better or worse, how it affects sleep, mood, work and movement, and what the person fears it means. Scores from zero to ten track change in one person but cannot compare people. Function is often a better measure than a number: can the person walk further, sleep longer, return to something they value? RED FLAGS needing urgent review include new weakness, numbness around the saddle area, loss of bladder or bowel control, fever, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, and severe pain after injury.

sections.heading: Medicines: the honest picture
sections.body: Medicines usually reduce pain rather than abolish it, and a realistic aim is a meaningful improvement in function. Simple analgesics and anti-inflammatory medicines suit many acute pains, taken as the label directs. Neuropathic pain responds better to certain antidepressants and anti-seizure medicines than to ordinary painkillers. OPIOIDS are valuable for severe acute pain, cancer pain and end-of-life care, but in long-term non-cancer pain the benefit is small and fades, while risks, including dependence, falls, constipation, hormonal changes and overdose, rise with dose and duration. Any opioid plan needs a clear goal and review date.

sections.heading: What works without medicines
sections.body: For most chronic pain the strongest evidence is for staying active. Graded exercise, physiotherapy, and pacing, which means spreading activity evenly rather than swinging between overdoing and collapse, improve function. Pain education reduces fear and disability. Cognitive behavioural therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy help people live well despite pain. Sleep, weight, mood and social contact all change pain. Heat, TENS machines, acupuncture and manual therapy help some people in the short term. Interventions such as nerve blocks and steroid injections have specific uses and limited duration.

sections.heading: Special situations
sections.body: Children, older adults and people who cannot speak still feel pain and show it through behaviour: guarding, grimacing, withdrawal, agitation or refusing food. Pain after surgery is best managed with a combination of methods so that less of any one medicine is needed. Complex regional pain syndrome is severe, disproportionate limb pain with colour, temperature and swelling changes after an injury, and early physiotherapy improves outcome. People with a history of addiction deserve pain treatment too, planned openly with one prescriber and close follow-up.

chapters.title: Wound Care & Tissue Viability
chapters.overview: Practical care of cuts, grazes, burns, surgical wounds, pressure injuries and leg ulcers: how wounds heal, how to clean and dress them, when to close them, and how to recognise infection and poor healing.

sections.heading: How a wound heals
sections.body: Healing runs through overlapping phases. HAEMOSTASIS stops the bleeding within minutes. INFLAMMATION clears debris and bacteria over the first few days, causing normal redness, warmth and swelling at the edges. PROLIFERATION fills the gap with new granulation tissue, which is red and bumpy, and new skin grows in from the edges. REMODELLING strengthens the scar for a year or more, though it never regains full original strength. Healing by primary intention means the edges are brought together; secondary intention means the wound fills from the base.

sections.heading: Cleaning and closing
sections.body: Press firmly with a clean cloth to stop bleeding. Rinse the wound thoroughly with clean running water; this matters more than any antiseptic. Remove loose dirt, pat dry, and cover with a non-stick dressing. Wounds that gape, are deep, are on the face or over a joint, or keep bleeding need professional closure with stitches, glue or strips, ideally within hours. Animal and human bites, deep punctures and heavily contaminated wounds are often left open because closing them traps infection. Check that tetanus vaccination is up to date.

sections.heading: Choosing a dressing
sections.body: A wound heals faster in a moist, clean environment than when left to dry and scab. The dressing is matched to the wound: films for shallow dry wounds, hydrocolloids to keep moisture in, foams and alginates to absorb fluid from wet wounds, hydrogels to soften dry dead tissue, and non-adherent layers to prevent sticking. Dressings are changed when they leak, slip or smell, not on a fixed daily habit. Surrounding skin is protected from becoming soggy. Negative-pressure therapy uses gentle suction through a sealed foam to help large or complex wounds.

sections.heading: Infection and delayed healing
sections.body: Signs of infection are spreading redness, increasing pain, swelling, warmth, pus, a bad smell and fever. A red streak tracking up a limb, a rapidly spreading area, severe pain out of proportion, or feeling very unwell needs urgent care. Healing is slowed by poor blood supply, diabetes, smoking, malnutrition, swelling, pressure, steroid medicines and dead tissue in the wound. DEBRIDEMENT removes dead tissue so healthy tissue can grow. A wound that has not improved in several weeks should be reassessed for an underlying cause.

sections.heading: Pressure injuries
sections.body: Pressure injuries develop where bone presses skin against a surface for too long, most often at the sacrum, heels, hips and elbows, in people who cannot move or feel well. They are staged from unbroken skin with redness that does not fade on pressing, through partial and full skin loss, to deep wounds exposing muscle or bone. Prevention is regular repositioning, pressure-relieving mattresses and cushions, keeping skin clean and dry, good nutrition and daily skin checks. Heels should be floated free of the bed. Most pressure injuries are preventable.

sections.heading: Leg and foot ulcers
sections.body: VENOUS ulcers, the commonest leg ulcers, sit around the inner ankle with swelling and brown skin staining, and heal with compression bandaging once the arterial supply has been checked. ARTERIAL ulcers are painful, punched-out wounds on the toes or foot with cold pale skin and weak pulses, and need a vascular opinion; compression can harm them. DIABETIC foot ulcers occur at pressure points on numb feet and can worsen quickly; they need offloading, infection control and urgent specialist foot-team review. Any ulcer that fails to heal may need a biopsy.

chapters.title: Sports & Exercise Medicine
chapters.overview: Using movement as medicine and looking after active bodies: exercise prescription, training principles, common sports injuries, concussion, heat and hydration, and the medical issues of athletes at every level.

sections.heading: Exercise as medicine
sections.body: Regular physical activity lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, depression, dementia and early death, and the biggest gain comes from moving from nothing to something. General public-health guidance for adults is about 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous aerobic activity a week, plus muscle strengthening on two days, and balance work for older adults. Moderate means you can talk but not sing. Activity can be built from short bouts. People with chest pain on exertion, fainting, or unexplained breathlessness should be assessed first.

sections.heading: Training principles
sections.body: Fitness improves through PROGRESSIVE OVERLOAD: asking the body to do slightly more than it is used to, then allowing recovery so it adapts. SPECIFICITY means the body adapts to exactly what it practises. Gains reverse when training stops. Most overuse injuries follow a sudden jump in volume or intensity, so load is increased gradually and hard days are balanced with easy ones. Sleep, enough energy intake and rest days are part of training, not a break from it. Strength training protects joints, bones and tendons at every age.

sections.heading: Sprains, strains and tendon problems
sections.body: A SPRAIN is a ligament injury; a STRAIN is a muscle or tendon injury. Early care is protection, relative rest, compression, elevation and ice for comfort, followed quickly by gentle movement and progressive loading, since prolonged rest delays recovery. Inability to bear weight, deformity, bony tenderness, a joint that gives way or locks, or numbness needs assessment for fracture or structural damage. TENDINOPATHY is a painful overloaded tendon, as at the Achilles or elbow, and responds best to a structured programme of progressive strengthening over weeks to months.

sections.heading: Concussion
sections.body: Concussion is a brain injury caused by a blow or jolt, with or without loss of consciousness. Symptoms include headache, dizziness, confusion, memory gaps, nausea, sensitivity to light and noise, and feeling slowed or foggy. Anyone suspected of concussion is removed from play that day: if in doubt, sit them out. After a short period of relative rest, activity is increased in stages only while symptoms stay settled, with return to learning before return to sport. Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, increasing drowsiness, weakness or unequal pupils is an emergency.

sections.heading: Heat, hydration and collapse
sections.body: Exertional heat illness ranges from cramps and exhaustion to HEAT STROKE, in which the core temperature is dangerously high and the person is confused or collapses. Heat stroke is treated by rapid cooling, ideally cold-water immersion, started at once: cool first, transport second. Drinking to thirst is adequate for most activity; drinking far more water than is lost can dangerously dilute blood sodium, causing headache, vomiting and confusion in endurance events. A collapsed athlete who is unresponsive and not breathing normally needs CPR and a defibrillator immediately.

sections.heading: Athlete health
sections.body: Relative energy deficiency in sport occurs when energy intake does not cover training, causing fatigue, stress fractures, low mood, frequent illness and, in women, missed periods; it affects all sexes. Screening for inherited heart conditions is considered where there is fainting on exertion, chest pain, or a family history of sudden death under fifty. Supplements are loosely regulated and can be contaminated with banned or harmful substances. Children are not small adults: growth plates are vulnerable, and early specialisation in a single sport raises injury and burnout risk.
