chapters.title: Podiatry & Foot Health
chapters.overview: Care of the feet and lower limbs: structure and gait, skin and nail problems, heel and forefoot pain, the diabetic foot, footwear and when a foot problem signals disease elsewhere.

sections.heading: Foot structure and walking
sections.body: Each foot has 26 bones, more than 30 joints, and arches held by ligaments, tendons and the plantar fascia, a strong band under the sole. In walking, the heel strikes, the foot rolls inward slightly to absorb shock, which is PRONATION, then stiffens and rolls outward, which is SUPINATION, to push off through the big toe. Flat feet and high arches are normal variations and need treatment only when they cause pain or problems. Pain that changes how a person walks often produces secondary pain in the knee, hip or back.

sections.heading: Skin and nail problems
sections.body: CORNS and CALLUS are thickened skin from pressure or friction; treatment is removing the cause with better-fitting shoes and padding, and careful reduction by a podiatrist. VERRUCAE are viral warts on the sole that often clear by themselves. ATHLETE'S FOOT is a fungal infection causing itching and peeling between the toes, treated with antifungal preparations and dry feet. Fungal nails are thick, discoloured and crumbly. An INGROWN TOENAIL is prevented by cutting nails straight across and may need a minor procedure under local anaesthetic if it recurs.

sections.heading: Heel and arch pain
sections.body: PLANTAR FASCIITIS causes sharp pain under the heel that is worst with the first steps in the morning or after sitting. It usually settles over months with calf and plantar fascia stretching, supportive cushioned shoes, heel inserts, and avoiding barefoot walking on hard floors. Achilles tendon pain at the back of the heel responds to progressive calf strengthening. A sudden snap at the back of the ankle with difficulty rising onto the toes suggests a ruptured Achilles tendon and needs same-day assessment. Heel pain in active children is often a growth-plate irritation.

sections.heading: Forefoot and toe problems
sections.body: A BUNION is a bony prominence at the base of the big toe as the toe drifts outward; wide shoes and padding ease symptoms, and surgery is for persistent pain rather than appearance. A MORTON'S NEUROMA is a thickened nerve between the toes giving burning pain or a pebble-in-the-shoe sensation. HAMMER TOES are bent smaller toes that rub. METATARSALGIA is pain under the ball of the foot. A hot, red, exquisitely tender big-toe joint coming on overnight suggests gout. A stress fracture causes focal bone pain that worsens with activity.

sections.heading: The diabetic and at-risk foot
sections.body: Diabetes can damage the nerves, so injuries go unfelt, and the arteries, so wounds heal poorly. People at risk should check their feet every day, including between the toes and the soles using a mirror, wear well-fitting shoes and never walk barefoot, test bath water with an elbow, and avoid corn plasters and sharp instruments. An annual foot check tests sensation and pulses. Any break in the skin, new swelling, redness, warmth or colour change needs review within a day. A hot swollen numb foot without a wound may be a Charcot foot, which is an emergency.

sections.heading: Footwear, orthoses and circulation
sections.body: A good shoe has room for the toes to spread, a firm heel counter, a fastening that holds the foot back, and a sole that bends at the ball of the foot, not the middle. Feet should be measured standing, later in the day. ORTHOSES are inserts that redistribute pressure or support the arch; simple ready-made ones work as well as custom devices for many problems. Calf pain on walking that eases with rest, cold pale feet, hair loss on the shins, or wounds that will not heal point to poor arterial circulation and need medical assessment.

chapters.title: Audiology & Speech-Language Therapy
chapters.overview: Hearing, balance, voice, speech, language and swallowing: how they are tested, what goes wrong at each age, hearing aids and implants, and the therapy that restores communication and safe eating.

sections.heading: How hearing is tested
sections.body: Sound passes through the ear canal, vibrates the eardrum and three tiny bones, and is turned into nerve signals in the cochlea. CONDUCTIVE hearing loss is a block in that mechanical chain, such as wax, fluid or a perforated drum. SENSORINEURAL loss is damage to the cochlea or nerve, as with ageing or noise. A pure-tone AUDIOGRAM charts the quietest sound heard at each pitch in each ear. TYMPANOMETRY measures eardrum movement and detects middle-ear fluid. Newborns are screened with automated tests that need no response from the baby.

sections.heading: Hearing loss through life
sections.body: In children, glue ear is the commonest cause of reduced hearing and usually clears, but persistent loss delays speech and learning. In adults, noise exposure causes permanent damage that is entirely preventable with ear protection. Age-related loss affects high pitches first, so speech sounds muffled and is hard to follow in background noise. Untreated hearing loss is linked with isolation, low mood, falls and faster cognitive decline. SUDDEN hearing loss in one ear over hours to days is an emergency, because early treatment improves the chance of recovery.

sections.heading: Hearing aids and implants
sections.body: Modern hearing aids are small digital amplifiers programmed to a person's audiogram; they help most with speech and take weeks of regular wear for the brain to adjust. Features include directional microphones, noise reduction, and wireless streaming from phones. A COCHLEAR IMPLANT bypasses a damaged cochlea by stimulating the hearing nerve directly, for severe to profound loss that hearing aids cannot help. Bone-conduction devices send sound through the skull. Communication tactics matter as much as devices: face the person, speak clearly without shouting, and reduce background noise.

sections.heading: Tinnitus and balance
sections.body: TINNITUS is the perception of sound, such as ringing or hissing, with no external source. It is common, usually accompanies hearing loss, and tends to become less intrusive as the brain learns to ignore it; sound enrichment, hearing aids and cognitive behavioural therapy help. Tinnitus that pulses with the heartbeat, or is in one ear only, should be investigated. The inner ear also houses the balance organs. Audiologists assess dizziness with tests of eye movement and head position, and vestibular rehabilitation exercises retrain balance after inner-ear disorders.

sections.heading: Speech, language and voice
sections.body: SPEECH is the physical production of sounds; LANGUAGE is understanding and using words and grammar. Children vary, but no babbling by twelve months, no single words by about eighteen months, no two-word phrases by two years, or loss of skills at any age warrants assessment, starting with a hearing test. STAMMERING is an interruption of the flow of speech and responds to early therapy. After stroke, APHASIA impairs language while intelligence is intact, and DYSARTHRIA is slurred speech from weak muscles. Hoarseness lasting more than three weeks needs examination of the voice box.

sections.heading: Swallowing problems
sections.body: DYSPHAGIA is difficulty swallowing, common after stroke, in Parkinson's disease, dementia, motor neurone disease and after head and neck cancer treatment. Signs include coughing or choking on food or drink, a wet gurgly voice after swallowing, food sticking, recurrent chest infections and weight loss. Material entering the airway is ASPIRATION and can cause pneumonia. Speech-language therapists assess swallowing at the bedside and with video X-ray or camera studies, then advise on posture, swallowing techniques and texture changes. Sitting upright, small mouthfuls and good mouth care lower risk.

chapters.title: Occupational Therapy & Rehabilitation Medicine
chapters.overview: Getting people back to the activities that make up a life after illness or injury: daily living skills, equipment and home adaptation, hand therapy, rehabilitation after stroke, brain and spinal injury, amputation, and return to work.

sections.heading: What occupational therapy does
sections.body: Occupation means everything a person needs or wants to do: washing, dressing, cooking, working, parenting, hobbies. Occupational therapists analyse where an activity breaks down, whether through weakness, pain, poor memory, low mood or an unsuitable environment, and then restore the skill, teach a new method, or change the task and surroundings. The focus is the person's own goals. ACTIVITIES OF DAILY LIVING are basic self-care; INSTRUMENTAL activities are the more complex tasks of independent life such as shopping, managing money and medicines, and using transport.

sections.heading: Equipment and home adaptation
sections.body: Small changes prevent falls and preserve independence: grab rails by the toilet and bath, a raised toilet seat, a shower chair, a second stair rail, good lighting, removal of loose rugs, and frequently used items stored between hip and shoulder height. Long-handled reachers, sock aids, kettle tippers and adapted cutlery reduce strain. Wheelchairs and seating are prescribed to fit the person's body and prevent pressure injury. Larger adaptations include ramps, stairlifts and level-access showers. A home assessment before hospital discharge identifies what is needed for a safe return.

sections.heading: Principles of rehabilitation
sections.body: Rehabilitation is an active, goal-directed process delivered by a team that may include doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech-language therapists, psychologists and social workers. Goals are specific, measurable and agreed with the person. The brain and body adapt most to practice that is frequent, task-specific and challenging, a property called NEUROPLASTICITY. Recovery is fastest in the first months but can continue for years. Rehabilitation starts early, in the acute hospital bed, because immobility itself causes muscle loss, stiffness, clots, pressure injuries and loss of confidence.

sections.heading: After stroke, brain and spinal cord injury
sections.body: After STROKE, therapy addresses weakness, balance, neglect of one side, vision, speech, swallowing, mood and fatigue, and survivors are taught to protect a weak shoulder and limb. After TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY, the hidden problems of memory, attention, planning, irritability and fatigue often limit return to work more than physical changes. SPINAL CORD INJURY is described by its level and completeness; rehabilitation covers mobility, skin care, bladder and bowel management, and recognition of autonomic dysreflexia, a dangerous surge in blood pressure in higher injuries triggered by something like a blocked catheter.

sections.heading: Hand therapy, amputation and prosthetics
sections.body: Hand therapists treat injuries, surgery and arthritis with custom splints, graded exercise, scar management and swelling control, and timing matters after tendon repair. Joint protection in arthritis means using larger joints, spreading loads and avoiding tight sustained grips. After AMPUTATION, rehabilitation covers wound healing, shaping the residual limb, managing phantom limb sensation and pain, and prosthetic fitting and training. A prosthesis demands extra energy to use, so fitness matters. Peer support from another person living with limb loss is consistently valued.

sections.heading: Fatigue, cognition and return to work
sections.body: FATIGUE MANAGEMENT teaches pacing, planning and prioritising: spreading demanding tasks across the week, building in rest before exhaustion, and simplifying jobs. Cognitive rehabilitation uses routines, diaries, phone reminders and a single place for important objects to compensate for memory and attention problems. Return to work succeeds more often when it is graded, starting with reduced hours or duties and building up, with adjustments agreed with the employer. Driving after illness or injury may require notifying the licensing authority and a formal assessment.

chapters.title: Clinical Psychology & the Talking Therapies
chapters.overview: How psychological therapies work, which therapy suits which problem, what happens in a session, and the self-help skills with good evidence. A companion to the psychiatry chapter, focused on therapy rather than medicines.

sections.heading: How therapy helps
sections.body: Psychological therapy is a structured collaboration to understand and change patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving that keep distress going. Across all types, the quality of the working relationship between person and therapist, called the THERAPEUTIC ALLIANCE, strongly predicts improvement. A FORMULATION is a shared map of how a person's difficulties developed and what maintains them, built from predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors. Therapy is not advice-giving; it teaches skills and understanding that the person continues to use. Feeling somewhat worse before better can happen as difficult material is faced.

sections.heading: Cognitive behavioural therapy
sections.body: CBT rests on the link between thoughts, feelings, body sensations and actions. It is practical, focused on the present, and uses work between sessions. Core methods include noticing and testing unhelpful thoughts, BEHAVIOURAL ACTIVATION, which schedules meaningful activity to lift depression, and graded EXPOSURE, which approaches feared situations step by step until the fear subsides. EXPOSURE AND RESPONSE PREVENTION is the specific form for obsessive-compulsive disorder. CBT has strong evidence for depression, anxiety disorders, panic, phobias, insomnia, eating disorders and chronic pain.

sections.heading: DBT, ACT and mindfulness-based therapy
sections.body: DIALECTICAL BEHAVIOUR THERAPY teaches four skill sets, mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, and was developed for people with intense emotions and self-harm. ACCEPTANCE AND COMMITMENT THERAPY aims to change a person's relationship with painful thoughts and feelings rather than their content, and to act on personal values. MINDFULNESS-BASED COGNITIVE THERAPY combines meditation practice with cognitive methods to reduce relapse in recurrent depression. COMPASSION-FOCUSED therapy targets shame and harsh self-criticism.

sections.heading: Trauma-focused and relational therapies
sections.body: For post-traumatic stress disorder, TRAUMA-FOCUSED CBT and EYE MOVEMENT DESENSITISATION AND REPROCESSING help the brain process a memory so it is recalled as past rather than relived. Stabilisation and safety come first. PSYCHODYNAMIC therapy explores how early relationships and unconscious patterns shape present difficulties. INTERPERSONAL therapy treats depression by working on grief, role changes, disputes and isolation. FAMILY and couple therapies treat the pattern between people, and are first-line for eating disorders in young people. SCHEMA therapy addresses deep, long-standing life patterns.

sections.heading: Psychological assessment
sections.body: Psychologists use interviews, observation and standardised tests. Questionnaires track the severity of symptoms over time. NEUROPSYCHOLOGICAL testing measures memory, attention, language, reasoning and executive function to clarify the effects of brain injury, dementia or developmental conditions. Assessment for autism and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder draws on developmental history, observation and reports from more than one setting. A RISK ASSESSMENT asks directly about thoughts of suicide and self-harm; asking does not plant the idea, and leads to a shared SAFETY PLAN.

sections.heading: Skills you can use today
sections.body: Slow breathing, with a longer out-breath than in-breath, calms the body's alarm system. GROUNDING brings attention to the present through the senses, for example naming five things you can see. Scheduling one small valued activity each day counters withdrawal. Writing a worry down and setting a fixed time to think about it reduces rumination. Regular sleep, movement, daylight and contact with others are treatments, not extras. If thoughts of ending your life are present, contact a crisis line such as 988 in the United States and Canada, or emergency services, now.

chapters.title: Men's Health & Andrology
chapters.overview: Conditions that affect men or affect them differently: prostate, testicular and penile problems, testosterone, fertility, sexual function, and why men present late and how to change that.

sections.heading: The prostate
sections.body: The prostate sits below the bladder around the urethra. BENIGN PROSTATIC ENLARGEMENT with age causes a weak stream, hesitancy, dribbling, frequency and getting up at night; it is treated with fluid and caffeine adjustment, medicines that relax or shrink the gland, or procedures. PROSTATITIS causes pelvic pain and urinary symptoms, sometimes with fever. PROSTATE CANCER is common and often slow-growing. The PSA blood test can detect it early but also rises with enlargement, infection and recent ejaculation, so testing is a shared decision that weighs possible overdiagnosis. Inability to pass urine at all is an emergency.

sections.heading: Testicles and scrotum
sections.body: Sudden severe testicular pain, often with nausea and a high-riding testicle, is TORSION until proven otherwise: the testicle has twisted on its blood supply and must be untwisted surgically within hours to be saved. EPIDIDYMITIS is a more gradual painful swelling, usually from infection. A VARICOCELE feels like a bag of worms above the testicle; a HYDROCELE is a painless fluid collection. TESTICULAR CANCER mostly affects men aged fifteen to forty-five, presents as a painless hard lump within the testicle, and is highly curable. A monthly self-check after a warm shower finds changes early.

sections.heading: Penile and foreskin problems
sections.body: PHIMOSIS is a foreskin too tight to retract; PARAPHIMOSIS is a retracted foreskin stuck behind the glans causing swelling, which is an emergency. BALANITIS is inflammation of the glans, often from yeast, irritation or diabetes. PEYRONIE'S disease is a scar plaque that bends the erect penis. An erection lasting more than four hours, PRIAPISM, is an emergency that can cause permanent damage. Any persistent sore, lump or colour change on the penis should be examined, since penile cancer, though uncommon, is treatable when found early.

sections.heading: Erectile and ejaculatory problems
sections.body: Erectile dysfunction is common and frequently has a physical cause. Because the arteries of the penis are small, it can be an early warning of heart and blood-vessel disease years before chest symptoms, so blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol should be checked. Other causes include diabetes, medicines, alcohol, smoking, low testosterone, pelvic surgery, anxiety and depression. Treatments include lifestyle change, tablets taken as prescribed, vacuum devices, injections and implants. Premature ejaculation responds to behavioural techniques, counselling and medicines.

sections.heading: Testosterone and fertility
sections.body: Low testosterone is diagnosed only when consistent symptoms, such as low libido, loss of morning erections, fatigue and reduced muscle, occur together with repeated low morning blood levels. Replacement can help confirmed deficiency but suppresses sperm production and requires monitoring, so it is unsuitable for men trying to conceive. Anabolic steroid use shrinks the testicles and impairs fertility. Male factors contribute to about half of couples' fertility difficulties; a SEMEN ANALYSIS is the first test. Heat, smoking, heavy alcohol, obesity and some medicines reduce sperm quality.

sections.heading: Why men present late
sections.body: Men on average see clinicians less often, attend later in an illness, and die younger, with higher rates of heart disease, injury and suicide. Barriers include the belief that seeking help is weakness, work patterns, and services that feel unwelcoming. Useful rules: a symptom lasting more than three weeks deserves a check; blood in the urine, stool or semen is never normal; chest pain on exertion should not be ignored; and persistent low mood, irritability, heavy drinking or risk-taking can be depression. Talking to someone is a strength.

chapters.title: Menopause & Women's Midlife Health
chapters.overview: The transition through perimenopause and beyond: what changes and why, symptoms, hormone therapy and its real risks and benefits, non-hormonal options, bone and heart health, and bleeding that needs investigation.

sections.heading: Perimenopause and menopause
sections.body: MENOPAUSE is defined as twelve months without a period and occurs on average around age fifty-one. PERIMENOPAUSE is the years before it, when ovarian hormone levels swing unpredictably and periods become irregular, heavier or lighter. Pregnancy remains possible until menopause is confirmed, so contraception is still needed. Menopause before forty is PREMATURE OVARIAN INSUFFICIENCY and needs hormone replacement to protect bones and heart unless there is a reason not to. Surgical removal of both ovaries causes an immediate menopause with often abrupt symptoms.

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.body: Hot flushes and night sweats, the VASOMOTOR symptoms, affect most women and last on average several years. Others include sleep disturbance, low mood, anxiety, irritability, difficulty concentrating, joint aches, palpitations, reduced libido, and weight shifting to the waist. GENITOURINARY SYNDROME OF MENOPAUSE is vaginal dryness, soreness, painful sex and urinary urgency or infections caused by falling oestrogen; unlike flushes it tends to worsen over time rather than fade. For women over forty-five, the diagnosis is made on symptoms and blood tests are usually unnecessary.

sections.heading: Hormone therapy: benefits and risks
sections.body: Menopausal hormone therapy replaces OESTROGEN and is the most effective treatment for flushes and sweats; it also protects bone. A woman who still has her womb must also take a PROGESTOGEN to protect its lining from overgrowth and cancer. Oestrogen through the skin, as patch, gel or spray, does not raise the risk of blood clots in the way tablets do. Combined therapy is associated with a small increase in breast cancer risk that grows with duration and falls after stopping. For most healthy women under sixty or within ten years of menopause, benefits outweigh risks. The decision is individual and reviewed regularly.

sections.heading: Non-hormonal and local treatments
sections.body: Low-dose VAGINAL OESTROGEN treats dryness and urinary symptoms with minimal absorption and can be used long term; moisturisers and lubricants help too. For flushes in women who cannot or prefer not to use hormones, certain non-hormonal prescription medicines, and cognitive behavioural therapy, reduce symptoms. Cooling strategies, layered clothing, less alcohol and caffeine, and stopping smoking help some. Evidence for herbal products is weak and their quality varies; some interact with medicines. Compounded 'bioidentical' hormone preparations are not better or safer than regulated products.

sections.heading: Bones, heart and long-term health
sections.body: Falling oestrogen speeds bone loss, raising the risk of OSTEOPOROSIS and fracture. Protection comes from weight-bearing and resistance exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D, not smoking, limited alcohol, and bone-density scanning for those at higher risk. Cardiovascular risk rises after menopause, so blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar and weight deserve attention in midlife. Pelvic-floor muscle training treats stress incontinence and mild prolapse. Midlife is also when cervical, breast and bowel screening invitations should be taken up.

sections.heading: Bleeding that must be checked
sections.body: Any vaginal bleeding after menopause, meaning more than twelve months after the last period, must be investigated promptly to exclude cancer of the womb lining, even if it is a single episode of spotting; an ultrasound to measure the lining and sometimes a biopsy are the usual tests. Before menopause, bleeding between periods, after sex, or very heavy or prolonged periods also deserve assessment. Persistent bloating, feeling full quickly, pelvic pain and needing to pass urine more often can be signs of ovarian cancer and should not be put down to the menopause.

chapters.title: Gender-Affirming Care & LGBTQ+ Health
chapters.overview: Respectful, evidence-informed care for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and gender-diverse people: language, the components of gender-affirming care, screening by anatomy, sexual health, and mental health and safety.

sections.heading: Language and respectful care
sections.body: SEX ASSIGNED AT BIRTH is recorded from a baby's body; GENDER IDENTITY is a person's own sense of their gender; SEXUAL ORIENTATION is whom a person is attracted to. These are separate. TRANSGENDER describes people whose gender differs from the sex assigned at birth; CISGENDER describes those for whom they match; NON-BINARY people do not identify simply as male or female. Good care uses the name and pronouns a person asks for, asks only questions relevant to the problem, and keeps records accurate. Fear of poor treatment causes many people to delay care.

sections.heading: What gender-affirming care includes
sections.body: Gender-affirming care is a range of support, not a single pathway, and each person chooses which parts, if any, are right for them. SOCIAL transition involves name, pronouns, clothing and presentation. Psychological support helps with exploration and with distress. Medical options include hormone therapy and, for some, surgery. Voice therapy and hair removal are important to many. GENDER DYSPHORIA is the distress that can arise from a mismatch between body or social role and identity. Care for people under eighteen follows separate, more cautious protocols that vary between jurisdictions.

sections.heading: Hormone therapy
sections.body: Feminising therapy uses oestrogen, usually with a medicine that lowers testosterone, producing breast growth, softer skin, redistribution of fat and reduced muscle over months to years. Masculinising therapy uses testosterone, producing a deeper voice, facial and body hair, increased muscle and cessation of periods. Some changes are permanent. Risks include blood clots with oestrogen and a raised red-cell count with testosterone, so blood tests and blood pressure are monitored. Hormones reduce fertility, so preservation of eggs or sperm is discussed beforehand. Testosterone is not a contraceptive. Hormones obtained without supervision carry added risk.

sections.heading: Surgery
sections.body: Surgical options include chest reconstruction or breast augmentation, removal of the womb, ovaries or testes, genital reconstruction such as vaginoplasty, metoidioplasty or phalloplasty, and facial and voice procedures. Not everyone wants surgery. Major genital surgery is performed in specialist centres, often in stages, and carries risks including bleeding, infection, narrowing or fistula of the urinary tract, and loss of sensation. After vaginoplasty, regular dilation is needed to keep depth. Recovery takes weeks to months, and long-term follow-up with a team that knows the procedures improves outcomes.

sections.heading: Screening by anatomy
sections.body: Screening follows the organs a person has, not the gender marker on a record. Anyone with a cervix needs cervical screening, and may need to request it if registered as male. Anyone with breast tissue, including trans women on long-term oestrogen, needs breast screening on the usual schedule. Trans women retain a prostate after surgery. Clinicians should explain why an examination is needed and offer choices that reduce distress, such as self-taken swabs. Bone health deserves attention when sex hormones are low for long periods.

sections.heading: Sexual health, mental health and safety
sections.body: Sexual health advice should be based on actual practices and anatomy, with access to testing, vaccination against hepatitis A and B and HPV, and HIV prevention. Rates of anxiety, depression, self-harm and suicidal thoughts are higher among LGBTQ+ people, driven by stigma, rejection and discrimination rather than by identity itself; family acceptance is strongly protective. So-called conversion practices are harmful and are banned in a growing number of places. Anyone in crisis can contact a helpline such as 988 or local emergency services.

chapters.title: Vascular Medicine & Surgery
chapters.overview: Diseases of the arteries, veins and lymphatics outside the heart: peripheral arterial disease, aneurysms, carotid disease, deep vein thrombosis, varicose veins, lymphoedema, and the limb- and life-threatening emergencies.

sections.heading: Peripheral arterial disease
sections.body: Narrowing of the leg arteries by atherosclerosis causes INTERMITTENT CLAUDICATION: cramping calf, thigh or buttock pain that comes on with walking and eases within minutes of rest. It marks disease throughout the body, so the main danger is heart attack and stroke. Treatment is stopping smoking, supervised walking exercise, and medicines to lower cholesterol, blood pressure and clotting risk. The ANKLE-BRACHIAL PRESSURE INDEX compares ankle and arm blood pressure to confirm the diagnosis. Pain at rest, especially at night and eased by hanging the foot down, ulcers or gangrene indicate critical ischaemia needing urgent revascularisation.

sections.heading: The acutely ischaemic limb
sections.body: A sudden blockage of a limb artery, by a clot that has travelled or formed on a narrowed vessel, threatens the limb within hours. The classic features are the six Ps: PAIN, PALLOR, PULSELESSNESS, PERISHING COLD, PARAESTHESIA (pins and needles or numbness) and PARALYSIS. Loss of sensation and movement are late signs. This is a surgical emergency: call for help at once and do not wait to see if it improves. Treatment is urgent blood thinning and removal or bypass of the blockage. Afterwards the limb is watched for dangerous swelling within its muscle compartments.

sections.heading: Aneurysms
sections.body: An ANEURYSM is a ballooning of an artery wall. The ABDOMINAL AORTIC ANEURYSM is the most important; it usually causes no symptoms until it leaks. Risk rises with age, male sex, smoking, high blood pressure and family history, and some countries offer a one-off ultrasound screen to older men. Small aneurysms are monitored; larger ones are repaired by open surgery or by a stent-graft placed through the groin arteries. Sudden severe abdominal, back or flank pain with collapse in an older person is a ruptured aneurysm until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: Carotid disease and stroke prevention
sections.body: Plaque in the carotid arteries of the neck can shed fragments to the brain. A TRANSIENT ISCHAEMIC ATTACK is a brief episode of weakness, speech disturbance or loss of vision in one eye that resolves completely; it is a warning that a stroke may follow within days and needs same-day assessment. When a symptomatic carotid artery is severely narrowed, CAROTID ENDARTERECTOMY to remove the plaque, done promptly, reduces stroke risk. Everyone with carotid disease benefits from antiplatelet and cholesterol-lowering treatment and blood-pressure control.

sections.heading: Veins: clots and varicose veins
sections.body: A DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS is a clot in a deep leg vein causing swelling, pain, warmth and redness of one calf or thigh; a piece can travel to the lungs as a PULMONARY EMBOLISM, causing sudden breathlessness, chest pain or collapse. Risks include immobility, surgery, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogen-containing medicines and long journeys. Diagnosis is by ultrasound and treatment is anticoagulation. VARICOSE VEINS are enlarged surface veins from failed valves; they cause aching and swelling and, in time, skin changes and ulcers. Treatments include compression and heat or foam closure.

sections.heading: Lymphoedema and vasospasm
sections.body: LYMPHOEDEMA is swelling from failure of lymph drainage, either inherited or after surgery, radiotherapy, infection or cancer. The skin thickens and the swelling does not fully pit. Management is lifelong compression garments, skin care, exercise, and specialised massage; cellulitis must be treated promptly because each episode worsens drainage. RAYNAUD'S phenomenon is spasm of small arteries in the fingers and toes on cold exposure, which turn white, then blue, then red. It is usually harmless, but onset in later life or with ulcers suggests an underlying connective tissue disease.

chapters.title: Environmental & Wilderness Medicine
chapters.overview: Illness and injury caused by the physical environment: heat, cold, altitude, water, lightning, bites and stings, air pollution, and how to prepare for emergencies far from help.

sections.heading: Heat illness
sections.body: Heat illness is a spectrum. HEAT EXHAUSTION brings heavy sweating, weakness, headache, nausea and a fast pulse; the person should rest in a cool place, loosen clothing, and sip fluids. HEAT STROKE is a life-threatening failure of temperature control with a very high body temperature and confusion, seizures or collapse; skin may be hot and dry or still sweating. Call emergency services and cool the person immediately by any means: cold-water immersion if possible, otherwise wet skin with fanning and ice packs to neck, armpits and groin. Older adults, infants, outdoor workers and people on certain medicines are most at risk.

sections.heading: Hypothermia and frostbite
sections.body: HYPOTHERMIA is a core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius. Shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech and confusion come first; as it deepens, shivering stops, consciousness fades and the heart becomes unstable. Move the person gently to shelter, remove wet clothing, insulate from the ground, cover the head, and give warm sweet drinks if fully alert. Handle a severely cold person very carefully, since rough movement can trigger a fatal heart rhythm. FROSTBITE is frozen tissue, white, hard and numb; rewarm in warm, not hot, water only when there is no risk of refreezing, and do not rub.

sections.heading: Altitude illness
sections.body: Above about 2,500 metres, the lower oxygen pressure can cause ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS: headache with nausea, fatigue, dizziness and poor sleep. The rules are to ascend gradually, never climb higher with symptoms, and descend if symptoms worsen. Two severe forms kill: HIGH-ALTITUDE CEREBRAL OEDEMA, with unsteadiness, confusion and drowsiness, and HIGH-ALTITUDE PULMONARY OEDEMA, with breathlessness at rest, cough and frothy sputum. Both demand immediate descent, with oxygen if available. Fitness does not protect, and anyone can be affected. Preventive medicines are prescribed by a travel clinician.

sections.heading: Drowning and diving
sections.body: Drowning is usually silent: the person cannot shout or wave, and slips under within a minute. Rescue without entering the water if possible, by reaching or throwing a float. A person pulled from water who is not breathing needs rescue breaths and CPR at once, since the problem is lack of oxygen. Anyone who has inhaled water and has a cough, breathlessness or drowsiness needs hospital observation. In scuba diving, ascending too fast causes DECOMPRESSION SICKNESS, with joint pain, rash, numbness or weakness, and ARTERIAL GAS EMBOLISM; treatment is oxygen and urgent recompression in a chamber.

sections.heading: Lightning, bites and stings
sections.body: Lightning victims carry no charge and are safe to touch; those who appear dead are treated first, because prompt CPR often succeeds. For snakebite, keep the person still, immobilise the limb, remove rings, and get to hospital; do not cut, suck or apply a tourniquet. Remove ticks with fine tweezers, gripping close to the skin and pulling steadily, and watch for an expanding rash or fever over the following weeks. Scrape away bee stings. Rinse jellyfish stings with seawater, and vinegar for box jellyfish. Any sting followed by breathing difficulty, facial swelling or collapse is anaphylaxis.

sections.heading: Air, smoke and being prepared
sections.body: Wildfire smoke and air pollution worsen asthma, lung and heart disease; on bad days stay indoors with windows closed, use a clean-air room or filter, and wear a well-fitted particle-filtering mask if you must go out. CARBON MONOXIDE from faulty heaters, generators or barbecues used indoors causes headache, dizziness and confusion in several people at once; get everyone into fresh air and call for help. For remote travel, leave a route plan, carry insulation, water, light and a means of signalling, and learn basic first aid. Survival priorities are shelter, warmth, water and signalling before food.

chapters.title: Medical Ethics, Consent & Patient Rights
chapters.overview: The principles behind good medical decisions and the rights every patient holds: consent, capacity, confidentiality, second opinions, complaints, advance care planning, and how to get the most out of an appointment.

sections.heading: The four principles
sections.body: Clinical ethics is often organised around four principles. AUTONOMY is a person's right to make their own informed decisions. BENEFICENCE is the duty to act for the patient's good. NON-MALEFICENCE is the duty to avoid harm. JUSTICE is fairness in how care and resources are shared. They frequently pull against each other, and ethical practice is the work of balancing them honestly in a particular case. Professionals also owe a DUTY OF CANDOUR: when something goes wrong, the patient should be told, receive an apology, and learn what will be done.

sections.heading: Consent
sections.body: Valid consent must be VOLUNTARY, INFORMED and given by a person with CAPACITY. Informed means understanding the nature of the treatment, its benefits, the risks that matter to that person, the alternatives, and what happens with no treatment. Consent is a conversation, not a signature, and can be withdrawn at any time. An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment, even life-saving treatment, for reasons others find unwise. In an emergency, when a person cannot consent and no wishes are known, clinicians may give immediately necessary treatment in the person's best interests.

sections.heading: Capacity and deciding for others
sections.body: Capacity is presumed in adults and is specific to the decision and the time. A person has it if they can understand the relevant information, retain it long enough, weigh it, and communicate a choice. An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity. When capacity is lacking, decisions are made by a legally appointed substitute decision-maker or attorney, or in the person's best interests taking account of their known values. Young people can often consent for themselves when mature enough to understand the decision; the rules vary by jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and your records
sections.body: Health information is confidential and is shared within the treating team only as needed for care. It may be disclosed without consent in limited circumstances defined by law, such as a serious and imminent risk of harm to others, certain infectious diseases, or a court order. In most countries patients have a legal right to see and obtain a copy of their records and to ask for errors to be corrected. A patient can usually say who may or may not be given information, including family members.

sections.heading: Advance care planning
sections.body: Advance care planning records what matters to a person in case they later cannot speak for themselves. An ADVANCE DIRECTIVE or living will sets out treatments a person would or would not want. A HEALTH CARE PROXY or power of attorney for personal care names someone trusted to decide. A do-not-attempt-resuscitation decision applies to CPR only and does not mean other treatment stops. These documents have legal requirements that differ by place. The most valuable step is the conversation itself, with family and with the clinical team, repeated as health changes.

sections.heading: Getting the most from care
sections.body: Before an appointment, write down your main concern, when it started, what you fear it is, and your three most important questions. Bring a current list of every medicine and supplement. Ask: What are my options? What are the benefits and harms of each? What happens if I do nothing? Repeat the plan back in your own words. You are entitled to an interpreter, a chaperone for intimate examinations, a second opinion, and a clear route to complain. Raising a concern should never affect your care.

chapters.title: Evidence-Based Medicine: Reading Research
chapters.overview: How to judge whether a health claim is trustworthy: types of study, bias, statistics in plain words, how guidelines are made, and a checklist for news stories, adverts and online claims.

sections.heading: Types of evidence
sections.body: Evidence varies in strength. A CASE REPORT describes one patient. A CASE-CONTROL study compares people with and without a disease, looking back for exposures. A COHORT study follows groups forward in time. These observational designs can show association but not prove cause. A RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIAL assigns people to treatments by chance, which balances known and unknown differences between groups and is the fairest test of a treatment. A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW gathers all relevant studies by a stated method, and a META-ANALYSIS pools their results. Laboratory and animal findings are a starting point only.

sections.heading: Bias and confounding
sections.body: BIAS is a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth. SELECTION bias arises when compared groups differ at the start. A CONFOUNDER is a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome: coffee drinkers once appeared to have more lung cancer because more of them smoked. BLINDING, where participants and assessors do not know who received which treatment, prevents expectations colouring results. The PLACEBO effect is real improvement from the expectation of treatment. PUBLICATION bias means positive studies are published more readily than negative ones, making treatments look better than they are.

sections.heading: Statistics in plain words
sections.body: A P VALUE is the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if the treatment truly had no effect; below 0.05 is the conventional threshold for statistical significance, but it does not measure importance. A CONFIDENCE INTERVAL gives the range within which the true effect plausibly lies; a narrow interval means a precise estimate. Statistical significance is not the same as CLINICAL significance: a large trial can detect a difference too small to matter to patients. Results from small studies, and surprising single studies, are often not repeated.

sections.heading: Outcomes that matter
sections.body: The best trials measure outcomes that patients feel: living longer, fewer heart attacks, less pain, better function. A SURROGATE outcome is a laboratory or scan measure, such as cholesterol or tumour size, standing in for these, and improving a surrogate does not always improve life. COMPOSITE outcomes bundle several events, and may be driven by the least important. INTENTION-TO-TREAT analysis counts everyone in the group they were assigned to, preserving the fairness of randomisation. Ask how long the study ran and whether the participants resemble you.

sections.heading: Guidelines and shared decisions
sections.body: Clinical guidelines combine evidence with judgements about benefit, harm, cost and patient values, and grade how strong each recommendation is. They describe what suits most people, not every person. CONFLICTS OF INTEREST, such as industry funding of studies or authors, should be declared and weighed. Evidence-based medicine was defined as the integration of the best research evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's own values and circumstances. A good decision is one made with accurate information and consistent with what matters to the person.

sections.heading: A checklist for health claims
sections.body: When you meet a health claim, ask: Who is making it, and what do they gain? Was it tested in people, and how many? Was there a fair comparison group? What was actually measured? How big is the effect in absolute numbers? Has anyone repeated it? What are the harms and the cost? Be wary of testimonials, 'secret' or 'miracle' cures, claims to treat many unrelated diseases, pressure to buy now, and attacks on all conventional medicine. Reliable sources name their authors, cite their evidence, and date their pages.

chapters.title: Newborn & Infant Care
chapters.overview: The first year: what is normal in a newborn, feeding, sleep and safe sleeping, jaundice, the unwell baby, growth and development, and looking after parents too.

sections.heading: The normal newborn
sections.body: A term baby is born between 37 and 42 weeks. Newborns breathe irregularly with short pauses, sneeze and hiccup often, and have cool bluish hands and feet in the first days. They lose up to about a tenth of birth weight in the first week and regain it by around two weeks. Common harmless findings include milia, small white spots on the nose; erythema toxicum, a blotchy rash; swollen breasts; and soft spots on the skull called fontanelles. The cord stump dries and falls off within one to three weeks. Vitamin K is given at birth to prevent a rare bleeding disorder.

sections.heading: Feeding
sections.body: Breast milk is the recommended sole food for about the first six months where possible, and any amount is valuable; formula is a safe alternative when prepared exactly as directed. Newborns feed eight to twelve times in twenty-four hours. Signs of enough milk are six or more wet nappies a day after the first week, regular yellow stools in the early weeks, contentment after feeds and steady weight gain. A good latch is wide-mouthed and not painful beyond the first seconds. Solid foods are introduced at around six months, alongside milk. Honey is avoided under one year because of botulism.

sections.heading: Sleep and safer sleeping
sections.body: To lower the risk of sudden infant death, place babies on their BACK for every sleep, on a firm flat mattress in their own cot in the parents' room for the first six months, with no pillows, bumpers, soft toys or loose bedding, and a smoke-free environment. Do not let the baby overheat. Never fall asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair. Sharing a bed is especially dangerous if a parent has had alcohol, sedating medicines or smokes. Newborns sleep in short stretches around the clock; longer night sleep develops over months.

sections.heading: Jaundice
sections.body: Yellowing of the skin and eyes is common from day two or three and usually fades within two weeks, as the baby's liver matures. It needs measuring, not guessing, because high bilirubin levels can damage the brain. Jaundice in the FIRST 24 HOURS of life is always abnormal and needs immediate assessment. Treatment when needed is phototherapy, a blue light that breaks bilirubin down. Jaundice lasting beyond two weeks, or with PALE stools and DARK urine, must be investigated for liver or bile-duct disease.

sections.heading: The unwell baby
sections.body: Young babies become seriously ill quickly and show it subtly. Seek urgent medical help for a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or more in a baby under three months; poor feeding or refusing feeds; fewer wet nappies; unusual sleepiness, floppiness or a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry; fast or laboured breathing, grunting, or pauses; blue, pale or mottled skin; a rash that does not fade when pressed; a bulging or sunken fontanelle; green vomit; or a seizure. Trust the feeling that something is wrong.

sections.heading: Growth, development and parents
sections.body: Growth is plotted on centile charts, and the trend along a line matters more than its position. Typical milestones include social smiling by about six to eight weeks, rolling by six months, sitting by about nine months, and first words and steps around a year; loss of a skill already gained always needs assessment. Routine immunisations begin in early infancy. Crying peaks at around six weeks; if it becomes overwhelming, put the baby safely down and step away, and never shake a baby. Persistent low mood, anxiety or frightening thoughts after birth are common, treatable, and nothing to be ashamed of.
